28: Regarding the phrase "paṭighaṃ tena pajahatīti" (one abandons resentment by that), one abandons resentment only through displeasure (domanassa). Indeed, there is no such thing as abandoning resentment by resentment itself, nor is there abandoning displeasure by displeasure itself. This monk, having undertaken one of the practices such as the three-month practice, reflects thus: "Monk, look! Is there any deficiency in your virtue (sīla), or in your energy (vīriya), or in your wisdom (paññā)? Is your virtue not perfectly pure? Is your energy not well-exerted? Is your wisdom not courageous and leading you?" Having reflected thus, he makes a firm effort, saying, "Now I will not allow this displeasure (domanassa) to arise again," and within three months, or six months, or nine months, he eradicates that displeasure with the Path of Non-Returning (Anāgāmi-magga). In this manner, it is said that one abandons resentment by resentment, and displeasure by displeasure. Regarding the passage "na tattha paṭighānusayo anuseti" (the underlying tendency to resentment does not lie latent there), the underlying tendency to resentment does not lie latent in such displeasure. It does not arise with that displeasure as its object; the meaning is that the underlying tendency to resentment has been abandoned therein. Regarding the phrase "avijjaṃ tena pajahati" (one abandons ignorance by that), in this Dispensation, a monk removes the underlying tendency to ignorance and enters the fourth jhāna. Having kept the underlying tendency to ignorance suppressed by the jhāna, he develops insight (vipassanā) and eradicates it completely with the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga). Although that ignorance is abandoned by the Path of Arahantship, because it was suppressed by the fourth jhāna, it is said not to lie latent in the fourth jhāna. Therefore, He said: "na tattha avijjānusayo anuseti." Now, wishing to ask a counterpart question (paṭibhāga-pucchā), he spoke the words beginning with "sukhāya pana ayye" (But for pleasure, lady...). In the answer to that problem, because pain is the opposite of pleasure and pleasure is the opposite of pain, He spoke of the dissimilar counterpart (visabhāga-paṭibhāga) regarding those two feelings. Equanimity (upekkhā), however, is like a mass of darkness, indistinct and difficult to point out. Since ignorance (avijjā) is also like that, He spoke of the similar counterpart (sabhāga-paṭibhāga) here. In as many places as ignorance creates darkness, in so many places knowledge (vijjā) dispels darkness; thus He spoke of the dissimilar counterpart (visabhāga-paṭibhāga). Regarding the phrase "avijjāya kho āvuso" (Of ignorance, friend...), since both these dhammas are taintless (anāsava) and supramundane (lokuttara), He spoke only of the similar counterpart (sabhāga-paṭibhāga). Regarding the phrase "vimuttiyā kho āvuso" (Of liberation, friend...), He spoke only of the similar counterpart (sabhāga-paṭibhāga) in the sense of being taintless, supramundane, and indeterminate (abyākata). Regarding the word "accayāsi," the meaning is that you have gone beyond the question. "Nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetuṃ" means he was unable to grasp the limit or measure of the questions; he asked for a counterpart to a dhamma that has no counterpart. Nirvana is...
70:
Unable to request the Blessed One themselves, who was so difficult to approach, those monks requested the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Friend Ānanda, it would be good..."

"Appeva nāma" means "it might be possible." Why did the Venerable Ānanda tell those monks, "You should approach the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka"? It was because the Buddha's actions were well-known to him. Indeed, the movements of the Dasabala were clear to the Elder. The Elder knew: "Today, the Blessed One, having stayed at Jetavana, will observe the day-abiding (divāvihāra) at Pubbārāma; today, having stayed at Pubbārāma, he will observe the day-abiding at Jetavana; today, he will enter for alms alone; today, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he will set out for a wandering through the countryside (janapadacārika) at this time." Did the Venerable Ānanda possess the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariyañāṇa) to know this? No, he did not. However, he knew by observing the actions performed and drawing inferences through reasoning (anumānabuddhi). On the day the Blessed One, having stayed at Jetavana, wished to observe the day-abiding at Pubbārāma, he would show signs of putting away the requisites of the lodgings. The Elder would then perform tasks such as sweeping and disposing of rubbish. The same method applied when the Buddha, having stayed at Pubbārāma, came to Jetavana for the day-abiding.

When he wished to enter for alms alone, he would attend to his physical needs early in the morning, enter the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), close the door, and sit having entered fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti). The Elder, knowing by that sign, "Today the Blessed One is sitting having seen a kinsman who is a being worthy of awakening (to the Four Noble Truths)," would signal the monks, "Friends, today the Blessed One wishes to enter for alms alone; you all prepare for the alms round." When he wished to enter surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he would sit having entered fruition attainment with the door of the Fragrant Chamber half-closed. The Elder, knowing by that sign, would signal the monks to take their bowls and robes. When he wished to set out for a wandering through the countryside, he would eat one or two morsels more than usual and would walk back and forth on the ambulatory path at all times. The Elder, knowing by that sign, would signal the monks, "Friends, the Blessed One wishes to wander through the countryside; perform your necessary duties."

During the period of the First Enlightenment (pathamabodhi), the Blessed One did not have a fixed residence for twenty years. Later, for twenty-five years, he resided continuously depending on Sāvatthī...
71:
The Blessed One would use two places in a single day. Having stayed at Jetavana during the night, on the following day, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he would enter Sāvatthī for alms through the South Gate, exit through the East Gate, and observe the day-abiding at Pubbārāma. Having stayed at Pubbārāma during the night, on the following day, he would enter Sāvatthī for alms through the East Gate, exit through the South Gate, and observe the day-abiding at Jetavana. Why did he do so? Out of compassion for two families. There was no one else among men like the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, nor any other woman like Visākhā, who had sacrificed wealth dedicated to the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Blessed One used these two places in a single day out of compassion for them. On that day, however, he stayed at Jetavana. Thus, the Venerable Ānanda thought: "Today, the Blessed One, after wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, will go to the Eastern Gatehouse (Pubbakoṭṭhaka) in the evening to pour water over his body. At that time, after I have poured water over the Blessed One and while he is standing, I will request him and lead him to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. In this way, these monks will have the opportunity to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One." Having thought thus, he spoke to those monks. 

Migāramātupāsāda refers to the palace of Visākhā. She was called Migāramātā (Migāra's Mother) because the merchant Migāra had placed her in the position of a mother. The phrase "He rose from his solitary seclusion" means: In that palace, the Blessed One's auspicious chamber was located between the auspicious chambers of the two Chief Disciples. The Elder opened the door, swept the inside of the chamber, removed the floral refuse, prepared the couch and stool, and gave a signal to the Teacher. The Teacher entered the auspicious chamber, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture (sīhaseyya) with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and after allaying the physical fatigue, he rose and sat having entered fruition attainment (phalasamāpatti), eventually rising from it in the evening. Referring to that rising, it is said, "He rose from his solitary seclusion."

"To pour water" (pariṣiñcituṃ) means: When a person bathes by rubbing the body with scented powder, clay, etc., or by scrubbing with a potsherd or fist, that person is said to be "bathing" (nhāyati). When one bathes normally without doing so, it is called "pouring water" (pariṣiñcati). Although no removable dust or dirt could adhere to the Blessed One's body, he entered the water solely to regulate the bodily temperature (utu). Therefore, it is said, "to pour water over his body." Pubbakoṭṭhaka refers to the Eastern Gatehouse.
72:
In Sāvatthī, the monastery is sometimes large and sometimes small. This is because during the time of Vipassī Buddha, that monastery was one league (yojana) in extent; in the time of Sikhī Buddha, it was three gāvutas; in the time of Vessabhū Buddha, it was half a league; in the time of Kakusandha Buddha, it was one gāvuta; in the time of Koṇāgamana Buddha, it was half a gāvuta; in the time of Kassapa Buddha, it was twenty usabhas; and in the time of our Buddha, it became eight royal karīsas (aṭṭhakarīsa) in extent. That city also is sometimes to the east, sometimes to the south, sometimes to the west, and sometimes to the north of that monastery. However, in the Gandhakuṭī of Jetavana, the place where the four legs of the bed are set remains immovable and fixed.

The four immovable shrine-sites (acalacetiyaṭṭhāna) are: the site of the Great Bodhi Throne, the site where the Wheel of Dhamma was first turned in the Isipatana Migadāya, the site where the stairs were set during the Descent from Heaven at the gate of Saṅkassa City, and the site of the legs of the bed. This Eastern Gatehouse (Pubbakoṭṭhaka) was the gatehouse at the eastern gate during the time of the twenty-usabha monastery of Kassapa Buddha. Even now, that gatehouse is well-known as the "Pubbakoṭṭhaka." During the time of Kassapa Buddha, when the Aciravatī River flowed around the city, upon reaching the Pubbakoṭṭhaka gatehouse, it breached the bank and created a large, deep lake that was level with the banks. In that lake, there were separate and delightful bathing places: one for the King, one for the citizens, one for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, and one for the Buddhas, all adorned with sandbanks resembling scattered silver plates.

Thus, the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda, went to the Pubbakoṭṭhaka gatehouse of such a nature to bathe his body. Then, the Venerable Ānanda offered the bathing cloth. The Blessed One removed the red double-layered undergarment and put on the bathing cloth. The Elder held the double-layered undergarment together with the outer robe (mahācīvara) in his hands. The Blessed One descended into the water. As soon as he descended, all the fish and turtles in the water became golden-colored. It was as if streams of liquid gold were being poured through mechanical pipes, or as if a sheet of gold was being spread out. Then, after the Elder had provided the bathing cloth to the Blessed One and he had bathed and emerged from the water, the Elder offered the red double-layered undergarment. The Blessed One put on that undergarment, tied the waistband which was like a flash of lightning, gathered the outer robe from its edges making it like a lotus bud, and stood holding it by the two corners that were offered. Referring to this, it is said: "Having bathed his body at Pubbakoṭṭhaka and emerged, he stood with a single robe."
73:
The body of the Blessed One, standing thus, shone with great beauty, like a lotus pond filled with newly bloomed paduma lotuses, like a Parijatta tree in full bloom, and as if mocking the glory of the sky illuminated by the radiance of all the stars. The series of thirty-two marks of a Great Man, beautiful with the circle of a fathom-wide radiance (vyāmappabhā), shone intensely like thirty-two moon-disks strung together, like thirty-two sun-disks, or like thirty-two Cakkavatti kings, thirty-two kings of gods, or thirty-two Great Brahmas standing in a row. This is called the Vaṇṇabhūmi (the section in praise of appearance). In such a context, a capable Dhamma-preacher should preach by supplementing the description of the beauty of the Buddhas' bodies or the beauty of their virtues with prose, verses, meanings, similes, and reasons. In such instances, the strength of a Dhamma-preacher is to be known.

'Gattāni pubbāpayamāno' means bringing the body to its natural state, making it free of water, or drying it. This is because if one wears the robe with a wet body, lumps (knots) appear on the robe and the requisite is damaged. On the bodies of the Buddhas, however, dust and sweat do not adhere. Like water drops on a paduma lotus leaf, the water rolls off and goes away. Even so, out of respect for the training (sikkhā-garavatā), the Blessed One, reflecting that 'this is the duty of a renunciant,' stood covering his body from the front, holding the outer robe (mahācīvara) by its two corners. At that moment, the Elder Ānanda thought: 'Once the Blessed One puts on the outer robe and sets his mind on going to the palace of Migāramātu (Visākhā), it will be difficult to turn him back. To thwart the intention of the Buddhas is as grave as stretching out one's hand to catch a solitary lion, as touching the trunk of a noble elephant in rut, or as seizing the neck of a cobra of fierce heat.' He planned, 'I will praise the excellence of the hermitage of Rammaka the Brahmin right here and request the Blessed One to go there.' He did so. Therefore, it is said: 'Then the Venerable Ānanda... (etc.) ...out of compassion.'

In that passage, 'anukampaṃ upādāya' means out of compassion for the five hundred monks who had gone to that hermitage thinking, 'We shall hear a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One,' and having felt pity for those monks. 'Dhammiyā kathāyā' refers to the ten perfections (pāramīs)...
74: (The monks) were assembled, praising the virtues of one of the thirty perfections and the virtues of the Great Renunciation. 'Āgamayamāno' means looking out for (waiting). The meaning of 'I am the Buddha' is that he did not enter hastily but stood until that talk was finished. 'Aggaḷaṃ ākoṭesi' means he gave a sign on the door-leaf with the tip of his fingernail (he knocked on the door). 'Vivariṃsu' means that because (the monks) were sitting listening attentively, they came and opened it at that very moment. 'On the prepared seat' means that in the time of the Buddha, wherever even a single monk dwelt, a seat for the Buddha was always prepared in every such place. Why? It is said that the Blessed One reflects on the monks who, having taken a meditation subject from him, dwell in a comfortable place: "This monk named so-and-so has gone after taking a meditation subject from me; will he be able to produce the special attainment or not?" Then, if he sees him having abandoned the meditation subject and thinking unwholesome thoughts, he thinks, "How indeed, while dwelling after taking a meditation subject from a Teacher like me, will unwholesome thoughts overcome this clansman and cause him to wander in the beginningless suffering of the round of rebirths?" For the sake of assisting him, he shows himself right there, admonishes that clansman, and having flown into the sky, returns to his own dwelling place. Those monks who were thus admonished thought: "The Teacher, knowing our minds, comes and shows himself standing right near us; at that moment, to search for a seat saying, 'Venerable Sir, sit here, sit here,' is a great burden." They dwell having already prepared a seat. He who has a stool prepares it. He who does not have one prepares a couch, a plank, a piece of wood, a stone, or a heap of sand. Not obtaining those, they even gather old leaves and spread a pāṃsukūla cloth there. Here, however, it refers to a seat prepared in the usual manner, thus it is said: "He sat on the prepared seat." 'Kāya nutthā' means with what talk were you sitting assembled? There is also a Pali reading 'Kāya netthā', which means what talk is there here? There is also a Pali reading 'Kāya notthā', which has the same meaning as the first. 'Antarākathā' is another kind of talk occurring in the midst of meditation, recitation, questioning, etc. 'Vippakatā' means unfinished, not having reached the conclusion because of my arrival. Then the Blessed One...
75: At that time, the Blessed One saw that monk who had abandoned his meditation subject and was thinking unwholesome thoughts. Then, thinking, "While dwelling after taking a meditation subject from a Teacher like me, unwholesome thoughts will overcome this clansman and cause him to wander in the beginningless suffering of the round of rebirths," for the sake of assisting that clansman, he showed himself right there, admonished him, and having flown into the sky, returned to his dwelling place. Those monks who were thus admonished knew: "The Blessed One, knowing our minds, comes and shows himself standing right near us." At that moment, since searching for a seat saying, "Venerable Sir, sit here," was a great burden, those monks dwelt having prepared a seat. A monk who had a stool prepared it. One who did not prepared a couch, a plank, a piece of wood, a stone, or a heap of sand. Those monks who did not obtain those things gathered old leaves and spread a pāṃsukūla cloth on that heap of leaves. In this hermitage of the Brahmin Dhammaka, however, there was already a seat prepared in the usual manner. Referring to that seat, it is said: "He sat on the prepared seat." "Sat on one side" means with what talk were you sitting together? In one Pali text, it appears as "With what talk were you sitting together?", and in that Pali, it should be understood according to the meaning previously mentioned. 'Antarākathā' is another talk spoken in the midst of meditation, learning the Pali, or learning the Commentary. 'Vippakatā' is a talk that has not reached its end because of the Blessed One's arrival. 'Anuppatto' means the Blessed One's arrival at the time when that talk was not yet finished. 'Dhammī vā kathā' is a Dhamma talk based on the ten subjects of talk (dasakathāvatthu). In the phrase 'Ariyo vā tuṇhībhavo', both the second jhāna and the original meditation subject are called Noble Silence. Therefore, a monk sitting after entering the second jhāna, as well as a monk sitting while firmly attending to the original meditation subject, should be known as sitting in Noble Silence. "Monks, there are these two searches," in this phrase, what is the connection (anusandhi)? Those monks, thinking they would listen to a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Blessed One, entrusted the burden to the Elder. The Elder also made the journey to the hermitage of the Brahmin Dhammaka for those monks. While those monks were sitting in that monastery, they did not speak talk that is contrary to the Path and Fruition, but sat only with Dhamma talk related to the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī), etc. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show, "This search of yours is called the Noble Search," began this teaching. In that Pali, in the phrase "Monks, what is the Ignoble Search?", it is like a man skilled in paths who, showing first the path to ruin that should be avoided, says, "Leave the left path and take the right." Similarly, because the Blessed One is skilled in teaching, he first explained the Ignoble Search which should be avoided, intending to explain the other, the Noble Search, later; thus, breaking the order of the summary, he spoke in this way. 'Jātidhamma' means having the nature of being born. 'Jarādhamma' means having the nature of aging. 'Byādhidhamma' means having the nature of illness. 'Maraṇadhamma' means having the nature of death. 'Sokadhamma' means having the nature of sorrow. 'Saṅkilesadhamma' means having the nature of being defiled. 'Puttabhariyaṃ' means sons and wives. This is the method in all terms. In the phrase 'Jātarūparajataṃ', 'jātarūpa' is gold, and 'rajata' is money such as copper coins used in trade. "Monks, these acquisitions (upadhi) are subject to birth" means he shows that all these five strands of sensual pleasure, called acquisitions, have the nature of being born. In the sections on the nature of illness, etc., gold and silver are not taken. The reason is that for gold and silver, there are no diseases such as headaches, no death called passing away (cuti) as for beings, and no sorrow arises. However, because they are defiled by impurities such as tarnish, they are included in the section on the nature of defilement. Likewise, because they are produced by seasonal conditions (utu), they are included in the section on the nature of birth; and because they age by gathering dirt, they are included in the section on the nature of aging.
76:
Monks, this quest should be known as the Noble Quest (ariya-pariyesanā) because it is faultless and because it is to be sought by the Noble Ones.

Why did He begin this teaching with "Monks, I too..."? It was to show His Great Renunciation (mahābhinikkhamana) from the very beginning. It occurred to the Blessed One: "Monks, I too formerly sought the ignoble quest (anariya-pariyesanā). Having abandoned that and sought the noble quest, I attained Omniscience (sabbaññuta). The group of five monks (pañcavaggiya) also formerly sought the ignoble quest. They too abandoned it, sought the noble quest, and reached the stage of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). You too have embarked upon the path of myself and the group of five monks. Your quest is also the Noble Quest." Thus, He began this teaching to show His Great Renunciation from the beginning.

In that passage, "daharo va samāno" means being just young. "Susu kāḷakeso" means having very black hair, having hair like the color of collyrium (añjana). "Bhadrena" means with a good (age). "Paṭhamena vayasā" means in the first of the three stages of life. "Akāmakānaṃ" means while (the parents) were unwilling; here the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard. "Assumukhānaṃ" means those with tears on their faces, those with tear-stained faces. "Rudantānaṃ" means while wailing and weeping. "Kiṃ kusalagavesī" means seeking "What is wholesome?". "Anuttaraṃ santivarapadaṃ" means seeking Nibbāna, the supreme object known as the excellent state of peace. In the phrase "yena Āḷāro Kālāmo", "Āḷāro" is the name of that ascetic. It is said he was tall and tawny (dīghapiṅgala), hence he was named "Āḷāra". "Kālāma" is his clan (gotta). "Viharatu āyasmā" means "Let the venerable one stay." "Yasmiṃ viññū puriso" means "In which doctrine a wise man." "Sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ" means "one's own teacher's doctrine." "Upasampajja vihareyya" means "should dwell having attained it." By this much, Āḷāra gave permission. "Taṃ dhammaṃ" means their doctrine and texts. "Pariyāpuṇiṃ" means "I learned it just by hearing."

"Oṭṭhapahatamattena" means just by the striking of the lips to receive what was said by the teacher, just by moving the lips back and forth. "Lapitalāpanamattena" means just by repeating what was spoken by the teacher. "Ñāṇavādaṃ" means the claim to knowledge, saying "I know"...
77:
...the claim (is meant). "Theravādaṃ" means a doctrine that is firm and stable, or the statement "I am an Elder (thera) in this doctrine." "I and others" means not only I, but many others also say this. "By mere faith alone" means without realizing it through wisdom, but by pure faith alone. It is said that while the Bodhisatta was learning the Dhamma orally, he realized: "The ascetic Kālāma does not have mere theoretical knowledge (pariyatti) of this Dhamma through speech; surely this venerable one is an attainer of the seven meditative attainments (samāpatti)." Because he knew this, the thought occurred to the Bodhisatta.

"Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ pavedesi" means "He made known to me the seven attainments ending with the Base of Nothingness." "Saddhā" means having faith for the purpose of producing these seven attainments. The same method applies to energy (vīriya) and so on. "Padaheyyaṃ" means "I should strive." "Soon, having realized that Dhamma for myself with direct knowledge, I attained and dwelt in it" means that the Bodhisatta, having exerted effort, produced the seven attainments within a few days, as if spreading out seven golden ladders. Therefore, he spoke thus.

"It is a gain for us, friend" means that this Kālāma was not envious. Therefore, without being envious and thinking "How did this newcomer produce this Dhamma so quickly?", he spoke thus, being pleased and wishing to express his appreciation. "Let us both lead this group" means "This group is large, let us both lead it," and thus he gave him equal status in the group. He divided it in the middle, saying, "I am an attainer of the seven attainments, and this Great Man is also an attainer of the seven. Let this many people learn the preliminary work (parikamma) from this Great Man, and let this many learn from me." "Uḷārāya" means excellent. "Pūjāya" means that the male and female attendants of Kālāma would come bringing scents, garlands, and so on. Kālāma would say, "Go and honor this Great Man." After honoring the Great Man, they would honor Kālāma with whatever remained. When they brought expensive couches and stools, he would have them given to the Great Man first, and only if there was a remainder would he take it for himself. Wherever they went, he would have the best dwelling prepared for the Bodhisatta and take the remaining place for himself. Thus, he honored him with grand honor. "This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment" and so on means that this Dhamma of the seven attainments does not lead to disenchantment with the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), nor to dispassion, nor to the cessation of lust and so on...
78:
This Dhamma does not lead to the stilling of defilements, it does not lead to the realization of the Dhamma known through higher knowledge, it does not lead to the realization of the Four Paths, and it does not lead to the realization of Nibbāna—this is the meaning.

'Only as far as rebirth in the Sphere of Nothingness' means it leads only to rebirth in the realm of the Sphere of Nothingness, which has a lifespan of sixty thousand eons; it does not lead beyond that. Thus, this Dhamma is of a nature that leads to returning again. That realm to which it leads is not free from rebirth, aging, and death, but is indeed encircled by the snare of Death. From that time on, the Great Being [Bodhisatta]—just as a man who is hungry in his belly, having obtained and enjoyed delicious food, might vomit it up due to bile, phlegm, or a fly, and would not even think of eating a single morsel of it again—likewise, even after achieving these seven attainments with great effort, seeing the danger in them such as the nature of returning again, he did not even give rise to the thought: 'I shall reflect on, enter into, resolve upon, emerge from, or review this Dhamma again.' 'Analankaritvā' means 'without adorning oneself with this Dhamma (without repeating it).' 'Nibbijjā' means 'having become weary (disenchanted).' 'Apakkamiṃ' means 'I departed.'

'Rāma (did not not know) this Dhamma'—here too, even while the Bodhisatta was learning that Dhamma, he knew: 'This Dhamma of the eight attainments is not merely words spoken by the ascetic Udaka; indeed, this ascetic Udaka is one who has truly attained the eight meditative attainments.' Therefore, this thought occurred to that Bodhisatta: 'Rāma... dwelt knowing and seeing.' The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

'To Uruvelā Senānigama (he went)'—here, 'Uruvelā' means a great bank or a great mound of sand. Alternatively, 'Uru' is said to be sand, and 'Velā' is said to be a boundary (shore). It should be understood that it is called 'Uruvelā' because of the vast amount of sand brought there by exceeding the boundary. In the past, before a Buddha had arisen, ten thousand young men of good family, having gone forth as ascetics and living in that region, gathered one day and made a pact: 'Physical and verbal actions are evident to others, but mental actions are not. Therefore, if anyone should think a sensual thought, a thought of ill-will, or a thought of cruelty, that person shall be by another...'
79:
...there is no one to accuse him; let that person himself accuse himself, and bringing sand in a leaf-cup, let him pour it out in this place; this shall be his punishment.' From that time on, whenever someone thought such a thought, he would pour sand there with a leaf-cup. In this way, a great mound of sand gradually formed in that place. Later, people who came after surrounded that sand mound and made it a site for a cetiya. With reference to that, it is said: 'Uruvelā means a great bank or a great mound of sand.' With reference to that same point, it is also said: 'Alternatively, Uru means sand, and Velā means a boundary (shore). Because there are many sands brought there by exceeding the boundary, it is called Uruvelā'—thus should the meaning be understood here.

'Senānigama' means the town (village) of the army. It is heard that the people of the first eon had an army camp in that place; therefore, that region is called Senānigama. There is also a variant reading 'Senānigāma.' 'Senānī' was the name of the merchant who was the father of Sujātā, and it means his village. 'Tadavasarim' means I descended (arrived) there. He saw a 'pleasant piece of ground' which means a delightful piece of ground, variegated with various kinds of water-born and land-born flowers in full bloom. He also saw a 'lovely woodland grove' that inspires devotion, resembling a peacock's tail. He saw the 'river Nerañjarā' flowing with clear, cool, blue water like a block of beryl. 'Setaka' (pure) means free from mud and clean. 'Supatittha' (with good fords) means endowed with beautiful fords that are gradually deep. 'Ramaṇīya' (delightful) means extremely beautiful to behold because of the sands spread out like silver plates and the abundance of fish and turtles. In the vicinity of that place, not far away, he saw an 'alms-resort village' (gocaragāma) that was easy to reach and where alms-food was easily obtainable for the ascetics who arrived. 'Alaṃ vata' means 'Indeed it is sufficient (Indeed it is suitable).' 'Sat right there' refers to his sitting on the Bodhi-pallanka (throne of enlightenment). For in the later suttas, 'right there' refers to the place where he performed austerities, but here it refers to the Bodhi-pallanka. Therefore, it is said: 'Sat right there.' The meaning is that he sat down after thinking, 'This place is suitable for striving.'

'Ajjhagamaṃ' means I attained or I reached. 'My knowledge and vision' means my Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), capable of seeing all phenomena, arose. 'My liberation (vimutti) is unshakable (akuppā)' means my liberation of the Fruit of Arahantship is unshakable because of its own nature and because its object is unshakable. It is 'unshakable' because it cannot be disturbed by lust and so on, and it is 'unshakable' because its object is the unshakable Nibbāna. 'This is the last birth' means this is the final birth of all births.
80:
"Now there is no more rebirth for me"—thus He shows the arising of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) within Him.

*Adhigato* means realized (through self-evolved knowledge). *Dhammo* refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. *Gambhīro* (profound) is a term that rejects the state of being superficial. *Duddaso* (hard to see) means it is difficult to see precisely because it is profound; it is to be seen with difficulty, and cannot be seen easily. Because it is hard to see, it is *duranubodho* (hard to understand); it is to be awakened to with difficulty, and cannot be awakened to easily. *Santo* (peaceful) means the extinguishing of defilements. *Paṇīto* (sublime) means not causing distress. Both these terms are spoken with reference only to the supramundane Dhamma. *Atakkāvacaro* (beyond the sphere of reasoning) means it is not to be known or delved into through reasoning; it is not something to be entered by [ordinary] intellect, but is to be realized only through wisdom. *Nipuṇo* (subtle) means fine. *Paṇḍitavedanīyo* (to be experienced by the wise) means it is to be known only by the wise who have undertaken the right practice (sammāpaṭipadā).

*Ālayarāmā* (delighting in attachment) means that beings are attached to the five cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, those five cords of sensual pleasure are called *ālaya* (attachments). The 108 modes of craving are also called *ālaya*. Because they delight in these attachments, they are called *ālayarāmā*. Because they take pleasure in attachments, they are called *ālayaratā*. Because they greatly rejoice in attachments, they are called *ālayasammuditā*.

For example, just as a king who enters a well-prepared garden, filled with trees laden with flowers and fruits, delights in those various excellences, rejoices increasingly, does not get weary, and does not wish to leave even in the evening; in the same way, these beings delight in the attachment to sensual pleasures and the attachment to craving, and they live in the round of rebirths (saṃsāravaṭṭa) rejoicing and without weariness. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show them the two kinds of attachment as if they were garden grounds, spoke the words beginning with "*ālayarāmā*."

*Yadidaṃ* is a particle. With reference to its place, the meaning should be understood as "*yaṃ idaṃ*" (which is this), and with reference to dependent origination, as "*yo ayaṃ*" (which is this). *Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo* refers to the causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and so on, which are the conditions for these effects. *Idappaccaya* (this condition) itself is called *idappaccayatā* (specific conditionality). The combination of both specific conditionality and dependent origination is called *idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo*. This is a designation for the causal factors such as volitional formations (saṅkhāra) and so on.

All terms beginning with *sabbasaṅkhārasamatha* (the stilling of all formations) are names for Nibbāna alone. Because all the agitations of formations are stilled and calmed by depending on that Nibbāna, it is called *sabbasaṅkhārasamatha*. Furthermore, because all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all cravings are exhausted, all defilements and lust fade away, and all suffering ceases by depending on that Nibbāna, it is called *sabbūpadhipaṭinissagga* (the relinquishment of all acquisitions), *taṇhākkhaya* (the destruction of craving), *virāga* (dispassion), and *nirodha* (cessation). That craving, however, binds rebirth to rebirth, or kamma together with its fruit...
81:
Because it binds (in existence), it is called *vāna* (weaving/binding); because it is the departure from that craving called *vāna*, it is called *Nibbāna*. "That teaching would be a weariness to me" means that teaching those who do not know or understand would be a weariness to me; that teaching would be a trouble to me. This means it would only result in physical weariness and physical distress. In the mind, however, neither of these exists for the Buddhas. *Apissu* is a particle in the sense of addition; it shows that "not only did this thought occur, but these verses also appeared (in my wisdom)." *Maṃ* means "to me" (*mama*). *Anacchariyā* means (verses) that are repeatedly wonderful. *Paṭibhaṃsu* means they became the objects of the wisdom called intuition (paṭibhāna); they reached the state of being repeatedly contemplated.

*Kicchena* means with difficulty; it does not mean through the painful practice (*dukkhapaṭipadā*). For all four paths of the Buddhas are only pleasant practices (*sukhapaṭipadā*). However, this was said with reference to the practice leading to the attainment (*āgamaniyapaṭipadā*), such as when filling the perfections (pāramīs), the Bodhisatta, while still possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion, gave to various supplicants his decorated head after cutting it off, drew out his throat-blood, uprooted his well-anointed eyes, and gave away his son who was like the lamp of the lineage and his wife of pleasing conduct, as well as undergoing cutting and breaking of the body in existences such as that of the Preacher of Patience (Khantivādī). *Halaṃ*: in this word, the letter '*ha*' is merely a particle, and the meaning is *alaṃ* (enough). *Pakāsituṃ* means to teach. Thus, it means: "It is not worth teaching the Dhamma attained with such difficulty; what is the use of teaching the Dhamma that has been mastered?"

*Rāgadosaparetehi* means those overwhelmed by lust and hatred, or those followed by lust and hatred. *Paṭisotagāmi* (going against the stream) refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths which proceeds as impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness, which is the opposite (upstream) of permanence and so on. *Rāgarattā* means those infatuated with sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. *Na dakkhanti* means they will not see through this nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness; who would be able to make those who do not see take it up in this way (as impermanent, etc.)? *Tamokhandhena āvuṭā* means those enveloped by the mass of ignorance. *Appossukkatāya* means through lack of concern, meaning through the desire not to teach the Dhamma. 

But why did the Buddha's mind incline in this way (not to teach)? Did He not (previously think), "Having been liberated, I will liberate others; having crossed over, I will cross others over"?

"What use is there for me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown guise? Having attained omniscience, I will cross over the world of beings together with the devas."
82:
If it is said, 'Did I not make the aspiration, fulfill the perfections (pāramīs), and reach the state of omniscience (sabbaññuta) with the thought: "Having crossed over the fourfold flood myself, I shall help other beings to cross; having attained the state of an Omniscient Buddha, I shall deliver the multitude of devas and humans"?', it is indeed true that He became a Buddha by fulfilling the perfections in such a way. However, due to the power of the knowledge reflecting upon the profundity of that Dhamma, the Blessed One's mind inclined in this way (towards remaining inactive and not teaching the Dhamma). Indeed, to the Blessed One who, after attaining omniscience, reflected on the state of beings being entangled in the thicket of defilements (kilesas) and the profundity of the Dhamma, the thickness of beings' defilements and the profundity of the Dhamma became apparent in every aspect. Then, to the Blessed One who thought, 'These beings are filled with defilements and are extremely defiled, like a dried gourd filled with sour gruel, like a large pot filled with buttermilk, like an old cloth soaked in fat and oil, or like a hand smeared and stained with eye-ointment; they are enamored with lust (rāga), corrupted by hatred (dosa), and deluded by ignorance (moha); how indeed will they be able to penetrate (this Dhamma)?', His mind inclined in this way also due to the power of the knowledge reflecting on the thicket of defilements.

'Furthermore, this Dhamma is as profound as the great mass of water that supports the earth; it is as difficult to see as a mustard seed hidden by a mountain; it is as difficult to understand as aligning the tips of a hair that has been split a hundred times. Was there any gift I did not give, any virtue (sīla) I did not guard, or any perfection (pāramī) I did not fulfill while striving to penetrate this Dhamma? Even while I was defeating the forces of Māra as if without effort, the earth did not tremble; it did not tremble when I recollected my past lives (pubbenivāsa) in the first watch of the night, nor did it tremble when I purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) in the middle watch. However, in the last watch, as soon as I penetrated the law of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. Thus, if this Dhamma was penetrated only with difficulty even by one with such sharp wisdom as myself, how will the worldly masses penetrate it?' It should be understood that His mind inclined in this way also due to the power of the knowledge reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma.

Moreover, His mind also inclined in this way because of His desire to teach only when requested by a Brahma. For the Blessed One knew: 'If my mind inclines towards remaining inactive, the Great Brahma will request me to teach the Dhamma. These beings hold Brahma in high regard; they will listen respectfully, thinking, "The Teacher was reportedly unwilling to teach the Dhamma, but the Great Brahma requested Him to do so; oh, how peaceful is the Dhamma! Oh, how sublime is the Dhamma!"' It should be understood that His mind inclined towards remaining inactive because of this reason, and not because He truly did not wish to teach the Dhamma.

Regarding 'Sahampatissa': It is said that in the dispensation (sāsana) of the Blessed One Kassapa, he was a thera named Sahaka who, having attained the first jhāna, was reborn as a Brahma with a lifespan of an aeon in the realm of the first jhāna. There, he was known as Brahma Sahampati. That...
83:
Referring to [Brahma Sahampati], He said, 'Brahmuno Sahampatissa' (of Brahma Sahampati). It is said that when that Brahma uttered the words, 'Alas, friends, [the world] is perishing!', he did so with such a voice that all the Brahmas in the ten-thousandfold world system heard it and assembled. 'Yatra hi nāma' means 'in which world'. 'Purato pāturahosi' means he appeared together with those ten thousand Brahmas. 'Apparajakkhajātika' refers to those whose nature is to have only a little dust of lust, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom. 'Assavanatā' means because of not hearing the Dhamma. 'Bhavissanti' indicates that those who have performed meritorious deeds (puññakiriya) under previous Buddhas and fulfilled their perfections are like mature lotuses waiting for the sun's rays; they are waiting for the teaching of the Dhamma, and at the end of a single four-line verse, those worthy of entering the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya-bhūmi) will not be just one or two, but hundreds of thousands who will become understanders of the Dhamma. 'Pāturahosi' means he appeared.

'Samalehi cintito' means the doctrine devised by the six teachers who possessed impurities (defilements). They, having arisen earlier, taught the impure Dhamma of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, as if spreading thorns or pouring poison. 'Apāpuretaṃ' means 'Open this [door]'. 'Amatassa dvāraṃ' refers to the Noble Path (ariya-magga) which is the door to the Deathless (Nibbāna). 'Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhaṃ' is the request: 'May these beings hear the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths realized by the Stainless One (the Buddha) who is free from the impurities of defilements.'

'Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito' means just like one standing on the summit of a solid rocky mountain. For such a person standing there, there is no need for efforts such as craning or stretching the neck to see. 'Tathūpamaṃ' means having a similar comparison to that rocky mountain. The summary of the meaning here is: Just as a man with sight standing on the summit of a rocky mountain would see the people all around, so too, O Sumedha (the Buddha), You who are the Blessed One with the All-Seeing Eye (samanta-cakkhu) through the wisdom of omniscience, having ascended the palace of Dhamma and being Yourself free from sorrow, look upon, consider, and examine the multitude of beings who are immersed in sorrow and overcome by birth and old age. The meaning here is: For example, suppose people made a large field all around the foot of a mountain, built small huts on the field-dykes, and lit fires at night. There would be a fourfold darkness. Then, a man with sight standing on the top of that mountain, looking down at the ground, would not be able to see the field, the dykes, the huts, or the people sleeping in those huts. In the small huts...
84:
It would be as if only the flame of a fire were visible. Similarly, for the Tathāgata who has ascended the Palace of Dhamma and looks upon the assembly of beings, those beings who have not performed meritorious deeds, even if they are sitting right beside His right knee in the same monastery, do not come into the range of the Buddha-eye; they are like arrows shot at night. However, those veneyya persons (those to be guided) who have performed meritorious deeds, even if they are far away, come into the range of His vision; they are prominent like a fire or like the Himalayan mountains. And this was also said - 

“The good shine from afar like the Himalayan mountains; the wicked are not seen here, like arrows shot at night.” (Dhp. 304).

With the word “Rise up” (Uṭṭhehi), he speaks requesting the Blessed One to set out on a journey for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Among the words beginning with “Vīra”, the Blessed One is called “Vīra” because of His possession of energy (vīriya). He is called “Vijitasaṅgāma” (Victor in battle) because He has conquered the Māras of the deity (Devaputta), death (Maccu), and defilements (Kilesa). He is called “Satthavāha” (Caravan leader) because He is capable of leading the caravan of veneyya beings to escape from the wilderness of birth (jāti) and so forth. He should be known as “Aṇaṇa” (Debtless) because of the absence of the debt of sensual desire (kāmacchanda).

“Ajjhesana” means request. “Buddha-cakkhu” (Buddha-eye) refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of their latent tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa). These two knowledges are called the “Buddha-eye”; omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is called the “All-seeing eye” (samanta-cakkhu); and the three lower path knowledges are called the “Dhamma-eye” (dhamma-cakkhu). Among the words beginning with “Apparajakkha” (those with little dust), those who have little dust of passion (rāga) etc. in their eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu) according to the method already mentioned are called “Apparajakkha”. Those for whom that dust is great are called “Mahārajakkha”. Those whose faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) etc. are sharp are called “Tikkhindriya”. Those whose faculties are weak are called “Mudindriya”. Those whose dispositions such as faith etc. are good are called “Svākāra”. Those who can note the meaning of what is taught and can be easily made to understand are called “Suviññāpaya”. Those who are accustomed to seeing danger in the next world and in faults are called “Paralokavajjabhayadassāvī”.

In this context, the Pali text is - “A person with faith has little dust; a person without faith has much dust. One who has aroused energy..., one who is lazy..., one who is mindful..., one who is forgetful..., one who is concentrated..., one who is unconcentrated..., one who is wise..., a person who is unwise has much dust. Likewise, a person with faith has sharp faculties... etc... a person who is wise sees danger in the next world and in faults; a person who is unwise does not see danger in the next world and in faults.”
85:
The world (loka) refers to the world of aggregates (khandha-loka), the world of bases (āyatana-loka), the world of elements (dhātu-loka), the world of success in existence (sampatti-bhava-loka), the world of the origin of success (sampatti-sambhava-loka), the world of failure in existence (vipatti-bhava-loka), and the world of the origin of failure (vipatti-sambhava-loka). The world as one is the fact that “all beings subsist on nutriment.” The world as two is mind and matter (nāma and rūpa). The world as three is the three feelings (vedanā). The world as four is the four nutriments (āhāra). The world as five is the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). The world as six is the six internal bases (āyatana). The world as seven is the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). The world as eight is the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). The world as nine is the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). The world as ten is the ten bases (āyatana). The world as twelve is the twelve bases (āyatana). The world as eighteen is the eighteen elements (dhātu).

Fault (vajja) means all defilements (kilesa) are faults, all misconduct (duccarita) are faults, all volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are faults, and all kamma leading to rebirth (bhavagāmikamma) are faults. Thus, in this world and in this fault, a sharp perception of danger (bhaya-saññā) is established. For example, it is like seeing a murderer with a raised sword. Through these fifty modes, He knows, sees, and penetrates these five faculties. This is the “Knowledge of the higher and lower faculties” (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) of the Tathāgata, as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

“Uppaliniyaṃ” means in a lotus pond. The same method applies to the remaining words. “Antonimuggaposīni” refers to lotuses that grow while remaining submerged within the water. “Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni” refers to lotuses that stand having risen above the water. Among them, those that stand having risen above are lotuses that will bloom this very day, awaiting the touch of the sun's rays. Those that stand level with the water are lotuses that will bloom tomorrow. Those that have not yet emerged from the water but are growing while submerged are lotuses that will bloom on the third day. There are also other diseased or afflicted lotuses that cannot emerge from the water; those will not bloom and will only become food for fish and turtles. Although those lotuses are not mentioned in the Pali text, they are brought forward and shown for the sake of comparison.

Just like those four types of lotuses, there are four types of persons: the one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), the one who is trainable (neyya), and the one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama). Among them, “the person for whom the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurs at the very moment of the teaching is called an ugghaṭitaññū person. The person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is analyzed in detail is called a vipañcitaññū person. The person for whom, through learning, questioning, and wise attention...”
86:
A person who, through associating with good friends, repeatedly attending to them, learning and questioning the Pali and Commentaries, and through proper attention, gradually attains the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, is called a 'Neyya' (one to be led) person. A person who, even though they hear much, recite much, memorize much, and teach much of the Dhamma, does not attain the penetration of the Four Noble Truths in that very life, is called a 'Padaparama' (one for whom the word is the maximum) person.

Among those four types of persons, when the Blessed One looked upon the ten thousand world systems, which were like a forest of lotuses, He saw: "The Ugghaṭitaññū person is like the lotuses that will bloom today; the Vipañcitaññū person is like the lotuses that will bloom tomorrow; the Neyya person is like the lotuses that will bloom on the third day; and the Padaparama person is like the lotuses that are food for fish and tortoises." Having seen thus, He saw in every aspect: "This many persons have little dust of defilements; this many persons have much dust of defilements; and among them, this many are Ugghaṭitaññū persons."

Among those persons, the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One brings fulfillment of benefit to the first three types of persons in this very life. For Padaparama persons, however, it serves to instill habitual tendencies (vāsanā) for the sake of benefit in future lives. Then, the Blessed One, knowing the Dhamma teaching that could bring benefit to these four types of persons and having the desire to teach, once again divided all beings in the three realms into two groups: those capable of liberation (bhabba) and those incapable of liberation (abhabba).

Referring to this division, it was said: "What kind of beings are abhabba? Those beings who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma (kammāvaraṇa), the obstruction of defilements (kilesāvaraṇa), and the obstruction of results (vipākāvaraṇa); who lack faith, lack desire, and are weak in wisdom; they are incapable of entering the right path (niyāma/magga) of wholesome states. These are called abhabba beings. What kind of beings are bhabba? Those beings who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma, etc. ... These are called bhabba beings." In making this distinction, He set aside all abhabba persons and, encompassing only bhabba persons with His knowledge, He divided them into six groups: "This many are those of lustful temperament; this many are those of hateful, deluded, speculative, faithful, and intellectual temperaments." Having done so, He thought, "I shall teach the Dhamma in this way."

'Paccabhāsi' means He replied. 'Apārutā' means they are opened. 'Amatassa dvārā' refers to the Noble Path (ariya magga). He showed that the Noble Path is the door to Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless (amata), and that He had opened that door. 'Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ' means let all people release their faith (let them place their faith). The meaning of the last two phrases is: I, thinking that it would be wearying for the body and mind to teach this sublime and supreme Dhamma, which I have mastered and well-developed myself...
87:
...did not teach. But now, let all people bring the vessel of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations.

Monks, to me, this thought occurred: "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?" This thought related to the teaching of Dhamma arose. When did it arise? It arose in the eighth week after becoming a Buddha.

In this regard, the sequential account is as follows: It is said that on the day of the Great Renunciation, the Bodhisatta, seeing the harem lying in disarray, was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). He called the minister Channa, saying, "Bring the horse Kanthaka," and together with Channa, he mounted the back of the noble horse and departed from the city. After pointing out the place where the Kanthakanivattana Cetiya would be built and crossing three great kingdoms, he went forth as a monk on the banks of the Anomā River. While wandering in due course, he went for alms in Rājagaha and stayed at Pandava Hill. When the King of Magadha asked his name and lineage and offered, "Please accept this kingdom's wealth," he replied, "Enough, Great King, I have no need for the kingdom's wealth. I have come forth having abandoned the kingdom to strive for the benefit of the world and to be one who removes the veil of ignorance in the world." Then the King took a promise from him, saying, "If that is so, when you become a Buddha, please come to my kingdom first."

Afterwards, he approached the sages Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta, but finding no essence in their teachings, he departed from there. While performing great austerities (dukkharacariyā) for six years in the Uruvelā forest, he was unable to penetrate the Deathless. Therefore, by consuming solid food, he restored his physical body.

At 그at time, in the village of Uruvelā, a householder's daughter named Sujātā had made a vow at a banyan tree: "If I go to a home of equal status and obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I shall perform a ritual offering." Her prayer was fulfilled. On the morning of the full moon day of Vesākha, she prepared thick milk-rice (ghana-pāyasa) to perform the offering even during the pre-dawn watch of the night. While that milk-rice was being cooked, large bubbles emerged and moved in a clockwise direction. Not even a single drop spilled outside. The Great Brahma held an umbrella over it. The four Great Guardian Kings stood guard with swords in hand. Sakka gathered firewood and lit the fire. The deities gathered the essence from the four great continents and...
88:
The deities gathered the divine essence from the four continents and infused it into that milk-rice. The Bodhisatta, awaiting the time for alms-round, went early and sat at the foot of the tree. The nursemaids, who had gone to clean the foot of the tree, returned and informed Sujātā, "A deity is sitting at the foot of the tree." Sujātā, having adorned herself with all her ornaments, placed the milk-rice in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces of money], covered it with another golden bowl, and carrying it on her head, went there. Seeing the Great Being, she placed the bowl in his hands, paid homage, and said, "Just as my wish has been fulfilled, so may your wish also be fulfilled," and then departed.

The Bodhisatta went to the bank of the Nerañjarā River, placed the golden bowl on the bank, bathed, and after coming out, made forty-nine morsels and consumed the milk-rice. He then said, "If I am to become a Buddha today, may this golden bowl float upstream," and threw it. The golden bowl floated upstream, stayed for a while, and then entered the abode of Kāla, the King of Nagas, where it struck the golden bowls of the three [previous] Buddhas and remained there.

The Great Being spent the day in a forest grove, and in the evening, taking the eight handfuls of grass given by Sotthiya, he ascended the Bodhimaṇḍa and stood on the southern side. That spot shook like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. The Great Being thought, "This spot is unable to bear my virtues," and went to the western side; that spot also shook in the same way. He went to the northern side; that spot also shook in the same way. He went to the eastern side; there, the place for the throne remained firm and motionless like a deeply planted sacrificial post (indakhīla). The Great Being thought, "This is the place where all the Buddhas destroy and demolish the defilements," and taking the grass by the tips, he shook it out. The grass became arranged as if drawn by a painter's brush. The Bodhisatta, resolving with fourfold energy, "I will not break this posture until I attain Enlightenment," sat down cross-legged on the throne.

At that very moment, Māra created a thousand arms, mounted the elephant named Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty leagues in height, and taking an army of Māra nine leagues long, approached, looking askance and overwhelming like a great mountain. The Bodhisatta [thought], "To me who has fulfilled the ten perfections, no other ascetic..."
89:
"...whether a brahmin, a deity, Māra, or Brahmā, there is no witness. However, during my life as King Vessantara, the great earth was my witness seven times. Now too, this great earth, though insentient and like a log of wood, is my witness," and he stretched out his hand. At that moment, the great earth roared and shook, emitting hundreds and thousands of sounds like a bronze bowl struck with an iron rod, causing Māra's army to be scattered to the edge of the universe. Even before the sun set, the Bodhisatta conquered Māra's army. In the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsanussatiñāṇa); in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (dibbacakkhu); and in the last watch, he applied his knowledge to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Contemplating the cycle and its cessation (the Four Noble Truths), he became a Buddha at dawn. Reflecting, "For the sake of this throne, I have striven for a duration of more than a hundred thousand times ten million aeons," he sat on that single throne in a single cross-legged posture for seven days. Then, a doubt arose in some deities: "Are there other qualities that make one a Buddha?"

Then, on the eighth day, the Blessed One arose from his meditative attainment and, knowing the doubt of the deities, ascended into the air to dispel their doubt. He performed the Twin Miracle (yamaka pāṭihāriya) and dispelled their doubt. Standing on the northern side, slightly leaning towards the east from the throne, he spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at the throne and the Bodhi tree, the place where he achieved the fruit of the perfections fulfilled for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons. That place became known as the Animisa Cetiya. Then, he spent seven days walking to and fro on a jeweled walkway (ratanacaṅkama) that stretched east to west between the throne and the place where he had stood. That place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya. After that, on the western side, the deities created a jeweled house (ratanaghara). Sitting there cross-legged, he spent seven days contemplating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, especially the Paṭṭhāna (the Book of Relations) with its infinite methods. That place became known as the Ratanaghara Cetiya. Having thus spent four weeks near the Bodhi tree, in the fifth week, he went from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla banyan tree. There too, he sat contemplating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation. While contemplating the Dhamma, he reviewed the sequence of the Abhidhamma as follows: first, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī; then the Vibhaṅga; the Dhātukathā; the Puggalapaññatti; the Kathāvatthu; the Yamaka; and the Mahāpakaraṇa, which is the Paṭṭhāna.
90:
When the mind of the Blessed One entered the subtle and profound subject of the Paṭṭhāna in that Great Treatise, joy (pīti) arose. With the arising of joy, his blood became clear. When the blood became clear, his skin became clear. When the skin became clear, rays of light, the size of a pinnacled hall (kūṭāgāra) and such, emanated from the front of his body and sped through the infinite world systems in the eastern direction like a herd of Chaddanta elephants running through the sky. Rays emanated from the back of his body towards the western direction, from the edge of the right shoulder towards the southern direction, and from the edge of the left shoulder towards the northern direction, speeding through infinite world systems. From the soles of his feet, rays the color of coral sprouts emerged, piercing the great earth, splitting the mass of water in two, penetrating the mass of air, and speeding into open space. From his head, a circle of blue rays, like a well-coiled string of jewels, emerged, piercing the six deva worlds, the nine Brahma worlds, the Vehapphala realm, and the five Suddhāvāsa realms, passing through the four formless realms, and speeding into open space. On that day, all the infinite beings in the infinite world systems appeared golden in color. Those rays that emanated from the Blessed One's body on that day continue to travel through infinite world systems even to this day.

Thus, after spending seven days at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, the Blessed One sat at the foot of the Mucalinda tree for another seven days. As soon as he sat down, a great unseasonal cloud arose, filling the entire interior of the world system. It is said that such a great cloud rains only at two times: when a Wheel-turning Monarch appears or when a Buddha arises. Here, it arose at the time of the Buddha's arising. When that great rain arose, Mucalinda the Naga King thought: 'This great rain has arisen just as my Lord, the Buddha, entered my abode; it is proper to provide a dwelling for the Buddha.' Although that Naga King was capable of creating a palace made of the seven jewels, he thought: 'By doing so, there will not be great fruit for me; I will perform personal service (veyyāvacca) for the body of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala).' He created a large body, coiled around the Teacher seven times, and held his hood over him from above. The space inside the coils was as large as the Lohapāsāda palace below. The Naga King's intention was: 'May the Teacher stay in whatever posture he desires.' Therefore, he enclosed such a large space. In the middle, a jeweled throne was prepared; above, there was a canopy of cloth decorated with golden stars, fragrant garlands, flower wreaths, and cloth ceilings. In the four corners, lamps of scented oil were lit; opening on the four sides...
91:
pots of sandalwood perfume were placed. Thus, the Blessed One spent those seven days at the foot of that tree, and for another seven days, he sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree.

In the eighth week, he used the tooth-stick and the medicinal yellow myrobalan (harītakī) brought by Sakka, King of the Devas, washed his mouth, and partook of the alms-food and cakes offered by the brothers Tapussa and Bhallika in the precious stone bowls presented by the four Guardian Kings of the World. Having returned and sitting at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, this thought, which is the habit of all Buddhas, arose in the Blessed One.

In that text, 'Paṇḍita' means one endowed with wisdom. 'Byatta' means one endowed with proficiency. 'Medhāvī' means one endowed with wisdom that understands the circumstances. 'Apparajakkhajātika' means a pure being of a nature free from defilements because they have been suppressed by meditative attainment. 'Ājānissati' means he will note, he will penetrate and understand. 'Knowledge arose in me' means the Knowledge of Omniscience arose in me. It is said that the Blessed One, not reaching a conclusion solely based on what the deity said, looked for himself with his Knowledge of Omniscience and saw that [Āḷāra Kālāma] had passed away seven days ago from today and was reborn in the Realm of Nothingness. Referring to that vision, he said: 'Knowledge and vision arose in me.' 'Mahājāniya' means a great loss, because he fell away from the Path and Fruit that could have been attained within those seven days; thus he is called 'one of great loss.' Because he was reborn in a place that is not an opportune moment (akkhaṇa), he has no ear-sensitivity to hear the Dhamma even if one went and preached it, nor are there feet to come to this human realm where Dhamma is preached; thus he showed that there is a loss of the noble benefit of the Path and Fruit. 'Abhidosakālaṅkata' means one who passed away at midnight. 'Knowledge arose in me' means the Knowledge of Omniscience arose in me. Here too, it is said that the Blessed One, without making a decision based on the deity's words, looked with his Knowledge of Omniscience and saw: 'Yesterday at midnight, Udaka Rāmaputta passed away and was reborn in the Realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.' Therefore, he spoke thus. The rest of the phrasing is just as before. 'Bahukārā' means they were of great help. 'Padhānapahitattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu' means they attended to the one who had committed himself to striving (the Bodhisatta) for the sake of his exertion, by sweeping the dwelling place and its surroundings, taking his bowl and robes and following him, and providing water for washing the face and tooth-sticks, etc. Who are those known as the Group of Five (Pañcavaggiya)? Those who...
92:
Rāma, Dhaja, Lakkhaṇa, Jotimanta,
Yañña, Subhoja, Suyāma, and Sudatta—
These eight Brahmins existed at that time;
Proficient in the Vedas with their six limbs, they reflected upon and interpreted the Vedic texts.

At the time of the Bodhisatta's birth, there were eight Brahmins who were readers of dreams and readers of marks. Among those eight, three Brahmins gave a dual prediction: "One endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti); if he renounces, he will become a Buddha." However, five Brahmins gave a single-pointed prediction: "One endowed with these marks will not remain in the household life; he will certainly become a Buddha." Among them, the first three spoke only according to what was in the Vedic texts, but these five went beyond the Vedic texts and decided [that he would definitely become a Buddha]. They gave away the offerings they had received to their relatives and, thinking without doubt, "This Great Man will not live the household life; he will certainly become a Buddha," they ordained as recluses intending to follow the Bodhisatta. It is also said that they were the sons [of the original sign-readers]. That statement is rejected in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

It is said that these men mastered many Vedas even in their youth, and therefore those Brahmins were placed in the position of teachers. They reflected that in the future it would not be easy for them to renounce after being entangled with wives and children, so they ordained while still young and lived making use of pleasant dwellings. From time to time, they would ask, "Sirs, has the Great Man gone forth in the Great Renunciation?" People would say, "Where would you see the Great Man? In three palaces, amidst various types of dancers, he is enjoying prosperity like a god." Hearing this, they lived unconcerned, thinking, "The Great Man's wisdom is not yet mature."

In this context, why did the Blessed One say, "These Group of Five (Pañcavaggiya) were very helpful to me"? Does he preach the Dhamma only to those who have been helpful and not to those who have not? It is not that he does not preach to others; he certainly does. Indeed, the Blessed One first looked for Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta because of his past association with them. However, in this Buddha-field, setting aside the Venerable Aññā Koṇḍañña, there was no one else capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths first. Why? Because of having such supporting conditions (upanissaya).
93:
In the past, during a time of performing meritorious deeds, there were two brothers. They worked the fields together. There, the elder brother had the thought: 'I shall give the first-fruit offering (agga-dāna) of this single crop nine times.' At the time of sowing, he gave the first of the seeds. At the time when the rice was in the 'embryo' stage, he consulted with his younger brother, saying, 'Let us split the rice stalks and give an offering during the embryo stage.' The younger brother said, 'Do you wish to destroy the young crop?' Knowing that the younger brother would not follow his wish, the elder brother divided the field and, from his own portion, split the rice stalks, extracted the milky fluid, mixed it with ghee and molasses, and gave it as an offering. At the time of making parched rice, he made parched rice and gave it. At the time of harvest, he gave the first of the harvest; at the time of binding, the first of the binding; at the time of making sheaves, the first of the sheaves; at the time of piling on the threshing floor, the first of the threshing floor; at the time of threshing, the first of the grain; at the time of winnowing, the first of the winnowed grain; and at the time of storing in the granary, the first of the granary. In this way, he gave the first-fruit offering nine times from a single crop. The younger brother, however, gave only after harvesting the rice. Among those two brothers, the elder became the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña, and the younger became Subhadda the Wanderer. Thus, because he had given the first-fruit offering nine times from a single crop, setting aside that Elder, there was no other capable of realizing the Dhamma first. As for the words, 'These Group of Five were very helpful,' this was said merely out of recollection of their past service.

Regarding 'Isipatane Migadāye': In that place, before the arising of a Buddha, Paccekabuddhas would spend seven days in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana. Emerging from cessation, they would chew the 'nāgalatā' tooth-stick, wash their faces at Lake Anotatta, take their bowls and robes, and arrive through the air to descend there. Having put on their robes there, they would wander the city for alms, and after finishing their meal, they would fly up from that very spot and depart. Thus, because seers (isi) descend (nipata) and ascend (uppata) here, the place came to be known as 'Isipatana.' Because it was given as a sanctuary for deer, it is called 'Migadāya' (Deer Park). Therefore, it is said, 'Isipatane Migadāye.'

'Antarā ca Gayaṃ antarā ca Bodhiṃ' means in the space between Gayā and the Bodhi tree, a distance of three gāvutas. From the Bodhi-maṇḍa to Gayā is three gāvutas. To Vārāṇasī, it is eighteen yojanas. Upaka saw the Blessed One between the Bodhi-maṇḍa and Gayā. Because of the association with the word 'antarā,' the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) is used. In such contexts, grammarians usually use the word 'antarā' only once, as in 'antarā gāmañca nadiñca yāti' (he goes between the village and the river), yet that word should be understood as connecting with the second term as well.
94:
If not associated with the word 'antara', the accusative case (upayogavacana) would not apply. However, here it is expressed as being associated. 'Addhānamaggapaṭipanna' means one who has set out on a long journey known as 'addhāna' (dīghamaggapaṭipanna). Regarding the time of traveling a long journey, because of the statement in the Vibhaṅga, 'One should eat, thinking, "I will travel half a yojana,"' even a distance of half a yojana is called 'addhānamagga'. From the Bodhimanda to Gayā, the distance is three gāvutas.

'Sabbābhibhū' means remaining having overcome all things of the three planes of existence. 'Sabbavidū' means having known all things of the four planes of existence. 'Sabbesu dhammesu anupalitto' means being unstained by the smear of defilements in all things of the three planes of existence. 'Sabbaṃ jaho' means remaining having renounced all things of the three planes of existence. 'Taṇhākkhaye vimutto' means being liberated by taking Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, as an object. 'Sayaṃ abhiññāya' means having known all things of the four planes of existence by oneself. 'Kamuddiseyya' means 'Whom else should I point to, saying, "This is my teacher"?'

'Na me ācariyo atthi' means 'In the supramundane Dhamma, I have no teacher.' 'Natthi me paṭipuggalo' means 'I have no person who is my equal.' 'Sammāsambuddho' means having realized the Four Truths by oneself through the method of causality. 'Sītibhūto' means having become cool by extinguishing the fires of all defilements. He is called 'Nibbuta' (Extinguished) because the defilements have been extinguished. 'Kāsinaṃ pura' refers to the city of Vārāṇasī in the Kāsī kingdom. 'Āhañchaṃ amatadundubhiṃ' means 'I go to beat the drum of the Deathless to attain the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.' 'Arahasī anantajino' means 'You deserve to be the Infinite Conqueror (Anantajina) who has conquered endless defilements.' 'Hupeyya pāvuso' means 'Friend, it may be so.' 'Pakkāmi' means he went to the country called Vankahāra.

There, he lived depending on a certain village of deer-hunters. The head hunter attended to Upaka. In that country, there were fierce gadflies. Then, they had Upaka stay inside a large jar. When the deer-hunter went to the distant forest to hunt deer, he commanded his daughter named Chāva, 'Do not neglect our Arahant,' and went away with his sons and brothers. That hunter's daughter was beautiful and possessed of perfect limbs. On the second day, when Upaka came to the house, that girl performed all the services and...
95:
...seeing Chāva approaching to serve the meal, he was overcome by lust and was unable even to eat. Taking the food in a bowl, he went to his dwelling place, set the food in a suitable spot, and thought, 'If I get Chāva, I shall live; if not, I shall die.' Thus, he lay down without food. On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter about Upaka. She said, 'He came only for one day and has not come again.' The hunter, thinking he would go and inquire of Upaka in the same state he had arrived, went immediately and asked while massaging Upaka's feet, 'Venerable sir, what is your discomfort?' Upaka only groaned and rolled from side to side. The hunter said, 'Speak, venerable sir; whatever I can do, I will do it all.' Upaka said, 'If I get Chāva, I shall live; if not, it is better to die right here.' The hunter asked, 'Venerable sir, if that is so, do you know any craft?' He replied, 'I do not.' The hunter said, 'Venerable sir, it is not possible to establish a household and live in the world without knowing any craft.'

Upaka said, 'Though I know no craft, I will be the one who carries meat for you, and I will also sell the meat.' The hunter said, 'We also like this very idea of meat-carrying and selling.' He gave Upaka an upper garment, took him to the house, and gave him his daughter. Through their living together, a son was born. They named him Subhadda. When the young son cried, Chāva mocked Upaka with a lullaby to soothe the child, saying, 'Son of a meat-carrier, son of a deer-hunter, do not cry,' and so on. Upaka said, 'Dear lady, do you think I am one without a refuge? I have a friend named Anantajina. I shall go to him.' Knowing that Upaka was weary, Chāva spoke in that manner again and again. One day, without informing anyone, Upaka set out towards the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa).

At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Great Monastery of Jetavana in Sāvatthī. Then, the Blessed One pre-emptively commanded the monks, 'Monks, if anyone comes asking for "Anantajina," show me to him.' Upaka, inquiring 'Where does Anantajina live?', eventually arrived at Sāvatthī, stood in the middle of the monastery, and asked, 'Where is Anantajina?' The monks led him to the presence of the Blessed One. Seeing the Blessed One, he said, 'Does the Blessed One recognize me?' 'Yes, Upaka, I recognize you. But where have you been living?' 'In the Vankahāra country, Bhante.' 'Upaka, you have become old; will you be able to ordain?' 'I will ordain, Bhante.' The Blessed One ordained him and gave him a meditation subject. While practicing the meditation subject, he established himself in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala), and after passing away...
96:
He was reborn in the Aviha realm. At the very moment of rebirth, he attained the fruit of Arahantship. Indeed, there are seven persons who attained Arahantship just upon being reborn in the Aviha realm; he was one of them.

Regarding this matter, it is stated:
"There are seven monks who, having reached the Aviha realm, are liberated;
With greed and hatred exhausted, they have crossed over the craving (visattikā) in the world.
They are Upaka, Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti—these three—
And Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi, and Saṅgiya.
Having abandoned the human body, they have transcended the divine bonds (divvayogam)."
Thus it is stated (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

"Saṇṭhapesuṃ" means they made an agreement. "Bāhulliko" refers to one who practices for the sake of an abundance of robes and so on. "Padhānavibbhanto" means one who has strayed, fallen away, or declined from the practice of meditation. "Āvatto bāhullāya" means one who has returned for the sake of an abundance of robes and so on. "Api ca kho āsanaṃ ṭhapetabbaṃ" means, "Indeed, for him who is born of a noble family, only a seat should be prepared," so they said. "Nāsakkhisuṃ" means that being overwhelmed by the majesty and power of the Buddha, they were unable to stand by their own agreement. "Nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācaranti" means they addressed him by name and by the term "friend" (āvuso), saying "Gotama" and "Friend." The meaning is that they spoke such words as: "Friend Gotama, when you were practicing austerities in the Uruvelā forest, we carried your bowl and robes as we followed you; we gave you water for washing and tooth-sticks; we swept the precinct where you stayed. Later, who performed the major and minor duties for you? Did you not think of us when we departed?"
