"Iriyāya" refers to the difficult posture. "Paṭipadāya" refers to the difficult practice. "Dukkarakārikāya" refers to performing difficult tasks such as consuming a handful of food or bean soup. "Abhijānātha me no" is a question: "Do you recognize this state of mine?" "Pabhāvitametaṃ" refers to this kind of sentence structure. The intention is: "When I was practicing meditation in the Uruvelā forest, did I ever come to you by night or by day to support you or to prevent you from being weary, and say such words as, 'Friends, do not worry; the light of insight or the sign of meditation has appeared to me'?"

Upon hearing just those words, they regained their mindfulness and respect arose. Believing that "Indeed, this person has truly become a Buddha," they said, "No, Bhante." "Bhikkhus, I was able to make the group of five monks understand..."
97:
Bhikkhus, I was able to make the group of five monks know that I am the Buddha. At that time, the Blessed One arrived on the very Uposatha day of the full moon of Āsāḷha. Having made his Buddhahood known and having made Elder Koṇḍañña a personal witness, he taught the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. At the end of the Sutta, the Elder, along with eighteen crores of Brahmas, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching was concluded while the sun was still visible. The Blessed One entered the rains retreat (vassa) right there.

The words beginning with "Bhikkhus, I also exhort two monks" were spoken to show that from the first day of the waning moon, they did not even enter the village for alms. This was because the Blessed One stayed only within the monastery to clear away the impurities that arose in the meditation of those monks. Whenever impurities of meditation arose, those monks went to the presence of the Blessed One and asked him. The Blessed One also went to the place where they were staying and removed the impurities. Then, while those monks were being exhorted by the Blessed One who partook of the food brought to him, Elder Vappa became a Stream-enterer on the first day of the waning moon. Elder Bhaddiya became one on the second day, Elder Mahānāma on the third day, and Elder Assaji on the fourth day. On the fifth day of the fortnight, he gathered all of them together and taught the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta. At the end of the Sutta, all the monks were established in the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, he said: "Bhikkhus, then the group of five monks, being thus exhorted by me... reached Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage... now there is no more rebirth." The Blessed One previously taught this entire sequence of discourse to show this single connection (anusandhi): "You too have embarked on the path of myself and the group of five; your quest is the Noble Quest (Ariya-pariyesanā)."

Now, however, it is not only for householders that the search for sensual pleasures occurs. Even for those who have gone forth, if they consume the four requisites without reflection, it becomes an Ignoble Quest (Anariya-pariyesanā) by the power of the five cords of sensual pleasure. To show this, he said: "Bhikkhus, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure." In that regard, among new bowls, robes, and so on, the four cords of sensual pleasure such as forms cognizable by the eye are found. The "taste" (rasa) here, however, is the "taste of usage" (paribhoga-rasa), which is the joy and satisfaction arising from use. In delicious almsfood and medicine, all five are found. In lodgings, as in the case of robes, four are found; here too, the taste is only the taste of usage. Why did he begin with the words "Bhikkhus, whoever..."? Having thus shown the five cords of sensual pleasure, he now spoke to refute those who might say, "Since the time of going forth, how can there be an Ignoble Quest? For those who have gone forth, there is only the Noble Quest." For those who have gone forth, the consumption of the four requisites without reflection is...
98:
He undertook this teaching to show that the use of the four requisites without reflection is indeed an ignoble quest (anariyapariyesana). In that text, 'gadhita' means being greedy through the greed of craving. 'mucchita' means being infatuated through the infatuation of craving. 'ajjhopannā' means being overwhelmed by craving. 'anādīnavadassāvino' means not seeing the danger. 'anissaraṇapaññā' means that 'escape' is called the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa); those people are devoid of that knowledge of reviewing.

Now, wishing to show a simile to clarify that meaning, he spoke the words beginning with 'seyyathāpi bhikkhave'. In that simile, the comparison between the simile and the thing illustrated should be understood thus: Ascetics and Brahmins are like wild deer; the four requisites are like a snare set by a hunter in the forest; the time when those monks and Brahmins consume the four requisites without reflection is like the time the deer lies down covering the hunter's pile of snares. The time when Mara can do as he pleases with the ascetics and Brahmins is like the time when the deer cannot go where it wishes when the hunter arrives; the meaning is that they have fallen under the power of Mara. However, the consumption of the four requisites with reflection by ascetics and Brahmins should be understood as like the time an unbound deer lies upon the pile of snares; just as the deer can go where it wishes when the hunter arrives, so too the ascetics and Brahmins do not fall under the power of Mara. 'vissattha' means fearless and without suspicion. The meaning of the remaining words is clear in all the Pali texts.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Pāsarāsi Sutta is finished.
## This Sutta is also known as the Ariyapariyesana Sutta.
## 7. Explanation of the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta

The Sutta beginning with 'evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta. In that Sutta, 'sabbasetena vaḷavābhirathena' means: 'The horses were white and harnessed, with white ornaments. The chariot was white, with white ornaments and white surroundings. The reins were white, the goad was white, the sunshade was white, the turban was white, the clothes were white, the sandals were white, and he was fanned with a white yak-tail fan.' As it is said, it means with a chariot that is entirely white and harnessed with four mares.
99:
There are two types of chariots: war chariots (yodharatha) and ornamental chariots (alaṅkāraratha). Among them, the war chariot is square-shaped, not very large, and capable of carrying two or three people. The ornamental chariot is large, long in length, and wide in breadth. In that chariot, eight or ten people, such as the umbrella bearer, the yak-tail fan bearer, and the palm-leaf fan bearer, can comfortably stand, sit, or lie down; this chariot is also an ornamental chariot. All its parts, including the wheels, the carriage body, and the railing, were covered with silver plates. The mares harnessed to it were naturally white in color. The decorative accessories were likewise made of silver. The reins were also well-wrapped with silver threads. The goad was also covered with silver plates. The Brahmin, having dressed in white cloth, wore a white upper robe, applied white unguent, wore white flowers, and had rings on his ten fingers and earrings in his ears; thus, all the ornaments of this Brahmin were also made of silver. His retinue of about ten thousand Brahmins likewise had white clothes, white unguents, white flowers, and white ornaments. Therefore, it is said, 'with an all-white chariot drawn by mares'.

'Departing from Sāvatthī' means that the Brahmin reportedly makes a clockwise circumambulation (padakkhiṇa) of the city once every six months. An announcement is made beforehand: 'From today, in so many days, he will circumambulate the city.' Hearing that announcement, those who have not yet left the city do not depart. Those who have already left also return, saying, 'We shall see the glorious prosperity of the meritorious one.' On the day the Brahmin wanders through the city, early in the morning, they sweep the city streets, spread white sand, scatter flowers including popped rice as the fifth kind, place full pots (puṇṇaghaṭa), set up banana trees and banners, and perfume the entire city with incense. The Brahmin, having washed his head early in the morning and eaten his breakfast, adorns himself with white clothes and so forth as described, descends from the palace, and mounts the chariot. Then, those Brahmins adorned with all-white clothes, unguents, flowers, and ornaments surround him, holding white umbrellas. Then, to gather the multitude, they first scatter various large and small fruits for the children; after that, they scatter bean-shaped coins (māsaka); after that, they scatter kahāpaṇa coins. The multitude gathers. Shouts of joy and the waving of cloths (celukkhepa) occur. Then the Brahmin performs auspicious acts such as the Maṅgalika and Sovatthika...
100:
While they were making auspicious greetings related to good fortune, that Brahmin wandered through the city with great splendor. Meritorious people, having ascended multi-storied mansions, opened window shutters that resembled the wings of a parrot and looked out. The Brahmin also headed towards the southern gate, as if overwhelming the city with the glory of his retinue and fame. Therefore, it is said, "He departs from Sāvatthī."

'Divā divassa' means the day of the day, at the time of midday. In the phrase 'Pilotikaṃ paribbājakaṃ', Pilotika is a wanderer who received this name through the usage of the feminine gender. It is said that this wanderer was a young man in his first stage of life, with a golden complexion, who served the Buddha. Early in the morning, after attending to the Blessed One and the Great Elders, he took his requisites such as the triple staff and water pot, and departed from the Jetavana monastery, heading towards the city. That Brahmin saw the wanderer coming from afar.

'Etadavoca' means that, knowing he had approached in due course, he spoke these words, mentioning his clan: "Friend Vacchāyana, from where does the venerable one come?" 'Paṇḍito maññe' means, "Does the venerable Vacchāyana consider the ascetic Gotama to be wise, or does he not?"

"Friend, who am I to know the power of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom? By what means could I know the power of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom?" Thus, he demonstrates his own ignorance in every way. 'Sopi nūnassa tādisova' means that one who could know the power of the ascetic Gotama's wisdom must surely be a Buddha like him, who has fulfilled the ten perfections and attained omniscience. Just as one who wishes to measure Mount Sineru, the Himālayas, the earth, or the sky needs to obtain a staff or a rope of suitable size, so too, one who wishes to know the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama needs to obtain omniscience equal to his knowledge. Here, it is repeated out of respect.

'Uḷārāya' means noble or excellent. "Friend, who am I to praise the ascetic Gotama? For what reason could I praise the ascetic Gotama?" he said. 'Pasatthapasattho' means he is praised by his own qualities, which are superior to those praised by all the people of the world; there is no need for him to be praised by others. Just as a jasmine flower, a blue water lily, a lotus, or red sandalwood, by their own...
101:
...color, scent, and splendor, are delightful and fragrant, and there is no need to praise them with external colors or scents; and just as a precious gem or the moon shines by its own light, and there is no need for them to be made to shine by another light; in the same way, the ascetic Gotama is praised by his own qualities which are praised by the whole world, and he is praised and has reached the state of being the most excellent in the entire world. There is no further need for him to be praised by others. Alternatively, 'Pasatthapasattho' means he is praised by those who are themselves praised.

Who are those who are praised? King Pasenadi of Kosala is praised by the inhabitants of Kāsi and Kosala. King Bimbisāra is praised by the inhabitants of Aṅga and Magadha. The Licchavī princes of Vesālī are praised by the inhabitants of the Vajjī country. The Mallas of Pāvā, the Mallas of Kusinārā, and other nobles are praised by the inhabitants of their respective districts. Brahmins such as Caṅkī are praised by groups of Brahmins. Lay followers such as Anāthapiṇḍika are praised by hundreds of lay followers. Laywomen such as Visākhā are praised by hundreds of laywomen. Wanderers such as Sakuludāyī are praised by hundreds of wanderers. Great female disciples such as the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā are praised by hundreds of bhikkhunīs. Great male disciples such as the Elder Sāriputta are praised by hundreds of monks. Devas such as Sakka are praised by many thousands of devas. Brahmas such as Mahābrahma are praised by many thousands of Brahmas. All of them praise, extol, and laud the Buddha who is endowed with the ten powers (Dasabala). Therefore, the Blessed One is called 'Pasatthapasattho'.

'Atthavasaṃ' means the benefit or advantage. Then the wanderer, wishing to explain the reason for his devotion, said: "Sir, just as a skilled elephant-woodsman..." and so on. In that passage, 'Nāgavanika' refers to a man who lives in the elephant forest but has not yet mastered the craft. Later, a man who has mastered the craft of catching elephants is called 'Nāgavanika'. 'Cattāri padāni' means the four footprints of knowledge (four points known through wisdom).

In the terms such as 'Khattiyapaṇḍita', 'Paṇḍita' refers to one endowed with wisdom. 'Nipuṇa' refers to those with subtle and profound intellect, capable of penetrating subtle meanings. 'Kataparappavāda' refers to those who have well understood the doctrines of others and are experienced in debating with others. 'Vālavedhirūpa' refers to those who are like hair-splitting archers. Just as they wander about, breaking and destroying (with their intellect)...
102:
It means they conduct themselves as if destroying the very subtle views of others with their own wisdom, just as an archer who can hit a hair-tip. 'They prepare problems' means they construct questions consisting of two, three, or four parts. 'We will lay blame' means they intend to find fault. 'They do not ask the Samaṇa Gotama questions'—why do they not ask? It is said that while the Blessed One is teaching the Dhamma in the midst of an assembly, He observes the inclinations and dispositions of the audience. Then He sees: 'These wise nobles have come having made secret, profound questions like precious treasure hidden in a waist-fold.' Even before they have asked, the Blessed One—knowing that there are this many faults in asking such questions, this many in answering, and this many regarding the meaning, phrasing, and syllables—thinks, 'If one wishes to ask, one should ask thus; if one wishes to answer, one should answer thus.' Thus, He incorporates those questions brought like hidden treasure into the midst of His Dhamma discourse and dismantles them. The wise nobles then become joyful, thinking, 'It is indeed great for us that we did not ask these questions; for if we had asked, the Samaṇa Gotama would have cast us down, leaving us with no footing.'

Furthermore, when Buddhas teach the Dhamma, they suffuse the assembly with loving-kindness (mettā). Due to this suffusion of loving-kindness, the minds of the multitude gain confidence in the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers. Buddhas are endowed with supreme appearance, perfection of form, a melodious voice, a gentle tongue, and well-aligned lips; they preach the Dhamma as if pouring nectar into the heart. Then, those whose minds are clear due to the suffusion of loving-kindness think: 'We shall not be able to take a hostile stance or argue with the Blessed One, who speaks such unambiguous, fruitful, and liberating words.' Thus, out of their own state of devotion, they do not ask.

'Aññadatthu' means certainly. 'They become disciples' means they become disciples by way of taking refuge. 'Tadanuttaraṃ' refers to that unsurpassed fruit of Arahatship. 'Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ' is the fruit of Arahatship, which is the consummation of the holy life of the Path; for the sake of that fruit of Arahatship, those clansmen go forth. 'O friends, if we had not approached, we would have been lost by merely not approaching and not attending.' The second phrase is a synonym for the first. In the phrases such as 'Assamaṇāva samānā,' they are 'non-recluses' because they have not calmed evil. They are 'non-brahmins' because they have not removed evil. They are 'non-arahants' because they have not killed the enemies of defilements.

'Udānaṃ udānesi' means He uttered an inspired utterance. Just as oil that cannot be contained in a measure overflows and runs out, that overflowing is called 'avaseka'...
103:
...and just as water that cannot be contained in a lake overflows and sweeps along, that is called a flood (ogha). In the same way, when a word born of joy cannot be contained in the heart and, becoming excessive, cannot stay within but comes out, that word is called an 'udāna' (inspired utterance). It means He uttered such a word born of joy.

'Hatthipadopamo' means the 'Simile of the Elephant's Footprint,' because this Dhamma has the elephant's footprint as its simile. It shows that this Dhamma has not yet reached completion in detail by this much alone. 'Nāgavanika' refers to a man who has learned the elephant-craft and frequents the elephant forest to catch elephants. Even so, why is he not called 'skilled' (kusala) here? Because the distinction will be shown later: 'He who is skilled.' Any person might enter, but one who is skilled does not immediately reach a conclusion. Therefore, he is not called 'skilled' here but is called so later.

'Vāmanikā' refers to female elephants that are not long in length but are short and large-bellied. 'Uccā ca nisevitaṃ' refers to a place on the trunks of trees like the banyan, about seven or eight cubits high, where elephants have rubbed themselves. 'Uccā kāḷārikā' refers to female elephants that are tall with legs like poles, called 'kāḷārikā' because of their irregular tusks. It is said that one of their tusks is high and the other is low. Both are also sparse and not close together. 'Uccā ca dantehi ārañjitāni' refers to places on the trunks of trees like the banyan, about seven or eight cubits high, which have been gashed by tusks as if struck by an axe. 'Uccā kaṇerukā nāma' refers to female elephants that are tall with long legs like poles, called 'kaṇerukā' because their tusks are like buds. They are called 'kaṇerukā' because they have bud-like tusks.

'So niṭṭhaṃ gacchati' means that elephant tracker can conclude: 'I have followed the tracks of a certain elephant; this is that very elephant, and no other.' Just as when I first saw the footprint, I did not reach a conclusion that 'this must be the footprint of the dwarf elephants'; and when I saw footprints further on, I did not reach a conclusion that 'it must be of the kāḷārikā or the kaṇerukā'; but only upon seeing the great elephant did I reach the conclusion that all those footprints belong to this very great elephant.

'Even so'—here is the comparison of the simile: The Dhamma teaching from the beginning until the abandoning of the hindrances should be understood like the elephant forest. The practitioner (yogāvacara) is like the skilled elephant tracker; the Fully Enlightened Buddha is like the great bull elephant; the jhanas and direct knowledges are like the large elephant footprint. Just as the elephant tracker, though seeing footprints here and there, does not reach a conclusion that 'it must be the footprint of the vāmanikā, the kāḷārikā, or the kaṇerukā,' so too for the yogi, these jhanas and direct knowledges...
104:
It should be understood that for external wanderers, there is a state of not reaching a conclusion [regarding the six supernormal powers]. Just as an elephant-tracker reaches a conclusion only upon seeing the great elephant, thinking, 'The footprint I have seen is indeed that of this great elephant and no other,' so too should it be understood that a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) reaches a conclusion only upon attaining the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). This comparison and connection can be made at the end of the sutta, but it is also appropriate to make it at this point. Taking the Pali terms as they appear in sequence, it is done right here.

In that Pali, the word 'idha' is an indeclinable (nipāta) indicating a place. This word 'idha' is used in some places in reference to the world (loka). For instance, as it is said: 'In this world, a Tathāgata arises.' In some places, it is used in reference to the Dispensation (sāsana). For instance, as it is said: 'Monks, only in this sāsana is there a recluse (samaṇa), only in this sāsana is there a second recluse.' In some places, it is used in reference to a location (okāsa). For instance, as it is said: 'Standing in this place, I who have become a deva have regained my life; know this, sirs.' In some places, it is merely a filler (padapūraṇa). For instance, as it is said: 'Monks, here I would have finished my meal and refused further food.' In this sutta, however, it should be understood as being said in reference to the world. The intended meaning is: 'Brahmin, in this world, the Tathāgata arises, the Arahant... the fully Enlightened Buddha, the Blessed One.'

In that Pali, the term 'Tathāgata' has been explained in detail in the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, and terms such as 'Arahaṃ' have been explained in the Visuddhimagga. Regarding the phrase 'arises in the world' (loke uppajjati), 'world' (loka) is threefold: the world of space (okāsaloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). Here, the world of beings is intended. Even when arising in the world of beings, the Tathāgata does not arise in the deva worlds or the brahma worlds, but only in the human world. Even in the human world, he does not arise in other world-systems (cakkavāḷa), but only in this world-system. Even there, he does not arise in all places, but only in the following described area: 'In the eastern direction is the market town named Gajaṅgala. To the west of it is Mahāsāla (the great sal tree); beyond that are the border regions (paccantima janapada), and on this side (the inner side) is the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). In the south-eastern direction is the river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. In the southern direction is the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. In the western direction is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country.'
105:
'In the northern direction is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country' (Mahāvagga, 259). Thus, he arises in the Middle Country, which is defined as being three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. It is not only the Tathāgata who arises in the Middle Country; Paccekabuddhas, the chief disciples (aggasāvaka), the eighty great elders (mahāthera), the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, the Universal Monarch (cakkavatti), and other noble brahmins and householders also arise only in this Middle Country.

In that context, from the time the Blessed One partook of the honey-milk-rice offered by Sujātā until the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), he is said to be 'arising' (uppajjati). At the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), he is said to have 'arisen' (uppanno). Alternatively, from the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahantship; or from the passing away from the Tusita realm until the Path of Arahantship; or from the time at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the Path of Arahantship, he is said to be 'arising'. At the Fruit of Arahantship, he is said to have 'arisen'. Here, 'arises' is said in reference to being the very first to arise among all beings; that the Blessed One arises in the world of beings is the meaning here.

'So imaṃ lokaṃ' means that the Blessed One points out this world which is about to be described. 'Sa-devakaṃ' means together with the devas. Likewise, 'sa-mārakaṃ' means together with Māra. 'Sa-brahmakaṃ' means together with Brahma. 'Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ' means together with recluses and brahmins. Because of arising in various ways, it is called 'pajā' (generation/beings); it refers to that world of beings. 'Sa-devamanussaṃ' means together with devas and humans.

In that Pali, by the word 'sa-devaka', it should be understood as including the five sense-sphere deva realms. By the word 'sa-māraka', it should be understood as including the sixth sense-sphere deva realm, Vasavatti. By the word 'sa-brahmaka', it should be understood as including the Brahma-kāyika and other brahma groups. By the word 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇi', it should be understood as including the recluses and brahmins who are enemies and opponents of the Sāsana, as well as the recluses who have calmed evil and the brahmins who have expelled evil. By the word 'pajā', it should be understood as including the world of beings (sattaloka). By the word 'sa-devamanussa', it should be understood as including conventional devas (sammuti-deva) and the remaining humans. Thus, here, by three terms, the world of beings together with the world of space is included; by two terms, only the world of beings is included by way of 'pajā'.

Another method: By including 'sa-devaka', the formless deva world (arūpāvacara) is included. By including 'sa-māraka', the six sense-sphere deva worlds are included. By including 'sa-brahmaka', the fine-material brahma world (rūpī brahma-loka) is included. By including 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇa' etc., the human world together with conventional devas by way of the four assemblies, or all the remaining world of beings, is included.
106:
Alternatively, in this context, by the word 'sadevaka' (with devas), he speaks of the state of having realized the entire world through a supreme definition. Then, to dispel the doubts of those who thought, "Māra is of great power, the lord of the six heavens of the sense sphere, who can bring others under his control; has even this Māra been realized by the Venerable Gotama?", he said 'samāraka' (with Māra). To dispel the doubts of those who thought, "The Great Brahmā is of great power; with one finger he can spread light through a thousand world systems, with two... ten fingers through ten thousand world systems, and he experiences the bliss of the supreme meditative attainments; has even this Brahmā been realized?", he said 'sabrahmaka' (with Brahmā). Then, to dispel the doubts of those who thought, "There are many ascetics and brahmins who are enemies of the Dispensation; have they also been realized?", he said 'sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ' (the generation of ascetics and brahmins). Having thus shown the realization of the most excellent beings, he then said 'sadevamanussaṃ' (with devas and humans), wishing to manifest the realization of the rest of the world of beings, starting from conventional devas (kings) and the remaining humans, by way of supreme definition. This is the sequence of meaning in this context.

The ancient teachers, however, said: by the word 'sadevaka', the rest of the world together with the devas is meant; by the word 'samāraka', the rest of the world together with Māra; by the word 'sabrahmaka', the rest of the world together with the Brahmās. Thus, having included all beings belonging to the three realms in three ways within three terms, and wishing again to encompass them without remainder by two terms, he said "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajaṃ sadevamanussaṃ". In this way, by means of five terms, the three realms (tedhātuka) are completely encompassed in various ways.

In the phrase "sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti" (having realized it himself through higher knowledge, he makes it known): "sayaṃ" means by himself, not being led by another. "Abhiññā" means having known with higher knowledge. "Sacchikatvā" means having witnessed it for himself. By saying this, inference (anumāna) and so forth are rejected. "Pavedeti" means he makes it known, makes it understood, proclaims it. That Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, gives up even the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion and "teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... good in the end". Whether he teaches a little or much, he teaches it only in a manner that is good in the beginning and so forth. In the beginning, he teaches it making it good and faultless. In the middle and in the end also, he teaches it making it good and faultless. This is the intended meaning.
107:
In that passage, there is the beginning, middle, and end of the Teaching (desanā), and there is the beginning, middle, and end of the Dispensation (sāsana). Firstly, in the Teaching, in a verse of four lines, the first line is called the beginning, the next two lines are called the middle, and the one line at the end is called the end. Of a sutta with a single connection, the introduction (nidāna) is the beginning, the conclusion "Idamavoca" is the end, and the sequence of words between the two is the middle. Of a sutta with many connections, the first connection is the beginning, the connection at the end is the end, and the one, two, or many connections in the middle are simply the middle.

In the Dispensation, however, virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and insight (vipassanā) are called the beginning. This has also been said: "What is the beginning of wholesome states? It is well-purified virtue and straight view (insight)." The Noble Path, spoken of as "Bhikkhus, there is a middle way (majjhima-paṭipadā) fully awakened to by the Tathāgata," is called the middle. Fruition (phala) and Nibbāna are called the end. For in this text, "Brahmin, this holy life (brahmacariya) has this fruition as its benefit, this fruition as its essence, this fruition as its end," fruition is called the end. In this text, "Friend Visākha, the holy life is lived as that which merges into Nibbāna, has Nibbāna as its destination, and Nibbāna as its end," Nibbāna is called the end.

In this passage "He teaches the Dhamma," etc., the beginning, middle, and end of the Teaching are intended. For the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, shows virtue in the beginning, the path in the middle, and Nibbāna at the end. Therefore, it is said: "That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end."

Therefore, another Dhamma preacher, when preaching the Dhamma:
"Should show virtue in the beginning,
Should clarify the path in the middle,
Should show Nibbāna at the end;
This is the established order for preachers."

"Sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ" (with meaning and with phrasing) means: if someone's teaching is dependent on praising gruel, rice, women, men, and so forth, he does not teach a Dhamma that is "with meaning." The Blessed One, however, having abandoned such a way of teaching, teaches the Dhamma dependent on the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth. Therefore, it is said, "He teaches the Dhamma with meaning." If someone's teaching is joined with only a single syllable, or consists only of labial syllables, or only of very broad or only of nasal (niggahīta) syllables, his teaching is called "without phrasing" (abyañjanā) because of the absence of perfection in phrasing, like the languages of the Damila, Kirāsa, Vara, and other barbarians (milakkha). The Blessed One, however—
108:
It is stated (in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary 1, 190): 'There are ten varieties of syllables to be understood: sithila (unaspirated), dhanita (aspirated), dīgha (long), rassa (short), garu (heavy), lahu (light), niggahīta (nasal), sambandha (connected), vavatthita (distinct), and vimutta (released).' Preaching the Dhamma without destroying these ten types of syllables and using only complete syllables is why it is said, 'He preaches the Dhamma with its syllables (savyañjana).'

In the term 'kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ,' 'kevala' means 'entire' or 'whole.' 'Paripuṇṇa' means 'neither deficient nor excessive.' This means He preaches only the entirely complete Dhamma; not even a single teaching is incomplete. 'Parisuddha' means being free from the impurities of defilements. If someone preaches this Dhamma with the desire to obtain gains and honors, their preaching is an impure teaching. The Buddha, however, preaches without regard for worldly gains, with a heart softened by the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā) and a desire to spread welfare, and with a mind characterized by the nature of uplifting (beings from saṃsāra). Therefore, it is said, 'He preaches the pure Dhamma.'

In the phrase 'brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti,' 'brahmacariya' refers to the entire Dispensation (sāsana) encompassed by the threefold training (sikkhāttaya). Therefore, it should be understood that while the Buddha preaches the Dhamma that is 'good in the beginning,' etc., He is manifesting the holy life, which is the entire Dispensation encompassed by the threefold training. 'Brahmacariya' means 'noble conduct' in the sense of being excellent. Or, it means the conduct of those who have become noble, such as the Buddhas.

'Taṃ dhammaṃ' refers to that Dhamma endowed with the aforementioned qualities. In the passage 'A householder or [the son of a householder] hears [that Dhamma],' why is the householder mentioned first? It is because they have humbled their pride and because they are numerous. Generally, those who go forth from royal families (khattiya) tend to be proud of their birth. Those who go forth from brahmin families tend to be proud of their mantras (Vedas). Those who go forth from low-born families are unable to remain steady (in the Dhamma) because of their low birth. Householder's sons, however, have had their pride and arrogance humbled by plowing the earth until sweat poured from their armpits and salt crystals formed on their backs. When they go forth, they do not act with pride or arrogance, but learn the Buddha's word to the best of their ability and, by practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), are able to establish themselves in the fruit of Arahatship. Furthermore, those who go forth from other families are not many; householders are the most numerous. Thus, because of their humbled pride and their prevalence, the householder is mentioned first.

'Aññatarasmiṃ vā' means in one or another of the other families. 'Paccājāto' means born. 'Tathāgate saddhaṃ paṭilabhati' means acquiring faith in the Buddha (after hearing the pure Dhamma).
109:
Having heard the Dhamma from the Lord of Dhamma, the Tathāgata, he acquires faith in the Buddha, thinking, 'The Blessed One is indeed perfectly enlightened.' 'He reflects thus' means he contemplates in this manner. 'Household life is confined' means that even if a husband and wife live in a house sixty cubits wide or even a hundred leagues apart, household life is still confined for them because of the nature of anxiety and impediments. 'It is a path of dust' means it is the place where the dust of passion (rāga), etc., arises, as stated in the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā). It can also be called the path through which defilements come. Because it is free from attachment and is like an open space, it is called 'the state of a monk which is like the open air.' In truth, even if a monk lives in a gabled house, a jeweled palace, or a celestial mansion with closed doors and windows, he does not cling, get stuck, or become bound. Therefore, it is said, 'Going forth is like the open air.' Alternatively, household life is confined because there is no opportunity for performing meritorious deeds. It is a path of dust because it is a gathering place for the dust of defilements, just like a place where dust collects if not swept. Going forth is like the open air because there is ample opportunity to perform meritorious deeds as one pleases.

In the passage 'This [holy life] is not easy to practice... if only I could go forth,' the summary is as follows: This holy life, consisting of the threefold training, is 'entirely complete' because it must be practiced without breach for even a single day until the final consciousness (death). It is 'entirely pure' because it must be practiced without being stained by the impurity of defilements for even a single day until the final consciousness. This holy life, which should be practiced to be like a polished and washed conch shell, is not easy for one living in a house to practice with such entire completeness. (He reflects:) 'If only I could shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron-colored robes suitable for those practicing the holy life, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.' Here, the activities of those living in a house, such as plowing and trading, are called 'agāriya' (household affairs), and these do not exist in the state of a monk. Therefore, the state of a monk should be known as 'anagāriya' (homelessness). 'I should go forth' means 'I should practice.' 'Small' means wealth less than a thousand is called small; from a thousand upwards, it is called great. Because of the sense of binding, relatives themselves are called a 'circle' (parivaṭṭa); this is known as the circle of relatives. If that circle of relatives is less than twenty, it is called small; from twenty upwards, it is called great.

'One who has entered the training and livelihood of monks' refers to the training known as the higher virtue (adhisīla) of monks, and the livelihood in which they live together...
110:
(Bhikkhus) have a similar livelihood and a similar way of life. Because they have attained that sājīva, known as the training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed by the Blessed One, and because they are trained in that training, they are called sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno (endowed with the training and livelihood of monks). Samāpanno means attaining both by fulfilling the training and not transgressing the livelihood. In the words beginning with "pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya" (abandoning the taking of life), the explanation of taking life and so on has already been detailed below. Pahāya means having abandoned this lack of virtue (dussīlya) known as the intention to take life. Paṭivirato hoti means that from the time of abandoning (taking life), one is indeed abstinent and turned away from that lack of virtue.

Nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho means one who has laid down the rod and the weapon because he does not carry a rod or a weapon to harm others. Here, except for the rod, all other implements that can harm beings should be understood as "weapons" (sattha). Although monks travel carrying a walking staff, a knife for cutting tooth-sticks, or a small knife (pipphalaka), these are not for harming others. Therefore, he is still referred to as nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho.

Lajjī means being endowed with shame (hiri) characterized by the loathing of evil. Dayāpanno means having reached the state of having a compassionate and loving mind. Sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī means being constantly sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings. Because of reaching such compassion, it means having a mind that desires the welfare of all living beings. Viharati means he maintains his postures; he protects (his virtue).

He is called dinnādāyī because he takes only what is given. He is called dinnapāṭikaṅkhī because even in his mind, he desires only what is given. He is called a thief (thena) because he steals. Athenena (by not stealing) means being pure precisely because of the state of not stealing. Attanā means by his own self; it means he lives by making his own self pure and without theft.

Abrahmacariya means the ignoble practice. He is called brahmacārī because he practices the noble conduct. Ārācārī means one who practices far away from the ignoble practice. Methuna refers to the low practices (asaddhamma) called sexual intercourse because they are practiced by those who are called "sexual partners" (methunaka) due to their similarity through being overwhelmed by lust. Gāmadhamma means the practice of villagers.

He is called saccavādī because he speaks the truth. He is called saccasandho because he connects truth with truth; it means he does not speak lies in between. For if a person sometimes speaks lies and sometimes speaks the truth, his truth is interrupted by lies, and thus he cannot (connect) truth with truth...
111:
(The speech) is connected. Therefore, such a person is not called saccasandho (one who is bound to truth). But this person is not like that; even for the sake of life, he does not speak a lie and always connects truth with truth; therefore, he is called saccasandho. Theto means firm, meaning one whose speech is steady. Some individuals do not have steady speech, like a cloth dyed with turmeric, like a stump fixed in a heap of chaff, or like a pumpkin placed on a horse's back. Some individuals have steady speech, like an inscription on stone or like a deeply fixed threshold pillar (indakhīla). Even if his head is being cut off with a sword, he does not speak two different words; such a person is called theto. Paccayiko means one whose words are trustworthy, meaning reliable. Some individuals are not trustworthy; if it is asked, "Who said this? So-and-so said it," one arrives at the situation where it must be said, "Do not believe his words." Some individuals are trustworthy; if it is asked, "Who said this? So-and-so said it," one arrives at the situation where it must be said, "If he said it, this itself is the standard; there is no need to investigate further; it must be exactly as he said." Such a person is called paccayiko. Avisaṃvādako lokassa means that because of speaking the truth in that way, he does not deceive the people. Imesaṃ bhedāya means for the purpose of dividing those from whom he heard (the speech), as implied by the phrase "having heard from here."

A reconciler of those who are divided (sandhātā) is one who, when two friends or fellow disciples of the same preceptor are divided for some reason, approaches each of them and says, "For people like you, born of such families and possessing such great learning, this is not proper," and thus reconciles them. Anuppadātā means one who further strengthens the reconciliation. When he sees two people in harmony, he says, "For people like you, born of such families and endowed with such qualities, such harmony is truly appropriate," and thus makes the bond firmer. One who delights in concord is called samaggārāmo. It means he has no desire even to live in a place where there is no concord. There is also a Pali reading "samaggarāmo"; the meaning is the same. One who rejoices in concord is called samaggarato; it means he has no desire to leave those people and go elsewhere. One who is glad when seeing or hearing of those in concord is called samagganandī. One who speaks words that create concord, or words that highlight the virtues of harmony, and does not speak otherwise, is called samaggaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā.

Nelā refers to the fault called ela; it means faultless speech, pure speech. It is like the word nela mentioned in the phrase "nelaṅgo setapacchādo."
112:
Kaṇṇasukha (pleasant to the ear) means that because of the sweetness of the syllables, it is pleasant to the ears; it does not cause earache like being pierced by a needle. It is called Pemanīya (lovable) because, due to the sweetness of the meaning, it does not cause anger in the whole body but generates love. It is called Hadayaṅgama (heart-pleasing) because it enters the mind easily without obstruction. It is called Porī (urbane/polite) because it is speech that is excellent due to being full of virtue; or it is called Porī because it is delicate like a lady raised in a great city; or it is called Porī because it belongs to the city, meaning the speech of city-dwellers. For city-dwellers have appropriate speech; they call one who is like a father 'Father,' one like a mother 'Mother,' and one like a brother 'Brother.' Such speech is called Bahujanakantā (beloved by many) because it is desired by many people. Because it is desirable and increases the joy of many people's minds, it is called Bahujanamānapā (pleasing to many).

He is called Kālavādī (speaking at the right time) because he speaks at the appropriate time; it means he speaks after noting the time suitable for what should be said. He is called Bhūtavādī (speaking the truth) because he speaks only according to reality. He is called Atthavādī (speaking what is beneficial) because he speaks only in connection with the welfare of the present and the future. He is called Dhammavādī (speaking Dhamma) because he speaks in connection with the nine supramundane states. He is called Vinayavādī (speaking Vinaya) because he speaks in connection with the Vinaya of restraint and the Vinaya of abandonment. A place for keeping is called Nidhāna; because his speech has a reason to be stored, it is called Nidhānavatī, meaning he speaks words worthy of being treasured in the heart. Even when speaking such words, he does not speak at the wrong time thinking 'I will speak words worth treasuring,' but speaks only after reflecting on the appropriate time. Sāpadesa means speaking with illustrations and with reasons. Pariyantavatī means speaking in a way that the limits are clear by showing the boundaries. Atthasaṃhita means speech endowed with meaning that cannot be exhausted even when analyzed in various ways; or, because it is connected with the benefit that the Atthavādī person speaks of, he speaks Atthasaṃhita speech; it means he does not set aside one thing and speak another.

Bījagāma-bhūtagāma-samārambhā means he is one who abstains from damaging the five kinds of seed-groups (root-seeds, trunk-seeds, joint-seeds, bud-seeds, and grain-seeds) and the groups of living plants such as green grass and trees, by way of cutting, breaking, or cooking. Ekabhattika (one-meal-er) means there are two meals: the morning meal and the evening meal. Among them, the morning meal is defined as being within the period before noon, and the other meal is within the period after noon and before dawn. Therefore, within the period before noon, ten times...
113:
Even if one eats ten times within the period before midday, it is still considered eating only one meal; with reference to such single-meal eating, it is called 'Ekabhattika.' Eating at night is called 'Ratti'; because he abstains from that night-eating, he is called 'Rattūparata.' Eating from after midday until sunset is called 'Vikālabhojana' (Eating at the wrong time). Because he abstains from eating at such an improper time, he is called 'Vikālabhojanā virata' (One who abstains from eating at the wrong time). Seeing things that are like thorns or obstacles because they are inconsistent with the Dispensation (Sāsana) is called 'Visūkadassana' (Distracting shows).

'Naccagīta-vādita-visūkadassana' refers to dancing, singing, and music performed by oneself or by causing others to perform, or even watching such things as peacock dances, which are like thorns. Engaging in dancing, etc., by oneself, causing others to engage in them, or watching them being performed is not permissible for monks or nuns.

Among the terms such as 'Mālā,' 'Mālā' refers to any kind of flower. 'Gandha' refers to any kind of fragrant substance. 'Vilepana' refers to anointing the skin to make it beautiful. One who wears these flowers, etc., is called 'one who carries' (dhāreti). One who applies them to fill in deficient areas is called 'one who adorns' (maṇḍeti). One who enjoys them for the sake of scent or for beautifying the skin is called 'one who beautifies' (vibhūseti). 'Ṭhāna' means cause. Therefore, it means he abstains from wearing garlands, etc., which the general public does with the intention of violating virtue.

A place that exceeds the prescribed measurements is called 'Uccāsayana' (High beds). Unallowable rugs or coverings are called 'Mahāsayana' (Large beds). It means he abstains from these high and large beds. 'Jātarūpa' refers to gold. 'Rajata' refers to kahāpaṇa, copper coins, lac coins, or wooden coins used in trade. He abstains from accepting both; it means he does not take it himself, does not have others take it, and does not take pleasure in it being placed near him.

'Āmakadhañña-paṭiggahaṇa' means abstaining from accepting the seven kinds of raw grain: hill rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, varaka, and kudrūsa. Not only is accepting these seven grains improper, but even touching them is not permissible for monks. In the term 'Āmakamaṃsa-paṭiggahaṇa,' except for meat specifically allowed for monks, accepting raw meat and raw fish is not permissible for monks, but touching them is not impermissible (it is permissible).

In the term 'Itthikumārika-paṭiggahaṇa,' 'Itthi' refers to a woman who has a husband; others are called 'Kumārikā' (Maidens). Accepting them or touching them is not permissible. In the term 'Dāsidāsa-paṭiggahaṇa,' accepting them as female or male slaves is not permissible; however, if one says, 'I give a kappiyakāraka (attendant)' or 'I give an ārāmika (monastery worker),' then it is permissible. Regarding goats and sheep...
114:
In the terms ending with "field" (khetta) and "site" (vatthu), the method of what is allowable (kappiya) and what is not allowable (akappiya) should be investigated through the power of the Vinaya teachings. Among those terms, "khetta" (field) refers to the land where grains (pubbaṇṇa) grow. "Vatthu" (site/land) refers to the land where pulses (aparaṇṇa) grow. Alternatively, if both grains and pulses grow in a certain area of land, that land is called "khetta." The undeveloped portion of land intended for planting those grains and pulses is called "vatthu." In this context, under the names of "khetta" and "vatthu," ponds, threshing floors, and reservoirs are also included. The work of a messenger is called "dūteyya." It is the act of taking the letters or messages of laypeople and going to various places. The minor act of going from house to house as directed is called "pahiṇagamana." Engaging in both of these is called "anuyoga." Therefore, in this context, the meaning should be understood as being devoted to the work of messengers and errands.

"Kayavikkaya" refers to buying and selling. In terms such as "tulākūṭa," "kūṭa" means deception. Among them, cheating with scales (tulākūṭa) is of four types: rūpakūṭa, aṅgakūṭa, gahaṇakūṭa, and paṭicchannakūṭa. Among these four, "rūpakūṭa" means making two scales of similar appearance and, when buying, taking with the large scale, and when selling, giving with the small scale. "Aṅgakūṭa" means when buying, pressing the back of the scale with the hand, and when selling, pressing the front of the scale. "Gahaṇakūṭa" means when buying, holding the base of the scale-string, and when selling, holding the tip. "Paṭicchannakūṭa" means making the beam of the scale hollow and putting iron filings or mercury inside; when buying, making those iron filings move to the back, and when selling, making them move to the front. A gold bowl is called "kaṃsa." Cheating with such a gold bowl is called "kaṃsakūṭa." How does one cheat? Having made one genuine gold bowl, one makes two or three other copper bowls to look like gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering a wealthy family, one says, "Please buy gold bowls." When asked the price, they offer to sell at a very cheap price. Then, when those people ask, "How can we know these are genuine gold?" the seller says, "Buy them only after testing," and after rubbing the genuine gold bowl on a touchstone, sells all the bowls and leaves.

"Mānakūṭa" (cheating in measurement) is of three types: hadayabheda, sikkhābheda, and rajjubheda. Among these three, "hadayabheda" is found when measuring ghee, oil, etc. The one buying those items uses a measure with a hole at the bottom, says "Pour slowly," and lets much of it leak into his own vessel. When selling, he plugs the hole, fills it quickly, and gives it. "Sikkhābheda" is found when measuring sesame, rice, etc. The one buying those items slowly raises the peak and takes it, while the one selling fills it quickly and cuts off the peak. "Rajjubheda" is found when measuring fields and sites. When they do not receive a bribe, they measure the field to be large even if it is not.
115:
Among the terms such as "ukkoṭana," "ukkoṭana" means taking a bribe to make an owner a non-owner, or a non-owner an owner. "Vañcana" means deceiving others by various means. Regarding this deception, there is this story: It is said that a hunter caught a large deer and a young deer and was coming along. Then a rogue asked, "Friend hunter, how much is the large deer, and how much is the young deer?" When the hunter said, "The large deer is two kahāpaṇas and the young deer is one," the rogue gave one kahāpaṇa, took the young deer, went a little way, and returned. He said, "Friend hunter, I have no need for the young deer; give me the large deer." The hunter said, "Then give me two kahāpaṇas." The rogue said, "Friend hunter, did I not give you one kahāpaṇa first?" The hunter replied, "Yes, you did." The rogue said, "Take back this young deer as well; thus, the one kahāpaṇa I gave and this young deer worth one kahāpaṇa will together make two kahāpaṇas." The hunter, thinking that he was speaking a valid reason, took the young deer and gave him the large deer.

"Nikati" means cheating with counterfeits by means of trickery or illusion, making what is not a head-ornament into a head-ornament, what is not a gem into a gem, and what is not gold into gold. "Sāciyoga" means engagement in crookedness. This name "sāciyoga" is also a name for those acts like "ukkoṭana." Therefore, in this context, the meanings should be understood as ukkoṭana-sāciyoga, vañcana-sāciyoga, and nikati-sāciyoga. Some teachers say that showing one object and exchanging it for another is "sāciyoga." However, that is included within "vañcana" (deception). Among the terms such as "chedana," "chedana" means cutting off hands, etc. "Vadha" means killing. "Bandha" means binding with ropes, etc. "Viparāmosa" (robbery) is of two types: himaviparāmosa (robbing by hiding with snow) and gumbaviparāmosa (robbing by hiding with bushes). Robbing travelers while being concealed by snow when snow falls is called "himaviparāmosa." Robbing while being concealed by bushes, etc., is called "gumbaviparāmosa." Plundering villages, market towns, etc., is called "ālopa." "Sahasākāra" means acts of violence, such as entering a house, placing a weapon on people's chests, and taking the desired goods. In this way, that monk abstains from cutting... (etc.) and acts of violence.

"That monk is content" means that this monk is endowed with the twelvefold contentment with whatever requisites are obtained among the four requisites mentioned above. For a monk endowed with this twelvefold contentment with whatever requisites are obtained, the eight requisites (parikkhāra) are allowable. They are: three robes, an alms-bowl, a small knife (for cutting tooth-sticks or sewing robes), a needle, a waist-band, and a water-filter. Thus it has also been said:
116:
“The three robes, the bowl, the razor/knife, the needle, the belt, and the water filter—these eight requisites are allowed for the monk devoted to spiritual practice.” (He preached).

All those requisites are both body-sustaining and belly-sustaining. How? Firstly, the three robes are called 'Kāyaparihārika' (body-sustaining) because they sustain the body when worn and used while traveling. They are called 'Kucchiparihārika' (belly-sustaining) when used to filter water with the corner of the robe for drinking, or when used to hold various fruits to be eaten. The bowl is also body-sustaining when used to carry water for bathing or when repairing the monastery floor and such; it is belly-sustaining when receiving and consuming food. The razor/knife is also body-sustaining when cutting tooth-sticks, or when preparing parts of beds and chairs, legs, robe-racks, or monastery poles; it is belly-sustaining when cutting sugarcane or opening coconuts and the like. The needle is also body-sustaining when sewing robes; it is belly-sustaining when used to pierce cakes or fruits for eating. The belt is body-sustaining when worn while traveling; it is belly-sustaining when used to tie and carry sugarcane and the like. The water filter is body-sustaining when filtering water for bathing or when preparing the monastery bedding; it is belly-sustaining when filtering drinking water, or when using it to carry and eat sesame, rice, parched rice, and the like. This is the extent of the requisites for a monk who carries the eight requisites.

For a monk who carries nine requisites, a bedsheet or a key is allowed when entering the sleeping quarters. For a monk with ten requisites, a sitting cloth (nisīdana) or a piece of skin is allowed. For a monk with eleven requisites, a walking stick or an oil tube is allowed. For a monk with twelve requisites, an umbrella or sandals are allowed. Among these, it should not be said that only the monk with eight requisites is content, while the others are discontented, greedy, or heavily burdened. For those monks are also of few wishes, contented, easy to support, and lead a light life. However, the Blessed One did not teach this sutta by way of them, but by way of the monk with eight requisites. That monk, having placed the small razor, needle, and water filter (inside the filter), and placing them inside the bowl, hangs the bowl on his shoulder, and making the three robes inseparable from his body, goes happily wherever he wishes. There is nothing for him to have to turn back and fetch...
117:
Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to show the light livelihood of this monk, spoke the words beginning with "He is contented with the robes that maintain the body." In that Pali, "kāyaparihārikena" means merely for the purpose of maintaining the body. "Kucchiparihārikena" means merely for the purpose of maintaining the stomach. "Taking them with him, he departs" means he takes all those eight requisites, making them attached to his body, and goes. He has no attachment or bond such as "My monastery, my precinct, my supporters exist." Like an arrow released from a bowstring, or like a rutting bull elephant that has left the herd, he stays alone, sits alone, and is solitary without a companion in all postures, making use of whatever monastery, forest grove, foot of a tree, or mountain cleft he desires. 

"He goes to the four quarters and is without resentment, being contented with whatever he gets; enduring hardships and undaunted, he should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros." (Sutta Nipāta 42). In this way, he attains the state of wandering like a rhinoceros horn as praised.

Now, wishing to establish that meaning with a simile, He spoke the words beginning with "Seyyathāpi." In that Pali, "pakkhĩ sakuᅇo" means a bird equipped with wings. "ူeti" means it flies up. The summary of the meaning in this simile is: Birds, knowing that "the trees in such a place have ripe fruit," come from various directions and eat the fruits of that tree, piercing and shaking them with their claws, wings, and beaks. They do not think, "This fruit is for today, this fruit is for tomorrow." When the fruit is exhausted, they do not keep guard over the tree, nor do they leave behind a wing, a claw, or a beak there. Instead, being without longing for that tree, they fly away to whatever direction they desire, with only the burden of their wings. In the same way, this monk departs without attachment and without longing. Therefore, it is said, "Taking them with him, he departs." "Ariyena" means faultless. "Ajjhattaᅃ" means within his own person. "Anavajjasukhaᅃ" means faultless happiness.

He, the monk endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, having seen a form with the eye, means he sees a form with eye-consciousness. Everything that should be said regarding the remaining terms has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. "Abyāsekasukhaᅃ" means...
118:
Happiness untainted by defilements is also called unmixed happiness (avikiṇṇasukha). Indeed, the happiness of sense restraint (indriyasaṃvarasukha) is unmixed because it occurs by way of "merely seeing" etc., regarding forms and so forth. That monk, endowed with the restraint of the six senses, including the mind as the sixth, acts with clear comprehension (sampajānakārī) through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension in these seven instances, such as going forward and returning. Everything that should be said regarding "going forward, returning," etc., has already been stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

What is shown by the words beginning with "He, by this..." (so iminā ca)? It shows the fulfillment of conditions (paccayasampatti) for one living in the forest. For a monk who lacks these four conditions, living in the forest does not succeed. He comes to live together with animals or forest-dwellers (hunters). Deities residing in the forest make terrifying sounds, thinking, "What is the use of forest-dwelling for such an evil monk?" They strike his head with their hands and make him flee. Ill-fame spreads: "This monk entered the forest and committed such and such evil deeds." But for one who possesses these four conditions, forest-dwelling succeeds. When he reviews his own virtue and sees no stain or blemish, joy arises; contemplating that joy in terms of its rise and fall, he enters the stage of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi). Deities residing in the forest speak his praise with delight. His fame spreads like a drop of oil poured onto water.

In that context, "secluded" (vivittaṃ) means empty, quiet, and without the noise of people. Regarding this seclusion, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Secluded means even if the lodging is near a village, if it is not crowded with laypeople or monastics, it is called secluded because of that lack of crowding." It is called "lodging" (senāsana) because one sleeps (seti) and sits (āsati) there. This is a designation for beds, benches, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Lodging means a bed is a lodging, a bench, a mattress, a pillow, a dwelling (vihāra), a curved house (aḍḍhayoga), a long house (pāsāda), a flat-roofed house (hammiya), a cave (guhā), a watchtower (aṭṭa), a pavilion (māḷa), a shelter (leṇa), a bamboo thicket, the foot of a tree, or a mandapa—wherever monks reside, all that is lodging." Furthermore, "dwelling, curved house, long house, flat-roofed house, cave" are called dwelling-lodgings (vihārasenāsana). "Bed, bench, mattress, pillow" are called bed-and-bench lodgings (mañcapīṭhasenāsana). "Mat, skin-rug, grass-mat, leaf-mat" are called spread-out lodgings (santhatasenāsana).
119:
"Or wherever monks reside"—this place is called open-space lodging (okāsasenāsana). Thus, there are four types of lodging, and all are included under the term "lodging." Wishing to show the lodging suitable for this monk, who is like a bird and can go unhindered in the four directions, the Buddha said "a forest, the foot of a tree," and so forth.

In that context, "forest" (arañña) refers to the forest mentioned in the context of nuns, meaning everything outside the town gate. However, "a forest lodging should be at least five hundred bow-lengths away"—this type of forest is suitable for this monk. The characteristics of such a forest lodging are stated in the Visuddhimagga in the description of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅganiddesa). "Foot of a tree" (rukkhamūla) refers to the foot of any tree that is secluded and has cool shade. "Mountain" (pabbata) refers to a rocky mountain. There, having performed his water duties in the rock pools and sitting in the cool shade of a tree, as the various directions become clear and he is fanned by the cool breeze, the monk's mind becomes concentrated. In the word "cleft" (kandara), "ka" means water; thus, it is a mountain area broken or split by water, also called a small river or a river bend. In such a place, there are sands like silver plates, a forest canopy above like a jeweled ceiling, and water flowing like a block of beryl. Having descended into such a gorge, drunk water, cooled his body, cleared the sand, spread his rag-robe, and sat down to practice the recluse's Dhamma, the monk's mind becomes concentrated.

"Mountain cave" (giriguha) refers to the space between two mountains, or a large tunnel-like cavity in a single mountain. The characteristics of a cemetery (susāna) are stated in the Visuddhimagga. "Forest wilderness" (vanapattha) refers to a place beyond the outskirts of human habitation, where there is no plowing or sowing. Therefore, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "Forest wilderness is a name for distant lodgings," and so forth. "Open air" (abbhokāsa) refers to an unsheltered, open space; a monk who desires it may live there by making a hut of robes. "Straw heap" (palālapuñja) refers to a pile of straw. Monks pull straw from a large heap to make a shelter like a mountain cave or a grotto; they also place straw over bushes and thickets and sit beneath them to practice the recluse's Dhamma. It is in reference to such places that this was said.

"After the meal" (pacchābhatta) means after eating. "Returned from the almsround" (piṇḍapātapāṭikkanta) means one who has returned from seeking alms. "Cross-legged" (pallaṅka) means sitting with the thighs locked all around. "Having folded" (ābhujitvā) means having bound or locked. "Keeping the body upright" (ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya) means setting the upper body straight.
120:
One should place the eighteen vertebrae end to end in a row (keeping them straight). For one sitting in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Because they do not bend, the painful feelings that might arise moment by moment due to the bending of skin, flesh, and sinews do not occur. When those painful feelings do not occur, the mind becomes concentrated, and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) does not fall away but grows and increases. 

'Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā' means having established mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject, or having placed mindfulness at the tip of the nose or near the mouth (the upper lip). Therefore, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: 'This mindfulness is well established at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth; therefore, it is said: parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā.' Alternatively, according to the method shown in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'pari' has the sense of embracing, 'mukha' has the sense of leading out (egress), and 'sati' has the sense of establishing. Therefore, it is called 'parimukhaṃ sati.' The summary of this phrase is: 'having established mindfulness that embraces the meditation subject which leads out from saṃsāra.'

In the phrase 'abhijjhā loke' (covetousness in the world), the five aggregates of clinging are called 'the world' because of their nature of breaking up and crumbling. Therefore, the meaning here is abandoning greed and removing sensual desire (kāmacchanda) regarding the five aggregates of clinging. 'Vigatābhijjhena' means (observing) with a mind free from covetousness because it has been abandoned through the abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna); it does not refer to a mind like eye-consciousness. 'Abhijjhāya cittaṃ parisodheti' means liberating the mind from covetousness. It means acting in such a way that covetousness releases the mind and, once released, does not take hold of it again. 

The same method applies to terms like 'byāpāda-padosaṃ pahāya' (having abandoned ill-will and malice). Because of this state, the mind perishes; it is called 'byāpāda' because it gives up its original natural state, like spoiled barley and so on. It is called 'padosa' because it becomes corrupted through transformation or because it destroys others. Both of these are synonyms for anger (kodha). 'Thina' is the sickness of the mind, and 'middha' is the sickness of the mental factors (cetasika). The combination of these two is called 'thina-middha' (sloth and torpor). 

'Āloka-saññī' (perceiving light) means being endowed with a pure perception free from hindrances, being able to perceive light at night just as it was seen during the day. 'Sato sampajāno' means being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom. These two are mentioned because they are helpful to the perception of light. The combination of 'uddhacca' (restlessness) and 'kukkucca' (remorse) is called 'uddhacca-kukkucca.' 'Tiṇṇavicikiccho' means one who stands having crossed over and transcended doubt. One is called 'akathankathī' (free from 'how-is-this') because thoughts like 'How is this? How is that?' no longer occur. 'Kusalesu dhammesu' refers to wholesome states that are blameless. It means having no doubt or hesitation such as 'Are these states wholesome? How are these wholesome?' This is the summary here, but regarding these (hindrances)...
121:
Everything that should be said regarding these hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by way of word-definition, characteristics, and so on, has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

'Paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe' means that when these five hindrances arise, they do not allow the unarisen mundane and supramundane wisdom to arise, and they also cut off and cause the already arisen eight attainments (samāpatti) or five higher powers (abhiññā) to fall away; therefore, they are called 'states that weaken wisdom.' Similarly, 'tathāgatapadaṃ' is also called the footprint of the Tathāgata's knowledge, the track of his knowledge, or the place trodden by his knowledge. 'Tathāgatanisevitaṃ' is the place rubbed by the flank of the Tathāgata's knowledge. 'Tathāgatārañjitaṃ' is the place stroked by the tusk of the Tathāgata's knowledge.

'Yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti' means knowing according to the true nature. 'The noble disciple has not yet reached a conclusion' means that since these jhānas and higher powers are common even to those outside the Dispensation (titthiyas), one has not yet reached a conclusion by that alone. Even at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), because the task is not yet finished, one has not yet reached a conclusion. However, 'is reaching a conclusion' means that at the moment of the Path, like an elephant-hunter seeing a great elephant, one is reaching a conclusion regarding the Triple Gem through this mode: 'The Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One.' 'Has reached a conclusion' means that having been reaching a conclusion at the moment of the Path, and because all tasks are finished at the moment of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-khaṇa), one has reached a conclusion regarding the Triple Gem in every way. The remaining words have clear meanings.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta is finished.
## 8. Explanation of the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta

The sutta beginning with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' is the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta. Therein, 'jaṅgalānaṃ' means of those creatures that move on the surface of the earth. 'Pāṇānaṃ' means of those creatures that have feet. 'Padajātāni' means footprints. 'Samodhānaṃ gacchanti' means they come to be included (placed within). 'Aggamakkhāyati' means it is called the foremost. 'Yadidṃ mahantattena' means it is called the foremost because of its greatness, and the meaning is that it is not by way of quality. 'Ye keci kusalā dhammā' means whatever wholesome...
122:
Whether mundane or supramundane, wholesome states come to be included. In this context, there are four types of inclusion: inclusion by kind (sajātisaṅgaha), inclusion by origin (sañjātisaṅgaha), inclusion by action (kiriyasaṅgaha), and inclusion by calculation (gaṇanasaṅgaha).

Among these four, inclusion by the power of common birth, such as saying, "Let all Khattiyas come, let all Brahmins come," is called sajātisaṅgaha. Inclusion by the power of the place of origin, such as saying, "All those from Kosala, all those from Magadha," is called sañjātisaṅgaha. Inclusion by the power of common action, such as saying, "All charioteers, all archers," is called kiriyasaṅgaha. The inclusion stated as, "Into which aggregate-calculation does the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) fall? The eye-base falls into the calculation of the form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha). If the eye-base falls into the calculation of the form-aggregate, then indeed, one should say the eye-base is included in the form-aggregate," is called gaṇanasaṅgaha. In this context as well, it is this very [type of] inclusion that is intended.

In answering the question, "Among the Four Noble Truths, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?", it is stated that the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) is unwholesome, the truth of the path (magga-sacca) is wholesome, the truth of cessation (nirodha-sacca) is indeterminate, and the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Therefore, wholesome states occurring in the four planes pertain only to one and a half truths (diyaddha-sacca). This being so, one might ask: Why did the Great Elder say, "They fall into the calculation of the Four Noble Truths"? It is because they are contained within the truths.

For example, it is said: "Monks, these more than one hundred and fifty training rules (sikkhāpada) come to be recited every fortnight, in which clansmen desiring their own benefit train. Monks, there are these three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā)." In this context, although these more than one hundred and fifty training rules are only the training in higher virtue, it is shown that one who trains in that training in higher virtue trains in all three trainings. This is because they are contained within the trainings.

Just as the footprints of foxes, rabbits, deer, and so on, which enter into one, two, three, or all four parts of a single elephant's footprint, are simply gathered into the elephant's footprint. This is because they do not escape the elephant's footprint and are contained within that very elephant's footprint. In the same way, states that fall into the calculation of one, two, three, or four truths are simply said to fall into the calculation of the Four Noble Truths. This is because they are contained within the truths. Therefore, although wholesome states fall into the calculation of one and a half truths, it is said, "All those states come to be included in the Four Noble Truths." In the summary terms (uddesa-pada) such as "In the Noble Truth of Suffering," and in the explanatory terms (niddesa-pada) such as "Birth is also suffering"...
123:
What needs to be said has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. However, in this context, only the sequence of the teaching (desanānukkama) should be understood.

For example, a skilled bamboo worker (vīlivakāra) obtains a well-grown bamboo, cuts it into four parts, sets aside three of those parts, and takes one part to split into five strips. From those five strips, he sets aside four, takes one, and while splitting it, makes five splints (bamboo layers). From those five splints, he sets aside four, takes one, and splits it into two parts: the inner part and the outer part. Then, setting aside the outer part, he takes the inner part and makes various bamboo utensils such as caskets, square fans, and round fans. It should not be said that the bamboo worker will not use the outer part, the other four splints, the other four strips, or the other three bamboo parts for his work. However, it is impossible to use them all at once; he will use them in due sequence.

In the same way, this Venerable Sāriputta, the Great Elder, like the bamboo worker who obtains a good bamboo and cuts it into four parts, began this extensive discourse and established the matrix (mātikā) by way of the Four Noble Truths. Just as the bamboo worker sets aside three parts and takes one to split into five, it should be noted that the Elder sets aside three Noble Truths and takes one, the Truth of Suffering, to analyze it into five parts by way of the five aggregates. Then, just as the bamboo worker sets aside four strips and takes one to split into five, the Elder sets aside the four immaterial aggregates and, wishing to analyze the form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha), makes a fivefold division into the four great elements and derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) based on the four great elements. Then, just as the bamboo worker sets aside four splints and takes one to split into two as the inner and outer parts, the Elder sets aside derived materiality and three elements, and when analyzing the single earth element (pathavī-dhātu), shows it in two ways by way of the internal (ajjhattika) and the external (bāhira). Just as the bamboo worker sets aside the outer part and takes the inner part to make various bamboo utensils, the Elder sets aside the external earth element and, in order to analyze and show the internal earth element through twenty aspects, preached the words beginning with, "Friends, what is the internal earth element?"

Just as the bamboo worker [will use] the outer part, the other four strips, the other four parts, and the other...
124:
He will proceed in due order with the task, for it is not possible to proceed all at once. Likewise, the Elder Sāriputta will also show by analyzing in due order the external earth element, the remaining three elements, the derived form, the remaining four immaterial aggregates, and the remaining three Noble Truths; for it is not possible to show them all at once. Furthermore, this sequence should be made clear by the simile of the princes:

It is said that there was a certain Great King who had more than a thousand sons. Having placed the ornaments and requisites for those princes in four chests, he handed them over to his eldest son, saying, "Dear son, these are the ornaments for your brothers. When a festival occurs and they ask you, 'Please give us the ornaments,' you should give them."

The eldest son replied, "Very well, your majesty," and stored them in the inner treasury. On the day of such a festival, the princes went to the King and said, "Father, please give us the ornaments; we wish to celebrate the festival."

The King said, "Dear sons, I have placed the ornaments in the hands of your eldest brother. Have them brought from him and wear them."

They agreed, went to the eldest brother, and said, "It is said that our ornaments are in your hands; please give them to us."

The eldest brother said, "I shall do so," and opened the treasury. He brought out the four chests, set aside three, and opened one. From that one chest, he brought out five caskets, set aside four, and opened one. From there, he brought out five boxes, set aside four, and opened one. Placing the lid to the side, he took out various ornaments such as those for the hands and feet and gave them. Although he did not immediately distribute the ornaments from the remaining four boxes, four caskets, and three chests, he gave them in due order, for it is not possible to give them all at once.

In this simile, the Great King should be seen as the Blessed One. Thus it was said: "Sela, I am a king, the supreme King of Dhamma" (Sutta Nipāta). The eldest son should be seen as the Elder Sāriputta.
