Thus it was said: "Monks, if one speaking rightly were to say of anyone, 'He is the Blessed One's own son, born of his mouth, born of the Dhamma, created by the Dhamma, an heir to the Dhamma, not an heir to material things,' it is of Sāriputta alone that one could rightly say this" (Majjhima Nikāya). The thousand-plus princes should be seen as the Saṅgha of monks. Thus it was said:
125:
"More than a thousand monks attend the Sugata, as he teaches the stainless Dhamma, the Nibbāna that is free from fear" (Saṃyutta Nikāya).

Just as the King placed the ornaments of those sons in four chests and entrusted them to the eldest son, the Blessed One entrusted the proclamation of the Four Truths to the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, Sāriputta is capable of explaining, teaching, proclaiming, establishing, revealing, analyzing, and making clear the Four Noble Truths in detail" (Majjhima Nikāya).

Just as the princes approached the King to ask for ornaments on such an occasion, the time when the Saṅgha of monks comes and requests a Dhamma teaching at the approach of the rains residence (vassa) should be understood. Indeed, this sutta was taught when the rains residence was near. Just as the King said, "Dear sons, I have placed your ornaments in the hands of your eldest brother; take them and wear them," the Buddha also sent the monks to the General of the Dhamma, saying: "Monks, associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna; monks, serve Sāriputta and Moggallāna. These wise monks are helpers to their fellow practitioners."

Just as the princes, having heard the King's words, went to the eldest brother to ask for the ornaments, the monks, having heard the Teacher's words, approached the General of the Dhamma to request a Dhamma teaching. Just as the eldest brother opened the treasury and brought out the four chests, the General of the Dhamma began this sutta by establishing the matrix (mātikā) by way of the Four Noble Truths. Just as setting aside three chests and opening one to bring out five caskets, setting aside three Noble Truths and analyzing the Noble Truth of Suffering by showing the five aggregates should be understood. Just as setting aside four caskets and opening one to bring out five boxes, setting aside the four immaterial aggregates and analyzing the one aggregate of form by showing the five divisions through the four great elements and derived form should be understood.

Just as setting aside four boxes, opening one, placing the lid to the side, and giving ornaments for the hands and feet, setting aside the three great elements and derived form and analyzing the single earth element, while setting aside the external [earth element] like a lid...
126:
The words beginning with "Friends, what is the internal earth element?" are spoken to show the internal earth element in twenty modes according to its various characteristics.

Just as ornaments are given to a prince after being taken out in sequence from four caskets, four boxes, and three chests, it should be understood that the Elder Sāriputta also shows the remaining three great elements, the derived matter (upādā-rūpa), the four immaterial aggregates, and the three Noble Truths by analyzing them in sequence later. In the passage beginning with "Friends, what is the internal earth element?", both terms 'ajjhatta' (internal) and 'paccatta' (personal) are synonyms for what belongs to oneself. 'Kakkhaḷa' means hard. 'Kharigata' means rough. 'Upādinna' (appropriated) does not refer only to matter produced by kamma; rather, it is a general term for all matter existing in the body. Whether the matter existing in the body is kamma-born or not, it is all called 'upādinna' because it is grasped and touched by the misapprehension of wrong view.

These are: hair, body hair... [to] gorge, and feces. This is the analysis of the meditation subject by way of the internal earth element for a clansman who practices the meditation on the elements. Everything that should be done by a practitioner who wishes to attain Arahantship by initiating attention and developing insight in this regard has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. Although the brain (matthalunga) is not included in this Pali text, one should also take that brain and define it by way of its color, shape, etc., as stated in the Visuddhimagga, and attend to it as: "This brain is also non-sentient, indeterminate (abyākata), void, and is merely the hard earth element."

The phrase "or whatever else there may be" is said to include the earth element that follows in the other three parts. "That which is the internal earth element" refers to the internal earth element of the aforementioned types. "That which is the external earth element" refers to the external earth element mentioned in the Vibhaṅga in the manner of "iron, copper, tin, lead," and so on.

By this much, the Elder has shown the internal earth element in detail through twenty modes according to its various natures, while showing the external earth element only briefly. Why? Because in whatever place the attachment, desire, longing, obsession, grasping, and misapprehension of beings are strong, the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddhas give a detailed discourse to remove those attachments and so on. But where they are not strong, they speak briefly because there is no task to be performed. For example, when a farmer is plowing a field, at a place where the plow gets stuck because the roots are strong, he stops the oxen, clears away the soil, and cuts the roots...
127:
...cutting and pulling them out. Where those roots do not exist, he does not exert great effort but simply plows while tapping the back of the ox. The fulfillment of this analogy should be understood in this way.

"This is just the earth element" means that because it has the same characteristics of hardness, roughness, and coarseness, both types of earth element are just the earth element. In saying "Friends," he shows the internal earth element by connecting it with the external earth element. Since the non-sentient nature of the external earth element is obvious, but not that of the internal, it becomes easy for one to grasp it as being just non-sentient, similar to the external earth element. How? Just as an untamed ox yoked with a tamed ox struggles and quivers for only two or three days and then soon becomes tamed, even so, for one who considers the internal earth element as being similar to the external, its non-sentient nature may not be apparent for only two or three days, but soon after, its non-sentient nature becomes clear. "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self"—thus it should be seen with right wisdom as it really is. "As it really is" means according to its true nature. Since that earth element has the nature of impermanence, etc., it should be seen as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; this is the meaning.

Why did he begin the discourse "Friends, there is such a time"? To show the destruction of the external earth element by the power of the external water element, and then to show, by way of a more superior distinction, the destruction of the earth element existing in the clung-to (upādinna) body. "Disturbed" means it increases and becomes disturbed by the power of the destruction by water (āpo-saṃvaṭṭa). "At that time the external earth element disappears" means at that time, in a hundred thousand million world systems (cakkavāḷa), all the earth element existing in the form of mountains, etc., dissolves in the salty water, follows the water, and disappears. Having dissolved, it becomes only water. "So great" means of such great magnitude.

Two hundred and forty thousand (yojanas),
This earth is said to have such thickness.

Just as it is great in thickness, in extent it is the size of a hundred thousand million world systems. "Impermanence" means the state of non-existence after having come to be. "Subject to decay" means the nature of decaying...
128:
It is the state of having the nature of moving towards destruction. Vaya-dhammatā means the state of having the nature of moving towards destruction. Vipariṇāma-dhammatā means the state of having the nature of abandoning the original state. Thus, by all these terms, only the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) is spoken of. Whatever is impermanent is suffering (dukkha). Whatever is suffering is non-self (anatta). In this way, all three marks are indeed included.

Mattaṭṭhakassa means of brief duration (parittaṭṭhitika). In that context, the brief duration of this body should be understood through two reasons: brevity of the period of existence (ṭhiti-parittatā) and inherent brevity (sarasa-parittatā). This personality (attabhāva) lived in a past mental moment (cittakkhana), it does not live now, and it will not live in the future. It will live in a future mental moment, it does not live now, and it did not live in the past. It is living in the present mental moment, it did not live in the past, and it will not live in the future.

'Life-faculty, personality,
And pure pleasure and pain,
Are joined with a single mental moment;
That moment passes quickly.'

This is said to show the brief duration of that personality. Thus, the brief duration should be understood by the brevity of the period of existence.

The inherent brevity of this body should be understood through its connection with the in-breath and out-breath, and so on. The life of beings is connected with the in-breath, connected with the out-breath, connected with both in-breath and out-breath, connected with the four great elements, connected with nutriment, and connected with consciousness; this is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Taṇhupādinnassa means that which is grasped, held, and misapprehended by craving as 'I', 'mine', or 'I am'. However, when that monk sees by applying the three marks in this way, the threefold grasping of craving, conceit, and views (taṇhā, māna, diṭṭhi) such as 'I' does not occur at all regarding the internal earth element. Just as there is disappearance through the power of the water element, so too there is the disappearance of the external earth element through the power of the fire element and the air element. Although only the water element appears in this sutta, the other elements should also be understood by way of meaning.

'If, friends' (tañce āvuso): here, it shows the power [of the monk] starting from the comprehension of the object at the ear-door of that monk who practices the meditation on elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna). 'They revile' (akkosanti) means they revile with the ten grounds for reviling. 'They threaten' (paribhāsanti) means they threaten with words such as 'You have done such and such, and we will do such and such to you.' 'They annoy' (rosenti) means they strike or provoke. 'They harass' (vihesenti) means they cause suffering; it refers to all kinds of verbal provocation. That monk, in this way...
129:
The monk who practices the meditation on elements understands thus: 'This (reviling, etc.) has arisen in me now, both by way of being present and by way of appearing through the power of an undesirable (aniṭṭha) object.' He understands that the feeling in the ear-door impulsion (sota-dvāra-javana-vedanā) and the contact (phassa) born of ear-contact (sota-samphassa) are impermanent. He sees ear-contact as impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. Feelings and so on associated with ear-contact should also be understood in the same way.

'Dhātārammaṇam-eva' means only the object known as the element. 'Pakkhandati' means he plunges into. 'Pasīdati' means he becomes clear in that object; or this is merely a locative usage. Although it is said as 'dhātārammaṇam-eva' by the power of euphonic combination (vyañjana-sandhi), the meaning here is 'dhātārammaṇe-yeva' (only in the object of the element). 'Adhimuccati' means he gains resolution by the power of the element; he is not lustful, he is not angry. When an object comes into range at the ear-door, this monk performs comprehension by way of defining the root cause and by way of its being adventitious and temporary. The detailed explanation of that was given in the section on mindfulness and clear comprehension (Satisampajañña-pabba) of the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Although it was spoken there by way of the eye-door, here it should be understood by way of the ear-door.

For the practitioner of element meditation who has performed such comprehension and possesses strong insight, if unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) arises when an object comes into range at the eye-door and so on, the mind, after reaching the determining stage (votthabbana) and obtaining repetition (āsevana) once or twice, sinks into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); it does not arise by way of lust and so on. This person is one of sharp insight who has reached the summit. For another, impulsion (javana) runs once by way of lust and so on. But at the end of the impulsion, because he adverts, 'Such impulsion associated with lust has run in me,' the object is already comprehended, and it does not run like that a second time. For another, even though he adverts once, the impulsion still runs a second time by way of lust and so on. But at the end of the second impulsion, because he adverts, 'Impulsion has run in me,' the object is already comprehended, and it does not arise like that a third time. Among these three, the first person is very sharp, and the third person is very dull. The meaning should be understood by way of the second person in this sutta, in the Laṭukikopama Sutta, and in the Indriyabhāvanā Sutta.

Having shown the power of the practitioner of element meditation by way of comprehension at the ear-door, now, wishing to show it at the body-door, he said, 'If, friends' (tañce āvuso), and so on. When encountering an undesirable object, one is troubled at two doors: the ear-door and the body-door. Therefore, just as a man who is the owner of a field, taking a hoe...
130:
Just as a man who is a landowner, while wandering through the fields holding a hoe, does not place a clod of earth just anywhere, but breaks the earth with the hoe only at weak spots such as the bunds and places a clod of earth along with grass; in the same way, the Great Elder (Venerable Sāriputta), intending that the sons of good family in the future who wish to fulfill the three trainings and will strive in the practice of meditation may establish restraint in these doors (ear and body) and quickly make an end of birth, aging, and death, began this teaching with the desire to show firm restraint in these two doors.

In that text, 'samudācaranti' means they make an effort. 'Pāṇisamphassena' means by striking with the hand; the same method applies to the other types of striking. 'Tathābhūto' means having such a nature. 'Yathābhūtasmiṃ' means in the true nature. 'Kamanti' means they occur. In the passages beginning with 'evaṃ buddhaṃ anussarato', one who reflects by the method beginning with 'iti pi so bhagavā' is said to be recollecting the Buddha; one who reflects on 'vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā' is also certainly recollecting [the Buddha]. One who reflects by the method beginning with 'svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo' is said to be recollecting the Dhamma; one who reflects on the Kakacūpama-ovāda (The Advice on the Simile of the Saw) is also certainly recollecting [the Dhamma]. One who reflects by the method beginning with 'suppaṭipanno' is said to be recollecting the Saṅgha; one who reflects on the virtue of a monk enduring being cut by a saw is also certainly recollecting [the Saṅgha].

In the phrase 'upekkhā kusalanissitā na saṇṭhāti', insight equanimity (vipassanūpekkhā) is intended. In the phrase 'upekkhā kusalanissitā saṇṭhāti', however, six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) is intended. Although that six-factored equanimity occurs in an Arahant by way of non-attachment to desirable and undesirable objects, because this monk, through the power of energy and the success of meditation, establishes his insight in the position of the six-factored equanimity of the Arahants, insight itself comes to be called six-factored equanimity.

In the description of the water element (āpodhātu-niddesa), 'āpogataṃ' refers to the characteristic nature of moisture present in all water. Everything that should be said regarding bile, phlegm, etc., along with the method of meditation, has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. 'Pakuppati' means increasing by way of a flood, or the rising of water from the ocean; this is its natural disturbance (pakopa). However, at the time of the world-destruction by water (āposaṃvaṭṭa), a hundred thousand million world systems are filled only with water. 'Ogacchanti' means they go down; it means they reach exhaustion and destruction like water placed on a stove. The rest should be understood in the same way as the previous methods.
131:
In the description of the fire element (tejodhātu-niddesa), 'tejogataṃ' refers to the characteristic of heat present in all fire. Alternatively, fire itself having reached the state of fire is called 'tejogataṃ'. The same method applies to the previously mentioned 'āpogataṃ' and the later 'vāyogataṃ'. 'Yena ca' means by which fire element. When that fire element is disturbed, this body burns intensely; it becomes possessed of heat through states such as one-day fevers. 'Yena ca jīrīyati' means that by which this body ages and decays, reaching the state of derangement of the faculties, loss of strength, wrinkling, and greying of hair. 'Yena ca paridahyati' means that by which this body is intensely scorched due to the disturbance [of that fire element]; that person, crying out 'I am burning! I am burning!', yearns for the application of ghee washed a hundred times, Gosīta-sandalwood, and the breeze from a palm-leaf fan. 'Yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchati' means that by which the eaten food such as rice, the drunk liquids such as beverages, the chewed food such as snacks, and the tasted food such as ripe mango, honey, and molasses reach proper digestion; it means they reach differentiation into essence (rasa) and so on. This is the summary here. Everything that should be said in detail, along with the method of meditation, has been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

'Haritantaṃ' means a green place. It means it is extinguished upon reaching green grass and so on. 'Panthantaṃ' refers to the main road. 'Selantaṃ' refers to a mountain. 'Udakantaṃ' refers to water. 'Ramaṇīyaṃ vā bhūmibhāgaṃ' refers to an open ground or area of land free from grass, bushes, and so on. 'Anāhārā' means without fuel, without sustenance (upādāna). This also refers to the disturbance of the fire element in its natural state. However, at the time of the world-destruction by fire (tejosaṃvaṭṭa), it burns a hundred thousand million world systems so that not even ash remains. 'Nhārudaddulena' refers to a piece of hide/sinew fallen from a cow. 'Aggim gavesanti' means they seek fire by taking such subtle fuel; even if it obtains a tiny amount of heat, it blazes up. The remaining points in this section on fire should also be understood in the same way as the previous method.

In the description of the air element (vāyodhātu-niddesa), 'uddhaṅgamā vātā' are the up-going winds that cause belching, hiccups, and so on. 'Adhogamā vātā' are the down-going winds that expel feces, urine, and so on. 'Kucchisayā vātā' are the winds situated outside the intestines. 'Koṭṭhāsayā vātā' are the winds situated inside the intestines. 'Aṅgamaṅgānusārino' are the winds that circulate through the major and minor limbs of the entire body following the network of nerves/veins (dhamanī), producing bending, stretching, and so on. 'Assāso' means the inward...
132:
Inhaling air through the nose is called assāsa. Exhaling air through the nose is called passāsa. This is merely a summary here. The full explanation, including the method of meditation, has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

'It carries away the village' means it takes away the entire village, reducing it to powder. The same applies to towns and so forth. In this section on the wind element (vāyo-dhātu), the transformation of the wind element that destroys a hundred thousand million world systems during the world-destruction by wind (vāyo-saṃvaṭṭa) is shown. 'Vidhūpanena' means by a fan. 'Ossavana' refers to the edge of the roof (thatch-end); because water flows from that edge, it is called 'ossavana.' The remaining explanations should be understood by applying the previous method.

'Friends, just as...'—what does this show? It shows the non-sentient nature (nissatta-bhāva) of the great elements mentioned below. 'Wood' refers to the timber used for building a house. 'Vines' refers to the creepers used for binding. 'Grass' refers to the thatch for the roof. 'Earth' refers to the fine clay smeared on the outside. 'Space is enclosed' means that space exists surrounding those pieces of wood, etc., inside and out. 'It comes to be known as a house' means that 'house' is merely a designation (paññatti). When wood and other materials are piled separately, they are only called a pile of wood or a pile of vines. Similarly, space surrounding bones and other parts, inside and out, based on those bones, etc., comes to be known as 'form' (rūpa) and is referred to as 'body' (sarīra). Just as when it is called a house based on wood, etc., it is called a king's house or a brahmin's house, so too this body is called a king's body or a brahmin's body, but in reality, there is no being (satta) or soul (jīva) here.

'Friends, the internal eye...'—why is this discourse (desanā) started? Because the derived form (upādā-rūpa), the four immaterial aggregates (nāma-kkhandha), and the three Noble Truths have not yet been mentioned; this discourse is started to explain them now. In that text, 'the eye is unimpaired' means that even if the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) has ceased or is damaged, or is oppressed by bile, phlegm, or blood, the eye cannot be a condition for eye-consciousness and is considered impaired. Only the eye-sensitivity capable of being a condition for eye-consciousness is called 'unimpaired eye' (aparibhinna-cakkhu). 'External forms' refers to forms produced by the four causes. 'The resulting attention' refers to the attention (manasikāra) that arises by turning the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) based on that eye and those forms.
133:
In the eye-door, it refers to the functional mind-element (kiriya-manodhātu) [the five-door adverting]. That adverting consciousness does not arise for one whose mind is elsewhere or because forms do not come into focus. 'Tajja' means corresponding to that [adverting]. 'Viññāṇabhāga' means the group of consciousness.

In the passages beginning with 'For one who has become thus,' the Four Truths are shown by way of the doors. Therein, 'for one who has become thus' means one who is possessed of eye-consciousness. 'Form' (rūpa) means that since eye-consciousness does not produce form, at the moment of eye-consciousness, form produced by three causes (ti-samuṭṭhāna) is obtained, and at the moment of the consciousness immediately following it, form produced by four causes (catu-samuṭṭhāna) is also obtained. 'Comes into the category' (saṅgahaṃ gacchati) means it is counted. Feelings and others associated with eye-consciousness, and consciousness itself being eye-consciousness, are thus counted. Here, by 'formations' (saṅkhāra), only volition (cetanā) is meant. 'Saṅgaha' means collecting together; 'sannipāta' means the meeting of conditions; 'samavāya' means a heap of causal factors.

'He who sees Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda)' means he who sees the causes (paccaya). 'He sees the Dhamma' means he sees the effects arisen from causes (paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma). All terms like 'desire' (chanda) are synonyms for craving (taṇhā). Craving is called 'desire' (chanda) by way of making a wish; 'abode' (ālaya) by way of making an attachment; 'inclination' (anunaya) by way of making a leaning; and 'obsession' (ajjhosāna) by way of overwhelming and swallowing. The discipline of desire and lust, and the abandoning of desire and lust, are synonyms for Nibbāna. Thus, the three Truths appear directly in the Pali text. The Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) should be understood by way of its meaning. In these three places, whatever right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this development and penetration—is the Path. 'Much has been done' means that by this much, much of the Buddha's dispensation has been fulfilled. The same method applies to the sections beginning with 'Friends, the internal ear...'

In the mind-door, the internal 'mind' refers to the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta). Even if that life-continuum has ceased, if it is incapable of being a condition for adverting consciousness and proceeds weakly, it is called 'impaired' (pari-bhinna). If it is capable of being a condition for adverting, it is called 'unimpaired' (aparibhinna). 'External mental objects' (bāhirā ca dhammā) refers to the dhammārammaṇa. The phrase 'not yet corresponding to that' is spoken only in relation to the time of the life-continuum. The second section refers to one whose mind is elsewhere, such as when reflecting on a mastered Jhana, or attending to a mastered meditation subject, or reciting mastered Buddha-word. In this section, 'form' (rūpa) can also refer to form produced by four causes, because mind-consciousness produces form. Feeling and others are associated with mind-consciousness. Consciousness is mind-consciousness itself. Here, formations are...
134:
Sankhāras are taken only by the power of contact (phassa) and volition (cetanā). The rest of the explanation should be understood in the manner already stated. Thus, the Great Elder (Venerable Sāriputta), having come after contemplating only a part of the teaching below, and standing at this point, showed the division of all the incomplete teachings below by way of the respective sense-doors, and concluded the Sutta with the appropriate connection (anusandhi).

## 9. Commentary on the Mahāsāropama Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Mahāsāropama Sutta. In that Sutta, "acirapakkante" means not long after he had split the Sangha and committed the act of causing [the Buddha's] blood to flow, while he was still in his own form and separate.

In the phrase "monks, a certain son of a good family (kulaputta) in this teaching," although not specifically designated as such-and-such a son of a good family, it should be understood that this was spoken with reference to Devadatta alone. For he is a "son of a good family by birth" (jāti-kulaputta) because he was born into the Okkāka dynasty, the unbroken lineage of King Mahāsammata. "Otiṇṇo" means one into whom birth (rebirth) has entered; such a person is called "descended into birth" (jātiyā otiṇṇo). The same applies to old age (jarā) and so forth. In the phrase "gain, honor, and fame," "gain" (lābha) refers to the four requisites. "Honor" (sakkāra) refers to the well-prepared state of those same requisites. "Fame" (siloka) refers to the speaking of praise (commendation). "Abhinibbatteti" means produces (uppādeti). "Apanñātā" means they are not well-known even where two people stand; they do not even obtain mere food and clothing. "Appesakkhā" means those with few followers; they do not have anyone to follow them in front or behind.

"Sārena sārakaraṇīyaṃ" refers to any utility such as an axle, wheel, yoke, or plow made from the heartwood of a tree. In the phrase "takes the branches and leaves of the holy life," the four requisites of the holy life of the Dispensation (sāsana-brahmacariya), which has the essence of the path and fruit (magga-phala-sāra), are called "branches and leaves"; he takes those. "And with that, he reaches satisfaction" means that just by obtaining those four requisites, he becomes satisfied, thinking "I have attained the essence," and comes to a stop.

Devadatta was one who attained the five superknowledges (abhiññā). The attainment of the peak of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and the five superknowledges is called "knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassana) in this Sutta.
135:
It is said (in the commentary): "Living without knowing or seeing" means living without knowing any subtle form, and at the very least, without even seeing a dust-demon (paṃsupisācaka).

"Attains the timeless liberation (asamayavimokkha)" means: "What is timeless liberation? The four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna; this is timeless liberation"—thus, as taught (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga), one attains, fulfills, and acquires these nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma).

Indeed, mundane attainments (lokiya-samāpatti) are liberated from opposing states only at the moment of their respective absorption. Therefore, it is said: "What is temporary liberation (samayavimokkha)? The four jhānas and the four immaterial attainments; this is temporary liberation"—thus they are called temporary liberation. Supramundane states, however, are liberated for all time. Indeed, once the paths and fruits are liberated, they remain liberated. Nibbāna is eternally liberated from all defilements. Therefore, these nine states are called timeless liberation.

"Unshakable deliverance of mind (akuppā cetovimutti)" refers to the liberation of the fruition of arahantship (arahattaphala-vimutti). "This fruition of arahantship is the purpose of this dispensation"—because of this meaning, this holy life (brahmacariya) has the fruition of arahantship as its purpose. It means this fruition of arahantship is the goal of this noble dispensation. "This is the essence" means this fruition of arahantship is the essence of the holy life. "This is the end" means this fruition of arahantship is the culmination of the holy life; this is the peak, and there is no state to be reached beyond this—thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching in accordance with the sequence of the discourse.

## 10. Explanation of the Cūḷasāropama Sutta

"Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Cūḷasāropama Sutta. Therein, "Piṅgalakoccha" means that Brahmin has a golden-brown (piṅgala) complexion. "Koccha" is his name; therefore, he is called "Piṅgalakoccha". In the words "saṃghino" and so forth, those who have a Saṅgha, which is defined as a group of renunciants, are called "saṃghino". Those who have such a group (gaṇa) are called "gaṇino". Because they are teachers of that group by way of instructing in conduct and training, they are called "gaṇācariya" (group-teachers). "Ñātā" means those who are well-known and famous. "Fewness of wishes, contentment..."
136:
They are called 'Yasassī' (renowned) because they possess widespread fame arising from such practices as not wearing clothes due to fewness of wishes. 'Titthakara' refers to the heretical teachers who establish their own doctrines. 'Sādhusammata' refers to those who are regarded as very good and virtuous people. 'Bahujanassa' means (according to the wishes) of the multitude of unlearned and blind worldlings.

Now, wishing to show who they are, the Buddha said, "Seyyathidaṃ pūraṇo" and so forth. In that passage, 'Pūraṇa' is the name of the person who claims to be a teacher, and 'Kassapa' is his clan (gotta). It is said that he was born as a slave who completed the number of one hundred in a certain family, and therefore they named him 'Pūraṇa' (the filler). Because he was an auspicious slave, no one would say to him, "It is badly done," nor would they say, "It is not done," even if it was not done. He thought, "Why should I live here?" and fled. Then, thieves robbed him of his clothes. Not knowing how to cover himself even with leaves or grass, he entered a village in his original state (naked). When people saw him, they approached him with cakes, rice, and other offerings, saying, "This monk is an Arahant, he has few wishes; there is no one like this monk." He thought, "This honor and gain have arisen for me because of my not wearing clothes." From then on, even when he obtained a cloth, he did not wear it, and he adopted that very state of nakedness as his monkhood. Five hundred other men also went forth under him; referring to him, it is said, "Pūraṇa Kassapa."

'Makkhali' is his name. He received the second name 'Gosāla' because he was born in a cow-shed. It is said that while he was walking on muddy ground carrying a pot of oil, his master said, "Dear, do not slip (mā khali)." Due to negligence, he slipped and fell, and out of fear of his master, he began to flee. The master ran after him and caught the hem of his garment. He abandoned the garment and fled naked; the rest of his story is just like that of Pūraṇa.

'Ajita' is his name. He is called 'Kesakambala' because he wears a blanket made of human hair. Thus, combining the two names, he is called "Ajita Kesakambala." In that context, 'Kesakambala' means a blanket made of human hair; there is no garment more loathsome than that. As it is said: "Monks, of all woven garments, the hair-blanket is said to be the worst. Monks, a hair-blanket is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, of ugly color, of bad smell, and unpleasant to the touch."
137:
'Pakudha' is his name, and 'Kaccāyana' is his clan (gotta). Thus, by combining the name and the clan, he is called "Pakudha Kaccāyana." He is one who rejects cold water; even after defecating, he does not perform the duty of washing with water, but does so only when he obtains hot water or sour gruel. If he crosses a river or water on the road, he thinks, "My virtue is broken," and after making a sand stupa and re-undertaking his virtue, he proceeds. He is one who holds such an inglorious view.

"Sañjaya" is his name. Because he is the son of Belaṭṭha, he is called "Belaṭṭhaputta." He is called "Nigaṇṭha" (free from knots) by virtue of the name he acquired by saying, "We have no knots of defilements, no fetters of defilements; we are those who are free from the knots of defilements." Because he is the son of Nāta, he is called "Nātaputta." "Abbhaññaṃsu" means they knew according to their own claims. This is what is meant: if their claim was leading out of suffering (niyyānika), they would all have known it. If not, they would not have known it. Therefore, the meaning of this question is: "Is their claim leading out of suffering or not?" Then the Blessed One, considering it useless to speak about the fact that their doctrines do not lead out of suffering, dismissed it by saying, "Enough," and wishing to teach only the Dhamma by making the meaning known through a simile, said, "Brahmin, I will teach you the Dhamma."

In that text, "sacchikiriyāya" means for the sake of realization. "Na chandaṃ janeti" means he does not produce the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda). "Na vāyamati" means he does not make an effort or strive. "Olīnavuttiko ca hoti" means he is of sluggish disposition. "Sāthaliko" means one who takes up the practice loosely, not firmly.

"Here, Brahmin, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures..." Why are these states such as the first jhāna superior to knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana)? Because they are the basis for the attainment of cessation (nirodha). For the states such as the first jhāna mentioned earlier were the basis for insight (vipassanā), but here they are the basis for the attainment of cessation; therefore, they should be understood as superior. Thus, the Blessed One concluded this sutta according to the sequence of the discourse. At the end of the teaching, the Brahmin was established in the refuges.

138:
## 4. Mahāyamakavagga
## 1. Explanation of the Cūḷagosinga Sutta

"Thus have I heard" and so forth is the Cūḷagosinga Sutta. Therein, "staying at Nātika" means (staying) in one of the two villages belonging to two cousins (sons of paternal uncles), which are situated near a lake named Nātika. "In the Brick House (Giñjakāvasatha)" means in a dwelling made of bricks. It is said that on one occasion, the Blessed One, while wandering in the Vajji country to benefit the people, arrived at Nātika village. The people of Nātika, having given a great offering to the Blessed One and heard the Dhamma, were inspired with faith. They consulted each other, saying, "We shall build a residence for the Teacher," and using only bricks, they constructed a palatial building (pāsāda), showing figures of wild animals and such on the walls, stairs, and pillars. Having plastered it with lime, completed the artistic work of floral and creeper designs, and arranged floor coverings, couches, and benches, they offered it to the Teacher.

Furthermore, the people built night-quarters, day-quarters, pavilions, and walking paths for the Saṅgha of monks. Thus, that monastery became very large. Referring to that, it is said: "In the Brick House".

"In the Gosinga Sal-wood Forest" (Gosingasālavanadāya): There, from the trunk of the largest tree, a branch grew out in the shape of a cow's horn (gosinga). Based on that tree, the entire forest came to be known as the Gosinga Sal-wood Forest. "Dāya" is a general name for a forest. Therefore, "Gosingasālavanadāye" means in the Gosinga Sal-wood Forest.

"They are staying" means they are living while experiencing the flavor of unity (sāmaggi-rasa). The period when these clansmen were worldlings (puthujjana) is told in the Uparipaṇṇāsa; here, however, the period when they were Arahants (khīṇāsava) is taught. For at that time, they were Arahants who had attained the flavor (of Dhamma), found a firm footing, and reached the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), and they lived there experiencing the flavor of unity. It is with reference to this that it was said.

"Approached the Gosinga Sal-wood Forest": Without inviting anyone, not even the General of the Dhamma Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, or the other eighty great disciples, nor even the Treasurer of the Dhamma Venerable Ānanda, the Buddha took his bowl and robes by himself and set out, like a great elephant leaving the army, or like a maned lion leaving the herd...
139:
...or like a cloud severed by the wind, he approached alone. Why did the Blessed One go there himself? Because the three noble sons were living enjoying the taste of harmony; he went to encourage them, out of compassion for future generations, and because of his respect for the Dhamma. The Blessed One had this thought: 'I will encourage these noble sons, praise them, greet them joyfully, and then I will preach the Dhamma to them.' Thus, he went primarily to encourage them. Furthermore, the Blessed One had this thought: 'In the future, noble sons will think, "The Fully Enlightened One himself went to the presence of those living in harmony, greeted them, preached the Dhamma, and encouraged those three noble sons. Who would not live in harmony?" Considering that they must live in harmony, they will quickly make an end of suffering.' Thus, he also went out of compassion for future generations. Buddhas are those who respect the Dhamma, and their respect for the Dhamma is well-known from the Rathavinīta Sutta. Thus, because of this respect for the Dhamma, he went thinking, 'I will honor the Dhamma.'

'Dāyapālo' means a forest guard. That forest guard sits at the gate of the fenced forest to protect it, so that people cannot enter as they wish and take flowers, fruits, resin, or timber. Therefore, he is called 'Dāyapāla'.

'Attakāmarūpā' means living with a nature of desiring one's own welfare. In this Dispensation, one who ordains but makes a living through the twenty-one types of wrong livelihood (anesana) such as practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, or running errands, is not called 'attakāmarūpa'. However, one who ordains in this Dispensation, abandons the twenty-one types of wrong livelihood, stands in the fourfold purity of virtue (caturpārisuddhisīla), learns the word of the Buddha, undertakes suitable ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), takes a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that pleases his mind from among the thirty-eight objects, leaves the village and enters the forest, produces meditative attainments (samāpatti), and lives practicing insight (vipassanā)—such a person alone is called 'attakāma' (one who desires his own welfare). Those three noble sons were also such persons. Therefore, it is said 'Attakāmarūpā viharanti'.

'Mā tesaṃ aphāsumakāsi': He stopped the Blessed One from making them uncomfortable, saying, 'Do not make them uncomfortable.' The forest guard had this thought: 'These noble sons live in harmony. In the places where some people go, quarrels, strife, and disputes occur; they wander like a fierce bull with sharp horns, goring others. Then, even two people walking on one path...'
140:
“By doing this, do not ever destroy the harmonious living of these noble sons. This person is inspiring and has a complexion like gold; I think he might be greedy for good flavors. From the time he arrives, he might destroy the diligent living (appamāda-vihāra) of these noble sons by speaking words of praise about his own attendants who offer excellent alms-food and the like. The dwelling places of these noble sons are also permanently designated; there are three leaf-huts, three walkways (caṅkama), three day-quarters, and three couches and stools. This monk is large in body and appears to be a senior. He might make these noble sons rise from their dwellings at an improper time. In this way, it will be uncomfortable for them in every respect.” Thinking thus and not wishing for any of that, he stopped the Blessed One, saying, “Do not make it uncomfortable for them.”

When asked whether this park keeper stopped Him knowingly or unknowingly, it was unknowingly. The reason is that although miracles such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems occurred from the time the Tathāgata took conception, the weak-minded people living in the forest are occupied only with their own work and are unable to notice those miracles. It is only when the Perfectly Enlightened One travels displaying the Buddha-majesty with the glory of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, the eighty minor marks, and the fathom-long radiance (byāma-pabhā), surrounded by many thousands of monks, that He can be recognized without asking, “Who is this?” However, at that time, the Blessed One concealed all that Buddha-majesty within the chamber of His robes, like the full moon covered by a mass of clouds, and He went in an unrecognized form, carrying His own bowl and robes. Thus, the park keeper stopped Him only because he did not know Him.

Regarding the words “Etadavoca” (he said this), it is said that as soon as the Venerable Anuruddha heard the park keeper’s words, “Monk, do not come,” he thought: “We three people dwell here; there are no other renunciants. This park keeper is speaking as if with a renunciant; who could it be?” Rising from his day-quarter and standing at the door, he looked at the path and saw the Blessed One. As soon as the Blessed One saw the Elder, He released rays from His body; the fathom-long radiance, adorned with the eighty minor marks, shone like a spread-out golden cloth. The Elder thought, “This park keeper, like one stretching out his hand to grab a hooded cobra by the neck, does not know he is speaking with the Supreme Person in the world, but thinks he is speaking with an ordinary monk.” Thinking thus, he spoke the words beginning with, “Friend park keeper, do not [stop Him].”
141:
“Tenupasaṅkami” (He approached Him): Why did he approach the Blessed One without first going out to welcome Him? It is said that this thought occurred to him: “We three people live in a harmonious dwelling. If I alone were to go out to welcome Him, it would not be a harmonious dwelling. I will go out to welcome Him only after taking my dear friends. Just as the Blessed One is dear to me, may He also be dear to my companions.” Thus, desiring to welcome Him together with them, he did not do so alone but approached Him [with them].

Some teachers, however, say that the path of the Blessed One’s arrival was at the end of the walkways by the doors of those Elders’ leaf-huts; therefore, the Elder went while giving a signal to those Elders.

“Abhikkamatha” means “Come this way.” “Pāde pakkhālesi” (He washed His feet) means that with His hands, which were beautiful like blooming lotuses and resembled golden cylinders, He took emerald-colored water, poured it over His golden-colored feet, and washed them by rubbing one foot against the other.

Why did the Blessed Ones wash their feet when no dust or dirt ever clings to their bodies? It was to balance the elements (utu) of the body and to gladden the hearts of those monks. Thinking, “The Blessed One washed His feet and made use of the water brought by us,” the hearts of those monks would be satisfied by the power of strong joy; therefore, He washed them.

“The Blessed One said this to the Venerable Anuruddha”: It is said that he was the eldest among those three monks. When honor is shown to him, it is shown to the rest as well; therefore, He spoke the words beginning with “Is it well with you, Anuruddha?” to the Elder alone. 

In that passage, “kacci” is an interrogative particle. “Vo” is a possessive pronoun. This is what is meant: “Anuruddha, are you keeping well? Is your posture comfortable? Is it supportable? Is your life proceeding and functioning well? Do you not struggle for alms-food? Is alms-food easily obtained by you? Seeing you arrive, do people think that a spoonful of gruel or a ladle of rice should be given?” Thus He asked about the duties of alms-gathering. Why? Because one can practice the Dhamma of a recluse only when not struggling for the four requisites; or else, this is simply the custom of renunciants.

Then, after the reply was given, He asked about the essence of harmony, saying, “Anuruddha, are you [living] in harmony?” and so on, thinking: “Anuruddha, you are those who have gone forth from royal families and possess great merit. If people do not think of giving to you who dwell in the forest, to whom else would they think of giving? But after eating that alms-food, do you live clashing with one another like young deer, or is there harmony among you?”

In that passage, “khīrodakībhūtā” (become like milk and water) means just as milk and water blend with each other and do not remain separate but attain a state of oneness, so too, by the power of harmony...
142:
"Do you live with minds that have attained oneness?" (ekattūpagatacittuppādā) is the question He asks. "With eyes of love" (piyacakkhūhi) refers to eyes that look after having established a mind of loving-kindness (metta); these are called eyes of love. "Do you live looking at one another with eyes of such a nature?" is what He asks. "Taggha" is an indeclinable meaning "certainly." It means, "Certainly, Bhante, we (live in such a way)." In the phrase "How then is it?" (yathā kathaṃ pana), "yathā" is merely an indeclinable. "Kathaṃ" is an inquiry into the cause. It means, "How do you live thus? For what reason do you live so? Tell me that reason."

"Bodily action of loving-kindness" (mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ) is bodily action performed by the power of a mind of loving-kindness. "Both openly and secretly" (āvi ceva raho ca) means both in the presence [of others] and in their absence. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

In this context, bodily and verbal actions in the presence [of others] are obtained while living together, while those in their absence are obtained when separated. Mental action (manokamma) is obtained in all circumstances. For among those living together, if one sees a couch, a bench, a wooden utensil, or a clay utensil left outside improperly by another, and instead of being contemptuous by asking "Who used this?", takes it and puts it away as if he had left it improperly himself, or if he cleans a place that ought to be cleaned, this is called bodily action of loving-kindness in the presence [of others]. When someone has departed, if another puts away the bedding and requisites that the former left improperly, or cleans a place that ought to be cleaned for him, this is called bodily action of loving-kindness in his absence. For one living together, speaking words that are pleasant, joyful, memorable, and connected with the Dhamma, or performing the chanting of verses, discussion, asking questions, and answering questions with others—this is called verbal action of loving-kindness in the presence [of others]. When the elder monks have departed, speaking of their virtues, such as "My dear friend Venerable Nandiya or Venerable Kimbila is thus endowed with virtue, thus endowed with conduct," is called verbal action of loving-kindness in their absence. For one who reflects and attends thus: "May my dear friend Venerable Nandiya or Venerable Kimbila be free from enmity, free from ill-will, and be happy," there is indeed mental action of loving-kindness both in their presence and in their absence.

"Bhante, our bodies are indeed different" (nānā hi kho no, bhante, kāyā) means that it is not possible to knead bodies together like clay or dough to make them one. "But I think our mind is one" (ekaဉ္ca pana maññe cittaṃ) shows that their minds are as if one, because of having the same welfare, being continuous, being without conflict, and being in harmony. How then do they live according to the minds of others, having set aside their own minds? If a stain appears on one's bowl, or if one's robe is soiled, or if there is work to be done on the border of a robe—at that time, if the one whose bowl has a stain says, "Friend, a stain has appeared on my bowl, it should be cleaned," and the others [who might have their own] robe...
143:
...is soiled and must be washed, or "My robe-border must be made," they enter the forest, bring wood, cut it, and having prepared the fine clay in a bowl-pot, they apply the clay. After that, they wash the robe or make the robe-border. Even if one says beforehand, "Friend, my robe is soiled, it should be washed," or "My leaf-hut is dirty, it should be plastered with clay," it is the same way.

The Blessed One said, "Sādhu, sādhu, Anuruddha." Previously, when they said, "Venerable Sir, we are not weary of alms-food," He did not give a "Sādhu." Why? Because this edible food (kabaḷīkāro āhāro) which serves beings is a common practice for these beings in the woeful planes, as well as in the human and deva worlds. However, beings in this world mostly fall into disputes. In the woeful planes, and in the human and deva worlds, these beings are often at odds; a time of harmony for them is rare and occurs only occasionally. Therefore, because of the rarity of living in harmony, the Blessed One gave the "Sādhu" in this instance.

Now, wishing to ask about the characteristics of their diligence, He said, "Anuruddha, do you..." and so on. In that phrase, "vo" is either an indeclinable or a nominative case meaning "you." "Amhākaṃ" means "among the three of us." "Returns for alms" means returning after wandering for alms in the village. "Avakkārapāti" refers to washing and setting out a tray-like bowl to set aside surplus alms-food.

"He who comes back last" means that those elders do not enter for alms-round together. Indeed, they delight in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Having performed their bodily ablutions early in the morning and fulfilled their duties, they enter their dwellings, set a time limit, and sit down having entered the attainment of fruition. Among them, the one who sat down first rises first according to his set time limit. Having wandered for alms and returned, he comes to the place for eating and knows, "Two monks will come later; I have arrived first." Then, having covered his bowl, he prepares the seats and so on. If the alms-food in his bowl is just enough for himself, he sits and eats. If there is a surplus, he puts it into the refuse-bowl (avakkārapāti), covers the bowl, and eats. Having finished his meal, he washes the bowl, wipes it dry, puts it in its bag, takes his bowl and robes, and enters his own dwelling. The second one also knows upon arrival, "One has arrived first, and one will come later." If the food in his bowl is just the right amount, he eats. If it is too little, he takes from the refuse-bowl and eats. If...
144:
If there is leftover food, he places it in the scrap-bowl (avakkārapāti), eats only as much as is sufficient, and like the elder who arrived first, enters his own dwelling place. When the third elder arrives, he knows, "Two have arrived first; I am the one who arrived later." Like the second elder, after he has finished eating, he washes the alms bowl, wipes it dry, places it in its bag, and folds away the seats. He pours out any remaining water from the drinking water jars or the utility water jars and turns the jars upside down. If there is leftover food in the scrap-bowl, he discards it as previously described, washes and puts away the bowl, and sweeps the dining hall. Then, after discarding the rubbish, he places the broom in a place free from termites where it will not be destroyed, takes his bowl and robes, and enters his dwelling place. This is the duty (vatta) to be practiced by the elders in the dining hall of a forest monastery outside the main monastery. It is with reference to this duty that the words beginning with "Yo pacchā" (He who [arrives] later) were spoken.

The words beginning with "Yo passati" (He who sees) should be understood as the duty to be practiced by those elders within the monastery. In that context, "vaccaghaṭa" refers to the ablution pot. "Ritta" means empty. "Tuccha" is a synonym for the same word. "Avisayha" means something so heavy that it cannot be lifted. "Hatthavikārena" means by making hand gestures (signals). It is said that those elders, taking whichever jar among the drinking water jars was empty, would go to the pond, wash it inside and out, filter the water, place it on the bank, and then summon another monk using hand gestures; they would not make any sound, whether directed at someone or not. Why did they not make a sound directed at someone? Because they feared the sound might disturb that monk. Why did they not make a sound even without directing it at someone? Because if a sound were made without direction, both might come out saying, "I first, I first!" In that case, the work of the third monk would be interrupted in a task that should be done by two. Instead, walking with restrained footsteps, one would go near the other monk's daytime resting place, and upon knowing he had been seen, would make a hand gesture. Because of that gesture, the other monk would come. Then, the two of them, joining hands and placing the object on their four hands, would carry it. With reference to this, it was said: "Having summoned a second monk with a hand gesture, they carry it by joining hands (hatthavilaṅghaka)."

Regarding the phrase "Pañcāhikaṃ kho pana," listening to the Dhamma on the 14th, 15th, and 8th days is a regular, customary duty. Without breaking that custom, every fifth day, the two elders would bathe before it got too late and go to the dwelling of the Venerable Anuruddha. There, all three would sit together and, concerning one of the three Pitakas, they would ask each other questions...
145:
...asking each other and answering each other. While they were doing so, dawn would break. This was said with reference to that dawning of the day. By this sequence of words, when the Elder was asked by the Blessed One about the characteristic of heedfulness (appamāda-lakkhaṇa), he answered regarding the characteristic of heedfulness specifically in situations where one might be heedless. For other monks, the time of entering for alms, the time of leaving, adjusting the undergarment, donning the robes, wandering for alms within the village, preaching the Dhamma, giving thanks (anumodanā), eating after leaving the village, washing the bowl, drying the bowl, and putting away the bowl and robes—these are matters that cause delay (papañca). Therefore, the Elder, wishing to show that for them there is no such thing as a time of heedlessness except for these few matters, answered regarding the characteristic of heedfulness in those very situations of potential heedlessness.

Then the Blessed One, having given approval (sādhukāra) to the Venerable Anuruddha, wishing to ask about the first jhana, spoke the words beginning with "Atthi pana vo." In that passage, "uttarimanussadhammā" refers to states superior to the ten wholesome courses of action of human beings. "Alamariyañāṇadassana-viseso" refers to a distinction in knowledge and vision capable of producing the state of a Noble One (ariya). The meaning is: "Venerable Sir, why should it not be realized? It has indeed been realized." "Yāva deva" means only as much as.

After the attainment of the first jhana had been explained in this way, wishing to ask about the second jhana and so on, He spoke the words beginning with "Etassa pana vo." In that passage, "samatikkamāya" means for the sake of transcending. "Paṭippassaddhiyā" means for the sake of tranquility. The rest should be understood in the same manner as already described in all places. In the final question, however, wishing to ask about the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) achieved through the power of supramundane knowledge and vision, He said, "alamariyañāṇadassana-viseso." The Elder also answered in accordance with the question. In that explanation, because unfelt happiness (avedayita-sukha) is more peaceful and more sublime than felt happiness (vedayita-sukha), he said, "We do not see any other pleasant dwelling (phāsuvihāra) that is superior or more sublime than this."

"Dhammiyā kathāyā" means with a Dhamma talk connected to the benefits of the essence of harmony (sāmaggi-rasa). Since all those monks had already completed their tasks regarding the Four Noble Truths, there was nothing further to be preached for their realization. However, by means of the essence of harmony, the Blessed One preached to them the benefits of harmony, saying, "This is such and such a benefit." "Bhagavantaṃ anusamyāyitvā" means having followed after the Blessed One. It is said that those elders, taking the Blessed One's bowl and robes...
146:
Those elders took the Blessed One's bowl and robes and followed him for a short distance. Then, when the Blessed One reached the edge of the monastery's precinct, he said, "Give me my bowl and robes; you stay right here," and departed. "Returning from there" means returning from the place where they were standing. "Why do we [speak] to the Venerable One?" means that although they had attained monkhood and other virtues by depending on the Blessed One, they spoke thus because they were weary of speaking about their own virtues and because of their fewness of wishes regarding their attainments. "Of these and those" refers to the mundane and supramundane states such as the first jhāna and so on. "Known by encompassing mind with mind" means knowing by distinguishing mind with mind thus: "Today the venerable ones spent their time in mundane attainments; today in supramundane attainments." "Deities also [told] me" means they reported, "Venerable Anuruddha, today the Venerable Elder Nandiya and today the Venerable Elder Kimila spent their time in such and such attainments." "When a question is asked" means whether I know that Dhamma myself or the deities told me, my face is ready with just this much; why do I not speak without being prompted or asked? However, when asked a question by the Blessed One, it was answered with mindfulness; he means, "Why do you not delight in my answering thus?"

## Dīgha is a deity king included among the twenty-eight Yakkha generals, as mentioned in the passage: "Maṇi Māṇivaro Dīgho, atho Serīsako sahā." "Parajana" is the name of that very deity. "Approached where the Blessed One was" means that while this Dīgha Parajana deity was going to this place, sent by King Vessavaṇa, he saw the Blessed One himself carrying his bowl and robes between the Giñjakāvasatha and the Gosinga Sāla forest. The Blessed One, carrying his bowl and robes himself, was going to the three clansmen in the Gosinga Sāla forest. Thinking, "Today there will be a great Dhamma discourse; I too must share in that teaching," he followed the Buddha's footsteps with an invisible body, stood at a short distance, and listened to the Dhamma. Even when the Teacher departed, he did not go but remained right there to see, "What will these elders do?" Then, seeing those two elders surrounding Venerable Anuruddha, he thought, "These elders, though they have attained all virtues such as monkhood by depending on the Blessed One, are stingy in revealing their virtues to the Blessed One; they cannot endure it and are hiding and concealing them excessively. Now I will not give these elders the opportunity to conceal them; from the earth..."
147:
"...up to the Brahma realm, I will make their virtues known," he thought and approached where the Blessed One was. "It is a gain for them, Bhante" means: "Bhante, for those inhabitants of the Vajjī country who get to see the Blessed One and these three young men of good family, get to pay homage, get to give gifts, and get to hear the Dhamma—it is a gain for them, Bhante, for the Vajjīs."

"Having heard the sound" means that the deva, by his own divine power, made a great sound that pervaded the entire Vajjī country and uttered those words. Because of that, the earth-dwelling deities (bhumma devatā) residing in trees, mountains, etc., heard the sound. With reference to that hearing, it is said: "Having heard the sound." "They made it heard" means having heard the great sound, they proclaimed it in turn. This method applies everywhere. "Up to the Brahma realm" means up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm.

"That family also" means: "These young men of good family, who went forth from our family, are thus endowed with virtue, qualities, conduct, and good Dhamma"—if that family also remembers these three young men of good family with a confident mind. This is how the meaning should be understood in all instances. Thus, the Blessed One concluded the teaching according to the sequence.

## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Cūḷagosinga Sutta is finished.
## 2. Mahāgosingasutta-vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāgosinga Sutta. Therein, the phrase "in the Gosinga Sāla forest park" is said to show the place of residence. In other suttas, it is customary to first show the alms-resort village, saying "The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery," and then show the place of residence. However, in this Mahāgosinga Sutta, the Blessed One's alms-resort village is not fixed; it could be any village. Therefore, only the place of residence is pointed out. This sutta should be known as one originating in the forest.

"Many" means a large number. "Renowned" means famous and well-known in all places. "Together with the elder disciples" means together with the venerable ones who are called "elders" (theras) because they are endowed with the qualities that make one firm, such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha, and "disciples" (sāvakas) because they have heard the Dhamma from the Buddha. Now those...
148:
Wishing to show the elders in their specific forms, he said "With the Venerable Sāriputta" and so forth. In that passage, the Venerable Sāriputta is well-known and famous in the Buddha's Dispensation for his virtues such as morality (sīla). To those with vision, he is as manifest and renowned as the sun or the moon positioned in the middle of the sky, or as the great ocean to those standing on its shore. The greatness of this Venerable Sāriputta should be understood not only through the qualities mentioned in this sutta, but also through the power of other suttas such as the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, Sīhanāda Suttas (Cūḷasīhanāda and Mahāsīhanāda), Rathavinīta Sutta, Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Cātuma Sutta, Dīghanakha Sutta, Anupada Sutta, Sevitabbāsevitabba Sutta, Saccavibhaṅga Sutta, Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta, Sampasādanīya Sutta, Saṅgīti Sutta, Dasuttara Sutta, Pavāraṇā Sutta, Susima Sutta, Therapañha Sutta, Mahāniddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Therasīhanāda Sutta, his Renunciation (Abhinikkhamana), and the Etadagga Sutta. For, regarding the position of being foremost (Etadagga), it was said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess great wisdom, this Sāriputta is the foremost."

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is also well-known, famous, and great like the [Venerable Sāriputta] through his virtues such as morality and the qualities mentioned in this sutta. Furthermore, his greatness should be understood through the power of these qualities: the Anumāna Sutta, Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, Māratajjanīya Sutta, the shaking of the Vejayanta palace, the entire Iddhipādasaṃyutta, the taming of the Naga king Nandopananda, his ascent to the celestial realm during the performance of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya), the Vimānavatthu, the Petavatthu, the elder's Renunciation, and his attainment of the Etadagga. For, regarding the position of being foremost, it was said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess psychic powers, this Mahāmoggallāna is the foremost."

The Venerable Mahākassapa is also well-known, famous, and great like the [Venerable Sāriputta] through his virtues such as morality and the qualities mentioned in this sutta. Furthermore, his greatness should be understood through the power of these suttas: the Cīvaraparivattana Sutta, Jiṇṇacīvara Sutta, Candopama Sutta, the entire Kassapasaṃyutta, the Mahāariyavaṃsa Sutta, the elder's Renunciation, and his attainment of the Etadagga. For, regarding the position of being foremost, it was said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who uphold the ascetic practices (dhutavāda), this Mahākassapa is the foremost."
149:
The Venerable Anuruddha is also well-known, famous, and great like the [Venerable Sāriputta] through his virtues such as morality and the qualities mentioned in this sutta. Furthermore, his greatness should be understood through the power of these matters: the Cūḷagosiṅga Sutta, Naḷakapāna Sutta, Anuttariya Sutta, Upakkilesa Sutta, Anuruddhasaṃyutta, Mahāpurisavitakka Sutta, the elder's Renunciation, and his attainment of the Etadagga. Regarding the position of being foremost, it was said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), this Anuruddha is the foremost."

In the words "and with the Venerable Revata," there are two Revatas: Khadiravaniya Revata and Kaṅkhārevata. Among them, Khadiravaniya Revata is the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta; he is not intended here. Only the elder who had many doubts, thinking, "Molasses is unallowable, mung beans are unallowable," is intended here as Revata. He is also well-known, famous, and great like the [Venerable Sāriputta] through his virtues such as morality and the qualities mentioned in this sutta. Furthermore, his greatness should be understood through his Renunciation and his attainment of the Etadagga. Regarding the position of being foremost, it was said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are meditators (jhāyī), this Kaṅkhārevata is the foremost."

The Venerable Ānanda is also well-known, famous, and great like the [Venerable Sāriputta] through his virtues such as morality and the qualities mentioned in this sutta. Furthermore, his greatness should be understood through the power of these matters: the Sekha Sutta, Bāhitika Sutta, Āneñjasappāya Sutta, Gopakamoggallāna Sutta, Bahudhātuka Sutta, Cūḷasuññata Sutta, Mahāsuññata Sutta, Acchariyabbhuta Sutta, Bhaddekaratta Sutta, Mahānidāna Sutta, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, Subha Sutta, Cūḷaniyalokadhātu Sutta, his Renunciation, and his attainment of the Etadagga. Regarding the position of being foremost, it was said: "Monks, among my monk disciples who are of great learning (bahussuta), this Ānanda is the foremost."

The phrase "and with other well-known [elders]" means that the Blessed One was staying in the Gosiṅga Sāla forest grove not only with these aforementioned elders, but also with many other disciple elders who were well-known for their great qualities. The Venerable Sāriputta, being himself of great wisdom, brought many other monks of great wisdom and stayed there at that time, surrounding the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala).
150: The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was himself endowed with psychic power. The Venerable Mahākassapa was himself a proponent of ascetic practices. The Venerable Anuruddha himself possessed the divine eye. The Venerable Revata himself delighted in meditative absorption (jhāna). The Venerable Ānanda himself was of great learning. Taking other monks of great learning as well, they dwelt surrounding the Buddha (the Ten-Powered One) at that time. Thus, it should be understood that at that time, these and other well-known Great Elders, numbering about thirty thousand monks, dwelt surrounding the Buddha.## "Emerging from seclusion" (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito) means emerging from the seclusion of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). When the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna emerged from seclusion and looked toward the western world-element, he saw the sun's orb, fifty yojanas in size, setting like an earring falling from the ear of a king intoxicated with luxury playing at the edge of a forest; like a red woolen blanket being folded and placed in a chest; and like a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand [pieces] falling from a jeweled peg. Then, looking toward the eastern world-element, he saw the moon's orb, forty-nine yojanas in size, adorned with the sign of the hare, rising over the summit of the Eastern Cakkavāḷa mountain from the womb of the cloud-colored ocean, like a silver wheel being turned by its rim; like a stream of milk flowing from a silver peak; and like a white swan flapping its wings and soaring into the sky. Then he looked at the Sāla forest. At that time, the Sāla trees were in full bloom from root to tip, appearing as if draped in fine white cloth or entwined with strings of pearls. The ground was adorned as if with an offering of flower-carpets, and because of the pollen falling here and there, it was as if sprinkled with lac-dye. Swarms of bumblebees and honeybees, intoxicated by the flower pollen, wandered through the forest as if singing. That day was also an Uposatha day. Then the Elder thought, "In what kind of delight shall I spend the night today?" Noble disciples are indeed those who delight in hearing the Dhamma. Then the thought occurred to him: "Today, I shall go to the presence of my elder brother, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), the Elder Sāriputta, and spend the time in the delight of the Dhamma." However, instead of going alone, he thought, "I will go taking my dear friend, the Elder Mahākassapa," and rising from his seat, he shook out his leather sitting-mat and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa.
151: "Very well, friend," said the Venerable Mahākassapa. Since that Elder was also a noble disciple who cherished hearing the Dhamma, upon hearing those words, he said, "Let us go, friend," without making any excuses such as "Friend, my head aches" or "my back hurts," but with a joyful heart, he said, "Very well, friend." Having agreed, he rose from his seat, shook out his leather sitting-mat, and followed Mahāmoggallāna. At that time, the two Great Elders, walking in succession, shone like two moon orbs, like two sun orbs, like two Chaddanta elephant kings, like two lions, or like two tigers.## The Elder Anuruddha, sitting in his daytime retreat, saw the two Great Elders going to the presence of the Elder Sāriputta. Looking toward the western world-element, [he saw] the sun entering the forest (which was like an earring falling from the ear of a king intoxicated with luxury, like a red blanket stored in a chest, or like a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand falling from a jeweled peg). Looking toward the eastern world-element, [he saw] the moon rising from the forest (which was like a turning silver wheel, like a stream of milk from a silver peak, or like a white swan soaring in the sky). Looking at the Sāla forest, he saw the Sāla forest in full bloom (which was like being draped in fine white cloth, adorned with pearl strings, or sprinkled with lac-dye due to the pollen). He thought, "Today is the Uposatha day. These elder brothers of mine are going to the presence of the General of the Dhamma. There will surely be a great Dhamma talk. I, too, shall share in hearing the Dhamma." Rising from his seat, he shook out his leather sitting-mat and followed closely behind the Great Elders. Therefore, it is said: "Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, and the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Sāriputta." They approached shining like three moons, three suns, or three lions standing in succession.## As the Great Elders were thus approaching, the Venerable Ānanda, sitting in his own daytime retreat, saw them and thought, "Today there will be a great Dhamma talk. I, too, must share in it. However, I shall not go alone; I will go taking my dear friend, the Elder Revata." The details should be understood in full, just as described for the approach of Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, and Anuruddha. Thus, those two persons approached, shining like two moons, two suns, or two lions in succession. Therefore, it is said: "The Venerable Sāriputta saw [the Venerable Ānanda]," and so on. "Seeing the Venerable Ānanda, he said this" means that having seen him from afar, as he gradually reached the range of conversation, he spoke the words, "Come, Venerable," and so forth. In the phrase "Delightful, friend (is this Sāla forest)," there are two kinds of delightfulness: the delightfulness of the forest and the delightfulness of the person. Therein, the forest is...
152:
A forest that is covered with trees such as Nāga, Salala, Sāla, and Campaka, possessing thick shade, filled with various trees bearing flowers and fruits, abundant in water, and situated far from a village—this is called vanarāmaṇeyyaka (the delightfulness of the forest). With reference to such a forest, it was said (in Dhammapada, 99): 

“Delightful are the forests where the worldling finds no joy; 
Those free from passion will find delight there, for they are not seekers of sensual pleasures.” 

Furthermore, even if a forest is in a rough place, without water, with sparse shade, and overgrown with thorns, if the Buddha and other Noble Ones (Ariyas) reside there, this is called puggalarāmaṇeyyaka (delightfulness due to the person). With reference to that statement, it was said (in Dhammapada, 98): 

“Whether in the village or in the forest, in the vale or on the hill, 
wherever the Arahants dwell, that ground is indeed delightful (bhūmirāmaṇeyyaka).” 

In this Gosinga forest, however, both types of delightfulness are found. At that time, the Gosinga Sāla forest was in full bloom from root to tip and was fragrant with the scent of flowers. The Fully Enlightened Buddha, the Supreme Person in the world including the devas, was also residing there together with about thirty thousand well-known monks. With reference to that forest, it was said: “Friend Ānanda, the Gosinga Sāla forest is delightful.” 

“Dosinā” means being free from faults. It refers to being free from the five stains (upakkilesa), namely: clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. “Sabbapāliphuallā” means blooming everywhere in the entire tree. It means there is no place from the root up to the top that is not in bloom. “As if divine scents are wafting” means that scents like those of the divine Mandārava flowers, Koviḷāra, Pāricchattaka, and sandalwood powder are wafting all around; it means it is as fragrant as the place where Sakka, Suyama, Santusita, Nimmānarati, Paranimmitavasavatti devas, and Mahābrahmā descend. 

When asking, “Friend Ānanda, what kind of monk (would illumine this forest)?” the Elder Ānanda was the junior-most (saṅghanavaka) among those five elders. Why did the Elder Sāriputta ask him first? It was because of his affection (mamāyitattā). Indeed, those two elders cherished one another. The Elder Sāriputta cherished the Elder Ānanda, thinking, “He performs the service to the Teacher that should be done by me.” The Elder Ānanda also cherished the Elder Sāriputta, thinking, “He is the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples.” He would have the youths of good family who were ordained under him take the Elder Sāriputta as their preceptor (upajjhāya). The Elder Sāriputta did the same. In this way, each other's...
153:
There were five hundred monks who were given their bowls and robes, ordained, and made to take him as their preceptor. Whenever the Venerable Ānanda received excellent robes and so on, he would give them only to the Elder (Sāriputta). 

It is heard that a certain Brahmin once thought: “The offerings to the Buddha-gem and the Sangha-gem are well-known, but how should the Dhamma-gem be honored?” He approached the Blessed One and asked about this matter. The Blessed One said: “Brahmin, if you wish to honor the Dhamma-gem, honor a monk who is very learned (bahussuta).” When he asked the Sangha, “Venerable sirs, please point out a learned monk,” he approached the Sangha and said, “Venerable sirs, please point out a learned monk.” (The monks) said, “Brahmin, it is the Elder Ānanda.” The Brahmin then honored the Elder with a robe worth a thousand pieces. The Elder took that robe and went to the Blessed One. The Blessed One asked, “Ānanda, where did you get this?” He replied, “Venerable sir, it was given by a Brahmin; I wish to give this to the Venerable Sāriputta.” When the Buddha said, “Give it, Ānanda,” he replied, “Venerable sir, he has gone on a journey.” The Buddha said, “Give it when he returns.” He then said, “Venerable sir, a training rule has been laid down.” When asked, “When will Sāriputta return?” he replied, “He will return in about ten days.” Therefore, the Buddha laid down the training rule: “I allow you, Ānanda, to keep an extra robe for at most ten days.” The Elder Sāriputta also, whenever he received anything pleasing, would give it to the Elder Ānanda. Thus, those two great elders cherished one another, and because of this affection, (Sāriputta) asked him first. 

Furthermore, this kind of “questioning for opinion” (anumatipucchā) should be asked starting from the youngest. Therefore, the Elder thought: “I will ask Ānanda first; Ānanda will answer according to his own intuition (paṭibhāna). Then I will ask Revata, Anuruddha, Mahākassapa, and Mahāmoggallāna. Mahāmoggallāna will answer according to his own intuition. Then the five elders will ask me in return, and I will also answer according to my own intuition.” Even with this much, this Dhamma teaching will not yet have reached its peak or its fullness. “Then we shall all approach the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers, and ask Him; the Teacher will answer with His Omniscient Knowledge. Only then will this Dhamma teaching reach its peak and its fullness.” For example, when a legal case arises in a district, it reaches the village headman; if he is unable to decide, it reaches the district governor; if he is unable, it reaches the chief judicial minister; if he...
154:
If the general is unable, [it goes] to the viceroy; if the viceroy is unable to decide, it reaches the king. From the time the king decides, the case does not move here and there but is settled by the king's word alone.
