In the same way, I will first ask the Venerable Ānanda... then we shall all approach the Blessed One, who is endowed with the Ten Powers, and ask Him. The Teacher will explain with His Omniscient Knowledge. By this much, this Dhamma teaching will reach its pinnacle and fullness. Thus, the Elder Sāriputta, wishing to ask for formal approval, first questioned the Elder Ānanda.

"Bahussuto" means having much hearing. It means having learned the nine-fold Dispensation of the Teacher according to the sequence and context of the Pali. "Sutadharo" means being a repository of what is heard. For one who loses what is learned here when reaching another place, like water in a leaky pot, and is unable to preach or teach even a single Sutta or Jātaka in the midst of an assembly, such a person cannot be called a "Sutadhara." For one whose learned Buddha-word remains just as it was when learned, and does not vanish even if not recited for ten or twenty years, such a person is called a "Sutadhara." "Sutasannicayo" means one who has accumulated what is heard. For one whose heard Dhamma is firmly established in the casket of the heart like an inscription on stone, or like lion's fat placed in a golden pot, such a person is called a "Sutasannicayo." "Dhātā" means being firm and proficient. For some, the learned Buddha-word is not retained, proficient, or unshakable. When told, "Preach this Sutta or this Jātaka," such a person says, "I will know after reciting, comparing, and contemplating repeatedly." For others, the retained and proficient Buddha-word is like the flow of the subconscious (bhavaṅgasota). When told, "Preach this Sutta or this Jātaka," they can bring it forth and preach it immediately. Referring to such a person, it is said: "Dhātā."

"Vacasā paricitā" means recited verbally by way of groups of ten suttas, ten chapters (vaggas), or ten groups of fifty (paṇṇāsas). "Manasānupekkhitā" means repeatedly contemplated by the mind. When one thinks of the Buddha-word recited verbally, it becomes clear in various places. It appears through wisdom just as forms appear to one who has lit a great lamp. Referring to such a person, it is said: "Vacasā paricitā manasānupekkhitā." "Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā" means well-penetrated by wisdom in terms of both meaning and reason.
155:
In the phrase "parimaṇ|alehi padabyañjanehi," the word (pada) itself is called "padabyañjana" because it manifests the meaning. When it is spoken with complete syllables and without diminishing the ten types of consonant sounds, it is called "parimaṇ|ala" (well-rounded). It means "with such words and syllables." Furthermore, when a monk preaching Dhamma in the midst of an assembly sets aside a Sutta or Jātaka and brings in another Sutta that causes obstruction, he tells an analogy for that [new] Sutta. For that purpose, he sets it down, takes this Sutta, places it in the context of what was taken, carries it on one-sidedly, and then rises when he knows the time. But the Sutta that was set aside remains merely set aside. His speech is called "aparimaṇ|ala" (incomplete).

However, a monk who sets down a Sutta or Jātaka without letting even a single word go outside, without violating the context and sequence of the Pali, staying within the method given by the teachers, proceeds like one demarcating with a brush, or like one releasing water through a deep channel, or like a noble Sindh horse striking its hooves. That monk's speech is called "parimaṇ|ala" (well-rounded). Referring to such speech, it is said: "parimaṇ|alehi padabyañjanehi."

In the word "anuppabandhehi," when a monk preaching Dhamma starts a Sutta or Jātaka, from the time he begins, he proceeds very rapidly like one rubbing fire-sticks, or like one eating hot food. In the context and sequence of the Pali, he treats what is taken as taken and what is not taken as not taken, striking here and there like one flushing out a monitor lizard roaming among old leaves, bringing it to an end, and then leaving. Another monk, while preaching Dhamma, sometimes speaks fast, sometimes slow, sometimes loud, and sometimes soft. Just as a ghost-fire (petaggi) sometimes blazes and sometimes goes out, so in this Dispensation, he is called a "ghost-fire Dhamma-preacher" (petaggi-dhammakathika). When the assembly wishes to rise, he starts again and again. Another monk, while preaching, expands here and there, preaching as if moaning and weeping. The speech of all these is called "appabandha" (disconnected).

However, a monk who starts a Sutta, stays within the method given by the teachers, and makes it a continuous flow like the current of a river, or makes his speech continuous like water falling from the celestial Ganges (Ākāsagaṅgā)—that monk's speech is "anuppabandha" (continuous). Referring to that speech...
156:
It is stated as “anuppabandhehi.” (Anuppabandha means) producing speech continuously like a river's current while remaining within the method provided by the teachers, speaking in succession. “Anusayasamugghātāya” means for the purpose of eradicating the seven underlying tendencies (anusaya). A monk endowed with such great learning (bahussuta) could beautify the Gosinga Sāla forest by sitting with a hundred or a thousand such learned monks, with the corners of their robes touching or sitting cross-legged with their knees touching. In this same manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

Because seclusion is a place of delight for that person, he is called “paṭisallānārāma” (one who delights in seclusion). Because he rejoices in seclusion, he is called “paṭisallānarata” (one who is devoted to seclusion).

“Sahassaṃ lokānaṃ” refers to a thousand world systems. Although the Elder Anuruddha habitually contemplates this extent through constant practice, if he so desires, he can indeed look upon many thousands of world systems. “Upari-pāsāda-vara-gato” refers to one who has reached the top of a noble palace of seven or nine stories. “Sahassaṃ nemimaṇḍalānaṃ volokeyya” is like opening a window and looking at a thousand wheel rims that are positioned on their hubs and touching rim to rim in the palace courtyard. To such a person, the hubs, the spokes, the intervals between the spokes, and the rims are clearly visible. In the same way, friend, this monk with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), with the divine eye that is purified and surpasses that of humans, looks upon a thousand worlds. Just as the wheel hubs are clear to the person on the palace, the thousand Sineru mountains are clear in the thousand world systems. The great islands are clear like the spokes. The people living on the islands are clear like the intervals between the spokes. The Cakkavāḷa mountains are clear like the rims.

“Āraññiko” refers to one who has undertaken the ascetic practice of a forest-dweller (āraññaka-dhutaṅga). In the remaining terms, the method is the same.

“No ca saṃsādenti” means they do not sink (do not falter). One who is unable to ask or answer a question with its reasons and causes is said to “saṃsādeti.” The meaning is that they do not do so. “Pavattinī hoti” means it flows and occurs like a river's current.
157:
“By whatever dwelling attainment” (yāya vihārasamāpattiyā) refers to living by whatever mundane dwelling attainment or by whatever supramundane dwelling attainment.

“Sādhu sādhu Sāriputta”—this exclamation of approval is given to the Elder Ānanda. However, the Blessed One is addressing the Elder Sāriputta. This is the method in all instances. “Yathā taṃ Ānandova” means that just as Ānanda himself would answer when answering correctly, so Ānanda has answered in a way that is suitable to himself and in accordance with his own inclination (ajjhāsaya). For the Elder Ānanda is himself very learned, and his inclination is thus: “O, that the fellow practitioners in the Dispensation might be very learned!” Why? Because for a learned monk, what is allowable and unallowable, what is blameworthy and blameless, what is a heavy offense and a light offense, and what is a curable offense and an incurable offense, become clear. A learned monk, having reflected on the word of the Buddha he has mastered, knows: “In this place, virtue (sīla) is taught; in this place, concentration (samādhi); in this place, insight (vipassanā); in this place, the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna.” Thus, he fulfills virtue where virtue is mentioned, fulfills concentration where concentration is mentioned, develops the foundation of insight where insight is mentioned, and by developing the Path, he realizes the Fruit. Therefore, the Elder’s inclination is: “O, that the fellow practitioners might learn one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas and, by reflecting on them, fulfill virtue and so on where they are mentioned, and gradually realize the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna!” In the remaining sections, the method is the same.

The Venerable Revata is one whose inclination is toward jhāna and who delights in jhāna. Therefore, his wish is: “O, that the fellow practitioners might sit alone, perform the preparatory work for kasiṇa meditation, produce the eight attainments, and by developing insight based on jhāna, realize the supramundane Dhamma!” That is why he answered in that way.

The Venerable Anuruddha possesses the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). His wish is: “O, that the fellow practitioners might develop the light, and with the divine eye, see beings passing away and being reborn in many thousands of world systems, and having moved their minds to spiritual urgency (saṃvega) through the fear of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-bhaya), develop insight and realize the supramundane Dhamma!” That is why he answered in that way.
158:
Venerable Mahākassapa was one who spoke in praise of ascetic practices (dhutavāda). It occurred to him: "It would be well if my fellow practitioners were speakers on ascetic practices, and through the power of the ascetic limbs (dhutaṅga), they could thin out the craving for the four requisites, destroy various other kinds of defilements, develop insight (vipassanā), and realize the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma)." Therefore, he answered in that manner.

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had reached the peak of the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramī). Indeed, the subtle distinctions of the mind (cittantara), the distinctions of the aggregates (khandhantara), the distinctions of the elements (dhātvantara), the distinctions of the sense bases (āyatanantara), the jumping into meditative absorptions (jhānokkanti), the jumping into objects (ārammaṇokkanti), the defining of factors (aṅgavavatthāna), the defining of objects (ārammaṇavavatthāna), the shifting of factors (aṅgasaṅkanti), the shifting of objects (ārammaṇasaṅkanti), the single-sided increase (ekatovaddhana—taking a triad and placing it in a triad), and the double-sided increase (ubhatovaddhana—increasing both triads and dyads) are clear only to a teacher of Dhamma who has studied the Abhidhamma (ābhidhammika). One who has not studied the Abhidhamma, when preaching the Dhamma, does not know, "This is my own view, this is the view of others." Intending to show his own view, he shows the view of others; intending to show the view of others, he shows his own view, thus misrepresenting the specific Dhamma. An Abhidhamma student, however, can show his own view as his own and the view of others as the view of others, without misrepresenting the specific Dhamma. Therefore, it occurred to that Elder: "It would be well if my fellow practitioners were students of Abhidhamma, and by applying their knowledge to subtle matters, they could develop insight and realize the supramundane Dhamma." Therefore, he answered in that manner.

Venerable Sāriputta had reached the peak of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī). Only a wise person can bring the mind under his own control; an unwise person cannot. An unwise person, following the whims of the mind that has arisen, wavers here and there, and within just two or three days, returns to the lay life and reaches ruin and destruction. Therefore, it occurred to that Elder: "It would be well if my fellow practitioners, not following the whims of the mind but keeping the mind under their own control, could destroy all the waverings of defilements, and without allowing the mind to wander outside even slightly, develop insight and realize the supramundane Dhamma." Therefore, he answered in that manner.

"Sāriputta, the words of all of you are good in a certain sense (pariyāyena)," the Buddha said. Sāriputta, the reason is that a monastery (saṅghārāma) has cause to be beautified by monks who are very learned (bahussuta), by those who delight in meditative absorption (jhāna), by those with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), by those who practice asceticism (dhuta), by those who study Abhidhamma, and by those who can bring the mind under their own control. Therefore...
159:
A monk who studies Abhidhamma shows his own view and the views of others only by the specific characteristics of those views. He does not cause the specific Dhamma to be misrepresented. Therefore, because Venerable Mahāmoggallāna desired, "It would be well if my fellow practitioners were students of Abhidhamma, applying their knowledge to subtle matters, developing insight, and realizing the supramundane Dhamma," he answered in this way. Venerable Sāriputta had reached the peak of the perfection of wisdom. Only a wise monk can bring his mind under his control; an unwise one is not capable. This is because an unwise person, by following the whims of the mind that has arisen, wavers here and there, and within two or three days, returns to the lay life and reaches ruin and destruction. Therefore, because Venerable Sāriputta desired, "It would be well if my fellow practitioners, not following the whims of the mind but keeping the mind under their own control, could destroy the waverings of defilements, and without letting the mind wander outside even slightly, develop insight and realize the supramundane Dhamma," he answered in this way.

"Sāriputta, the words of all of you are well-spoken indeed according to those various reasons (pariyāyena); they are not ill-spoken. However, listen also to my words. 'I will not break this cross-legged posture (until I reach the fruit of Arahantship)' means that I, having resolved upon the four-factored energy (caturaṅga-vīriya), will not break or abandon this cross-legged posture (pallaṅka) that I have taken up."

It is said that the Blessed One, having renounced the royal splendor with his matured knowledge and gone forth, gradually ascended the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Resolving upon the four-factored energy and sitting firmly upon the unconquered throne (aparājita-pallaṅka) which the King of Māras could not defeat, he destroyed the heads of the three Māras. At the time of dawn, making the ten-thousandfold world system resound, he penetrated the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). He said this with reference to his own Great Bodhi Throne. Alternatively, he said this out of compassion for future generations and to show the good worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) who possesses the essence of practice for the sake of Nibbāna.

The reason is that the Blessed One saw: "In the future, noble sons with such an inclination (ajjhāsaya) will reflect: 'When the Blessed One was preaching the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta here, he said: Sāriputta, a monk here, after his meal... Sāriputta, by such a monk would the Gosiṅga Sāla-wood be beautified. We shall take up the Blessed One's intention.' After returning from the alms round, they will firmly resolve upon the four-factored energy and think: 'We shall perform the recluse's duties, thinking: We will not break this posture until we reach Arahantship.' Those who practice thus will, in just two or three days, reach the end of birth, aging, and death." Seeing this, he said this out of compassion for future generations and to show the good worldling who possesses the essence of practice.

"Sāriputta, only by such a monk, without any other reason (directly), would the Gosiṅga Sāla-wood be beautified." Thus, he concluded the teaching with a fitting connection (anusandhi).

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Mahāgosiṅga Sutta is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Mahāgopālaka Sutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Mahāgopālaka Sutta. In that sutta, there are three ways of explaining the meaning: Ekanāḷika, Caturassa, and Nisinnavattika. Among these three, reciting the Pali and then explaining the meaning of each word is called Ekanāḷika. Showing the unwise cowherd...
160: The teaching structured in four parts—showing the unwise monk, showing the wise cowherd, and showing the wise monk—is called Caturassa. Showing the unwise cowherd and reaching the conclusion, showing the unwise monk and reaching the conclusion, showing the wise cowherd and reaching the conclusion, and showing the wise monk and reaching the conclusion—this is called Nisinnavattika. This sequence of practice is the custom of all teachers in this matter. "By eleven, bhikkhus" means by eleven unwholesome factors (limbs). "Gogaṇa" refers to a herd of cattle. "Pariharituṃ" means to wander while looking after them. "Phātiṃ kātuṃ" means to make them increase and prosper. "Idha" means in this world. "Na rūpaññū" means not knowing the forms (rūpa) either by number or by color. Not knowing by number means not knowing the count of one's own cows, whether they are a hundred or a thousand. When the cows are stolen or run away, that cowherd does not count the herd and think, "Today this many cows are missing," and does not wander between two or three villages or in the forest to search for them. Even when his herd enters among others' cows, he does not count the herd and drive them out with a stick, thinking, "This many cows are not ours." The lost cows of that cowherd remain lost. When the owners of the cows see him wandering with their cows, they threaten him, saying, "This man has taken our cows for so long," and take their cows away. His herd decreases, and he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow (pañcagorasa). Not knowing by color means not knowing: "This many cows are white, this many are red, this many are black, this many are brindled, this many are brown." When the cows are stolen and so forth... he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow. "Not skilled in marks" means not knowing the marks made on the bodies of the cows, such as bows, spears, or brands. When the cows are stolen or run away, that cowherd does not [think], "Today cows with such and such marks are missing" ... he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow. "Not removing fly eggs (āsāṭika)" means that wounds often occur on cows in places struck by stumps, thorns, and so forth. There, blue flies lay eggs; these are called āsāṭika. Those eggs must be removed with a stick and treated with medicine.
161:
An unskilled cowherd does not do so (apply medicine, etc.); therefore, it is said, 'He is not one who removes fly eggs.' The wounds of his cattle increase and become deep, and maggots enter their bellies. Being afflicted by disease, the cows are unable to eat as much grass as they need or to drink water. Consequently, the cows' milk fails, the strength of the bulls diminishes, and the lives of both are endangered. In this way, his herd of cattle diminishes, and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.

'He is not one who covers wounds' means that a wound that has arisen in the manner already described should be treated with medicine and covered by binding it with bark or a coarse cloth. A foolish cowherd does not do so. Then, pus and blood flow from the wounds of his cattle, and they rub against one another; because of this rubbing, wounds also arise in other cattle. Thus, the cows are afflicted by disease and are unable to eat as much grass as they need ... (pe) ... he is excluded.

'He is not one who makes smoke' means that during the rainy season when gnats, mosquitoes, and the like are abundant, when the herd enters the pen, smoke should be made here and there. An unwise cowherd does not do so. The herd, being harassed all night by gnats and the like, does not get any sleep; the next day, they lie down and sleep under trees and such in the forest. Being unable to eat as much grass as they need ... (pe) ... he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow.

'He does not know the ford' (na titthaṃ jānāti) means he does not know whether a watering place is level or uneven, or whether it is dangerous with crocodiles and predators or safe. That cowherd makes the cows go down at a place that is not a proper ford. Their feet are broken as they step on stones and such at an uneven ford. Cows that descend into a deep ford where there are crocodiles are seized by crocodiles and other predatory creatures. He comes to the state of having to say, 'Today, this many cows are lost; today, this many cows are lost.' In this way, his herd of cattle diminishes, and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.

'He does not know what has been drunk and what has not' means he does not know whether they have drunk or not. Indeed, a cowherd should know, 'This cow has drunk, this one has not; this cow got a turn at the watering place, this one did not.' But this man, having looked after the herd in the forest during the day, thinking 'I will give them water,' goes to the river...
162:
Otherwise, he might lead them to a pond. At that pond, the great bulls, young bulls, and strong cows strike the weak and old cows with their horns or flanks to make space for themselves. They enter the water up to their thighs and drink as much as they desire. The remaining cows, unable to find a place, stand on the bank and drink water mixed with mud, or they do not get to drink at all. Then the cowherd beats them on their backs and drives them back into the forest. In that forest, the cows that did not drink become parched with thirst and are unable to eat as much grass as they need. Then, the cows' milk is cut off, the speed of the bulls declines... and so on... he is excluded from enjoying the five products of the cow.

'Not knowing the path' means not knowing: 'This path is even and safe; this path is uneven, doubtful, and dangerous.' That cowherd avoids the even and safe path and leads the herd of cattle onto the other path. On that path, the cows, oppressed by the scent of lions, tigers, and the like, or by the danger of thieves, stand with their necks raised like frightened deer. They neither eat as much grass as they need nor drink water. Then, the cows' milk is cut off... and so on... he is excluded.

'Not being skilled in pastures' means a cowherd must be skilled in pastures. He must know the five-day cycle or the seven-day cycle. Having grazed the herd in one place, he should not graze them in that same place the next day. For a place grazed by a large herd becomes as bare as the surface of a drum, devoid of grass, and the water becomes turbid. Therefore, he should graze them there again only on the fifth or seventh day. Only after such a period does the grass regrow and the water become clear. This cowherd, however, does not know the five-day or seven-day cycle and grazes them every single day in the same place they have already grazed. Then his herd does not get green grass but eats dry grass and drinks water mixed with mud; thus, the cows' milk is cut off... and so on... he is excluded.

'One who milks dry' means a wise cowherd should leave one or two teats for as long as the flesh and blood of the calf are sustained, milking in a way that leaves a remainder. This cowherd, however, milks everything without leaving anything for the calf. The calf, which depends only on milk, becomes parched with thirst for milk and, being unable to stand...
163:
...trembling, it falls before its mother and dies. The mother cow, seeing her young calf, thinks, 'My little calf did not even get to drink its own mother's milk,' and out of grief for her offspring, she is unable to eat as much grass or drink as much water as she needs. Then, the milk in her udders is cut off. In this way, that cowherd's herd also declines and perishes, and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.

They are called 'Gopitara' because they stand in the place of fathers to the cows. They are called 'Gopariṇāyaka' because they lead the cows wherever they desire. 'Na atirekapūjāya' means: a wise cowherd honors such bulls with extra honor; he gives them choice fodder, decorates them with five-finger marks of scented paste, adorns them with garlands, fits gold or silver casings on their horns, and at night, lights a lamp and lets them sleep under a cloth canopy. But this foolish cowherd does not perform even one of these honors. The bulls, not receiving extra honor, do not protect the herd and do not ward off dangers. In this way, that cowherd's herd declines and he is excluded from the five products of the cow.

'Idha' means in this Dispensation. 'Na rūpajñū hoti' means: he does not know 'form'—described as 'the four great elements and the material form derived from the four great elements'—in two ways: by number or by origin (samuṭṭhāna). Not knowing by number means: he does not know the twenty-five groups of form mentioned in the Pali texts, namely: the eye-base, the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-bases; the visible form-, sound-, odor-, flavor-, and tangible-bases; the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty; bodily intimation, vocal intimation; the space element, the water element; lightness, malleability, and readiness of form; integration, continuity, decay, and impermanence of form; and nutriment.

Just as that cowherd does not know the appearance of the cows by number, this monk should be understood as being very similar to that cowherd. That monk, not knowing form by number, is unable to bring his meditation to its peak by grasping form, defining mentality, grasping both mentality and form, discerning the causes, and applying the characteristics. Just as that cowherd's herd does not increase, so too this monk does not increase in this Dispensation through virtue, concentration, insight, the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna. Just as that cowherd is excluded from the five products of the cow, so too this monk is excluded from the five aggregates of Dhamma: the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, the aggregate of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
164:
Not knowing by way of origin (samuṭṭhāna) means not knowing that "this much form arises from one cause, this much form arises from two causes, this much form arises from three causes, this much form arises from four causes, and this much form does not arise from any cause at all." Just as that cowherd does not know the appearance of cows by their color, this monk is similar to that cowherd. That monk, not knowing form by way of its origin, while performing the grasping of form and the defining of mentality, etc., remains outside (the Dispensation).

"He is one unskilled in characteristics" means not knowing that wholesome and unwholesome kamma, as it is said, "A fool is characterized by the kamma he performs; a wise man is characterized by the kamma he performs," is the characteristic that distinguishes the wise from the foolish. Such a monk, not knowing this, does not avoid fools and does not associate with the wise. Because he does not avoid fools and does not associate with the wise, he does not know what is allowable and what is not, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, what is blameworthy and what is blameless, what is a heavy offense and what is a light offense, what is a curable offense and what is an incurable offense, and what is a cause and what is not a cause. Not knowing these things, he is unable to take up a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and develop it. Just as that cowherd's herd of cows does not increase, similarly, in this Dispensation, he cannot increase in virtue (sīla) and so forth as mentioned. And like the cowherd who is excluded from the five products of the cow, he remains outside the five aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha).

"He is one who does not remove the unwholesome thoughts that should not be delighted in" means he does not dispel sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) and so forth when they arise. That monk, without removing these unwholesome thoughts, which are like fly eggs (āsāṭika), wanders about under the influence of thoughts and is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it. That monk, just like that cowherd... remains outside.

"He is one who does not dress a wound" means, for example, when seeing a form with the eye, he grasps at its signs (nimitta), and in this manner, he grasps at signs in all sense objects. Just as that cowherd does not dress a wound, so this monk does not fulfill the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara). Wandering with the doors of his senses open, he is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it... remains outside.

"He is one who does not make smoke" means that just as that cowherd does not make smoke, this monk does not make the "smoke" of Dhamma teaching. He does not give Dhamma talks, chant in the sarabhañña style, give talks to those sitting nearby, or perform the sharing of merits (anumodanā). Because he does not do so, people do not know him as "one of great learning" or "one of virtue." Those people, not knowing whether he has virtues or not, do not support him with the four requisites. That monk...
165:
That monk, being weary due to the lack of the four requisites, is unable to recite the Buddha's words (Buddhavacana), to fulfill the duties and practices (vatta-paṭipatti), or to take up a meditation subject and develop it... he remains outside the Dispensation.

Not knowing the ford (tittha) means not approaching learned monks who are like a ford. Even if he approaches them, he does not ask or inquire, "Venerable sir, how should this syllable (byañjana) be placed? What is the meaning of this statement? What does the Pali text say in this place? What does the meaning illustrate in this place?" Thus, he does not make himself known. To that monk who does not inquire in this way, those learned elders do not open up the meaning that has not yet been opened, they do not analyze and show it, they do not make clear the meaning that is obscure and hidden, and they do not make manifest what is not manifest. Regarding the various things that are grounds for doubt, they do not dispel even a single doubt. Doubts themselves are called "things that are grounds for doubt." The meaning is that they do not remove even one of those doubts. That monk, without approaching the "ford" of the learned, being full of doubt, is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it. Just as that cowherd does not know the ford, so this monk does not know the "ford of Dhamma." Not knowing it, he asks questions about things that are not his concern. Approaching a monk who is an expert in Abhidhamma, he asks about what is allowable and what is not (Vinaya). Approaching a monk who is a master of the Vinaya, he asks about the definition of mentality and materiality (Abhidhamma). Those persons, being asked about things that are not their field, are unable to answer. That monk, having doubts himself, is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it... remains outside the Dispensation.

Not knowing what is drunk means that just as that cowherd does not know whether the cows have drunk or not, so this monk does not know or obtain the joy (pāmojja) connected with the Dhamma. He does not find the benefit based on the "ground for making merit" (puññakiriyavatthu) consisting in hearing the Dhamma. Even when he goes to the place of Dhamma preaching, he does not listen respectfully; he dozes off while sitting, he talks, or his mind is elsewhere. That monk, because he does not listen to the Dhamma respectfully, is unable to take up a meditation subject and develop it... remains outside the Dispensation.

Not knowing the path (vīthi) means that just as that cowherd does not know the right or wrong path, so this monk does not truly know the Noble Eightfold Path, thinking, "This is mundane (lokiya), this is supramundane (lokuttara)." Not knowing it, he becomes attached only to the mundane path and is unable to produce the supramundane... remains outside the Dispensation.

Not being skilled in pastures (gocara) means that just as that cowherd does not know the pastures to be frequented every five or seven days, so this monk does not truly know the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), thinking, "These are mundane, these are supramundane." Not knowing it, in subtle matters...
166:
By exercising one's own knowledge and being firmly established in the mundane foundations of mindfulness (lokiya-satipaṭṭhāna), one is unable to bring about the supramundane (lokuttara) state... and thus becomes an outsider to the Dispensation.

'He is one who milks dry' (anavasesadohī ca hoti) means that when receiving the four requisites, he does not know the proper measure and takes everything without leaving any remainder. In the descriptive section (niddesavāra), it is said of that monk, 'They invite him to take' (abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavārenti), meaning they bring [the requisites] forward and invite him. Here, there are two kinds of invitations: verbal invitation (vācābhihāra) and invitation with requisites (paccayābhihāra). Verbal invitation means people go to the monk and invite him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please tell us what you need.' Invitation with requisites means they take clothes, or oil, molasses, etc., go to the monk, and say, 'Venerable sir, please take as much as you need.' In such an invitation, 'the monk does not know the measure' means the monk does not know the proper amount of those four requisites. As stated in the Rathavinīta Sutta, 'One must know the donor's wish, one must know the measure of the gift, and one must know one's own capacity'; instead of taking in accordance with the proper measure, he takes everything that is brought. People become dissatisfied and do not invite him again by bringing requisites. That monk, being weary due to the lack of requisites, is unable to take up and develop the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna)... and thus becomes an outsider to the Dispensation.

'He is not a worshiper with extraordinary honor' (te na atirekapūjāya pūjetā hoti) means that just as that cowherd does not honor the great bulls, so too this monk does not honor the elder monks with extraordinary honor, such as bodily actions associated with loving-kindness, whether in their presence or absence. Because of this lack of honor, the elders reflect, 'These people do not show us respect,' and they do not favor the junior monks with the two kinds of hospitality (saṅgaha). They do not favor them with material hospitality (āmisa-saṅgaha), such as robes, alms-bowls, food contained in the bowl, or dwellings. Even when the junior monks are weary and fading, they do not look after them. They do not teach them the Pali, the Commentaries, the sequence of Dhamma talks, or the profound texts. The junior monks, receiving neither of these two kinds of hospitality from the elders, are unable to remain established in this Dispensation. Just as that cowherd's herd of cattle does not increase, so too their virtues (sīla) and other qualities do not increase. And just as that cowherd is excluded from the five flavors of cow's milk, so too they are excluded from the five aggregates of the Dhamma (dhamma-kkhandha). The 'bright side' (sukka-pakkha) should be understood by applying the reverse of the method described for the 'dark side' (kaṇha-pakkha).

## In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī,
## the Explanation of the Mahāgopālaka Sutta is finished.
167:
## 4. Commentary on the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta

This discourse beginning with 'Thus have I heard' (Evaṃ me sutaṃ) is the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta. Therein, 'in Ukkacelā' (Ukkacelāyaṃ) means in the city of that name. It is said that while that city was being built, at night, a fish from the current of the Ganges reached the dry land. People soaked cloths in oil-bowls, made torches (ukkā), and caught that fish. When the city was completed, those who named it did so based on the event: 'On the day we took possession of the city site, a fish was caught with cloth-torches (celukkā)'; thus they named it Ukkacelā.

'He addressed the monks' (bhikkhū āmantesi) refers to the place where the Blessed One was sitting, from which the entire Ganges was clearly visible. At such a sandy landing on the Ganges, in the evening, sitting surrounded by a large Saṅgha of monks and looking at the great Ganges flowing in full—He reflected, 'Has anyone in the past reached growth or decline in dependence on this Ganges?' He saw that in the past, in dependence on a foolish cowherd (bāla-gopālaka), hundreds of thousands of cattle fell into the whirlpools of this Ganges and perished in the great ocean. On the other hand, he saw that in dependence on a wise cowherd (paṇḍita-gopālaka), hundreds of thousands of cattle attained safety, growth, and health. Having seen this, He thought, 'I will teach the Dhamma to the monks based on this matter,' and then He addressed the monks.

'A Magadhan' (māgadhako) means a resident of the Magadha country. 'One of unwise nature' (duppaññajātiko) means one who is naturally without wisdom, foolish, and extremely deluded. 'Without investigating' (asamavekkhitvā) means without noting, without considering. 'He caused them to cross' (patāresi) means he made an effort to make them cross. 'To the northern shore of the Videhans' (uttaraṃ tīraṃ suvidehānaṃ) means that on this side of the Ganges is the Magadha country, and on the other side is the Videha country. Thinking, 'I will take the cattle from Magadha to Videha and protect them,' he made them cross to the northern shore. With reference to that crossing, it is said, 'to the northern shore of the Videhans.' 'Having made a circle' (āmaṇḍalikaṃ karitvā) means having made them go in a circle (into a whirlpool). 'They met with disaster and ruin' (anayabyasanaṃ āpajjiṃsu) means they did not prosper but reached destruction; they entered the great ocean itself. Indeed, when that cowherd was making the cattle cross, he should have observed whether the landing on this side of the Ganges was level or uneven. In the middle of the Ganges, he should have noted two or three sandbanks for the cattle to rest. Likewise, on the other side, he should have noted three or four landings, thinking, 'If they miss this landing, they will take this one; if they miss that one, they will take this one.' However, this foolish cowherd, without even observing whether the landing where the cattle descended on this side was level or uneven...
168: Without marking two or three sandbanks in the middle of the Gaṅgā for the cattle to rest, and without considering the four or five landing places on the opposite bank, he made the cattle cross from a place that was not a landing. Then, because the great bull of that cowherd was endowed with speed and strength, he crossed the current of the Gaṅgā diagonally and reached the opposite bank. Seeing the broken bank and the dense thicket of thorns, and realizing 'This place is difficult to descend,' he turned back because he could not even find a place to plant his front feet. The cattle, saying 'The great bull has turned back, let us also turn back,' also turned back. At the place where the large herd of cattle turned back, the water was cut off and a whirlpool arose in the middle of the Gaṅgā. The herd of cattle entered the whirlpool and reached only the ocean. Not even a single ox was free from harm or disease. Therefore, it is said: 'Right there they met with disaster and ruin.' 'Unskilled in this world' means being unskilled in the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana) in this world. The same applies to the world beyond. The states belonging to the three planes of existence are called 'Māradheyya' (the realm of Māra). The nine supramundane states are called 'Amāradheyya' (not the realm of Māra). 'Maccudheyya' (the realm of Death) also refers to the states of the three planes. The nine supramundane states are 'Amaccudheyya' (not the realm of Death). They are unskilled in that Māradheyya and so on. According to the word-meaning, the place of Māra is Māradheyya. 'Dheyya' means a place, a site, a permanent dwelling, or a range of activity (object). The same applies to Maccudheyya. 'Tesaṃ' refers to such recluses and brahmins. It should be understood that here the six teachers are shown. Having thus concluded the dark side, wishing to show the bright side, he said: 'Bhikkhus, in the past...' and so on. There, 'balavagāvo' refers to tamed bulls and cows. 'Dammagāvo' refers to young bulls to be tamed and heifers that have not yet calved. 'Vacchatare' refers to strong young bulls that have passed the stage of being calves. 'Vacchake' refers to young suckling calves. 'Kisābalake' refers to cattle with little flesh and blood and weak strength. 'Tāvadeva jātako' is a calf born on that very day. 'Mātugoravakena vuyhamāno' means the mother cow goes in front, making the sound 'huṃ-huṃ', caring for and giving a sign, cutting the water with her chest. The calf follows either out of respect for the mother or along the path of water cut by the mother's chest; this is called 'carried along out of respect for the mother'.
169:
"Having cut the stream of Māra" means having cut the stream of craving of Māra with the Path of Arahatship. "Gone to the far shore" means they have reached Nibbāna, the far shore of Saṃsāra, just as great bulls reach the far shore of a river. "They went to the far shore" means that at the moment the great bulls reached the far shore, having seen the great bulls standing after crossing two-thirds of the current of the Ganges and reaching the far shore, they followed the path they took and reached the far shore. "They will go to the far shore" means that having exhausted three portions of the defilements to be abandoned by the four paths, they will now cut the remaining stream of craving with the Path of Arahatship and reach Nibbāna, the far shore of Saṃsāra, just as strong oxen reach the far shore of a river. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all instances. The two types of persons, the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) and the faith-follower (saddhānusārī), are those possessed of the first path (the Path of Stream-entry).

"By the one who knows" means by the Buddha who knows all phenomena. "Well-proclaimed" means well-spoken. "Open" means revealed. "The door to the Deathless" is the Noble Path. It means that the door of the Noble Path has been opened for the sake of attaining Nibbāna. "Made into a non-reed" means the reed of vain conceit has been made to disappear. "Aspire for security" means aspire for Arahatship with the desire to act; the meaning is, be those who desire to act, who desire to bring it about. There is also a variant reading "pattatthā." According to that reading, it means that by having obtained such a Teacher, you are indeed those who have reached Arahatship. The remaining words are clear in all places. The Blessed One concluded the discourse according to the sequence of connections.

## In the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī,
## The Explanation of the Cūḷagopālaka Sutta is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta
"Thus have I heard" and so on is the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta. Therein, in the phrase "in the Great Wood, in the Pinnacled Hall," "Great Wood" (Mahāvana) refers to a large forest that is self-sown, not planted, and has defined boundaries. The Great Wood near Kapilavatthu, however, is continuous with the Himālayas, without boundaries, and stands reaching the great ocean. This one [in Vesālī] is not like that. It is called "Mahāvana" because it is a large forest with defined boundaries. The "Pinnacled Hall" (Kūṭāgārasālā) should be understood as the Blessed Buddha's Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), built within the monastery grounds depending on the Great Wood, with a pinnacled house inside and covered with swan-shaped roof tiles, endowed with all excellent features.
170:
Regarding the name Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta: In the past, it is said that a Nigaṇṭha and a Nigaṇṭhī, having each learned five hundred doctrines, traveled throughout Jambudīpa with the intention of engaging in and winning debates, and eventually met in the city of Vesālī. When the Licchavi princes saw them, they asked, "Who are you? Who are you?" The Nigaṇṭha replied, "I am traveling through Jambudīpa to engage in and win debates." The Nigaṇṭhī said the same. The Licchavi princes said, "Then engage in debate with each other right here." The Nigaṇṭhī asked the five hundred doctrines she had learned, and the Nigaṇṭha was able to answer. When the Nigaṇṭha asked, the Nigaṇṭhī was also able to answer. Neither won nor lost; they were both equal in ability.

The Licchavi princes said, "Since you are both equal in ability, why continue wandering? Stay right here in Vesālī." They gave them a house and provided them with provisions. From their union, four daughters were born: Saccā, Lolā, Paṭācārā, and Ācāravatī. These four daughters were also wise and mastered the five hundred doctrines each that their parents had learned. When the daughters reached maturity, they said to their parents, "Mother, in our family, there is no custom of sending daughters to a husband's house with gifts of gold and silver. If a layman can suppress and defeat our doctrines, we will become his wives and serve at his feet. If a monk can suppress and defeat our doctrines, we will ordain in his presence. What do you think, parents?" The parents replied, "We also agree to that."

The four daughters then took the form of female wanderers (paribbājikās) and, saying, "This Jambudīpa is known for its rose-apple (jambu) trees," they took rose-apple branches and set out on their travels. Whenever they reached a village, they would plant the rose-apple branch as a banner in a heap of dust or sand at the village gate and say, "Whoever is able to engage in and win a debate, let him trample and destroy this rose-apple banner," and then they would enter the village. Thus, traveling from village to village, they arrived at the city of Sāvatthī. In the same manner, they planted the rose-apple banner at the city gate, informed the people who arrived, and entered the city.

At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery near Sāvatthī. Then, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, having many duties such as attending to sick monks and sweeping areas that had not yet been swept, entered the city for alms later than the other monks when the sun was already high. Seeing the rose-apple banner planted at the city gate, he asked the children, "What is this?" The children explained the whole matter to him. "In that case, trample and destroy that banner," he said. The children replied, "Venerable sir, we do not dare; we are afraid."
171:
Venerable Sāriputta said, "Children, do not be afraid. If they ask, 'Who caused our rose-apple banner to be trampled?' tell them, 'The disciple of the Buddha, Venerable Sāriputta Thera, caused it to be trampled. If you wish to present your doctrines, go to the presence of the Elder at Jetavana Monastery.'" Hearing the Elder's words, the children trampled the rose-apple banner and discarded it. The Elder, after wandering for alms, returned to the monastery. The female wanderers, coming out of the village, asked, "Who caused our banner to be trampled?" The children told them the matter. The female wanderers entered the village again and, going through every street, announced, "It is said that the disciple of the Buddha named Sāriputta will debate with us. Let those who wish to listen come out." A great crowd came out, and together with that crowd, the female wanderers went to Jetavana.

The Elder thought, "It is not pleasant (not appropriate) for women to come to the place where we live," and sat in the middle of the monastery. The female wanderers went and asked the Elder, "Did you cause our banner to be trampled?" The Elder replied, "Yes, it is true that I caused it to be trampled." They said, "We will engage in a debate with you." He said, "Very well, do so. Who shall ask and who shall answer?" When they said, "It is our turn to ask questions," he replied, "You are women; you ask first." Those four female wanderers, standing in the four directions, asked the thousand doctrines they had learned from their parents.

The Elder answered all the questions they asked without any confusion or entanglement, like cutting a lotus stalk with a sword. After answering, he said, "Ask again." They replied, "Venerable sir, we only know this much." The Elder said, "You have asked a thousand doctrines and I have answered. Now I will ask only one question; you answer that question." Seeing the Elder's power, those female wanderers did not dare to say, "Ask, venerable sir, we will answer." They said again, "Speak, venerable sir; if we know, we will answer."

The Elder said, "This question is the first question taught to sons of good family after they have been ordained," and asked, "What is one?" Those female wanderers could see neither the beginning nor the end of it. When the Elder said, "Answer," they replied, "Venerable sir, we do not know." "You asked a thousand doctrines and I answered, but you cannot answer even one of my questions. In this case, who has won and who has lost?" he asked. "Venerable sir, you have won and we have lost," they replied. When he asked, "What will you do now?" the female wanderers, remembering their parents' words, replied, "Venerable sir, we will ordain in your presence." "Since you are women, it is not appropriate to ordain in my presence. However, in our Dispensation..."
172:
## 
(Venerable Sāriputta) said, "Listen to our words, go to the residence of the bhikkhunīs, and ordain." Those female wanderers replied, "Very well," and accepting the Elder's advice, they went to the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs and ordained. After ordaining, being heedful and possessing the energy that burns away defilements (ātāpī), they attained Arahantship before long.

This Saccaka was the younger brother of those four women. He was even more wise than those four women. Having learned a thousand doctrines from his parents and many more external systems of thought, he did not go elsewhere but lived in Vesālī, teaching the arts to the princes. Because he was so full of wisdom and knowledge, he feared that his belly might burst, and thus he traveled about with an iron band (ayapaṭṭa) wrapped around his abdomen. It is in reference to him that it is said, "Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta."

"Bhassappavādako" means one who is skilled in the path of discourse (kathāmagga). "Paṇḍitavādo" means one who is in the habit of saying, "I am a wise man." "Sādhusammato bahujanassa" means one who is highly regarded by the multitude as being of good views and excellent, because the predictions he makes based on the movements of the stars (astrology) are mostly correct. "Vādena vādaṃ samāraddho" means one who is censured through the path of discourse. "Āyasmā Assajī" refers to the Elder Assaji, who was the teacher of the Elder Sāriputta. "Jaṅghāvihāraṃ anucaṅkamamāno" means walking on foot from the houses of the Licchavi princes to various other houses. Why did he approach the place where Venerable Assaji was? It was for the purpose of knowing his doctrine (samaya).

Indeed, such a thought had occurred to him: "I have been wandering about thinking, 'I will refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama,' but I do not yet know his doctrine, so I have not refuted it. Only after knowing another's doctrine is refuting it called a well-made refutation. This Venerable Assaji is known as a disciple of the ascetic Gotama and is proficient in his teacher's doctrine. Therefore, I will question this Elder, establish a firm basis for the doctrine, and then refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama." Thus, he approached. "Vineti" (disciplines) is asked in the sense of: "How does he discipline? How does he train?" If the Elder were to say "suffering" (dukkha), there would be an opportunity for criticism. Even the paths and fruits are figuratively (pariyāyena) referred to as suffering. If the Elder said "suffering," Saccaka would ask, "Master Assaji, for what purpose have you ordained?" Then, if he replied, "For the sake of the paths and fruits," Saccaka would want to criticize him, saying, "Master Assaji, your teaching is not a teaching; it is a great slaughterhouse, it is a place that leads to hell; there is no prospect of happiness for you; you wander about merely wearing yourselves out with suffering every time you rise."
173:
## 
Therefore, it is not appropriate to speak in figurative terms (pariyāyakathā) to Saccaka, who has a habit of criticizing others. Thinking, "I will speak to him in direct terms (nippariyāyakathā) so that he will be without a foundation," the Buddha taught this discourse, "Monks, form is impermanent," solely by way of impermanence and non-self. "Dussuta" means words that are unfit to be heard.

"Santhāgāra" refers to the assembly hall where the princes are advised on their affairs. "Approached where those Licchavis were" means that Saccaka had this thought: "Previously, I did not refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama because I did not know it. Now, however, I know the doctrine as told by his great disciple (Assaji). These five hundred Licchavis, who are my students, are also assembled. I will go with them and refute (challenge) the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama." Thus, he approached.

"Ñātaññatarena" refers to one of the well-known Elders of the group of five (Pañcavaggiya), namely Assaji. "Patiṭṭhitaṃ" means as established by that Elder Assaji. Thinking, "Will it remain as established, or will he say something else? If so, what can I do?", he spoke even now while turning his back. "Ākaḍḍheyya" means pulling towards oneself. "Parikaḍḍheyya" means pushing forward. "Samparikaḍḍheyya" means pulling at one time and pushing at another.

"Soṇḍikākilañja" refers to a mat used in a tavern. "Soṇḍikādhutta" refers to a drunkard. A drunkard wishing to wash a liquor-strainer bag would hold it by both corners to shake out the dregs, shaking it downwards (odhuneyya), shaking it upwards (niddhuneyya), and shaking it repeatedly (nipphoṭeyya).

What is called "Sāṇadhovika" (hemp-washing) is as follows: People take hemp fibers to make hempen cloth, tie them into bundles, and soak them in water. On the third day, those bundles become well-softened. Then, people take sour gruel, liquor, etc., go to that place, hold the hemp bundles, and wash them by striking them alternately against three planks placed to the right, to the left, and in front, while eating and drinking the sour gruel and liquor. It is a great festive game. A royal elephant, seeing that game, entered deep water, took water with its trunk, and played by spraying it alternately on its forehead, its back, its two sides, and between its thighs. Based on that play, that festive activity is called "Sāṇadhovika."
174: Regarding the play called Sāṇadhovika, it is said: "He plays the game called Sāṇadhovika." Who is this Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta who would challenge the doctrine of the Blessed One? Is this Saccaka a Yakkha, or Sakka (Indra), or Brahma? An ordinary human is not capable of challenging the doctrine of the Blessed One; this is the meaning here. "Tena kho pana samayena" refers to the time when Saccaka entered the monastery. At what time did he enter? He entered at midday. Why were they walking to and fro at that time? They were walking to dispel sloth and torpor (thina-middha) caused by consuming fine food. Or, those monks were practitioners of meditation during the day. For such monks, after the meal, having walked, bathed, and let the body cool down, the mind becomes concentrated when they sit to practice the Dhamma. "Yena te bhikkhū" means that Saccaka, while looking around and going from one precinct to another asking, "Where does the ascetic Gotama live?", saw the rag-robe-wearing (paṃsukūlika) monks walking in the forest like elephants and went towards them. This is the reference for "Yena te bhikkhū," etc. "Kahaṃ nu kho bho" means in which monastery or in which pavilion does he reside. "Esa Aggivessana Bhagavā" means that at that time, the Blessed One, having arisen at dawn and entered the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti), spread the net of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) over the ten thousand world systems. While observing beings who were ready to be enlightened, he saw: "Tomorrow, Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta will come with a large company of Licchavis, desiring to challenge my doctrine." Therefore, having attended to his physical needs early in the morning, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he entered Vesālī for alms. After returning from the alms round, thinking, "I will sit in a comfortable place where a large crowd can sit," he did not enter the Gandhakuṭi but sat for the day-rest (divāvihāra) at the foot of a certain tree in the Mahāvana forest. Those monks, having performed their duties to the Blessed One, were returning when Saccaka questioned them. Pointing to the Blessed One sitting in the distance, they said, "Aggivessana, this is the Blessed One." "Mahatiyā licchaviparisāya saddhiṃ" means he was surrounded by about five hundred Licchavi princes, as mentioned below. Those Licchavis were merely his disciples. Within the city of Vesālī, Saccaka took the five hundred Licchavi princes and approached the Blessed One, desiring a debate. To hear the conversation of the two wise men...
175:
"Where is the Venerable Gotama?" means in which monastery or in which pavilion does he reside. At that time, the Blessed One, having arisen at dawn and entered the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti), spread the net of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) over the ten thousand world systems. While observing beings who were ready to be enlightened, he saw that on the next day, Saccaka, the son of a Nigaṇṭha, would come with a large company of Licchavis, desiring to challenge his doctrine. Therefore, having attended to his physical needs early in the morning, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he entered Vesālī for alms. After returning from the alms round, thinking, "I will sit in a comfortable place where a large crowd can sit," he did not enter the Gandhakuṭi but sat for the day-rest (divāvihāra) at the foot of a certain tree in the Mahāvana forest. Those monks, having performed their duties to the Blessed One, were returning when Saccaka questioned them. Pointing to the Blessed One sitting in the distance, they said, "Aggivessana, this is the Blessed One."

"With a large company of Licchavis" means he was surrounded by about five hundred Licchavi princes. Those five hundred Licchavis were merely Saccaka's disciples. Within the city of Vesālī, Saccaka took the five hundred Licchavi princes and approached the Blessed One, desiring a debate. Thinking, "We shall know the conversation of the wise men," most people came out, and so that assembly was large and of an indefinite number. This is said in reference to that assembly.

"Having raised their joined palms (añjali)" refers to those who were associated with both sides (wrong view and right view). They thought: "If those of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) should question us, 'Why did you salute the ascetic Gotama?', we shall reply, 'Does merely raising the joined palms constitute salutation?' If those of right view (sammādiṭṭhi) should question us, 'Why did you not salute the Blessed One?', we shall reply, 'Does salutation only occur by striking the ground with one's head? Is not the act of raising joined palms also a salutation?'"

"Name and clan" means they announced their names, saying, "Venerable Gotama, I am the son of such-a-one, named Datta, named Mitta, and I have come here." They announced their clans, saying, "Venerable Gotama, I am of the Vāsiṭṭha clan, of the Kaccāna clan." It is said that they did this because they were from poor families and wished to become well-known in the midst of the assembly by way of their name and clan.

Those who sat in silence were the cunning and the extremely foolish. Among them, the cunning ones thought: "If one engages in conversation once or twice, one becomes familiar; and when there is familiarity, it is not proper to refrain from giving alms once or twice." Thus, wishing to free themselves from the burden of giving alms, they sat in silence. The extremely foolish ones, due to their ignorance, sat in silence anywhere, like a lump of clay that has been cast down.

Indicating a certain reason or opportunity, the Blessed One then, encouraging the effort to ask questions, said: "Ask, Aggivessana, whatever you desire." The meaning is: "Ask if you desire; there is no burden for me in answering questions." Or else, "Ask whatever you desire, I will answer everything for you." Thus he made the invitation based on omniscience (sabbaññu-pavāraṇā), which is unique and not shared by Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, or great disciples. For they do not say, "Ask whatever you desire," but say, "We shall know after hearing." But the Buddhas say: "Ask, friend, whatever you desire," or "Ask, Great King, whatever you desire," or "Ask me any question, Vāsava, whatever you wish in your mind; I will bring an end to each and every question for you," or "Therefore, monk, sit in your own seat and ask whatever you desire."
176:
“To the Brahmin Bāvarī and to you all, the opportunity is granted to clear all your doubts; ask whatever you desire in your mind” (Sutta Nipāta 1036). Or, “Sabhiya, ask me whatever question you desire in your mind; I shall bring an end to each and every question for you (by answering them)” (Sutta Nipāta 517). Or, [the Buddha] extends the invitation of omniscience to various yakkhas, kings, devas, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers. It is not surprising that the Blessed One, having attained Buddhahood, should extend such an invitation. Even while standing in the stage of a Bodhisatta with partial knowledge (padesa-ñāṇa)—

“Koṇḍañña, explain the questions; these sages of good character entreat you. Koṇḍañña, this is the way among men: when one becomes wise, this burden [of answering] comes to him” (Jātaka 2.17.60)—thus, when entreated by the sages for the sake of Sakka and others—

“Sirs, the opportunity is granted; ask whatever question you have desired in your mind. Having personally known this world and the world beyond, I shall explain each question to you” (Jātaka 2.17.61).

Thus, during the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka and the Sambhava Jātaka, after wandering through the entire Jambudīpa three times without finding anyone capable of ending (answering) the questions, when the Brahmin asked the questions for a very long time and the opportunity was granted, [the Bodhisatta], though only seven years old and playing with dust in the street, sat cross-legged right there in the alley and said—

“Indeed, I shall explain your question just like an expert; however, the King knows it, and whether he acts upon it or not [is his concern]” (Jātaka 1.16.172)—thus he had already extended the invitation of omniscience.

When the Blessed One had thus extended the invitation of omniscience, [Saccaka], being delighted, asked the question, beginning with: “But how, Master Gotama?”
177:
Then, the Blessed One, wishing to prevent the Nigaṇṭha’s son Saccaka from having an opportunity to speak, as if to say: “Look, sirs, the disciple says one thing, and the teacher says another. Did I not say from the very beginning, ‘If he stands by what his disciple has established, then I will take up the argument’? But this man says something else; what can I do in such a case?”—and desiring to speak in the same manner as the Elder Assaji had spoken below, said: “Aggivessana, in this way I...” and so forth.

“Master Gotama, a simile occurs to me; I will present that simile,” he said. The Blessed One said: “Let it occur to you, Aggivessana. Aggivessana, present that simile boldly.”

“Balakaraṇီyā” refers to tasks such as plowing and trading that must be performed by physical strength. “Rūpattāyaṃ purisapuggalo” indicates a person who stands holding the view that form is the self, in the sense that “form is the self.” “Rūpe patiṭṭhāya” means standing (relying) on that form which is taken as the self. “Puññaṃ vā apuññaṃ vā pasavati” means he obtains (or produces) either merit or demerit. The same method applies to terms like “feeling as self” (vedanattā) and so on.

What is shown by this statement? These five aggregates are the support for these beings, like the earth. These beings, relying on these five aggregates, strive in wholesome and unwholesome kamma. “Do you, while denying such an existing self, show that the five aggregates are non-self?”—thus he presented the simile with great reasoning.

The simile presented by this Nigaṇṭha’s son Saccaka is indeed firm; no one other than an Omniscient Buddha is capable of cutting through Saccaka’s words and pointing out the fault in his argument. Truly, there are two kinds of persons: those to be tamed by a Buddha (buddha-veneyya) and those to be tamed by a disciple (sāvaka-veneyya). Disciples can tame those to be tamed by a disciple, and Buddhas can also tame them. However, disciples are not able to tame those to be tamed by a Buddha; only Buddhas can tame them. This Nigaṇṭha was also one to be tamed by a Buddha; therefore, no one else was capable of cutting through his argument and pointing out the fault. For that reason, the Blessed One himself, in order to show the fault in the argument, said: “Aggivessana, is it not the case that you...” and so forth.

Then the Nigaṇṭha thought: “The ascetic Gotama is firmly establishing my view; if there is any fault later on, he will suppress me alone. Let me place this view on the heads of the great multitude as well.” Therefore, he said: “Master Gotama, I too say thus: ‘Form is my self... consciousness is my self,’ and this great multitude also [says so].” The Blessed One, from the Nigaṇṭha...
178:
The Blessed One is superior in doctrine to Saccaka, the son of the Nigaṇṭha, by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or even a hundred thousandfold. Therefore, He thought: "This Nigaṇṭha is trying to excuse himself and cast the argument onto the heads of the multitude. I will not allow him to excuse himself; I will turn him away from the multitude and subdue him alone." Then He said to Saccaka: "Aggivessana, to you, some..." and so on. The meaning of this is: This multitude has not come to present my doctrine; you yourself have gathered all the people of Vesālī and come to present my doctrine. Therefore, you alone must explain your own doctrine; do not cast it upon the heads of the multitude. That Saccaka, wishing to acknowledge it, said: "Venerable Gotama, I..." and so on.

Thus, the Blessed One, having made Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son acknowledge his doctrine, began the questioning: "Aggivessana, if that is so..." In this context, "tena hi" is an indeclinable particle indicating a reason. The meaning is: "Since you acknowledge the five aggregates as the self, therefore..." "Sakasmiṃ vijite" means in one's own realm. "Ghātetāyaṃ vā ghātetuṃ" means to execute one who deserves to be executed, or who is fit for execution. "Jāpetāyaṃ vā jāpetuṃ" means to cause loss of wealth to one who deserves such loss, or to make one's wealth perish. "Pabbājetāyaṃ vā pabbājetuṃ" means to banish or expel from one's own realm one who deserves banishment. "Vattituñca arahati" means it follows one's will, and it is worthy of being made to follow one's will; it indicates that it is proper to be subject to one's will. Thus, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son, like a fool, emphasized and explained the very reason brought forward to destroy his own doctrine as if he were sharpening a weapon to kill himself.

"Let my form be thus" means let my form be of such a kind—delightful, beautiful, adorned, and pleasant to look at, like a golden gatepost or a well-prepared painting. "Let my form not be thus" means let my form not be of such a kind—ugly, ill-shaped, or filled with wrinkles, grey hair, and freckles.

"He remained silent" means that the Nigaṇṭha, realizing his mistake at this point, thought: "The ascetic Gotama has brought forward a reason to destroy my doctrine. Out of foolishness, I emphasized and explained that very reason. Now I am ruined. If I say (that form) follows my will, these kings will rise up and say, 'Aggivessana, you said you have power over your form. If you have power over your form, why do you not, like these kings...'
179:
"...these Licchavī kings, who shine with bodies like the Tāvatiṃsa gods, being very beautiful, graceful, and elegant—why do you not shine like that?" (they would say). If I say it does not follow my will, the ascetic Gotama will rise up and charge me, saying, 'Aggivessana, you previously said you have power over your form, and now you deny it.' Thus, if I say it follows my will, there is a fault; if I say it does not follow my will, there is also a fault." Thinking thus, he remained silent. The Blessed One asked a second time, and a second time he remained silent. Because the head of one who does not answer when asked by the Blessed One up to three times splits into seven pieces, and because Buddhas, having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons for the sake of beings, have great compassion for beings, the Blessed One, before asking for the third time, said to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son: "Answer now," and so on.

In that passage, "sahadhammikaṃ" means a statement accompanied by reasons and causes. "Vajirapāṇi" means one who has a thunderbolt weapon in his hand. "Yakkho" refers not to just any yakkha, but should be understood as Sakka, the king of gods. "Ādittaṃ" means having a color like fire; "sampajjalitaṃ" means intensely burning; "sajotibhūtaṃ" means glowing all around, meaning it has become a single mass of flame. "Ṭhito hoti" means he stood there having created a deformed appearance with a huge head, tusks like banana buds, and terrifying eyes and nose. Why did this Sakka come? He came to make him give up his view. Furthermore, when the Blessed One was inclined to be inactive in teaching the Dhamma, thinking, "If I were to teach the Dhamma and others did not understand me," Sakka came with Mahābrahmā and made a pledge: "Venerable Sir, teach the Dhamma. We will make those who do not follow your authority follow it. May you have the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhamma-cakka), and let us have the Wheel of Authority (Āṇā-cakka)." Therefore, he came today to terrify Saccaka and make him answer the question.

Only the Blessed One and Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha's son saw that Sakka. If others had seen him, it would have been a cause for blame. They might say, "The ascetic Gotama, knowing that Saccaka would not enter into his doctrine, summoned a yakkha and showed him, and then Saccaka spoke out of fear." Therefore, only the Blessed One and Saccaka saw him. Upon seeing him, sweat poured from Saccaka's entire body, and his insides felt as if they were turning upside down, and he cried out. He (thinking), "Do others see him too?"...
180:
Looking around, Saccaka did not see even a single person who showed even a sign of hair-standing-on-end (fear). Because of that, Saccaka thought: 'This danger has arisen for me alone. If I say "It is a Yakkha," they might say, "Do you alone have eyes? Do you alone see the Yakkha? Having not seen the Yakkha before, do you only see the Yakkha now when you are being defeated in a debate by the ascetic Gotama?"' Thinking thus, and realizing 'Now I have no other refuge here except the ascetic Gotama,' Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta then addressed the Blessed One with these words. 'Seeking protection (tāṇa)' means searching for a guard. 'Seeking shelter (leṇa)' means searching for a hiding place. 'Seeking refuge (saraṇa)' means searching for a resort. In this context, it is called 'tāṇa' because it protects. It is called 'leṇa' because one hides there. It is called 'saraṇa' because it destroys; the meaning is that it oppresses and destroys danger.

'Having taken to heart (manasi karitvā)' means having placed in the mind, reflected, and investigated. 'May my feeling be thus' means may it be only wholesome, may it be only pleasant. 'May my perception be thus' means may it be only wholesome, may it be only pleasant, and may it be associated only with joy. The same method applies to mental formations and consciousness. In the phrase 'May it not be,' the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what was previously stated. 'Is it fitting?' means 'Is it proper?' 'To regard' means to see through the power of craving, conceit, and views (taṇhā, māna, diṭṭhi) as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' 'No indeed, Master Gotama' means 'Master Gotama, it is not proper to regard it so.'

Thus, just as a clever snake charmer might draw out the venom caused by a snake bite by making that same snake bite again, the Blessed One, in that very assembly, made Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta admit with his own mouth that 'The five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.' 'One who clings to suffering' means clinging to the suffering of these five aggregates through craving and views. 'One who has reached and is obsessed' should also be understood through the power of craving and views. In phrases such as 'This suffering is mine,' the meaning is that one regards the suffering of the five aggregates through the power of craving, conceit, and views. 'Should fully understand' means one should completely know through the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. 'Having abandoned' means having brought to an end, to destruction, and to non-arising.

'Nava' means tender (new). 'Akukkukajāta' means that at the time of flowering, a solid stalk about the size of a thumb arises inside; it refers to being without that stalk. 'Hollow (ritta)' means empty, devoid of internal essence. Because it is empty, it is 'vain (tuccha).' 'Defeated (aparaddha)' means being like one who has lost a battle. 'Indeed, these [words] were spoken by you'—the Blessed One said this to him...
181:
The Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'Indeed, these [words] were spoken by you,' wishing to rebuke Saccaka by making his harsh-tongued nature evident. It is said that in the past, Saccaka used to approach the six great teachers, such as Pūraṇa, and ask them questions. Those teachers were unable to answer. Then, Saccaka would humiliate them greatly in the midst of the assembly, and rising from his seat, he would depart, proclaiming his victory. With the notion that he would harass the Fully Enlightened One in the same way, he approached and asked:

'O friends, what is the name of that tree, which has thin leaves and thorns,
Where, with a single blow, the head is split apart?'

Just as a soft-beaked bird that has only frequented trees without essence might peck at a khadira tree and suffer a broken beak, Saccaka, having struck against the Buddha who possesses the essence of omniscience, suffered the breaking of his 'beak of knowledge' and realized the firm and solid nature of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa). To make this clear in the midst of the assembly, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'Indeed, these [words] were spoken by you.' The phrase 'not now' does not mean that sweat is entirely non-existent in the physical body, but rather that at this moment while speaking with Saccaka, there was no sweat. In the phrase 'revealed his golden-hued body,' it does not mean he revealed his entire body. Usually, Buddhas preach the Dhamma to the assembly with their bodies securely covered, having fastened the buttons. Then, the Blessed One took the robe at the front of his neck and lowered it about four inches.

As soon as it was lowered, masses of golden-hued rays emerged, like a stream of liquid gold flowing from a golden pot, or like a flash of lightning from a red cloud. Circling the noble neck and head, which were like a small golden drum, they rose into the sky. Why did the Blessed One do this? It was to dispel the doubts of the multitude. For the people might have had doubts, thinking: 'The ascetic Gotama says he has no sweat, while Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputta is dripping with sweat like someone caught in a machine. However, the ascetic Gotama is sitting wrapped in a thick double-layered robe; how can we know whether there is sweat inside or not?' To dispel that doubt, he acted thus. 'Mankubhūta' means having become powerless and lusterless. 'Pattakkhandha' means with shoulders dropped. 'Appaṭibhāna' means not seeing any further answer. 'Nisīdi' means he sat scratching the ground with his big toe.

'Dummuakha' does not mean he became ugly (for he was handsome and pleasing to look at); it is just a name given to the state of his face being crestfallen at that time. 'Unfit to descend into that lotus pond again'—for all...
182:
It is shown that a crab with its joints (claws) broken and its movement severed is unable to descend into the pond again; it becomes food for crows, hawks, and so forth in that very place. 'Visūkāyikāni' refers to the thorns or spikes of views. 'Visevitāni' refers to the involvements or associations with views. 'Vipphanditāni' refers to the agitations or scurryings of views. In the phrase 'yadidaṃ vādādhippāyo', 'yadidaṃ' is merely a particle. It shows that he is unable to approach with the intention of finding fault, thinking 'I will find fault'; rather, he should approach for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma.

Regarding the statement, "He said this to Dummukha the Licchavi prince," why was it said? It is said that when Dummukha presented his analogy, the other Licchavi princes also thought: "This Nigaṇṭha has long insulted us in our place of learning. Now is the time to see the back of our enemy Saccaka. We too shall each bring an analogy and treat him in such a way that, like someone striking a person who has already been knocked down by a palm-strike with a club, he will not be able to lift his head in the midst of the assembly again." They prepared their analogies and sat waiting for the end of Dummukha’s speech. Saccaka, knowing their intention, thought: "All these Licchavi princes are sitting with their necks craned and their lips moving. If they get the chance to each bring an analogy, I will not be able to lift my head in the midst of the assembly again. Let me put down Dummukha so that no one else gets a chance, and by cutting off the turn of speech in this way, I will ask the ascetic Gotama a question." That is why he said those words. In that context, 'āgamehi' means "Wait! Do not speak again."

"Venerable Gotama, let this speech stand" means "Venerable Gotama, let that speech of ours and of many other ascetics and brahmins be set aside (leave it be)." "Vilāpaṃ vilapitaṃ maññေ" means this speech is like rambling or delirium; it means it is mere incoherent talk. Alternatively, in the phrase 'tiṭṭhatesā', the word 'kathā' (speech) should be brought in. In the phrase 'vācāvilāpaṃ vilapitaṃ maññေ', it means this utterance of words will likely be mere rambling.

Now, wishing to ask a question, he said the words beginning with 'kittāvatā'. In that context, 'vessārajjappatto' means one who has attained knowledge (one who has attained self-confidence).
