'Aparappaccayo' means one who does not go to another (one who is not dependent on others). Then, the Blessed One, wishing to answer the question for Saccaka, spoke the words beginning with "Aggivessana, in this dispensation," the meaning of which is very clear. Because it is said "he sees" in this passage, the stage of a trainee (sekkhabhūmi) is shown. Therefore, wishing to ask about the higher stage of an adept (asekkhabhūmi), he asked a second question, and the Blessed One answered that question as well.
183:
In that context (the second question), among the terms beginning with 'dassanānuttariyena', 'dassanānuttariya' (unsurpassed seeing) refers to mundane and supramundane wisdom. 'Paṭipadānuttariya' (unsurpassed practice) refers to mundane and supramundane practice. 'Vimuttānuttariya' (unsurpassed liberation) refers to mundane and supramundane liberation. Or, if taking only the supramundane, 'dassanānuttariya' refers to the Right View of the Path of Arahantship. 'Paṭipadānuttariya' refers to the remaining path factors. 'Vimuttānuttariya' refers to the liberation of the highest fruit (aggaphala-vimutti). Alternatively, the Arahant's seeing of Nibbāna is called 'dassanānuttariya'. The eightfold path is called 'paṭipadānuttariya'. The fruit of Arahantship is called 'vimuttānuttariya'. This is how it should be understood.

'Buddho so bhagavā' means that the Blessed One has himself awakened to the Four Noble Truths (Buddho). 'Bodhāya' means he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the awakening of others to the Four Noble Truths. Among the terms beginning with 'danto', 'danto' means the Blessed One is tamed, being free from the venom of defilements; 'damathāya' means he teaches for the sake of taming others. 'Santo' means the Blessed One is calmed through the subsiding of all defilements; 'samathāya' means he teaches for the sake of calming others. 'Tiṇṇo' means the Blessed One has crossed over the four floods; 'taraṇāya' means he teaches for the sake of helping others cross over. 'Parinibbuto' means the Blessed One is extinguished through the extinguishing of defilements; 'parinibbānāya' means he teaches for the sake of the extinguishing of defilements in others.

'Dhaṃsī' refers to those who destroy virtues. 'Pagabbhā' refers to those possessed of impudence or harshness of speech. 'Āsādetabbaṃ' means that which should be struck or challenged. 'Āsajja' means having struck or challenged. 'Natveva bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ' means that no one, after challenging the Venerable Gotama, is able to depart taking their own doctrine intact without it being destroyed. The Blessed One does not cause danger to anyone's life like an elephant or such. However, this Nigaṇṭha did not bring these three analogies to praise the Blessed One, but only to praise himself. For example, just as a king, after killing an enemy, might praise the enemy saying, "He must have been such a brave and powerful man," yet he is only praising himself.

In the same way, although Saccaka praised the Blessed One with words such as "Venerable Gotama, like a rogue elephant...", he was only praising himself, thinking: "Only we are the brave ones, only we are the wise ones, only we are the ones of great learning; that is why we approached the Fully Enlightened One for debate, who is like a rogue elephant, like a great mass of blazing fire, and like a cobra with its hood raised." Having thus praised himself, wishing to invite the Blessed One, he said the words beginning with "Please accept my (almsfood)." In that context, 'adhivāsetu' means "please accept." 'Svātanāya' means "for the sake of the merit, joy, and gladness that will arise tomorrow from my service (of almsfood, etc.) to you." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.
184:
The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent, without moving any limb of his body or organ of speech, maintaining patience only within himself. It means he accepted only with his mind for the sake of showing favor to Saccaka.

"Whatever you think is suitable for the recluse Gotama" means that those Licchavi princes used to bring five hundred pots of cooked alms-food as a regular meal for Saccaka. Referring to those very five hundred items, he said, "Tomorrow, you should bring whatever you think is suitable and allowable for the recluse Gotama; for you are the attendants of the recluse Gotama and you know what is allowable or unallowable, and what is suitable or unsuitable." "Bhattābhihāraṃ abhihariṃsu" means they brought the food that was to be brought. "Paṇītena" means with excellent (food). "Sahatthā" means with his own hand. "Santappetvā" means having satisfied well, making him full and satiated as much as desired. "Sampavāretvā" means having caused him to refuse well, making him decline with a hand gesture saying, "Enough, enough." "Bhuttāviṃ" means one who has finished eating. "Onītapattapāṇiṃ" means one who has removed his hand from the bowl; it means the hand is withdrawn from the bowl. There is also a variant reading "Onittapattapāṇiṃ," the meaning of which is: one whose bowl is separate from his hand is "onittapattapāṇī." It means the Blessed One who, having washed both hands and bowl, and having placed the bowl aside in a suitable place, was sitting. "Ekamantaṃ nisīdi" means knowing the Blessed One to be in such a state, he sat down in one place.

"Puññañca" means whatever merit there is in this gift, referring to the future resultant mental aggregates (vipāka-nāma-kkhandha). "Puññamahī" refers only to the retinue of those resultant mental aggregates. "Taṃ dāyakānaṃ sukhāya hotu" means may that merit be for the happiness of these Licchavi princes. It is said that Saccaka said this while dedicating it to them, thinking, "I am indeed a recluse, and it is not fitting for a recluse to dedicate his own gift (to others)." Then the Blessed One, because the gift was given by the Licchavis to Saccaka and not to the Blessed One, but was given by Saccaka to the Blessed One, wishing to clarify that matter, said, "Aggivessana, whatever merit..." and so on. Thus, the Blessed One dedicated the offering given to Himself to the Nigaṇṭha, independently of the Nigaṇṭha's own view; and that [act] will become a latent disposition (vāsana) for him in the future.

## The Explanation of the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
185:
## 6. Mahāsaccakasutta-vaṇṇanā

"Thus have I heard" and so on; this is the Mahāsaccaka Sutta. In this Mahāsaccaka Sutta, the three phrases "At one time" (ekaṃ samayaṃ), "At that time" (tena kho pana samayena), and "In the morning" (pubbaṇhasamayaṃ) refer to the same single period of time. Indeed, this is the time when monks, having performed their duties, washed their faces, taken their bowls and robes, and paid homage to the Cetiya, stand at the deliberation hall (vitakkamaḷaka) thinking, "Which village shall we enter for alms?" At such a time, the Blessed One, having dressed in his red double-layered undergarment, tied his waistband, and draped his rag-robe (pamsukūla) over one shoulder, emerged from the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) and stood at the front of the Fragrant Chamber surrounded by the community of monks. Referring to this standing, it is said: "At one time," "At that time," and "In the morning."

"Pavisitukāmo" means having made the resolution, "I will enter for alms." "Tenupasaṅkami" (approached him): Why did he approach? He approached with the intention of refuting (vādāropanajjhāsaya). It is heard that Saccaka had this thought: "Previously, due to my lack of wisdom, I took the entire assembly of Vesālī and went to the ascetic Gotama, only to be humiliated in the midst of the assembly. Now, I will not do that; I will go alone and challenge his doctrine. If I can defeat the ascetic Gotama, I will demonstrate my own view and achieve victory. If the ascetic Gotama wins, no one will know, like someone dancing in the dark." Thus, taking a "sleep-question" (niddā-pañha), he approached with this intention to refute.

"Anukampaṃ upādāya" (out of compassion) means out of compassion for Saccaka, the son of the Nigantha. It is said that the Elder Ānanda had this thought: "If the Blessed One sits for a moment, (Saccaka) will get to see the Buddha and hear the Dhamma. That will lead to his welfare and happiness for a long time." Therefore, he requested the Blessed One and, having spread out the four-fold rag-robe, said, "May the Blessed One sit down." The Blessed One, reflecting that "Ānanda is speaking for a reason," sat on the prepared seat.

"Bhagavantaṃ etadavoca" (said this to the Blessed One) means setting aside for a while the question he brought like a gold bag in his waist-pocket, and first considering from the side, he spoke the words: "There are, Master Gotama..." and so on. "Phusanti hi te, bho Gotama" means those ascetics and brahmins experience, obtain, and feel the painful physical sensations that have arisen in the body. "Ūrukkham bho" means the state of the thighs being like pillars, meaning stiffness of the thighs. Here, the future tense "bhavissati" is used in the sense of wonder. "Kāyanvayaṃ hoti" means...
186:
Following the will of the body is being under the control of the body. Insight (vipassanā), however, is called the development of the body (kāyabhāvanā); through that insight, there is no such thing as reaching a state of mental distraction. Thus, the Nigaṇṭha (Saccaka) spoke only of what is non-existent and untrue. Tranquility (samatha) is also called the development of the mind (cittabhāvanā); for a person endowed with concentration (samādhi), there is no such thing as stiffness of the thighs (ūrukkhampha) and so on. Thus, the Nigaṇṭha spoke only this untrue word. In the Commentary, however, it is said: "Just as for one who says, 'It happened in the past,' and then says, 'Stiffness of the thighs will also occur,' the future tense does not fit, so too the meaning does not fit; he speaks of what is non-existent and untrue."

The statement "there is no development of the body" was said with reference to the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga), such as the practice of the five fires (pañcātapa). This practice is what they call the development of the body. But what did Saccaka see that made him say this? It is said that he used to come to the monastery late in the day; at that time, the monks, having put away their bowls and robes, would go into seclusion in their respective night-quarters and day-quarters. Seeing those monks in seclusion, he thought, "These monks only practice the development of the mind; they have no development of the body," and thus he spoke in this way.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to cross-examine him, said, "Aggivessana, how have you heard about the development of the body?" Saccaka, elaborating on that statement, mentioned "Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca," and so on. In that context, Nanda is his name, and Vaccha is his clan (gotta). Kisa is the name, and Saṅkicca is the clan. Makkhali Gosāla has already been mentioned below. "These people" refers to those three individuals; they are said to have reached the pinnacle of foul ascetic practices of the body. "Excellent, excellent" refers to refined and superior foods. "They take" means they take in strength. "They increase" means they grow. "They make fat" means they produce body fat. "Abandoning the former practice" means abandoning the former practice of austerities (dukkharacariyā). "Later they accumulate" means later they satisfy themselves and grow with excellent foods and so on. "There is growth and decline" means there is increase and decrease; thus, only the mere growth and decline of this body—growth at one time and decline at another—is apparent, but the development of the body is not apparent. To show this, and wishing to ask about the development of the mind, the Buddha said, "Aggivessana, how have you heard about the development of the mind?" "Could not answer" means he was unable to answer fully, like a foolish worldling.
187:
How could you, who do not even know such a coarse and weak development of the body, know the subtle and profound development of the mind? At this point, Elder Codanālaya, saying, "This word is not the word of the Buddha," prepared to lay down his fan and leave. Then Elder Mahāsīva said, "Monks, the growth, decline, taking, and laying down of this body composed of the four great elements are apparent." Having heard this, he noted, "For one who comprehends the coarse body, it is appropriate to say that the insight (vipassanā) that arises is coarse."

"One attached to the essence of pleasure" (sukhasārāgī) means one endowed with lust associated with pleasant feeling. "From the cessation of pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises" does not mean it arises immediately (without interval). This is because the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) between pleasure and pain is prohibited in the Paṭṭhāna. However, because painful feeling cannot arise as long as pleasant feeling has not ceased, it is spoken of in this way here. "Overpowers and remains" (pariyādāya tiṭṭhati) means it stays after exhausting and taking over (the wholesome mind). "On both sides" (ubhatopakkha) means having two sides: pleasure as one side and pain as the other.

Even when pleasant feeling has arisen, it cannot overpower the mind and remain because the body has been developed. Even when painful feeling has arisen, it cannot overpower the mind and remain because the mind has been developed. In this context, development of the body is insight (vipassanā), and development of the mind is concentration (samādhi). Insight is the opposite of pleasure and is close to pain. Concentration is the opposite of pain and is close to pleasure. How? For one sitting and practicing insight, as time passes, it becomes like fire breaking out in various parts of the body; sweat flows from the armpits, and it becomes as if a column of steam is rising from the head. Then the mind is distressed, greatly distressed, and agitated. Thus, insight is the opposite of pleasure and close to pain. But when physical or mental pain has arisen, for one who has entered an attainment (samāpatti) after suppressing that pain, at the moment of attainment, the pain is far removed and an immeasurable pleasure descends. Thus, concentration is the opposite of pain and close to pleasure. Just as insight is the opposite of pleasure and close to pain, concentration is not like that. Just as concentration is the opposite of pain and close to pleasure, insight is not like that. Therefore, it was said, "Even when pleasant feeling has arisen, it [does not overpower] the mind..."
188:
Because the body has been developed, [pleasant feeling] cannot remain overwhelming the mind; because the mind has been developed, the arisen painful feeling also cannot remain overwhelming the mind, he said.

"Āsajja upanīya" means by both offending the virtues and by bringing them near. "Taṃ vata me" means "That mind is indeed my mind."

"Aggivessana, why should it not be so? It is indeed so. Do not have such a perception. Both pleasant and painful feelings do indeed arise in me, but when that feeling arises, I do not allow it to remain overwhelming the mind," he said. Now, wishing to preach the Dhamma that inspires confidence from the beginning to clarify this matter, he began with the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana). In that context, "Here, Aggivessana, before my enlightenment... I sat right there, this is enough for striving"—all this should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Pāsarāsi Sutta below. The difference here is that in that Sutta, the sitting at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka) is mentioned, while in this Sutta, the performance of austerities (Dukkarakārikā) is mentioned.

"Allakaṭṭha" means moist fig wood. "Sassneha" means being with sap. "Kāmehi" means by way of sensual objects (vatthukāma). "Avūpakaṭṭha" means not being withdrawn. In terms like "Kāmacchanda," sensual lust (kilesakāma) itself is called "desire" (chanda) by way of wishing, "affection" (sneha) by way of sticking, "infatuation" (mucchā) by way of intoxication, "thirst" (pipāsā) by way of thirsting, and "fever" (pariḷāha) by way of burning. "Opakkamika" means arising due to exertion. "For knowledge, for vision, for supreme enlightenment" (ñāṇāya dassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāya) are all synonyms for the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga).

The comparison of the similes here is as follows: Persons who are not yet withdrawn from sensual objects due to sensual lust are like moist fig wood with sap. Being immersed in water is like being wet with sensual lust. Not producing fire even when churning is like the inability to attain the supramundane path through feelings born of exertion for those not withdrawn from sensual objects due to sensual lust. Not producing fire even without churning is like the inability to attain the supramundane path even without feelings born of exertion for those persons. The second simile should also be understood in this same way. The difference here is that the first simile is for those who renounce with children and wives, while the latter is for those who renounce according to the Brahmanical Dhamma.
189:
In the third simile, "koḷāpa" refers to dry wood that is free from the sap of attachment and has no holes. "Thale nikkhittaṃ" means placed on a hill or on the ground. Here too, the correlation between the simile and the thing illustrated is as follows: Persons who have been liberated from sensual objects through [the removal of] sensual lust are like the dry koḷāpa wood; they are not wet with sensual lust, just as [the wood] is placed on dry land far from water. Just as fire is produced by rubbing, those who have been liberated from sensual objects through [the removal of] sensual lust attain the supramundane path through feelings born of exertion, such as the open-air practice (abbhokāsika-dhutaṅga) and the sitting practice (nesajjika-dhutaṅga). Just as fire is produced merely by rubbing with a dry branch of another tree, the attainment of the supramundane path is also possible through the pleasant practice (sukhā paṭipadā) without feelings born of exertion. The Blessed One spoke this simile for his own benefit.

Now, wishing to show his own performance of austerities, he said "Tassa mayhaṃ," etc. If one asks, "Could the Blessed One not have become a Buddha without practicing austerities?" He was indeed capable of becoming a Buddha whether he practiced them or not. Then why did he practice them? (He thought,) "I will show my exertion to the world including the devas. And the virtue of crushing [defilements] through energy will gladden me." Indeed, a kshatriya who receives a kingdom through traditional succession while just sitting in a palace is not as joyful as a king who, having taken an army and fought two or three battles in the field, crushes his enemies and gains the kingdom. For a king who has gained the kingdom in this way, while enjoying royal splendor, looks at his assembly and remembers his own exertion, thinking, "I performed such a deed in such a place, I pierced and struck such and such an enemy in this way, and thus I have attained this royal splendor," and great joy (somanassa) arises. In the same way, the Blessed One thought, "I will show my exertion to the world including the devas; that exertion will gladden me greatly and produce joy," and so he practiced austerities.

Furthermore, he practiced them out of compassion for future generations. Future generations will think, "The Sammāsambuddha, even after fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons, attained omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) only after exerting great effort; how much more should we put forth energetic striving!" If so, they will quickly make an end of birth, aging, and death. Thus, he practiced out of compassion for future generations.

"Dantebhidantamādhāya" means placing the upper teeth on the lower teeth. "Cetasā cittaṃ" means [crushing] the unwholesome mind with the wholesome mind. "Abhiniggaṇheyyaṃ" means should be restrained.
190:
## 
'Abhinipīḷeyyaṃ' means I should press hard (or squeeze). 'Abhisantāpeyyaṃ' means I should scorch, implying that I should torment myself by applying energy. 'Sāraddho' means being distressed (or weary). 'Padhānabhitunnassa' refers to one who is afflicted or destroyed by the energy of exertion.

'Appāṇakaṃ' means being breathless (without inhalation and exhalation). 'Kammāragaggarī' refers to a smith's bellows. 'Sīsavedanā honti' refers to severe headaches caused by winds that are unable to escape due to some reason. 'Sīsaveṭhaṃ dadeyya' means one would give a head-wrap (or tie a turban). 'Devatā' refers to the deities residing near the end of the Bodhisatta's walking path and around the precinct of the leaf-hut monastery.

At that time, it is said that the Bodhisatta fainted due to the occurrence of extreme bodily heat. The Bodhisatta fell while sitting on the walking path. Seeing him fall, the deities said, 'This is the way an Arahant lives,' and some said according to their belief, 'Arahants are like this, they resemble the dead.' Among those deities, those who said 'He is dead' went to King Suddhodana and informed him, 'Your son is dead.' The King asked, 'Did my son die after becoming a Buddha, or without becoming one?' The deities replied, 'He could not become a Buddha; he fell and died on the very ground of his exertion.' The King said, 'I do not believe it; there is no such thing as my son dying without attaining Enlightenment (Bodhi).'

In later times, after the Blessed One had turned the Wheel of Dhamma and gradually traveled to Rājagaha and then arrived at Kapilavatthu, King Suddhodana took the alms-bowl, invited Him to the palace, offered gruel and food, and during the interval after the meal, he reported this matter: 'Venerable Sir, while You were practicing exertion, deities came and said, "Great King, your son is dead."' The Buddha asked, 'Great King, did you believe those words?' The King replied, 'Venerable Sir, I did not believe them.' The Buddha said, 'Great King, now that you have seen wonders starting from the interpretation of the dreams, why would you believe it? I have now become a Buddha, and you have become the father of a Buddha. But in the past, when my knowledge was not yet mature and I was practicing the Bodhisatta's conduct as the youth Dhammapāla, when I went to learn the arts, people brought a goat's bone and showed it to you, saying, "Your son, the youth Dhammapāla, is dead; this is his bone." Even then, Great King, you said, "There is no such thing as untimely death for my son; I do not believe it."' Based on this incident, the Blessed One related the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka.
191:
## 
Deities said the words 'Mā kho tvaṃ mārisā' (Do not, dear sir) out of affection for me. It is said that for deities, 'mārisā' is an affectionate form of address. 'Ajajjitaṃ' means fasting (not eating). 'Halanti vadāmi' means 'Alanti vadāmi' (I say 'enough'). It carries the meaning of prohibition: 'Enough with this food, do not do this, I will subsist [on less].'

380-1. 'Maṅguracchavī' means having skin like the skin of a maṅgura fish. 'Etāva paramaṃ' means this much is the highest limit of those feelings. Regarding the words 'Pitu sakkassa kammante... paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharitā' (While at the work of his father... he dwelt having attained the first jhāna), I shall relate what has been heard. King Suddhodana had what is called the Ploughing Festival Day (Vappamaṅgaladivasa). On that occasion, they prepared various kinds of hard and soft food. They had the city streets cleaned, placed full water-pots, raised banners and flags, and decorated the entire city like a celestial mansion. All servants, laborers, and others, dressed in new clothes and adorned with perfumes and garlands, assembled at the royal palace. In the King's ploughing work, one hundred thousand ploughs were used. However, on that day, they used eight hundred ploughs less one (799). All the ploughs, along with the oxen's reins and ropes, were plated with silver, like the chariot of the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi. The plough held by the King was plated with red gold. The horns of the oxen, the reins, and the goads were also plated with gold. The King, departing with a great retinue, took his son with him.

At the place of the ploughing work, there was a Jambu (rose-apple) tree with thick leaves and dense shade. Having prepared the prince's bed under that tree, hung a canopy decorated with golden stars above it, surrounded it with a cloth curtain, and placed guards, the King, adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by a host of ministers, went to the place of ploughing. There, the King took the golden plough. The ministers took seven hundred and ninety-nine silver ploughs and ploughed here and there. The King ploughed from this side to that side, and from that side to this side. While great prosperity was unfolding at that place, the nurses who were sitting around the Bodhisatta went out from within the curtain to see the King's splendor. The Bodhisatta, looking here and there and seeing no one, quickly arose, sat in the cross-legged position, took up the meditation on inhalation and exhalation, and attained the first jhāna. The nurses, wandering among the various foods, were delayed for a short while.
192:
The shadows of the other trees had turned, but the shadow of that Jambu tree remained circular and stayed in place. The nurses, thinking 'The young master is alone,' quickly lifted the curtain and entered. Seeing the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged on the couch and witnessing that miracle, they went to the King and reported: 'Your Majesty, the Prince is sitting in this manner; the shadows of other trees have turned, but the shadow of the Jambu tree remains circular and still.' The King came quickly, saw the miracle, and bowed to his son, saying: 'Dear son, this is my second salutation to you.' This was said in reference to his attainment of the first jhāna: 'At the plowing festival of his father, the Sakyan King... he entered and dwelt in the first jhāna.' He reflected: 'Could this be the path to enlightenment? Could this first jhāna of mindfulness of breathing be the path to realizing omniscience?' Satanusārivijñāṇa (consciousness following mindfulness) refers to the consciousness that arises immediately after the mindfulness that has occurred once or twice, thinking: 'This knowledge of mine is not yet the path to enlightenment; it will only be the first jhāna of mindfulness of breathing.' 'That happiness' refers to the happiness of the first jhāna of mindfulness of breathing.

'Are present near' means they served him by performing duties such as sweeping the precinct of the leaf-roofed hut. 'One with many requisites' refers to one who practices to increase the four requisites. 'One who turns for abundance' refers to one who, being greedy for taste, turns for the sake of fine alms-food and so forth. 'They departed in weariness' means they left out of dissatisfaction, following the law of nature (dhamma-niyāma). They went by nature to provide the opportunity for physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) when the Bodhisatta was to attain omniscience. When they left, they did not go elsewhere but went only to the city of Vārāṇasī. After the group of five had departed, the Bodhisatta obtained physical seclusion for half a month, and sitting on the Unconquered Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, he penetrated omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

The passage beginning with 'Secluded from sensual pleasures' should be understood in the same manner as explained in the Bhayabherava Sutta.

'I know' is a separate connection (anusandhi). The Nigaṇṭha (Saccaka) thought: 'I asked the recluse Gotama one question. The recluse Gotama keeps speaking without showing an end, saying: "Agnivessana, there is another for me; Agnivessana, there is another for me." Is he angry?' Then the Blessed One, [saying] 'Agnivessana, when the Tathāgata is teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds...'
193:
There is not a single person who can say the recluse Gotama is angry. The Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma only for the purpose of making others understand and penetrate the Four Noble Truths. To show this, he began this Dhamma teaching. In that text, 'ārabbha' means 'referring to' (sandhāya). The word 'yāvadeva' indicates the determination of the purpose. This is the meaning: making others understand is the sole purpose of the Tathāgata's Dhamma teaching; therefore, he does not teach only one person, but teaches all beings, however many there are who can understand.

What is shown by the phrase 'tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ'? Saccaka thought: 'The recluse Gotama is very handsome and inspiring; his lips are well-formed, his tongue is soft, and his voice is sweet. I think he wanders about pleasing the assembly, but he lacks internal one-pointedness of mind (samādhi).' Then the Blessed One, to show that 'Agnivessana, the Tathāgata does not wander to please the assembly; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma even to an assembly as large as the universe, unattached, untainted, dwelling alone to this extent, and practicing the attainment of the fruit of emptiness (suññata-phala-samāpatti)', spoke in this way.

'Ajjhattameva' means only the internal object (gocara-ajjhatta). 'Sannisādemi' means 'I cause to settle.' Indeed, at the moment the assembly applauds, the Tathāgata enters the attainment of the fruit (phala-samāpatti) by pre-determination. Even before the sound of applause has ceased, he emerges from the attainment and continues teaching the Dhamma from where he stood. Because the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) of the Buddhas is swift, they enter the attainment in every breath. 'Yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ' means he dwells constantly in that concentration of the fruit of emptiness; it shows that he establishes and fixes the mind in that sign of concentration (samādhi-nimitta).

'Okappaniyametaṃ' means it is a believable statement. Having thus accepted the Blessed One's one-pointedness of mind, Saccaka now wished to ask the question he had brought like a treasure tied in his waist-cloth, and said: 'Does the Venerable Gotama know sleeping during the day?' For example, even if a dog has been fed to its fill with milk-rice made with undiluted milk mixed with ghee, it cannot help but eat dung if it sees it; if it does not eat it, it at least sniffs it before going; if it goes without even sniffing it, its head aches. In the same way, although the Teacher had given Saccaka this inspiring Dhamma teaching, which is like milk-rice, from the time of his renunciation until the destruction of taints, yet for such a person...
194:
Even after hearing the Dhamma teaching, not even a slight degree of faith in the Blessed One arose in him. Therefore, like a valuable treasure wrapped in his waist-cloth, he was unable to leave without asking the questions he had brought, and so he spoke thus. In this context, sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) are abandoned by all Arahants through the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). However, physical fatigue (kāya-daratha) occurs in both sentient bodies and non-sentient things. Indeed, lotuses such as the blue and white lotuses bloom at certain times and are in bud at others. At night, the leaves of some trees fold up, and in the morning, they expand. Thus, falling into the stream of the life-continuum (bhavaṅgasota) due to the fatigue of the physical body produced by kamma is what is meant here by 'sleeping'. Such sleep also occurs to Arahants. Referring to that sleep, he said, "I know," and so on. "They speak of living in delusion" means living with great confusion.

"Āsajja āsajja" means having struck against or having provoked. "Upanītehi" means by words spoken having brought them near. "Vacanappathehi" means by the pathways of speech or by words. "Abhinanditvā anumoditvā" means accepting with the mind and being pleased, and praising with the voice and being joyful. The Blessed One preached two suttas to this Saccaka Nigaṇṭha. The previous sutta was one bhāṇavāra (recitation section) long, and this sutta is one and a half bhāṇavāras long. Thus, even after hearing the Dhamma for two and a half bhāṇavāras, this Nigaṇṭha did not reach the realization of the Four Noble Truths, did not ordain, and did not even establish himself in the Three Refuges. Why did the Blessed One preach the Dhamma to him? It was to establish a habitual tendency (vāsanā) for the future. For the Blessed One saw: "Although this man does not yet have the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit, more than two hundred years after my Parinibbāna, the Sasana will be established in the island of Tambapaṇṇi. At that time, he will be born in a noble family, and upon reaching maturity, he will ordain, learn the three Pitakas, develop insight (vipassanā), and reaching Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), he will become a great Arahant named Kāḷabuddharakkhita." Seeing this, he preached the Dhamma to establish the habitual tendency for the future.

When the Sasana was established in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, that person passed away from the deva world and was born into a family of ministers in the village where the Dakkhiṇagiri Vihāra went for alms. Having ordained at an age suitable for monkhood, he learned the three Pitakas of the Buddha's word. While leading a group and surrounded by a large assembly of monks, he went to see his preceptor (upajjhāya). Then, his preceptor, wishing to admonish his pupil, did not even speak a single word of conversation face-to-face with that monk who had come after learning the three Pitakas of the Buddha's word. That monk, having risen at dawn, went to the elder and asked, "Venerable sir, although I have come to you after completing the work of studying the scriptures, you did not even speak a single word face-to-face..."
195:
...did not even speak. "What fault do I have, venerable sir?" he asked. The elder said, "Friend Buddharakkhita, do you think that just by learning this much of the Buddha's word, the task of your monkhood has reached its completion?" When he asked, "Venerable sir, what should I do?", the elder said, "Leave the group, cut off worldly proliferation (papañca), go to Cetiyapabbata Vihāra, and practice the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma)." That Kāḷabuddharakkhita, abiding by the instruction of his preceptor, reached Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Having great merit and being honored by the king, he lived at Cetiyapabbata Vihāra surrounded by a large assembly of monks.

At that time, King Tissa (Tissa Mahārāja), while observing the Uposatha precepts, was staying in the Royal Cave at Cetiyapabbata. He had given a signal to the monk who attended the elder: "When my noble lord answers a question or preaches the Dhamma, please give me a signal." On a certain day for hearing the Dhamma, the elder, surrounded by the assembly of monks, ascended to the courtyard of the Kaṇṭaka Cetiya, paid homage to the stupa, and stood at the foot of a Kāḷatimbaru tree. Then, a monk who was a pindapātika (alms-food gatherer) asked the elder a question regarding the Kāḷakārāma Sutta. The elder said, "Friend, is today not the day for hearing the Dhamma?" He replied, "Yes, venerable sir, it is the day for hearing the Dhamma." "If so, bring a chair; we shall listen to the Dhamma while sitting right here," the elder said. Then, they prepared a seat for him at the foot of the tree. The elder, after reciting the introductory verses, began the Kāḷakārāma Sutta. The young attendant monk also had the signal given to the king.

The king arrived even before the introductory verses were finished. Having arrived, he stood at the edge of the assembly in an unrecognizable guise and listened to the Dhamma while standing throughout the three watches of the night. When the elder said the words, "Thus the Blessed One said," the king uttered the cry of 'Sādhu'. The elder, realizing it, asked, "Great King, when did you arrive?" "Venerable sir, I arrived even while the introductory verses were being recited," he replied. "Great King, you have done a difficult thing," the elder said. "Venerable sir, this is not a difficult thing. If my mind had wandered elsewhere for even a single word since the time your reverence began the Dhamma talk, may I not be the lord of even a place as small as the prick of a goad in the island of Tambapaṇṇi," he swore.

Since the qualities of the Buddha were illustrated in that sutta, the king asked, "Venerable sir, are the qualities of the Buddha only this many, or are there others?" "Great King, the qualities that I have not preached are far more numerous and immeasurable than those I have preached," the elder replied. When the king requested, "Venerable sir, please give an analogy," the analogy is as follows:
196:
Great King, just as in a rice field of about a thousand karīsa, the remaining grains of rice are many compared to a single ear of rice, even so, the virtues of the Buddha I have spoken of are few, while those remaining unspoken are many.

“Venerable Sir, please provide another analogy,” he requested.

Great King, just as if one were to hold the eye of a needle against the great river Ganges full of flowing water, the water taken by the eye of the needle is very little, while the remaining water is vast; even so, the virtues of the Buddha I have spoken of are few, while those remaining are many.

“Venerable Sir, please provide another analogy,” he requested.

Great King, in this world, birds called cātaka (swallows) wander and play in the sky. That species of bird is very small. Is the space where that bird spreads its wings in the sky vast, or is the remaining sky small?

“Venerable Sir, what are you saying? The space where that bird spreads its wings is very small, while the remaining sky is indeed vast,” he replied.

Great King, even so, I have spoken only a few of the Buddha's virtues; the remaining virtues of the Buddha are many, infinite, and immeasurable.

“Venerable Sir, it is well spoken. The infinite virtues of the Buddha have been compared to the infinite sky. We are greatly devoted to the Venerable One, but we are unable to make a fitting offering. I offer this kingdom of three hundred yojanas in this island of Tambapaṇṇi, which is my poor gift, to the Venerable One,” he said.

Great King, you have shown your devotion. We, however, return this kingdom offered to us back to you. Great King, rule the kingdom with righteousness and justice.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Mahāsaccaka Sutta is finished.
## 7. Explanation of the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta

“Evaṃ me sutaṃ” and so forth is the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta. In that sutta, “pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde” means in the palace of Migāramātā (Visākhā) within the monastery known as Pubbārāma. Here is the sequential account (anupubbīkathā): One hundred thousand aeons ago, a female lay devotee invited the Blessed One Padumuttara and, having given a great gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and made an aspiration: “In the future, may I be the chief attendant of a Buddha like you.” That lay devotee wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and our...
197:
In the time of the Blessed One, she was conceived in the womb of Sumanadevī in the house of the banker Dhanañjaya, the son of the banker Meṇḍaka, in the city of Bhaddiya. When she was born, they named her Visākhā. When the Blessed One went to the city of Bhaddiya, Visākhā, along with five hundred young maidens, went to welcome the Blessed One, and upon her first sight of Him, she became a Sotāpanna.

Later, she went to the house of Prince PuṇṇavaḍḎhana, the son of the banker Migāra in Sāvatthī. In that house, the banker Migāra placed Visākhā in the position of a mother; therefore, she is called Migāramātā (Migāra's mother).

When she was going to her husband's house, her father had an ornament called Mahālatā made for her. In that ornament, four nāḷis of diamonds, eleven nāḷis of pearls, twenty-two nāḷis of coral, and thirty-three nāḷis of rubies were used. Thus, it was completed with these aforementioned jewels and other jewels of seven colors. When that Mahālatā ornament is worn on the head, it covers down to the tops of the feet. Only a woman possessing the strength of five noble elephants is able to wear that ornament. Later, Visākhā became the chief female attendant of the Dasabala (the Buddha). She gave up that ornament and, using ninety million (nine koṭis) in wealth, had a monastery built for the Blessed One, constructing a mansion on a piece of land the size of a karīsa. On the upper floor of that mansion, there were five hundred rooms, and on the lower floor, there were five hundred rooms; thus, it was adorned with one thousand rooms. Visākhā thought, "A mansion alone is not beautiful," and surrounding that mansion, she had five hundred two-pinnacled buildings, five hundred small mansions, and five hundred long halls built. The festival for the monastery was completed in four months.

There is no other woman who has sacrificed wealth in the Buddha's Dispensation like Visākhā, who stood in the state of a woman. There is no other man who has sacrificed wealth in the Buddha's Dispensation like Anāthapiṇḍika, who stood in the state of a man. That Anāthapiṇḍika spent five hundred and forty million (fifty-four koṭis) of wealth to build the Jetavana Mahāvihāra in a place similar to the Mahāvihāra of Anurādhapura, on the southern side of Sāvatthī. Visākhā built the Pubbārāma in a place similar to the Uttamadevī-vihāra, on the eastern side of Sāvatthī. The Blessed One, out of compassion for these two families, resided in these two monasteries regularly while staying near Sāvatthī. He would spend one rainy season at Jetavana and one rainy season at Pubbārāma. At this time, the Blessed One was staying at the Pubbārāma. Therefore, it is said, "In the mansion of Migāramātā in the Pubbārāma monastery."
198:
“Venerable Sir, to what extent [is one liberated through the destruction of craving]?” means “Venerable Sir, by how much?” “In brief, one is liberated through the destruction of craving” means that one is called ‘liberated through the destruction of craving’ because of the state of having a mind liberated by taking Nibbāna—the destruction of craving—as an object. To what extent, in brief, does this occur? He asks, “Please teach me in brief the preliminary practice of the path for a bhikkhu who is an Arahant, by which practice one becomes liberated through the destruction of craving.”

“Accantaniṭṭho” (One who has reached the ultimate goal) means those who have transcended the end known as destruction and passing away; thus they are called “accantā” (ultimate). Because that Arahant has completions that have reached the ultimate end, he is called “accantaniṭṭho.” It means one who has reached the absolute end, the eternal end. “Accantayogakkhemī” (One who has reached the ultimate security from bondage) means one who possesses Nibbāna, the absolute and eternal end of the four bondages (yogas). “Accantabrahmacārī” (One who has reached the ultimate holy life) means one who possesses the absolute and eternal noble practice of the Ariya Path. Since that Arahant has an absolute conclusion, he is called “accantapariyosāno” (One who has reached the ultimate end) according to the previous method.

“Seṭṭho devamanussānaṃ” (The best among devas and humans) means one who is noble and superior to both devas and humans. He requests the Blessed One, “To what extent does a bhikkhu of such nature reach Nibbāna, the destruction of craving? Please tell me the practice of that Arahant quickly and in brief.” Why did Sakka act with such haste? It was because he wished to enjoy the pleasures of the garden.

It is said that this Sakka, having ordered the preparations for garden-play, had the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā) set up guards in the four directions. Surrounded by hosts of devas from two deva worlds, together with twenty-five million celestial dancers, he mounted the elephant Erāvaṇa and, while standing at the garden gate, reflected on this question: “To what extent is the preliminary practice of the path to be attained in brief by an Arahant who is liberated through the destruction of craving?” Then it occurred to him: “This question is extremely glorious. If I enter the garden without having this question resolved, I will be agitated by the objects of the six sense doors and will not be able to reflect on this question again. Let the garden-play wait for a while; I will go to the Teacher, ask and learn this question, and only then play in the garden.” Thinking thus, he vanished from the elephant’s back and appeared in the presence of the Blessed One. Those four Great Kings remained standing exactly where they had taken up their guard. The surrounding hosts of devas, the dancers, and the elephant king Erāvaṇa also remained there at the garden gate. Thus, wishing to enjoy the play, he spoke in haste as follows.

In the phrase “Sabbe dhammā nālaṃ abhinivesāya” (All things are not fit for adhering to), “all things” refers to the five aggregates, the twelve sense bases, and the eighteen elements. All these, through the power of craving and views...
199:
(All things) are not fit for adhering to; they are not sufficient, not capable, and not suitable. Why? Because they do not remain according to the way they are grasped (by craving and views). Indeed, even though they are grasped as permanent, they turn out to be only impermanent; though grasped as pleasurable, they turn out to be only suffering; though grasped as self, they turn out to be only non-self. Therefore, they are not fit for adhering to.

“Abhijānāti” (He fully understands) means he fully understands through the ‘full understanding of the known’ (ñāta-pariññā) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. “Parijānāti” (He comprehends) means he comprehends in the same way through the ‘full understanding by investigation’ (tīraṇa-pariññā). “Yaṃkiñci vedanaṃ” (Whatever feeling) means experiencing any feeling, even a slight one associated with the fivefold consciousness. By this, the Blessed One shows Sakka, the King of Devas, the comprehension of mental phenomena (arūpa-pariggaha) by way of feeling. If the meditation on feeling (vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna) had not been taught below, it should be taught here. However, since it has been taught below, it should be understood according to the method stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

In the term “Aniccānupassī” (Contemplating impermanence), one should understand impermanence (anicca), the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), and the person contemplating impermanence (aniccānupassī). Among these three, ‘impermanence’ refers to the five aggregates; they are impermanent because they have the nature of arising and passing away. ‘Contemplation of impermanence’ is the knowledge that sees the five aggregates by way of their destruction and passing away. ‘One contemplating impermanence’ refers to the person endowed with that knowledge. Therefore, “aniccānupassī viharati” means he dwells repeatedly contemplating by way of impermanence; this is the meaning here.

In the term “Virāgānupassī” (Contemplating dispassion), there are two kinds of dispassion: dispassion through destruction (khaya-virāga) and ultimate dispassion (accanta-virāga). Among these, the repeated contemplation of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra) by way of their destruction and passing away, as well as the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) that sees Nibbāna—the ultimate dispassion—as dispassion, are both called ‘contemplation of dispassion.’ A person endowed with both is called ‘one contemplating dispassion.’ With reference to such a person, it is said “virāgānupassī,” meaning one who contemplates by way of dispassion. The same method applies to “Nirodhānupassī” (Contemplating cessation), for cessation is also of two kinds: cessation through destruction and ultimate cessation.

In the term “Paṭinissaggānupassī” (Contemplating relinquishment), relinquishment (paṭinissagga) is called ‘giving up’ (vossagga). That giving up is of two kinds: relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-vossagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-vossagga). Among these, ‘relinquishment as giving up’ is insight (vipassanā), for it gives up defilements and aggregates by way of ‘abandoning by substitution of opposites’ (tadaṅga-pahāna). ‘Relinquishment as entering into’ is the Path (magga), for it enters into Nibbāna by way of taking it as an object. Or, it is called ‘giving up’ for two reasons: because of giving up the aggregates and defilements by way of ‘abandoning by eradication’ (samuccheda-pahāna), and because of entering into Nibbāna. Therefore, because it gives up defilements and aggregates, it is ‘pariccāga-vossagga’; because the mind enters into the element of Nibbāna, which is cessation, it is ‘pakkhandana-vossagga.’ Both of these meet in the Path. A person endowed with both is called ‘one contemplating relinquishment’ because of being endowed with this contemplation of relinquishment. With reference to such a person, it is said “paṭinissaggānupassī.” Anything in the world...
200:
‘Upādiyati’ means that one does not cling to, take hold of, or misapprehend even a single conditioned thing (saṅkhāra) through the power of craving. ‘Anupādiyā na paritassati’ means that because of not clinging, one does not yearn or tremble with the agitation of craving. ‘Paccattaññeva parinibbāyati’ means that one attains peace by the extinguishing of defilements by oneself. By the words ‘Khīṇā jātī’ (birth is exhausted) and so forth, only the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) of that Arahant is shown. In this way, the Blessed One, having been asked by Sakka, the Lord of Devas, about the preliminary practice of an Arahant in brief, made it light and easy, and taught it quickly and concisely.

‘Avidūre nisinno hoti’ means sitting in an adjacent gabled chamber (kūṭāgāra). ‘Abhisameccā’ means knowing by penetrating with wisdom. By these words, the meaning is: ‘Did this Sakka rejoice with understanding, or did he rejoice without knowing?’ Why did such a thought occur to that Elder (Mahāmoggallāna)? It is because the Elder did not hear the Blessed One’s answer to the question, but only heard Sakka, the King of Devas, rejoicing and saying, ‘So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.’ Sakka, the King of Devas, rejoiced with a very loud voice. If so, why was the Blessed One’s voice not heard? It is because of the nature of making it known only to the assembly. Indeed, when the Buddhas teach the Dhamma, although the voice is heard by the assembly as far as the edge of the contiguous universe, it does not go out even a finger’s breadth beyond the assembly. Why? With the intention that such sweet words should not be in vain. At that time, the Blessed One was sitting in the auspicious state chamber (siri-gabbha) of the seven-jeweled gabled mansion of Migāramātū. To the right of that chamber was the gabled chamber where the Elder Sāriputta resided, and to the left was the gabled chamber of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Because there were no gaps or openings in between, the Elder did not hear the Blessed One’s voice, but heard only Sakka’s voice.

‘Pañcahi tūriyasatehi’ means with five hundred five-fold musical instruments. A five-fold musical instrument is one endowed with these five factors: ātata, vitata, ātatavitata, susira, and ghana. Among them, ‘ātata’ refers to one-sided drums covered with leather, such as the bheri. ‘Vitata’ refers to two-sided drums. ‘Ātatavitata’ refers to stringed instruments such as the lute (paṇava). ‘Susira’ refers to hollow instruments such as the flute. ‘Ghana’ refers to solid instruments such as cymbals. ‘Samappito’ means approached or endowed. ‘Samangībhūto’ is a synonym for that same word. ‘Paricāreti’ means enjoying that prosperity and directing the sense faculties toward various objects. By these words, it means being endowed with five hundred musical instruments that are played while surrounding him...
201:
...and enjoying divine bliss. ‘Paṭipaṇāmetvā’ means having removed them, or having made them silent. How so? Just as nowadays faithful kings, upon seeing a venerable monk, dismiss the dancers saying, ‘Such and such a venerable one is coming; friends, do not sing, do not play, do not dance,’ Sakka also did the same upon seeing the Elder.

‘It has been a long time, dear Moggallāna, since you made this turn to come here.’ Such words are naturally affectionate greetings in the world. Indeed, worldly people, seeing someone who has arrived after a long time, or someone of a pleasing nature who has come though they have never come before, are accustomed to say, ‘From where has the master come? The master has come after a long time! How did you know the way to come here? Did you lose your way and arrive?’ and so forth. But this Sakka spoke thus because the Elder had indeed come before. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna indeed used to travel to the deva realms from time to time. In that context, ‘pariyāyamakāsi’ means he made a turn or occasion. ‘To come here’ means ‘Venerable sir, it has been a long time since you made the turn to come here.’ Saying, ‘This seat is prepared,’ he had a jeweled throne (maṇipallaṅka) of one league in size spread out and spoke thus.

In the phrase ‘Many are the duties and things to be done,’ those who have many duties are called ‘bahukicca.’ ‘Bahukaraṇīya’ is a synonym for that same term. ‘By my own duty’ means that his own personal duty is small and slight, not much. However, the duties concerning the devas are many. Indeed, starting from the ground, disputes concerning wish-fulfilling trees (kalparukkha), celestial maidens, and so forth are settled in the presence of Sakka. Therefore, wishing to show the distinction, he said, ‘Only by the duties of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.’ For the devas, daughters and sons are born in their laps; women who will serve at their feet are born on their beds; celestial maidens who will provide ornaments for them are born surrounding the beds; and those who perform services (veyyāvaccakara) are born inside the mansion. For these, there are no disputes. However, those who are born on the boundaries between territories, being unable to decide ‘This is mine’ or ‘This is yours,’ create a dispute and ask Sakka, the King of Devas. That Sakka says it belongs to the one whose mansion is nearer. If the distance to both mansions is equal, he says it belongs to the one who was standing and looking at his mansion. If he was not looking at even one, Sakka takes it as his own for the sake of cutting off the quarrel between the two. Referring to that, he said, ‘Only by the duties of the Tāvatiṃsa devas.’ Moreover, such recreational activities are also his duties.
202:
"It disappears from us very quickly" means that it is not seen by us, just like a visual form in the darkness. By this statement, he shows: "Venerable Sir, I do not remember the answer to that question." The Elder, reflecting, "Why does this Sakka show that he does not remember? Is he trying to avoid it?" then understood: "Devas are indeed very deluded. Being oppressed by the objects arising at the six sense-doors, they do not even know whether they have eaten or not, or whether they have drunk or not. In such a state, what is so strange about them forgetting this matter?"

Some teachers, however, say: "Because the Elder is a person respected and honored by Sakka, he spoke thus out of fear, thinking, 'The Elder might rebuke me, saying: Just now you went to the presence of the Buddha, the Supreme Person in the world, to learn the question, and now you have entered among the dancers.'" However, such a way of speaking is called deceit (kohaṅña). Such deceit does not exist in noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka). Therefore, it should be understood that he did not remember only because of his state of great delusion. Why did he remember later? It should be understood that he remembered because the Elder generated in that Sakka a sense of urgency (saṃvega) accompanied by joy (somanassa) and removed the darkness of delusion.

Now, Sakka says "Bhūtapubbaṃ" (In the past) and so on, to inform the Elder of the cause of his past existence. In those words, "samupabyūḷho" means a gathered assembly. "Asurā parājiniṃsu" means the Asuras reached defeat. When were these Asuras defeated? It was at the time when Sakka was reborn. It is heard that in a previous life, Sakka was a youth named Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha. That youth was wise and clever, and his conduct was like the conduct of a Bodhisatta. He took thirty-three men and performed meritorious deeds. One day, reflecting with his own wisdom, he cleared the rubbish from both sides of the place where people gathered in the middle of the village and made that place very delightful. Again, he had a pavilion built in that very place. Later, he had a rest house built. Leaving the village, he traveled for a gāvuta, half a yojana, three gāvutas, and up to a yojana, and together with those companions, he made the uneven roads even. All of them, being of one mind, performed many meritorious deeds such as building bridges where bridges were needed, and constructing pavilions, rest houses, ponds, and planting flower gardens in appropriate places. Magha fulfilled the seven vows (vatapada) and, upon passing away, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm together with his companions.
203:
At that time, the hosts of Asuras lived in the Tāvatiṃsa deva realm. All those Asuras were equal in lifespan and appearance to the devas. Seeing Sakka with his retinue, those Asuras thought, "New young devas who have just been reborn have arrived," and they prepared a great amount of liquor. Sakka gave a sign to the young devas: "We are those who have performed meritorious deeds and should not share with others; do not drink the strong liquor, only act as if you are drinking." They did as Sakka said. The foolish Asuras drank the strong liquor, became intoxicated, and fell into a deep sleep. Sakka gave a sign to the devas, had them grab those Asuras by their feet, and had them thrown down to the foot of Mount Sineru. At the base of Mount Sineru, there is an Asura realm equal in size to the Tāvatiṃsa deva realm. The Asuras live there. They also have a tree called the Citta-pāṭali (trumpet flower tree). When that tree blooms, they realize, "This is not Tāvatiṃsa; we have been deceived by Sakka." Saying, "Seize that Sakka!" those Asuras surrounded Mount Sineru and, when the devas were aroused, they climbed up like termites coming out from the base of an anthill.

In that war, sometimes the devas won, and sometimes the Asuras won. When the devas were victorious, they pursued the Asuras as far as the surface of the ocean. When the Asuras were victorious, they pursued the devas as far as the foot of the pillars at the top of Mount Sineru. In this particular battle, however, the devas were victorious and pursued the Asuras as far as the surface of the ocean. Sakka, having made the Asuras flee, established guards in five places. Having thus provided protection, he placed statues of Indra (Sakka) holding the vajra weapon at the foot of the pillars. From time to time, the Asuras would come up, and seeing those statues, they would think, "Sakka remains vigilant," and they would retreat from that very place.

"Tato paṭinivattitvā" means retreating from the place of victory. "Paricārikāyo" means the goddesses who perform tasks such as providing flowers and perfumes.

The Great King Vessavaṇa, being a very close and trusted friend of Sakka, went along with Sakka. "Purakkhatvā" means placing in front. "Pavisiṃsu" means that after entering, they stood looking through the half-closed doors.

"Friend Moggallāna, look also at the delightfulness of this Vejayanta Palace" means: "Friend Moggallāna, look at the delightfulness of this Vejayanta Palace; look at the golden pillars, silver pillars, gem pillars, coral pillars, ruby pillars, cat's eye pillars, pearl pillars, and pillars made of the seven treasures; and also the figures of wild animals in the lotus-shaped bowls made of gold and so on, which are on those very pillars..."
204:
Showing the delightful nature [of the palace] starting from the rows of pillars, he said this. Regarding the phrase "Yathā taṃ pubbekatapuññassa," the meaning is: just as a place of enjoyment should be adorned for one who has performed merit in the past, so it is adorned in this very way. The phrase "Atibāḷhaṃ kho ayaṃ yakkho pamatto viharati" means that he dwells very heedlessly, being excessively intoxicated by the power of the success of the retinue of dancers in his own palace.

"Iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāsi" means he performed a feat of psychic power. Having entered the water-kasiṇa attainment, he resolved by psychic power that the place where the palace stood should become water, and then struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe. Just as a bowl placed on the surface of water, when struck on its rim with a finger, wobbles, moves to and fro, and does not remain still; in this very way, the palace shook, trembled, and quaked. The pillars, beams, rafters, pinnacles, and brackets emitted a 'kara-kara' sound as if they were about to fall. Therefore, it is said: "Saṅkampesi sampakampesi sampavedhesi."

"Acchariyabbhutacittajātā" means that amazement and wonder arose, thinking, "Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how marvelous!" and they were filled with satisfaction and strong joy. "Saṃviggaṃ" means agitated. "Lomahaṭṭhajātaṃ" means the occurrence of hair standing on end; the meaning is that the body was covered with hairs standing upright like gems or ivory pegs fixed on a golden wall. This standing of hair on end can occur due to joy and also due to distress; however, here it arose due to joy. For the Elder Mahāmoggallāna performed that miracle in order to stir Sakka with the force of joy. Therefore, the meaning is: knowing that he was agitated and his hair stood on end with the force of joyful emotion.

"Idhāhaṃ, mārisa" is said because now the Elder Mahāmoggallāna had generated joyful emotion in Sakka and dispelled his darkness [of heedlessness], and Sakka, having reflected, spoke thus. "Friend, is this your teacher, the Blessed One?" (the deities asked). When asked, "Friend, where did you go?" you said, "To the presence of my teacher." While you remain in this celestial realm as if standing on one foot, you speak in this way; therefore they asked, "Friend, is this your teacher, the Blessed One?" Regarding the phrase "Sabbahmacārī me eso," although the Elder is a homeless monk, one who has fulfilled his aspiration and is a Chief Disciple, and Sakka is a householder, they are fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) by virtue of the practice of the Path; therefore he spoke thus.
205:
"If even your fellow practitioner is so powerful, how much more powerful must your teacher, the Blessed One, be!" Thus, having developed a desire to see the psychic miracles of the Teacher, they spoke in this way.

"Ñātaññatarassa" means to one among the well-known ones; for Sakka is one among those who are well-known. The rest of the words are clear in all the Pali texts. The Blessed One concluded the discourse according to the sequence of connections.

## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya,
## The Explanation of the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta is finished.
## 8. Explanation of the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta. Therein, regarding "diṭṭhigataṃ," although in the Alagaddūpama Sutta it was spoken of as a mere view, in this sutta it refers to the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). That monk [in the Alagaddūpama Sutta] was very learned, but this monk [Sāti] is of little learning. Being a reciter of the Jātakas, he heard the Blessed One relating the Jātakas and concluding them by saying, "Monks, at that time I was King Vessantara, I was Mahosadha, Vidhurapaṇḍita, Senakapaṇḍita, and King Mahājanaka." Then it occurred to him: "These forms, feelings, perceptions, and formations cease right there in each existence, but consciousness (viññāṇa) alone runs and wanders from this world to the next, and from the next world to this world." Thus the eternalist view arose in him. Therefore he said: "It is this very consciousness that runs and wanders, and no other."

But it was said by the Fully Enlightened One: "Consciousness is dependently arisen; it arises when there is a condition; without a condition, there is no arising of consciousness." Therefore, this monk speaks what was not spoken by the Buddha, strikes at the Wheel of the Conqueror (Jinacakka), obstructs the Knowledge of Fearlessness (Vesārajja-ñāṇa), deceives the people who wish to hear the Dhamma, and falling across the path of the Noble Ones, he practices for the harm and suffering of many. Just as when a great thief arises in a king's realm, he arises for the harm and suffering of many, so too in the Dispensation of the Conqueror...
206:
He should be known as one who has arisen as a thief of wrong view in the Buddha's Dispensation, for the harm and suffering of the multitude. "Many monks" refers to those monks living in the countryside who are alms-food eaters. "They approached him" means that they approached immediately, without even sitting down from where they heard the news, thinking, "If this monk gains a following, he might cause the Dispensation to disappear; let us dissuade him from his wrong view before he gains a faction."

"Sāti, what is that consciousness?" means "Sāti, which consciousness do you refer to? What kind of consciousness is it?" "Venerable Sir, it is that which speaks and feels, experiencing the results of good and bad deeds here and there" means "Venerable Sir, it is this very consciousness that speaks and feels, which experiences the results of wholesome and unwholesome deeds in various lives; this is the consciousness I refer to." "From whom (did you hear this)?" means "From which of the khattiyas, brahmins, merchants, workers, laypeople, monks, devas, or humans did you hear me teaching this?"

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks. Why did he address them? It is said that this thought occurred to the monk Sāti: "The Teacher calls me a 'worthless man' (mogha-purisa), but just because he says 'worthless man,' it does not mean there is no support (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits. For the Blessed One also admonished Upasena, the son of Vaṅganta, with the words 'worthless man,' saying, 'Worthless man, you have turned back too quickly to a life of abundance.' That elder, by striving and exerting himself later on, realized the six higher powers (abhiññā). I, too, will exert such energy and produce the paths and fruits." Then the Blessed One, wishing to show that this man is one whose conditions are cut off and who will not grow in the Dispensation, addressed the monks. The meaning of "Usmīkato" and so forth is just as stated below.

"Atha kho bhagavā" (Then the Blessed One) is also a separate sequence. It is said that this thought occurred to the monk Sāti: "The Blessed One says I have no support for the paths and fruits. What can be done if there is no support? The Tathāgatas do not teach the Dhamma only to those with support; they teach it to anyone. I will receive the advice of the Sugata from the Buddha and perform wholesome deeds that lead to the bliss of heaven." Then the Blessed One, preventing him from receiving the Sugata's advice by saying, "Worthless man, I do not give you advice or instruction," began this discourse. Its meaning should be understood in the same way as stated below. Now...
207:
The Blessed One, wishing to purify the view of the assembly, said, "Monks, I will question you in this Dispensation," and so forth. All of that should be understood in the same way as stated below.

Now, to show the conditioned nature of consciousness, he said, "Monks, whatever..." and so forth. Therein, "manañca paṭicca dhamme ca" means dependent on the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-mana) together with adverting (āvajjana) and the mental objects of the three planes. "Kaṭṭhañca paṭicca" (dependent on wood) and so forth is said for the purpose of illustrating with a simile. What does he show with that simile? He shows the absence of transmigration from one door to another. For just as a fire that burns dependent on wood burns only when there is the condition of fuel, and when that is absent, it is extinguished right there due to the deficiency of conditions, and it does not move to wood chips and the like to be called a "wood-chip fire" and so forth; in the same way, consciousness that arises dependent on the eye and forms arises only when there are conditions known as the eye, forms, light, and attention in that eye-door. When those are absent, it ceases right there due to the deficiency of conditions, and it does not move to the ear and the like to be called "ear-consciousness" and so forth. This method applies to all sections. Thus, the Blessed One refuted Sāti, saying, "I do not speak even of the mere transmigration between doors in the arising of consciousness, yet this worthless man Sāti speaks of transmigration between lives."

Having thus shown the conditioned nature of consciousness, now, wishing to show the conditioned nature of all five aggregates, he said, "Bhūtamidaṃ" (This has come to be) and so forth. Therein, "bhūtamidaṃ" means this group of five aggregates has been born, has come to be, and has been produced. He said, "Monks, do you also see that this has come to be?" "Tadāhārasambhavaṃ" means this group of five aggregates is arisen from nutriment (conditions), arisen from conditions; he asks, "Do you see that it arises only when there is a condition?" "Tadāhāranirodhā" means from the cessation of that condition. "Bhūtamidaṃ no su" means "Has this come to be, or has it not come to be?" "Tadāhārasambhavaṃ no su" means "Is that group of five aggregates that has come to be arisen from conditions, or is it not?" "Tadāhāranirodhā" means from the cessation of that condition. "Nirodhadhammaṃ no su" means "Is that thing of a nature to cease, or is it not?" "Sammapрaññāya passato" means for one who sees rightly with insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) through the actual function and characteristics that "this group of five aggregates has been born, has come to be, and has been produced." "Paññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ" means well seen with insight-wisdom in the same way as stated. Thus, taking the acknowledgement of those who reflected on those questions, he shows the conditioned nature of the five aggregates.

Now, wishing to ask about the state of being free from craving for those five aggregates which have been well seen with that wisdom as being conditioned and subject to cessation, he said, "Imaṃ ce tumhe" (If you hold this...) and so forth. Therein, "diṭṭhiṃ" (view) means...
208:
Insight right view is pure through the seeing of nature. It is purified through the seeing of causes. "Allīyetha" means one would dwell clinging by means of craving and views. "Kelāyetha" means one would dwell playing or cherishing by means of craving and views. "Dhanāyetha" means one would fall into greed, desiring it like wealth. "Mamāyetha" means one would produce possessiveness by means of craving and views. "For the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of grasping" means that the Dhamma which I have taught, which is like a raft for the purpose of crossing over the four floods, was not taught for the purpose of grasping by the power of attachment. In the phrase "Would you then know it?", the white side (the side of purity) should be understood by way of the reverse.

Now, wishing to show the cause of those aggregates, he said, "Monks, there are these four nutriments," and so on. That too has the meaning already stated. For example, if a person is asked, "Do you know this person?", and he replies, "I know not only this person, but I also know his mother, and his mother's mother," thus knowing by way of lineage, he is said to know well. In the same way, the Blessed One knows not only the aggregates alone, but he also knows the cause of the aggregates, and the cause of those causes; thus he knows the entire succession of causes. Wishing to show that power of a Buddha, and now to show the succession of causes, he said, "Monks, these four nutriments also," and so on. That too has the meaning already stated. "Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be... p... the mass of suffering arises." In this place, the discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) should be expanded. That discourse has already been expanded in the Visuddhimagga.

"When this exists, that comes to be" means when this cause such as ignorance exists, this effect such as volitional formations comes to be. "With the arising of this, that arises" means with the arising of this cause such as ignorance, this effect such as volitional formations arises. Therefore, he said, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be... p... the mass of suffering arises." Having thus shown the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), now wishing to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), he said, "Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance," and so on. There, "avijjāya tveva" means only of ignorance. "Asesavirāganirodhā" means the remainderless cessation, the cessation by way of non-arising, through the Path (Magga) known as fading away (virāga). "Cessation of volitional formations" means the cessation of volitional formations by way of non-arising. With the cessation of volitional formations thus ceased, there is the cessation of consciousness. To show that with the cessation of consciousness etc., name-and-form etc. are also ceased, he said, "With the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness," and so on, and thus of this entire mass of suffering...
209:
...it is said, "there is cessation." In that phrase, "kevalassa" means entire, or pure, or devoid of a being. "Dukkha-kkhandhassa" means of the mass of suffering. "There is cessation" means there is non-arising.

"When this does not exist," and so on, should be understood by the method of the opposite of what was already stated.

Having thus spoken of the round and the cessation of the round, now, for one who knows this round of conditions with its twelve factors by means of the Path together with insight, that running back and forth which is abandoned—wishing to ask about the absence of that running back and forth, he said, "Monks, would you...", and so on. There, "knowing thus" means knowing thus by means of the Path together with insight. "Seeing thus" is a synonym for that same term. "Pubbanta" means the prior portion, meaning the past aggregates, elements, and bases. "Would you run back?" means would you run back by the power of craving and views? The rest has been expanded in the Sabbāsava Sutta.

Now, wishing to ask about their state of being unshakable in that knowledge of the Path and insight, he said, "Monks, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you say, 'The Teacher is our respected one (garu)'?", and so on. There, "garu" means one who is heavy/venerable, one who must be followed even if unwillingly. "Samaṇa" means the Buddha-Samaṇa. "Would you point to another teacher?" means having such a perception as "This teacher is not able to accomplish our task," would you point to another external teacher? "Of many recluses and brahmins" means having such a perception, (the doctrines) of many sectarian recluses and brahmins. "Vata-kotūhala-maṅgala" refers to the undertaking of vows, curiosity about views, and auspicious signs seen, heard, or sensed. "Would you return to those things as having essence?" means having such a perception as "These things are the essence," would you return to them? It means would you again take up those things that have been relinquished. "Known by oneself" means known by one's own knowledge. "Seen by oneself" means seen by one's own eye of wisdom. "Realized by oneself" means made clear and manifest by oneself. "I have led you" means, monks, I have led you to Nibbāna, I have made you reach it, by means of this Dhamma which has the nature of being visible here and now (sandhiṭṭhika) and so on. The meaning of the terms "sandhiṭṭhika" etc. has been expanded in the Visuddhimagga. "This was said in dependence on this" means this statement was said in dependence on the fact of its being known by yourselves and so on.

Why did he begin with the words, "Monks, as for the three..."? Was the teaching not already brought to its climax by way of the round and the cessation of the round below? Yes, it was brought to its climax. However, this is a separate...
210:
The connection (anusandhi) is as follows: All beings dwelling in this world are greatly confused regarding rebirth (paṭisandhi). Thinking, "I shall destroy the cause of their confusion and make rebirth clear," the Buddha began this teaching. Alternatively, ignorance (avijjā) is the root of the round of suffering (vaṭṭa), and the arising of a Buddha (buddhuppāda) is the root of liberation from the round (vivaṭṭa). Thus, even after showing ignorance as the root of the round and the arising of a Buddha as the root of liberation, He began this teaching with the intention, "Once more, I shall bring the teaching to its climax by way of the round and its cessation."

In that Pali, 'sannipātā' means by way of coming together in unison, as a group. 'Gabbhassa' refers to the being arising in the mother's womb. 'Avakkanti hoti' means the occurrence of arising. In some places, the word 'gabbha' refers to the mother's womb. As the Buddha said:

"The youth who dwells in the womb for the first night,
Goes forth as if rising from bed; as he goes, he does not return."

In some places, 'gabbha' refers to the being arising in the womb. As He said: "Ānanda, other women carry the fetus (gabbha) in their womb for nine or ten months and then give birth." In this context, only the being is intended; referring to that being, it is said 'gabbhassa avakkanti hoti' (the descent of the fetus occurs).

'Idha' means in this world of beings. The phrase 'mātā ca utunī hoti' (and the mother is in her season) is said in reference to the fertile period. It is said that in the place of women called the womb, when a child is about to be born, a large blood-clot forms, breaks, and flows out, whereby the site becomes pure. When the site is pure, if the parents come together even once, it is the time (khetta) when conception can occur for up to seven days. At such a time, a child can indeed be conceived even through physical contact such as holding hands, holding the hair-braid, or touching the limbs.

'Gandhabba' refers to the being who has arrived there. 'Paccupaṭṭhito hoti' (is present) does not mean standing nearby watching the union of the parents. The meaning here is that a certain being, driven by the mechanism of Kamma, is ready to be born in that place.

'Saṃsayena' means with great anxiety for life (doubt), thinking, "Will I be healthy, or will my son be?" The statement "Bhikkhus, this is blood" was spoken in reference to the fact that at that time, the mother's blood reaches that place and, due to the power of love for the child, becomes white milk.

'Vaṅkaka' is a small toy plow for children in small villages. 'Ghaṭikā' refers to the game of hitting a short stick with a long stick (tip-cat).
