'Mokkhacika' refers to the game of turning somersaults, either in the air by holding a stick or on the ground by placing the head down. 'Ciṅgulaka' refers to a windmill (fan) made of palm leaves or similar materials that revolves when hit by the wind.
211: A paper windmill (cingulaka) that revolves when struck by the wind is called paribbhamanacakkaṃ. Pattāḷhakaṃ refers to a small leaf cup; with that leaf cup, they play by measuring sand and so forth. Rathakaṃ is a small chariot. Dhanukaṃ is also a small bow. Sārajjati means it gives rise to lust (rāga). Byāpajjati means it gives rise to ill-will (byāpāda). Anupaṭṭhitakāyasati means not establishing mindfulness in the body (kāyasati). Parittacetaso refers to one with an unwholesome mind limited by defilements. Yatthassa te pāpakā means he does not know or attain that attainment of fruition in which those evil states cease. Anurodhavirodhaṃ refers to lust and hatred. Abhinandati means he delights through the power of craving; through the power of craving, he speaks excessively (abhivadati), saying “Oh, what happiness!” and so forth. Ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati means he remains attached, swallowing and finishing it by grasping through the immersion of craving. Whether it be pleasant feeling or neutral feeling, let him delight; but how does he delight in painful feeling? One who grasps, thinking “I am suffering, this is my suffering,” is said to delight in it. Uppajjati nandī means craving arises. Tadupādānaṃ means that very craving is called clinging (upādāna) in the sense of grasping. “With clinging as condition, existence...” and so forth; in showing the arising of the mass of suffering, the Blessed One once again shows the round of Dependent Origination with its two links and three sections. 410-4. Now, to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), He said: “Monks, here a Tathāgata arises in the world,” and so forth. Therein, appamāṇacetaso means one who has an immeasurable supramundane mind, meaning one endowed with the path-consciousness (maggacitta). “Monks, you should remember this teaching on the liberation through the destruction of craving (taṇhāsaṅkhaya-vimutti) taught by me in brief; do not be negligent,” He said. In this sutta, the teaching is called “liberation” (vimutti) because it is the cause for attaining liberation. Mahātaṇhājālataṇhāsaṅghāṭapaṭimukkaṃ: Craving itself is called “the great net of craving” (mahātaṇhājāla) in the sense of being woven together, and “snare” (saṅghāṭa) in the sense of being firmly joined. Thus, consider this monk Sāti, the fisherman's son, as caught in this net of craving, this snare of craving. It means he has entered into it, he is included within it. The remaining words have clear meanings. ## In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, ## The Explanation of the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta is finished.
212:
## 9. Commentary on the Mahā-assapura Sutta

This sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," is the Mahā-assapura Sutta. In that sutta, "Angesu" refers to the princes who were inhabitants of the Anga country; a certain district that was the dwelling place of those princes is also called "Angā" by way of popular usage; the meaning is "in that Anga country." A market town of the Anga country known by the city name Assapura is referred to as "Assapuraṃ nāma angānaṃ nigamo"; the meaning is that the Buddha dwelt making that market town his resort for alms. The Blessed One said this: He spoke these words, "Monks, people recognize you as 'recluses, recluses' (samaṇa, samaṇa)," and so forth.

Why did he say this? It is said that the people in that market town were faithful and devoted, cherishing the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. They praised even a novice (sāmaṇera) ordained that very day as if he were an elder (thera) of a hundred years. In the morning, when they saw the Saṅgha of monks entering for alms, even those who were going to the fields carrying fans, ploughs, and so forth, or those entering the forest carrying axes and so forth, would set aside those implements. They would sweep the rest house, the pavilion, or the foot of a tree which served as a sitting place for the Saṅgha of monks, prepare seats, set out clear drinking water, and having invited the Saṅgha of monks to sit, they would offer gruel, food, and so forth. Only after seeing off the Saṅgha of monks who had finished their meal would they take up those implements such as axes and fans and go to the fields or the forest to perform their work. Even at their place of work, they had no other talk besides that concerning the virtues of the Triple Gem.

The eight persons—the four established in the paths and the four established in the fruits—are called the Noble Saṅgha (Ariya-saṅgha). They spoke only in praise of the Saṅgha of monks, saying, "They are endowed with such virtue, such conduct, and such practice; they are conscientious, amiable, and possessed of noble qualities." Whether they were sitting in front of their houses after returning from work and having their evening meal, or whether they were sitting inside their bedrooms, they spoke only in praise of the Saṅgha of monks. The Blessed One, seeing the respectful service of those people, spoke these words wishing to urge the Saṅgha of monks toward [worthiness of] alms-food and respectful treatment.

"Ye dhammā samaṇakaraṇā ca brāhmaṇakaraṇā ca" means those qualities which, when undertaken and fulfilled, make one a recluse (samaṇa) whose evils are stilled, and a brahmin (brāhmaṇa) whose evils are barred. "Monks, these three are the things to be done by a recluse..."
213:
...things to be done by a recluse (samaṇakaraṇīya). What are the three? The undertaking of the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the undertaking of the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the undertaking of the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Thus (in the Anguttara Nikāya 3.82), he taught the things to be done by a recluse. Those qualities also indeed make one a recluse. In this [Mahā-assapura Sutta], however, the teaching is expanded by way of moral shame (hiri), moral dread (ottappa), and so forth. In the phrase "Evaṃ no ayaṃ amhākaṃ," the word "no" is merely a particle. The meaning is "Thus this [practice] is for us." The two terms "Mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā" (great fruit, great benefit) are identical in meaning. "Avañjhā" means not empty (amogha). The term "Saphala" (fruitful) is the same in meaning as "avañjhā." If a quality has no fruit, it is called "vañjhā" (empty). "Saudrayā" means a quality that has growth (savaḍḍhi). This term is a synonym for "saphalatā" (fruitfulness). "Evañhi vo bhikkhave sikkhitabbaṃ" means "Monks, thus you should train."

In this way, the Blessed One, through this much of the text, spoke in praise of the qualities such as moral shame and moral dread. Why did he speak so? He spoke for the purpose of cutting off the path of speech (to end disputes). If some foolish monk, newly ordained, were to say: "The Blessed One says, 'Live undertaking the qualities of moral shame and moral dread'; what indeed is the benefit in living by undertaking them?"—it is for the purpose of cutting off that monk's path of speech [that he spoke]. And this following is the benefit: because these qualities, when undertaken and fulfilled, make one a "Samaṇa" because of the stilling of defilements, and a "Brāhmaṇa" because of having barred evil. They bring about the gain of the four requisites. They fulfill the great benefit of the donors who offer the four requisites. They make the monkhood not empty, but fruitful and conducive to growth. Thus he spoke in praise. This is the summary of the commentary in this sutta. For the detailed explanation, it should be understood in the same manner as taught in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

"Hirottappena" means by way of moral shame (hiri) and moral dread (ottappa), which are explained in detail (in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī) as "that which is ashamed of what one should be ashamed of, and that which dreads what one should dread." Furthermore, in this context, moral shame has its origin within oneself (ajjhatta-samuṭṭhāna), while moral dread has its origin externally (bahiddhā-samuṭṭhāna). Moral shame has self as the governing principle (attādhipateyya), while moral dread has the world as the governing principle (lokādhipateyya). Moral shame is established in the nature of conscientiousness (lajjā), while moral dread is established in the nature of fear [of wrongdoing] (bhaya). The detailed explanation of this is given in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga. Moreover, these two qualities are called "world-protecting qualities" (lokapāla-dhamma) because they protect the world. As he said: "Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world. Which two? Moral shame and moral dread. Monks, these two bright qualities protect the world. Monks, if these two bright qualities did not protect the world, there would be no recognition here of 'mother,' or 'maternal aunt,' or 'paternal aunt,' or 'teacher's wife,' or 'wives of respected ones'..."
214:
The world would fall into confusion like goats, sheep, chickens, pigs, dogs, and jackals (Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.9). These very qualities are preached in the Jātaka as "Devadhamma" (Divine Virtues).

As it is said:
"Those endowed with shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), established in pure states, peaceful and good people in the world, are called 'Devadhamma'" (Jātaka 1.1.6).

For the Venerable Mahācunda, however, these were shown as the practice of effacement (sallekha-paṭipadā). As it is said: "Others may be shameless, but here we shall be shameful; thus effacement should be practiced. Others may be fearless of wrongdoing, but here we shall be fearful of wrongdoing; thus effacement should be practiced" (Majjhima Nikāya 1.83). These same qualities were shown as the ordination by exhortation (ovādūpasampadā) for the Venerable Mahākassapa. It was said: "Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'A keen sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing shall be present in me towards the elders, those of middle standing, and the newly ordained monks.' Thus, Kassapa, you should train yourself" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.154). In this Mahā-assapura Sutta, however, these are shown as the duties of a recluse (samaṇadhamma).

Since the goal of recluseship (sāmaññattha) does not reach its summit by this much alone, the Buddha said, "Bhikkhus, you might think thus," and so forth, in order to show other qualities that make one a recluse. In that text, regarding the goal of recluseship, first in the Saṃyutta Nikāya: "Bhikkhus, what is recluseship (sāmañña)? It is this Noble Eightfold Path. That is to say: Right View ... Right Concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called recluseship. And what, bhikkhus, is the goal of recluseship (sāmaññattha)? The destruction of greed, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion; this, bhikkhus, is called the goal of recluseship" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.36). Thus, the Path is called "sāmañña," while the Fruits and Nibbāna are called "sāmaññattha." In this context, however, it should be understood that both the Path and the Fruits together are spoken of as the goal of recluseship. "Ārocayāmi" means I declare. "Paṭivedayāmi" means I make known.

In the phrase "Our bodily conduct is pure," bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra) is of two kinds: pure and impure. When a monk kills living beings, takes what is not given, or engages in sexual misconduct, his bodily conduct is called impure; this is prohibited by way of the paths of action (kammapatha). When one strikes or harasses another with the hand...
215:
...with a clod, a stick, or a weapon, his bodily conduct is called impure; this also is prohibited by the boundaries of the training rules. In this Sutta, without speaking of both of those, only supreme effacement (parama-sallekha) is preached. When a monk, with the intention of threatening or driving away crows that are drinking water from a water pot or eating food from an alms-bowl, raises his hand, a stick, or a clod, his bodily conduct is impure. The opposite is called pure. "Uttāna" means evident or manifest. "Vivaṭa" means open or uncovered. Both terms illustrate purity. "Na ca chiddavā" means being consistent at all times, without gaps or flaws in between. "Saṃvuta" (restrained) means closed by shutting the doors against defilements, not for the purpose of concealing one's faults.

Regarding verbal conduct (vacīsamācāra), when a monk speaks lies, utters slander, speaks harsh words, or engages in idle chatter, his verbal conduct is called impure. This is prohibited by way of the paths of action (kammapatha). When a monk speaks disparagingly or insultingly using words such as "householder," "slave," or "servant," his verbal conduct is called impure. This is prohibited by the boundaries of the training rules. In this Sutta, without speaking of both of those, only supreme effacement is preached. When a monk, being asked by a junior monk or a novice, "Venerable sir, have you seen our preceptor?" replies with the intention of joking, "Friends, many monks and nuns were quarreling in a certain place; your preceptor has gone off carrying a bundle of vegetables for sale on his head," and so forth, his verbal conduct is impure. The opposite is called pure.

Regarding mental conduct (manosamācāra), when a monk is covetous, has a mind of ill-will, or holds wrong views, his mental conduct is called impure. This is prohibited by way of the paths of action. When a monk takes pleasure in gold and silver deposited nearby, his mental conduct is called impure. This also is prohibited by the boundaries of the training rules. In this Sutta, without speaking of both of those, only supreme effacement is preached. When a monk [harbors] sensual thoughts or...
216:
If one thinks thoughts of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) or thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka), that monk's mental conduct (manosamācāra) is impure. The opposite conduct is called pure.

Regarding livelihood (ājīva), if a monk, for the sake of livelihood, practices medicine, runs errands, performs surgery, applies ointments, cooks oil, or makes a living through the twenty-one types of improper search (anesanā), or if he eats by begging [improperly], his livelihood is called impure. This conduct is already prohibited by the bond of the training rules (sikkhāpada). In this sutta, however, without speaking of both of those, supreme effacement (parama-sallekha) is taught. Indeed, if a monk obtains ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, etc., and consumes them after storing them, thinking, 'It will be for tomorrow or the day after'; or if, seeing neem shoots and the like, he says to the novices, 'Eat the neem shoots,' and the novices, thinking 'The elder wishes to eat,' prepare them in a permissible way and offer them; or if he says to young monks or novices, 'Friends, drink some water,' and they, thinking 'The elder wishes to drink water,' wash the water-conch and offer it—the livelihood of one who consumes such things is also impure. The opposite livelihood is called pure.

'Knowing the measure' (mattaññū) means knowing the measure, knowing what is suitable, and knowing the proper amount in seeking, receiving, and consuming.

'Devoted to wakefulness' (jāgariyam-anuyutta) means dividing the night and day into six parts, allowing for sleep in only one part, and being devoted and applied to wakefulness in the remaining five parts. In the context of the 'lion's posture' (sīha-seyyā), there are four types of reclining: the sensualist's posture (kāmabhogī-seyyā), the hungry ghost's posture (peta-seyyā), the lion's posture (sīha-seyyā), and the Tathāgata's posture (tathāgata-seyyā). Among these four, 'Monks, for the most part, sensual beings sleep on their left side' refers to the sensualist's posture. Among them, there is almost no one who sleeps on the right side.

'Monks, for the most part, hungry ghosts sleep on their backs' refers to the hungry ghost's posture. Because hungry ghosts have very little flesh and blood and are bound by a mass of bones, they cannot sleep on one side and sleep only on their backs.
217:
“Monks, for the most part, the lion, the king of beasts, places its tail between its thighs and sleeps on its right side” (A.iv.246) refers to the lion's posture (sīha-seyyā). The lion, the king of beasts, being possessed of great power, places its two front paws in one place and its two back paws in one place, tucks its tail between its thighs, and after noting the position where the front paws, back paws, and tail are placed, it rests its head upon the front paws and sleeps. Even after sleeping the whole day, when it wakes up, it wakes without being startled. It raises its head and observes the position where its front paws and other limbs were placed. If any limb has moved from its original position, it becomes displeased, thinking, “This is not worthy of your birth or your courage,” and it sleeps right there again, not going out for prey. But if they remain unmoved, it becomes very joyful and satisfied, thinking, “This is worthy of your birth and your courage.” It then rises, stretches with a lion's grace, shakes its mane, roars the lion's roar three times, and departs for prey. Reclining in the fourth jhāna is called the Tathāgata's posture (tathāgata-seyyā). Among these, the lion's posture is presented here. This is called the noble posture because it is the posture of one with great power. “Foot upon foot” means the left foot upon the right foot. “Overlapping” (accādhāya) means placing it slightly beyond. This is because if ankle touches ankle or knee touches knee, pain frequently arises, the mind does not become one-pointed, and the reclining is uncomfortable. If placed overlapping so they do not touch, pain does not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the reclining is comfortable; therefore, it was said thus.

The passage beginning with “covetousness in the world” (abhijjhaṃ loke) was explained in detail in the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta.

In the simile, “Monks, just as...”, “having taken a debt” means borrowing money with interest. “Would make an end of it” means making it so that the ends are gone. This means one should return everything in its entirety, so that not even a farthing's worth of remnant remains for them. “Because of that” means because of being debt-free. Reflecting, “I am now debt-free,” he gains strong joy and attains strong happiness. Therefore, it was said, “He would gain joy, he would attain happiness.”

“Affliction” (ābādha) is so called because it oppresses all four postures as if cutting with a saw due to the arising of painful feelings; one who has that is called “afflicted” (ābādhika). Arising from that affliction...
218:
He is afflicted with suffering. 'Adhimattagilāno' means being severely ill. 'Nacchādeyya' means not enjoying (food) due to being oppressed by a severe disease. 'Balamattā' means mere strength; it implies that there is no strength in his body. 'Tatonidānaṃ' means because of the cause of being free from illness. Indeed, for that person who reflects, 'I am free from illness,' those two (joy and gladness) arise. Therefore, it is said, 'He would obtain joy, he would attain gladness.' 'Na cassa kiñci bhogānaṃ vayo' means that there would be no loss of his wealth, even as much as a kākaṇika coin. 'Tatonidānaṃ' means because of the cause of being released from bonds. The remaining terms should be understood in all instances according to the method already mentioned. 'Anattādhīno' means not being one's own master. It means not being allowed to do anything according to one's own wish. 'Parādhīno' means having to follow the will of others. It means existing only according to the will of another. 'Na yena kāmaṃ gamo' means that although there is a desire to go to a certain direction one wishes, one does not get the chance to go there. 'Dāsavyā' means from the state of a slave. 'Bhujisso' means being one's own master (owning oneself). 'Tatonidānaṃ' means because of the cause of being one's own master. 'Kantāraddhānamaggaṃ' means a long journey through a waterless desert. 'Tatonidānaṃ' means because of the cause of reaching a safe land.

In this passage, 'When these five hindrances are not abandoned,' the Blessed One shows the unabandoned hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) as being like a debt, and the remaining hindrances as being like disease and so on. The similarity in that simile is as follows: A man takes a debt from others and squanders it. When the creditors say, 'Pay the debt,' or speak harsh words, or when he is bound or beaten, he is unable to resist at all and must endure everything. Indeed, that debt itself is the cause of his endurance. In the same way, a person who is infatuated with an object through sensual desire clings to that object with the attachment of craving. Even if he is spoken to with harsh words by the owners of the house, or is bound or beaten, he must endure everything. Indeed, that sensual desire itself is the cause of his endurance. It is like women who are oppressed and beaten by the masters of the house. Thus, sensual desire should be seen as being like a debt.

Just as a person afflicted with bile disease, even when given honey, sugar, and so on, cannot enjoy their taste because of the bile disease, and only spits them out saying, 'How bitter! How bitter!' In the same way, a person with a corrupted mind (one with ill-will) does not accept the advice even when being slightly admonished by teachers and preceptors who desire his welfare, and saying things like, 'You are troubling me too much,' he leaves the monkhood. Just as that man afflicted with bile disease cannot enjoy the taste of honey and sugar...
219:
...because he is aching with anger, he does not enjoy the flavor of the Dispensation, such as the bliss of jhāna. Thus, ill-will (byāpāda) should be regarded as being like a disease. Furthermore, just as a man imprisoned in a jail on the day of a planetary festival does not see the beginning, middle, or end of the festival; even if he is released from prison the next day and hears people saying, 'Yesterday's festival was delightful, the dancing and singing were wonderful,' he cannot join the conversation. Why? Because he did not experience the festival. In the same way, a monk overcome by sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) does not know the beginning, middle, or end of the Dhamma being preached through various methods. When the Dhamma talk is over and he hears people praising the Dhamma, saying, 'The Dhamma preaching was wonderful, the reasons and similes were wonderful,' he cannot join the conversation. Why? Because he did not experience the Dhamma talk due to the power of sloth and torpor. Thus, sloth and torpor should be regarded as being like a prison.

Furthermore, a slave playing at a festival, if ordered, 'There is this urgent matter to be done, go there quickly; if you do not go, I will cut off your hands and feet or your ears and nose,' must go quickly and does not get to enjoy the beginning, middle, or end of the festival. Why? Because he is dependent on another's will. In the same way, a monk who is not proficient in the Vinaya enters the forest for the sake of seclusion (viveka), but if a doubt arises even regarding allowable meat, perceiving it as unallowable, he must abandon seclusion and go to a Vinaya expert to purify his virtue. That monk does not enjoy the bliss of seclusion. Why? Because he is oppressed by restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca). Thus, restlessness and remorse should be regarded as being like slavery.

Furthermore, a man traveling on a difficult journey, seeing places where people have been robbed and beaten by thieves, becomes suspicious and fearful even at the sound of a stick or a bird, thinking, 'The thieves have come.' He walks, stops, and turns back; the distance he has turned back is often more than the distance he has traveled. That person may or may not reach safety with great difficulty and hardship. In the same way, a person in whom doubt (vicikicchā) has arisen regarding the eight points, doubting in such ways as, 'Is he really the Buddha, or is he not?' cannot accept with faith and decision. Because he cannot accept it, he cannot reach the Path (magga) or the Fruit (phala).
220:
Just as on a long journey through a wilderness, one might repeatedly experience hesitation and wavering, thinking, "Are there robbers or not?" and being unable to penetrate with wisdom, thus giving rise to a state of agitation in the mind that hinders reaching a safe haven; in the same way, doubt (vicikicchā) also repeatedly causes hesitation and wavering, thinking, "Is he truly the Buddha or not?" and so on. By being unable to penetrate with wisdom and giving rise to a state of agitation in the mind, it hinders the attainment of the noble state (ariyabhūmi), which is a place of safety. Therefore, doubt should be understood as being like a long journey through a wilderness.

Now, regarding the phrase "monks, like freedom from debt," the Blessed One shows that the abandoning of the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) is like freedom from debt, and the abandoning of the remaining hindrances is like freedom from illness and so on. The similarity is as follows: Suppose a man takes a loan and engages in business. When his business prospers and succeeds, he thinks, "This debt is indeed a source of anxiety." He then pays back the debt along with the interest and has the record of the debt destroyed. From that time on, no one sends a messenger or a letter to him. Even if he sees the creditors, he may stand up from his seat if he wishes, or not stand up if he does not wish. Why? Because he no longer has any connection or attachment to those creditors. In the same way, a monk, reflecting that "this sensual desire is indeed a source of anxiety," develops the six things as taught in the Satipaṭṭhāna and abandons the hindrance of sensual desire. For the monk who has thus abandoned sensual desire, just as a man freed from debt feels no fear or agitation upon seeing his creditors, he no longer has any attachment or bond to the property of others. Even when seeing divine forms, defilements do not arise. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of sensual desire as being like freedom from debt.

Furthermore, just as a man afflicted with a bile-related illness recovers from that disease through medical treatment and thereafter enjoys the taste of honey, sugar, and so on; in the same way, a monk, reflecting that "this ill-will (byāpāda) indeed causes harm," develops the six things and abandons the hindrance of ill-will. For the monk who has thus abandoned ill-will, just as a man freed from a bile-related illness enjoys sweet things like honey and sugar with delight, when he learns the training rules such as the Ācārapannatti, he accepts them respectfully with his head and practices them with delight. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of ill-will as being like freedom from illness.
221:
Just as a man who was imprisoned on a festival day might think on a subsequent festival day, "In the past, due to the fault of negligence, I was imprisoned and could not enjoy that festival; now I shall be diligent," so that his enemies find no opportunity. Being thus diligent, he enjoys the festival and utters an exclamation of joy, "Oh, what a festival! Oh, what a festival!" In the same way, a monk, reflecting that "this sloth and torpor (thīna-middha) indeed causes great harm," develops the six things and abandons the hindrance of sloth and torpor. For the monk who has thus abandoned sloth and torpor, just as a man freed from bonds enjoys the beginning, middle, and end of a festival for seven days, he enjoys the beginning, middle, and end of the festival of the Dhamma and reaches Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of sloth and torpor as being like liberation from bonds.

Furthermore, just as a slave, relying on a friend, gives wealth to his masters and makes himself a free man (bhujissa), and from then on does whatever he wishes; in the same way, a monk, reflecting that "this restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) indeed causes great harm," develops the six things and abandons restlessness and remorse. For the monk who has thus abandoned restlessness and remorse, just as a free man does whatever he wishes and no one can prevent him by force, he practices the path of renunciation (nekkhamma-paṭipadā) as he pleases, and restlessness and remorse can no longer prevent him by force. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of restlessness and remorse as being like becoming a free man.

Just as a strong man, taking his portable wealth and being well-equipped with weapons and accompanied by a retinue, enters a wilderness, and robbers flee just by seeing him from afar; and that man safely crosses that wilderness and reaches a safe haven, being joyful and happy; in the same way, a monk, reflecting that "this doubt (vicikicchā) indeed causes harm," develops the six things and abandons doubt. For the monk who has thus abandoned doubt, just as a strong man, well-equipped with weapons and accompanied by a retinue, being fearless and regarding robbers as no more than blades of grass, safely departs and reaches a safe land; in the same way, having crossed the wilderness of misconduct (duccarita), he reaches the supreme safe land, the Deathless Nibbāna. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke of the abandoning of doubt as being like reaching a safe land.

"This very body" refers to this physical body (karajakāya). "Drenches" means he moistens and saturates it with the rapture and pleasure (pīti-sukha) that arises everywhere. "Suffuses" means he makes it flow all around. "Fills" means he fills it as one would fill a bellows with air. "Pervades" means everywhere...
222:
It pervades. 'Sabbāvato kāyassa' refers to the body of that monk, which consists of all its parts. In the place where the succession of clung-to matter (upādinnaka-rūpa) occurs, there is not even a tiny spot the size of an atom following the skin, flesh, and blood that is not pervaded by the bliss of the first jhāna. 'Dakkho' refers to a skilled bathman who is proficient in making, mixing, and kneading bathing powders. 'Kaṃsathāle' means in a vessel made of some kind of bronze. An earthen vessel is not used as a simile because it is not durable and tends to break when kneading. 'Paripphosakaṃ paripphosakaṃ' means by sprinkling water again and again. 'Sanneyya' means that one should hold the bronze vessel with the left hand and sprinkle water in the right proportion with the right hand, kneading it repeatedly to form a ball. 'Sinehānugatā' means followed by the moisture of water; 'sinehaparetā' means saturated with the moisture of water internally and externally; 'santarabāhirā' means pervaded by the moisture of water in all places, both inside and out. 'Na ca pagghariṇī' means that the water does not drip in drops. It means it can be held with the hand or with two or three fingers, and can even be placed in a waist-pocket.

In the simile for the bliss of the second jhāna, 'ubbhitodako' means having water welling up; it does not mean water that breaks through and rises from below, but rather water that wells up from within. 'Āyamukhaṃ' is the path through which water comes. 'Devo' refers to the rain. 'Kālenakālaṃ' means at all times, or once every half-month or once every ten days. 'Dhāraṃ' refers to the raindrops. 'Nānuppaveccheyya' means would not let enter, or would not rain down. 'Sītā vāridhārā ubbhijjitvā' means cool water welling up and filling that lake. Water rising from below breaks through repeatedly and agitates the water. Water entering from the four directions brings old leaves, grass, branches, and wood, making the water turbid. Rainwater also agitates the water with the falling of raindrops and the formation of bubbles. But water that arises as if created by psychic power, remaining calm, does not have any spot where it says 'it pervades here' and 'it does not pervade there.' Therefore, there is no place that is not pervaded. In that simile, the physical body (karajakāya) is like the lake, and the bliss of the second jhāna is like the water. The rest should be understood in the same manner as the previous method.
223:
In the simile for the bliss of the third jhāna, 'uppalinī' means that there are lotuses in this pond. The same method applies to the other two terms (paduminī, puṇဍarīkinī). In this context, among the white, red, and blue lotuses, any unspecified lotus is just an 'uppala.' A lotus with fewer than a hundred petals is called 'puṇဍarīka.' A lotus with a hundred petals is called 'paduma.' Alternatively, there is a decision here that regardless of the number of petals, a white lotus is 'paduma' and a red lotus is 'puṇဍarīka.' 'Udakānuggatāni' means those (lotuses) that have not emerged above the water. 'Antonimuggaposīnī' means growing and flourishing while remaining submerged under the water. The remaining words should be understood in the same manner as the previous method.

In the simile for the bliss of the fourth jhāna, in the phrase 'parisuddhena cetasā pariyodātena,' it should be understood as 'parisuddha' (purified) because it is free from the defilements, and 'pariyodāta' (bright/cleansed) because it is radiant. The phrase 'odātena vatthena' (with a white cloth) is spoken for the purpose of the pervasion of the 'utu' (physical essence/aura). Pervasion of 'utu' is not possible with a soiled cloth; the pervasion of 'utu' is strong only with a cloth that has been freshly washed and purified. In this simile, the physical body (karajakāya) should be understood as the cloth. The bliss of the fourth jhāna should be understood as the pervasion of 'utu.' Therefore, just as when a man who has bathed well sits down covering himself, including his head, with a clean cloth, the 'utu' (warmth/aura) from his body pervades the entire cloth so that there is no part of the cloth not pervaded; likewise, it should be understood here that there is no part of the monk's physical body not pervaded by the bliss of the fourth jhāna. Alternatively, the fourth jhāna mind is like the cloth, and the matter produced by that mind is like the pervasion of 'utu.' Just as in some places, even if the white cloth does not touch the body, the whole body is pervaded by the 'utu' produced from that body; likewise, it should be understood here that the entire physical body of the monk is pervaded by the subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa) produced by the fourth jhāna.

In the simile for the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), because the actions performed on that day are clear, only the three villages visited on that day are taken. There, the person who has attained the knowledge of past lives should be understood like the man who went to the three villages. The three realms of existence (tayo bhavā) should be understood like the three villages. Just as the actions performed by that man in the three villages on that day are clear to him, so too the actions performed in the three realms of existence are clear to the monk who sits with his mind directed toward the knowledge of past lives.
224:
In the simile of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), 'dve agārā' means two houses. 'Sadvārā' means having doors facing each other. 'Anucaṅkamante' means walking back and forth. 'Anuvicarante' means wandering here and there; alternatively, it should be understood as the act of exiting this house and entering that house, or exiting that house and entering this house.

In that simile, the two houses with facing doors are like death (cuti) and rebirth (paṭisandhi). The man with sight is like one who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa). Just as when a man with sight stands between two houses and looks, the people entering and exiting the houses are clear to him, so too, when one who has attained the knowledge of the divine eye increases the light and looks, it is the time when beings passing away and being reborn are clear. If it is asked, "Are those deaths and rebirths clear to the knowledge or to the person?", the answer is that they are clear to the knowledge. It is only because they are clear to that knowledge that it is said they are clear to the person.

In the simile of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), 'pabbata-saṅkhepe' means on a mountain peak. 'Anāvilo' means being free from mud. 'Sippi-sambukaṃ' refers to oysters and shells. 'Sakkhara-kathalaṃ' refers to gravel and potsherds. 'Maccha-gumbaṃ' refers to shoals and groups of fish. In the phrase 'tiṭṭhantampi carantampi', the gravel and potsherds only remain still, while the others both move and stay still. Just as when there are cows standing or lying down at intervals, one says "these cows are moving," referring to the moving cows and thereby including the others as moving; similarly, referring to the gravel and potsherds which are always still, the other two are also said to be still. And referring to the movement of the other two, the gravel and potsherds are also said to be moving. In that simile, just as oysters, shells, etc., are clear to a man with sight standing on the shore and looking, so should be understood the time when the Four Noble Truths are clear to a monk who sits directing his mind toward the destruction of the taints.

Now, wishing to mention the name of the one whose taints are destroyed (an Arahant) through seven aspects along with their characteristics and qualities, the Buddha said, "Monks, this monk is called an ascetic (samaṇa)..." and so on. In that passage, regarding "Monks, in this way a monk is an ascetic," etc.: Monks, in this way a monk is an 'ascetic' (samaṇa) because he has calmed (samita) evil. He is a 'brahmin' (brāhmaṇa) because he has barred (bāhita) evil. He is a 'bathed one' (nhātaka) because he has washed away the defilements. He is a 'knower' (vedagū) because he has gone beyond (or known) unwholesome states through the knowledges (vedas) known as the four path-knowledges. For that very reason, the Buddha said, "To him, they are known," and so on. He is a 'learned one' (sottiyo) because he has discarded the defilements,
225:
meaning because of being completely free (from them) and because of having abandoned them. He is a 'noble one' (ariya) because he has cut off the defilements, meaning because he has destroyed them. He is 'worthy' (arahaṃ) because he is far from those defilements, meaning because he has become distant from them. The remaining text is clear in all the Pali passages.

## In the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary known as Papañcasūdanī,
## the Explanation of the Mahā-assapura Sutta is finished.
## 10. Explanation of the Cūḷa-assapura Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Cūḷa-assapura Sutta. The reason for its delivery is the same as the previous (Mahā-assapura) sutta. 'Samaṇa-sāmīci-paṭipadā' means the practice that is suitable for ascetics, the practice that is in accordance with ascetics.

In the terms such as 'samaṇa-malānaṃ', those (unwholesome) states, when they arise, make the ascetics soiled and stained; therefore, they are called 'stains of an ascetic' (samaṇa-mala). Because of these states, ascetics are corrupted and severely defiled; therefore, they are called 'faults of an ascetic' (samaṇa-dosa). These states, having arisen, make the ascetics like dregs and devoid of essence, causing them to wither; therefore, they are called 'dregs of an ascetic' (samaṇa-kasaṭa). 'Āpāyikānaṃ ṭhānānaṃ' refers to the causes that lead to rebirth in the states of deprivation (apāya). 'Duggati-vedaniyānaṃ' refers to the causes for experiencing resultant feelings in the woeful planes (duggati).

Regarding the weapon named 'Mataja' (born of the dead): people take sharp iron and rub iron against iron, then mix those iron filings with meat and feed them to cranes (koñca-sakuṇa). Those birds, being unable to defecate, die. If they do not die, they are beaten to death. Then, their bellies are cut open, washed with water, and the filings are retrieved, mixed with meat, and fed to them again. In this way, they make a weapon with the iron filings obtained after feeding them seven times. Skilled blacksmiths, receiving a high wage, forge that weapon. Because it is produced from a dead bird, it is called 'Mataja'; it is extremely sharp. 'Pīta-nisitaṃ' means it has both 'drunk' water (been quenched) and been well-sharpened on a stone. 'Saṅghāṭiyā' means with a sheath. 'Sampārutaṃ' means covered. 'Sampaliveṭhitaṃ' means wrapped all around.
226:
*Rajojallika* refers to one who bears dirt and dust that has accumulated on the body. *Udakorohaka* refers to one who descends into the water three times a day (with the intention of washing away evil). *Rukkhamūlika* refers to one who habitually lives at the foot of a tree. *Abbhokāsika* refers to one who habitually lives in the open air. *Ubbhaṭṭhaka* refers to one who remains standing upright. *Pariyāyabhattika* refers to one who eats only once a month or once every half-month. All these are spoken of in terms of the practices of external sectarian views. This is because, in this Dispensation (Sāsana), a monk who wears robes is not called a "*Saṅghāṭika*" (in that external sense). Practices such as bearing dirt and dust do not exist in this Dispensation at all. The word of the Buddha is named only as "*Buddhavacana*," and not as Vedas (Mantras). Only the extent of being a tree-root dweller (*rukkhamūlika*) or an open-air dweller (*abbhokāsika*) is obtained here. Even those terms, *rukkhamūlika* and *abbhokāsika*, are spoken of in the context of external sects.

"*Jātam eva naṃ*" refers to that person who is just born on that very day. "*Saṅghāṭikaṃ kareyyuṃ*" means they should perform the act of wearing the *saṅghāṭi* by both dressing in and covering themselves with stitched cloth. This is the method in all Suttas.

Seeing oneself as pure is what is meant by "*visuddhamattānaṃ samanupassati*." However, one should not yet be called "pure" (*visuddha*) at that stage. "*Pāmojjaṃ jāyati*" means the arising of a state of gladness. "*Pamuditassa pīti*" means that for one who is glad, rapture arises, shaking the entire body. "*Pītimanassa kāyo*" refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*) of the person associated with rapture. "*Passambhati*" means becoming tranquil and free from distress. Experiencing physical and mental happiness is what is meant by "*sukhaṃ vedeti*." "*Cittaṃ samādhiyati*" means the mind of the person who is happy through this bliss of renunciation (*nekkhamma-sukha*) becomes concentrated, as if reaching absorption (*appanā*). "*So mettāsahagatena cetasā*" means that the teaching, which began below by way of the defilements, enters into the development of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra-bhāvanā*) by way of sequence, just as rainwater falling on a mountain flows into a river. Whatever should be said regarding that *brahmavihāra-bhāvanā* has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*. In the phrase "*Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, pokkharaṇī*," it should be understood that while in the *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta* the Path is compared to a lotus pond, in this Sutta, the Dispensation (*Sāsana*) is compared to it. "*Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hoti*" means that because all defilements have been stilled, one becomes a recluse in the ultimate sense (*paramattha-samaṇa*). The meanings of the remaining words are clear in all places.

## The Explanation of the Cūḷa-assapura Sutta is Finished.
## The Explanation of the Fourth Division is Finished.
227:
## 5. Cūḷayamakavagga

## 1. Sāleyyaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

This Sutta beginning with "*Evaṃ me sutaṃ*" is the *Sāleyyaka Sutta*. Therein, "*Kosalesu*" refers to the princes who reside in the region named Kosala. A single region that is the dwelling place of those princes is also called "Kosala" by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī-sadda*); (the Blessed One was staying) in that Kosala region. Ancient teachers, however, say: In the past, having heard that the prince named Mahāpanāda did not even smile upon seeing various dancers, the King said, "Whoever can make my son laugh, I shall adorn him with all ornaments." Then, even abandoning their plows, a great multitude of people gathered and showed various games for more than seven years, but they were unable to make the prince laugh. Then, Sakka sent a celestial dancer. That celestial dancer showed a divine dance and made him laugh. Then those people departed toward their respective dwelling places. When they saw friends and relatives on the way, they performed greetings and asked, "Sirs, is it well? Sirs, is it well?" (*Kaccì bho kusalaṃ?*). Therefore, taking that word "*kusalaṃ kusalaṃ*" as the basis, that region is called "Kosala."

"*Cārikaṃ caramāno*" means wandering on a journey at an unhurried pace. "*Mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ*" means together with a large community of monks, numbering hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands, without a fixed limit. "*Brāhmaṇagāma*" refers to both a village where Brahmins gather and a fief village of Brahmins. Here, a gathering village is intended. "*Tadavasarī*" means he arrived there, he reached it. Since a monastery is not specifically mentioned here, there must be a forest grove suitable for Buddhas not far from that village; it should be understood that the Teacher went to that forest grove. "*Assosuṃ*" means they heard or perceived; they knew according to the sequence of the sound of words reaching the ear-door. "*Kho*" is a particle used either for emphasis or merely as a filler. Therein, by way of emphasis...
228:
They simply heard; it should be understood that there was no obstacle to their hearing. It is merely the smoothness of the syllables to complete the sentence.

Now, to reveal the meaning of what they heard, it is said: "Friends, the ascetic Gotama..." and so on. In this context, he is known as "Samaᅀa" (ascetic) because he has calmed evil. "Khalu" is a particle used in the sense of hearsay. "Bho" is merely a form of address among them. "Gotama" is an indication of the Blessed One's clan. Therefore, in the phrase "Friends, the ascetic Gotama...", the meaning should be understood as "Friends, it is said that the ascetic of the Gotama clan has arrived." The word "Sakyaputta" indicates the Blessed One's noble family. "Sakyakulā pabbajito" indicates that he went forth out of faith. It means he went forth out of faith, having abandoned that family while it was still prosperous and not overcome by any loss. What follows has the same meaning as previously stated. In the phrase "Taᅁ kho pana", the accusative case is used in the sense of describing such a state; it means "of that Venerable Gotama". "Kalyāᅀa" means endowed with good qualities, meaning "excellent". "Kittisadda" is the sound of fame itself, or the sound of praise from devas and humans. "Abbhuggata" means it has risen, pervading the world including the devas. How? "Thus is that Blessed One... (pe)... the Buddha, the Blessed One."

In this context, this is the connection of the words: That Blessed One is "Arahaᅁ" for this reason, "Sammāsambuddha" for this reason... (pe)... "Bhagavā" for this reason. It means for such and such reasons. In that regard, because he is remote from defilements, because he has killed the enemies (the defilements) and destroyed the spokes (of the wheel of rebirth), because he is worthy of requisites, and because he does no evil in secret—for these reasons, that Blessed One should be known as "Arahaᅁ". Having laid down the matrix (mātikā) in this manner, all these words are explained in detail in the Buddhānussatiniddesa of the Visuddhimagga; therefore, the detailed explanation should be taken from there.

"Sādhu kho pana" means it is indeed good; it means it brings benefit and happiness. "Tathārũpānaᅁ arahataᅁ" means such as that Venerable Gotama is; of such Arahants who are rare to see even in hundreds of thousands of millions of aeons, whose bodies are delightful, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, adorned with the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, who are never tiring to behold, who have an extremely sweet voice of Dhamma, and who have gained the name "Arahant" in the world by attaining true qualities. "Dassanaᅁ hotĩ" means even the mere seeing by opening clear and gentle eyes is truly good. If, with a Brahma-voice endowed with eight factors...
229: ...thinking, "If we could hear even a single word of the Dhamma from the Blessed One as he preaches, it would be even better," they approached where the Blessed One was. This means they came with joyful minds, having abandoned all other tasks. "They said this"—there are two kinds of questions: the householder's question and the non-householder's (renunciant's) question. Among them, the householder's question comes in this way: "Venerable Sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome?" The non-householder's question comes in this way: "Venerable Sir, these five aggregates of clinging..." These brahmins and householders, wishing to ask a householder's question suitable for themselves, said: "Venerable Gotama, what is the cause, what is the condition?" and so on. To them, the Blessed One, wishing to answer the question briefly at first so that they would not be able to grasp it easily, said: "Householders, it is because of unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct," and so on. Why did the Blessed One answer in a way that they could not easily grasp? Because they considered themselves wise. If he had explained the meaning in detail so that they could grasp it without first setting down the matrix (mātikā), they might look down on the teaching, thinking it is too shallow. They might become people who say, "If we were to preach, we could preach just like this." Therefore, the Blessed One first answered the question briefly so that they could not grasp it easily. Then, when the brahmins and householders, unable to grasp it, requested a detailed teaching, he said: "Householders, in that case..." to teach in detail. In that passage, "Tena hi" is a particle in the sense of cause. It means "Because you request me (I shall preach)." "Threefold" means in three parts. "By body" means through the body-door. "Adhammacariyā visamacariyā" means uneven conduct known as unrighteous conduct. Here, the word-meaning is: practicing what is not Dhamma is "adhammacariyā", meaning the doing of unrighteousness. Practicing unevenly, or the practice of uneven kamma, is "visamacariyā". Because it is both unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, it is called "adhammacariyā visamacariyā". In this way, the meaning should be understood in all dark and bright terms. "Luddo" means a harsh person. "Dāruᅀo" means a cruel person. "Lohitapāᅀĩ" means the hands of one who deprives another of life are smeared with blood. Even if they are not smeared, such a person is still called "bloody-handed". "Devoted to killing and striking" means in the killing of others...
230:
He is one who is inclined towards and remains fixed in striking, killing others, and using weapons. Adayāpanno means one who has reached a state of being devoid of pity and compassion.

'Yaṃ taṃ parassa' refers to whatever property belongs to another. Paravittūpakaraṇaṃ refers to the kind of utility, requisites, or goods of another that produce pleasure. Gāmagataṃ vā means property kept within a village. Araṇyagataṃ vā means property kept in the forest, on treetops, mountain peaks, and so on. Adinnaṃ means property not given by those others, whether by body or by speech. In the term theyyasaṅkhātaṃ, thena means a thief (cora). The state of a thief is theyya; it is a designation for the intention to steal. The two terms saṅkhā and saṅkhāta are identical in meaning, being designations for a category (koṭṭhāsa), as in 'perceptions are the source of the categories of mental proliferation' (saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā), etc. Because it is both the state of stealing and a designation, it is called theyyasaṅkhāta. It means a specific mental category known as the intention to steal. Although this term is in the nominative case, because it stands in the sense of the instrumental case, it should be understood in meaning as theyyasaṅkhātena (with the intention to steal).

Māturakkhitā and the terms following it refer to a girl who, when her father is lost or dead, is looked after by her mother with food, clothing, etc., with the thought, 'When she reaches the proper age, I will give her to a suitable family'; such a girl is called māturakkhitā (guarded by the mother). In this same manner, piturakkhitā (guarded by the father) and others should be understood. Families of equal status make agreements even while the fetuses are in the womb: 'If I have a son and you have a daughter, she shall not go elsewhere; she shall be for my son only.' A woman thus reserved while still in the womb is called sassāmikā (having a master/husband). A woman for whom a penalty has been set regarding a village, a house, or a street, such as 'Whoever goes to the woman of such a name shall be fined this much,' is called saparidaṇḍā (subject to a fine). A woman who, at the very least, is encircled by even a mere garland by someone who throws it over her with the thought, 'This one shall be my wife,' is called mālāguṇaparikkhittā (encircled by a garland). One who commits a transgression with such women according to the characteristics of sexual misconduct mentioned in the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta is a wrongdoer.

Sabhāgato means one who is present in an assembly hall (sabhā). Parisāgato means one who is present in the midst of a gathering. Ñātimajjhagato means one who is present in the midst of relatives who are heirs. Pūgamajjhagato means one who is present in the midst of guilds (senī). Rājakulamajjhagato means one who is present in the midst of the royal court, in the High Court (Mahāvinicchaya).
231:
(He stands in the midst of) officials. Abhinīto means being brought for the purpose of questioning. Sakkhipuṭṭho means being questioned after being made a witness. 'Come, good man' is merely a form of address. 'For his own sake or for the sake of another' means for the sake of himself or another, due to reasons involving limbs such as hands and feet, or due to the reason of wealth (referring to telling lies). In the phrase āmisakiñcikkhahétu, āmisa is intended as gain. Kiñcikkha means any small bribe. It means for the sake of a bribe as small as a partridge, a quail, a lump of ghee, or a lump of fresh butter. He is one who speaks a lie even while knowing it.

'To divide these people' means speaking what was heard from these people to cause them to divide. 'To divide those people' means speaking what was heard from those people to cause them to divide. Thus, he is one who causes division among those who are united or between two friends. 'One who encourages those already divided to divide further' means one who provides support and shows reasons for those already divided not to reconcile, saying, 'You have done well by abandoning him; if you had not, within a few days he would have caused you great harm.' Vaggārāmo means having a place of delight in factions (division). Vaggarato means delighting in factions. Vagganandī means rejoicing upon seeing or hearing those who are divided. 'Speech that causes division' means speaking words that cause even united beings to divide or break apart, words that are the cause of quarrels.

Aṇḍakā (boils/excrescences) refers to words that arise like boils through the fault of speaking insults and disparagement, just as boils arise on a diseased tree. Kakkasā means rotten speech. Just as a rotten tree is rough and sheds powder, so too is this speech rough; it enters as if rubbing against the ear. Therefore, it is called 'harsh speech' (kakkasā). Parakaṭukā means speech that is bitter, unpleasant, and provocative of anger to others. Parābhisajjanī means speech that, like a crooked thorny branch, pierces the vital spots and causes others to be stuck, preventing even those who wish to leave from going. Kodhasāmantā means speech that is close to anger. Asamādhisamvattanikā means speech that does not lead to either absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). Thus, all these are synonyms for faulty speech.

Akālavādī means one who speaks at an improper time. Abhūtavādī means one who speaks what is not true. Anatthavādī means one who speaks what is not connected to a reason (unbeneficial). Adhammavādī means one who speaks what is not the nature of things (not in accordance with Dhamma)...
232:
An 'avinayavādī' is one who speaks words unrelated to the discipline of restraint (asaṃvara-vinaya). 'Anidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ' refers to one who speaks words that are not fit to be stored in the casket of the heart. 'Akālena' refers to one who speaks at an improper time, either before or after the appropriate time for speaking. 'Anapadesaṃ' refers to speech that is devoid of references to the Suttas. 'Apariyantavatiṃ' refers to speech that is without limit; setting aside the Sutta or Jātaka, one brings in an illustration or a story related to that Sutta and speaks only extraneous talk. The Sutta that was laid down remains merely laid down. One reaches a state where it must be said, 'Is he preaching a Sutta or a Jātaka? We see neither the end nor the beginning of that Sutta.'

For example, the branches of a banyan tree (nigrodha) send down aerial roots wherever they reach. Having taken root where they descended, they grow again. In this way, they spread for half a league or even a league. As they spread further and further, the original main tree perishes, and only the lineage of branches remains. Similarly, this Dhamma preacher is called a 'Banyan Dhamma preacher' (nigrodha-dhammakathika). Having merely introduced the Sutta, he proceeds by wandering around with peripheral talk. If a person, though speaking much, can bring out and explain, 'This was said for this meaning,' then it is proper for him to speak much. 'Anatthasaṃhitaṃ' refers to speech that is not connected with welfare.

'Abhijjhātā hoti' means one who looks with covetousness. 'Aho vata' is an indeclinable used in the sense of longing. In this covetousness, the course of action (kammapatha) is not yet broken merely by looking. However, when one inclines it towards oneself, thinking, 'O, may this thing be mine! May I have power over this thing!', then the course of action is broken; this is the meaning intended here.

'Byāpannacitto' means one with a ruined mind, a corrupt mind. 'Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappo' means one with mental intentions corrupted by ill-will. 'Hanyantu' means 'may they be killed.' 'Vajjhantu' means 'may they meet with destruction.' 'Mā vā ahesuṃ' means 'may they not exist at all.' Here too, the course of action is not broken merely by getting angry. It is only when one thinks, 'May they be killed,' etc., that the course of action is broken. Therefore, it is said thus.

'Micchādiṭṭhiko' means one with unwholesome vision. 'Viparītadassano' means one with perverted vision. 'Natthi dinnaṃ' is said with reference to the absence of the fruit of what is given. 'Yiṭṭhaṃ' refers to a great sacrifice. 'Hutaṃ' refers to an offering made with gifts. Both of these...
233:
...he rejects them with reference only to the absence of fruit. 'Sukatadukkhaṭānaṃ' means of wholesome and unwholesome deeds well-done or ill-done. 'Phalaṃ vipāko' means that which is called the fruit of benefit (ānisaṃsa-phala) or the fruit of result (vipāka-phala); he says that it does not exist. 'Natthi ayaṃ loko' means for one established in the next world, this present world does not exist. 'Natthi paro loko' means for one established in this world, the next world does not exist; it intends to show that all beings are annihilated right there in each existence. 'Natthi mātā natthi pitā' is said by way of the absence of fruit for right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) or wrong practice (micchā-paṭipatti) towards those parents. 'Natthi sattā opapātikā' means there are no beings who are born by way of passing away and reappearing. 'Sayam abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedenti' means those persons who, having realized for themselves through higher knowledge this world and the next world, proclaim them—he says they do not exist, thus showing the non-existence of Omniscient Buddhas. By this much, the ten-based wrong view is described.

'Pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya' and the other seven courses of action have been explained in detail in the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta. Non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) and the others have clear meanings.

'Sahabyataṃ upapajjeyyaṃ' means one should reach the state of being together. 'Brahmakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ' means of the Brahmas born in the plane of the first jhāna. 'Ābhānaṃ devānaṃ' means there are no separate Brahmas named Ābhā; it is just a designation for the Brahmas born in the Parittābhā, Appamāṇābhā, and Ābhassara realms. As for the term 'Parittābhānaṃ' etc., they are not taken together but are taken separately to distinguish those Brahmas. The same method applies to terms like 'Parittasubhānaṃ'. In this way, the Blessed One, having shown the destruction of the taints (āsava), concluded the teaching by crowning it with Arahantship.

Standing at this point in the Sutta, the celestial realms should be combined. First, by way of the three jhāna planes, there are nine Brahma worlds; five Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes) and four Ārūpa (Formless) realms make nine; thus there are eighteen. Together with the Vehapphala realm, there are nineteen. If the Asaññasatta (Unconscious) realm is included, there are twenty Brahma worlds. Thus, together with the six kāmāvacara (sensuous) heavens, there are twenty-six celestial realms. The Blessed One showed the arising of all those beings through the ten wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha).

Among those celestial realms, in the six kāmāvacara realms, arising occurs only through the ripening of the three types of good conduct (sucarita). In the higher celestial and Brahma realms, however, these courses of action act by way of strong dependence (upanissaya)...
234: The ten wholesome courses of action are taught as being virtue itself. This is because for one who possesses virtue, the preliminary preparation for kasiṇa meditation is successful. Established in virtue, having performed the preliminary preparation for kasiṇa and producing the first jhāna, one is reborn in the realm of the first jhāna. By developing the second jhāna and so forth, one is reborn in the realm of the second jhāna and so on. Making the fine-material sphere jhāna (rūpāvacara jhāna) the basis and developing insight (vipassanā), one established in the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is reborn in the five Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). Making the fine-material sphere jhāna the basis and producing the immaterial sphere attainments (arūpāvacara samāpatti), one is reborn in the four immaterial realms. Making the fine-material or immaterial jhānas the basis and developing insight, one reaches the fruit of arahantship (arahatta). However, the realm of unconscious beings (asaññasatta) is not mentioned here because it is the practice of ascetics and wanderers outside the Dispensation. The remaining words in all places have clear meanings. ## The Commentary on the Sāleyyaka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. ## 2. Verañjaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Verañjaka Sutta. Therein, 'Verañjakā' refers to the residents of Verañjā. 'For some business or other' (kenacid-eva karaṇīyena) means for some unspecified task. All the rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the previous sutta. Specifically, in this sutta, the teaching is given based on the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), such as 'one who walks unrighteously, one who walks unevenly.' In the previous sutta, however, the teaching was based on the Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna); this is the distinction. The remaining words are just the same. ## The Commentary on the Verañjaka Sutta in the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya, is finished. ## 3. Mahāvedalla Sutta Vaṇṇanā. The sutta beginning with 'Thus have I heard' is the Mahāvedalla Sutta. Therein, 'Venerable' (āyasmā) is a term of respect and deference. 'Mahākoṭṭhika' is the name of that Elder. 'Emerging from seclusion' (paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito) means emerging from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). In the phrase 'unwise, unwise' (duppañño duppañño), there is no such thing as 'corrupted wisdom'; it means one without wisdom, one devoid of wisdom. 'To what extent, indeed' (kittāvatā nu kho) is an inquiry into the delimitation of the cause; by how much measure thus...
235:
...is it said' is the meaning. That question (pucchā) is of five kinds: the question to illuminate the unseen (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā), the question to compare the seen (diṭṭhasandandanā-pucchā), the question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā), the question for seeking agreement (anumati-pucchā), and the question from the desire to explain (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). The distinction between these questions is as follows:

What is the question to illuminate the unseen? By nature, a characteristic is unknown, unseen, unweighed by knowledge, unjudged, unmanifested, and unclarified; one asks a question for the purpose of knowing, seeing, weighing, judging, manifesting, and clarifying that characteristic. This is called the question to illuminate the unseen.

What is the question to compare the seen? By nature, the characteristic of a thing is already known, seen, weighed by knowledge, judged, manifested, and clarified; yet one asks a question for the purpose of comparing it with other wise people. This is called the question to compare the seen.

What is the question to cut off doubt? By nature, one has fallen into uncertainty and doubt, being of two minds, thinking, 'Is it thus, or is it not? What is it? How is it?'; he asks a question for the purpose of cutting off that doubt. This is called the question to cut off doubt.

'What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent? Impermanent, Bhante.' A question asked during a Dhamma teaching after taking such an agreement from others is called the question for seeking agreement.

'Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?' A question of the Blessed One who, having himself asked the community of monks, desires to answer it himself, is called the question from the desire to explain. Among these questions, the question to compare the seen is intended in this sutta.

The reason is that the Elder, sitting in his day-quarters, formulated the questions himself and resolved them himself, bringing this sutta from the beginning to the end. Some people are only able to formulate a question but cannot resolve it; some can resolve it but cannot formulate it; some can do neither; and some can do both. Among them, the Elder was certainly able to do both. Why? Because of his great wisdom. Indeed, in this Dispensation, the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder Mahākaccāyana, the Elder Puṇṇa, the Elder Kumārakassapa, the Elder Ānanda, and this very Venerable Elder reached a distinguished position by relying on great wisdom. It is not possible for one endowed with only a little wisdom...
236:
For a monk to reach the pinnacle of the disciple's perfection of knowledge, it is possible only for one of great wisdom. Being such a person of great wisdom, the Elder Sāriputta attained that position. Indeed, there is no one equal to that Elder in wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One placed the Elder Sāriputta in the foremost position, saying: ‘Monks, among my disciple monks who possess great wisdom, Sāriputta is the foremost.’

Similarly, a monk endowed with only a small amount of wisdom is unable to analyze and elaborate in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One, in accordance with the Omniscient Knowledge. However, one of great wisdom is able to do so. Being such a person of great wisdom, the Elder Mahākaccāna became capable in that regard. Therefore, the Blessed One placed the Elder Mahākaccāna in the foremost position, saying: ‘Monks, among my disciple monks who elaborate in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief, Mahākaccāna is the foremost.’

Similarly, a monk endowed with only a small amount of wisdom is unable to preach the Dhamma by bringing forth the ten subjects of discourse and analyzing the seven purifications. However, one of great wisdom is able to do so. Being such a person of great wisdom, the Elder Puᅇᅇa sat upon the decorated Dhamma-seat in the midst of the fourfold assembly, holding an ornate fan, and preached the Dhamma with grace, like the full moon. Therefore, the Blessed One placed the Elder Puᅇᅇa in the foremost position, saying: ‘Monks, among my disciple monks who are Dhamma preachers, this Puᅇᅇa, the son of the Brahmin lady Mantāᅇĩ, is the foremost.’

Similarly, a monk endowed with only a small amount of wisdom, when preaching the Dhamma, cannot go beyond this or that point, moving like a blind man holding the end of a staff, or like someone walking on a narrow wooden bridge only a foot wide. One of great wisdom, however, can establish a single four-line verse, bring forth similes and reasons, and preach the Tipiᅡaka Word of the Buddha, turning it upside down and inside out. Being such a person of great wisdom, the Elder Kumārakassapa established a single four-line verse, brought forth similes and reasons, and connecting them together, preached the Tipiᅡaka Word of the Buddha, turning it upside down and inside out, as if making flowers of five colors bloom in a great lake, or as if lighting a lamp with a thousand wicks on the summit of Mount Sineru...
237:
...preaching while turning it upside down and inside out. Therefore, the Blessed One placed that Elder in the foremost position, saying: ‘Monks, among my disciple monks who are ornate speakers (cittakathika), Kumārakassapa is the foremost.’

Similarly, a monk endowed with only a small amount of wisdom is unable to learn even a four-line verse in four months. A monk of great wisdom, however, can learn a hundred or even a thousand words while standing on a single spot. Because of his great wisdom, the Elder Ānanda, while standing for the duration of a single step, could learn sixty thousand words and fifteen thousand verses at once, having heard them only once without asking again, as if pulling and gathering flowers from a vine. Whatever he learned of the Buddha's words remained exactly as it was learned, like an inscription carved on a stone slab, or like lion's fat placed in a golden jar. Therefore, the Blessed One placed the Elder Ānanda in the foremost position, saying: ‘Monks, among my disciple monks who possess a good course of action, who are mindful, who are resolute, who are of great learning, and who are attendants, Ānanda is the foremost.’

Similarly, a monk endowed with only a small amount of wisdom is unable to reach the pinnacle of the fourfold analytical insights. A monk of great wisdom, however, is able to do so. Because of his great wisdom, the Elder Mahākoᅡᅡhita reached the vast and infinite analytical insights through the power of penetration of the Path and Fruit, inquiry, hearing, and prior effort. Therefore, the Blessed One placed the Elder Mahākoᅡᅡhita in the foremost position, saying: ‘Monks, among my disciple monks who have attained the analytical insights, Mahākoᅡᅡhita is the foremost.’

Thus, because of his great wisdom, the Elder was capable of both raising questions and resolving them. That Elder Mahākoᅡᅡhita, sitting in his daytime retreat, raised all the questions himself and resolved them himself, bringing this Mahāvedalla Sutta to completion from the beginning. He thought: ‘This Dhamma teaching is indeed beautiful. I shall compare it with my elder brother, the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta. After such comparison, this Sutta, established with a single view and a single intention by the two of us, will be extremely profound and firm like a stone umbrella. It will be of great benefit, like a boat placed at a ferry for those wishing to cross the four floods, or like a noble chariot drawn by a thousand horses for those wishing to travel on a journey.’ Thus, he asked the questions for the purpose of comparing views. Therefore, it is said: ‘In this context, the questioning for the purpose of comparing views is intended.’
238:
Regarding the term "nappajānāti" (does not understand), the meaning is: because one does not understand distinctly, one is called "duppañño" (unwise or of poor wisdom). This same method should be understood for all terms. "Does not understand: 'This is suffering'" means: one does not distinctly understand the Truth of Suffering according to its true nature, function, and characteristic, such as "This is suffering," "This is the extent of suffering," and "There is no suffering beyond these phenomena of the three realms."

"Does not understand: 'This is the origin of suffering'" means: one does not distinctly understand according to its true nature, function, and characteristic that craving (taṇhā), which produces the suffering of the process of existence, is the Truth of the Origin, in the sense that "Suffering arises because of this cause."

"Does not understand: 'This is the cessation of suffering'" means: one does not distinctly understand according to its true nature, function, and characteristic that Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of both [suffering and its origin], is the Truth of Cessation, in the sense that "This suffering and this origin of suffering cease upon reaching this state called Nibbāna."

"Does not understand: 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering'" means: one does not distinctly understand the Truth of the Path according to its true nature, function, and characteristic, in the sense that "This practice of the Eightfold Path leads to Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering."

In the subsequent sections as well, the meaning should be understood in this same manner. In brief, it should be understood that here, the person who practices the meditation on the Four Noble Truths is being discussed.

Indeed, this person learns the Four Noble Truths by listening to them in the presence of a teacher. He learns and applies himself thus: "Excluding craving, the phenomena belonging to the three realms are the Truth of Suffering; craving is the Truth of the Origin; Nibbāna, which is the non-occurrence of both, is the Truth of Cessation; and the Path that leads to Nibbāna while fully understanding the Truth of Suffering and abandoning the Truth of the Origin is the Truth of the Path." Among those Four Truths, the first two truths (Suffering and Origin) are called the 'round' (vaṭṭa), and the latter two truths (Cessation and Path) are called the 'ending of the round' (vivaṭṭa). Insight (vipassanā) application occurs only in the 'round,' not in the 'ending of the round.' Therefore, when this person applies his mind, he applies it to the Truth of Suffering.

Defining the Truth of Suffering as the five aggregates such as materiality (rūpa), he enters through the method of meditation on the elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna) and defines: "The four great elements and the derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) based on the four great elements are called materiality." He defines feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa) that take that materiality as an object as 'mentality' (nāma). Thus, like splitting a twin palm tree, he defines: "These two phenomena alone are mentality and materiality (nāma-rūpa)."

Then, considering that this mentality-materiality is not without cause but has causes and conditions, he defines the causes and the conditionally arisen phenomena thus: "What is its cause? Phenomena such as ignorance (avijjā) and so forth." Having done so, he applies the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa): "All phenomena are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having been." Then, he applies the three marks: they are suffering (dukkha) because of the mode of being oppressed by rise and fall, and they are non-self (anattā) because of the mode of being uncontrollable. While investigating through the sequence of insight (vipassanā), he reaches the Supramundane Path (lokuttara-magga).
239:
At the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa), one penetrates the Four Noble Truths with a single penetration (ekapaṭivedha) and realizes them with a single realization (ekābhisamaya). One penetrates the Truth of Suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha). One penetrates the Truth of the Origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha), the Truth of Cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha), and the Truth of the Path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). One realizes the Truth of Suffering through the realization of full understanding (pariññā-abhisamaya), the Truth of the Origin through the realization of abandoning (pahāna-abhisamaya), the Truth of Cessation through the realization of realization (sacchikiriyā-abhisamaya), and the Truth of the Path through the realization of development (bhāvanā-abhisamaya).

That person penetrates three truths by way of function (kiccato) and penetrates the Truth of Cessation by way of object (ārammaṇato). At that moment of the Path, there is no discursive advertence, attention, or reflection such as "I am fully understanding suffering, I am abandoning the origin, I am realizing cessation, I am developing the path." However, even while comprehending [the object], the Path penetrates Cessation by way of object while simultaneously accomplishing the functions of full understanding and so forth regarding the [other] three truths.

Therefore, it is said "he is wise (paññavā)." In this context, at the lower limit, a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is indicated as wise, and at the upper limit, one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava, an Arahant) is indicated as wise. If a person learns the Word of the Buddha, the Tipitaka, by way of the Pali text, the meaning, the sequence, and the connection, and wanders about turning it over from top to bottom, yet lacks even a mere comprehension by way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self—is such a person to be called wise or unwise? Such a person is called "one who wanders in consciousness" (viññāṇacarita) and should not be called wise. On the other hand, if one applies the three marks and investigates through the sequence of insight, practicing with the thought "Today, this very day, I shall reach Arahantship"—is such a person to be called wise or unwise? When analyzed, such a person belongs to the side of the wise. However, in the Sutta, only one who has penetration (paṭivedha) is spoken of [as wise].

Why is the question "Consciousness, consciousness?" asked here? It is asked because one wishes to ask about the consciousness of insight (vipassanā-viññāṇa), which is the performing consciousness (kammakaraka-citta) that leads to the attainment of the Noble Path, by which consciousness one investigated the formations and became known as "wise."

"He understands it as 'pleasure'" means he also understands pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). The same method applies to the two subsequent terms. By this, the Elder taught the meditation on the formless (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by way of feeling as it appears in the method beginning with "Feeling a pleasant feeling, he understands: 'I feel a pleasant feeling.'" Its meaning should be understood exactly as stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta.
240:
