The Elder Tissa, entering for alms, saw them and asked, "Venerable sirs, did you receive alms?" They replied, "Friend, we have already made the rounds." Realizing they had received nothing, he said, "Venerable sirs, please wait right here until I return." They said, "Friend, the fifty of us did not even get enough to moisten our bowls." He replied, "Venerable sirs, those who reside permanently are capable; even if they do not receive, they know the nature of the alms-round path." The elders waited. The Elder entered the village. At the very first house, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk rice and was standing looking out for the Elder. As soon as the Elder reached the door, she filled his bowl and offered it. Elder Tissa took that milk rice, went to the elders, and said to the Sangha Elder, "Venerable sir, please accept this." The Sangha Elder thought, "So many of us received nothing, yet this monk has returned quickly with food; how can this be?" and looked at the faces of the other elders. Recognizing the meaning of that look, Tissa said, "Venerable sirs, this is alms-food obtained righteously. Please accept it without hesitation." Starting from the Sangha Elder, he gave as much as all the monks desired and then ate as much as he himself desired.

Then, after the meal was finished, the elders asked him, "Friend, when did you penetrate and realize the supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma)?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I have no supramundane states." They asked again, "Friend, are you an attainer of Jhāna?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I do not have this Jhāna either." They asked, "Friend, is this not a miracle (pāṭihāriya)?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, I have fulfilled the Sāraṇīyadhamma. By the power of that Dhamma..."
296:
"From the time [the Sāraṇīyadhamma] was fulfilled, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the alms-food in the bowl would not be exhausted," he said. "Excellent, excellent, virtuous one, this is suitable for you," the Elders said. This is the story regarding the phrase: "The alms-food in the bowl is not exhausted."

This same Elder went to the place of the Giribhaṇḍa Great Offering at Cetiya Mountain and asked, "What is the most excellent item in this place?" "Venerable sir, there are two cloths," they replied. "These will come to me," he said. Hearing this, a minister reported to the King, "A young monk spoke thus." The King said, "Such is the mind of a young monk; however, fine cloths are suitable for the Great Elders," and he set them aside, saying, "I will give them to the Great Elders." While the Saṅgha of monks stood in order, even though the King placed those cloths on top during the offering, they did not fall into the hands [of the Great Elders]; only other cloths did. However, when it was time to give to the young monk, they fell into his hands. The King placed them in the young monk's hands, looked at his face, invited him to sit, and after making the offering, dismissed the Saṅgha. He then sat near the young monk and asked, "Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma?" The young monk, not wishing to speak of a supramundane state (lokuttara dhamma) that he did not possess even by way of metaphor, said, "Great King, I have no supramundane Dhamma." "Venerable sir, did you not speak of it before?" the King asked. "Yes, Great King, I am one who fulfills the Sāraṇīyadhamma. From the time I fulfilled that Dhamma, the most excellent item comes to me whenever items are distributed," he said. "Excellent, excellent, venerable sir, this is suitable for you," the King said, paid homage, and departed. This is the story regarding the phrase: "He receives the most excellent item when items are distributed."

During the peril of Brāhmaṇatissa, the residents of Bhātara village fled without informing the Theri Nāgā. At dawn, the Theri said to the young nuns, "The village is extremely silent, without the sound of people; go and investigate first." They went and, realizing everyone had gone, returned and informed the Theri. Hearing this, she said, "Do not worry about their departure; just strive in your own studies, inquiries, and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra)." At the time for alms-round, she robed herself and, together with twelve other nuns, stood at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate. The deity dwelling in the tree offered alms-food to all twelve nuns and said, "Ladies, do not go elsewhere; always come right here." The Theri's...
297:
The Theri had a younger brother named Naga Thera. He thought, "The danger is great; it is not possible to survive here. We shall go to the other shore." Having set out from his residence with twelve other monks, he thought, "I will see the Theri before I go," and came to his sister's village. Hearing that "the Elders have arrived," the Theri went to them and asked, "Venerable sirs, why have you come?" Naga Thera told her the situation. She said, "Stay in the monastery for just one day today and go only tomorrow." The Elders went to the monastery.

The next day, after wandering for alms at the foot of the tree, the Theri approached the Elder and said, "Please partake of this alms-food." The Elder said, "It is not proper, Theri," and stood in silence. "Dear brothers, the alms-food was obtained righteously; partake of it without hesitation," she urged, but he only said, "It is not proper, Theri." The Theri took the bowl and tossed it into the air, and the bowl remained suspended in the sky. The Elder said, "Even if it stays at a height of seven palm-trees, it is still the food of a bhikkhunī." He added, "Danger does not last forever. When the danger has subsided and I am preaching the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma, if I am inwardly reproached with the thought, 'O monk who observes the dhutaṅga of alms-gathering, you spent your time eating the food of a bhikkhunī,' I will not be able to remain firm. Be diligent, Theris!" and he set out on his way.

The tree deity thought, "If the Elder partakes of the alms-food from the Theri's hand, I will not stop him. But if he does not partake, I will stop him." Seeing the Elder departing, the deity descended from the tree and said, "Venerable sir, give me the bowl." Taking the bowl, the deity led the Elder back to the foot of the tree, prepared a seat, offered alms-food, and after making him promise to complete the meal, supported the twelve bhikkhunīs and twelve bhikkhus for seven years. This is the story regarding how deities take interest [in the virtuous]. In that story, the Theri was one who had fulfilled the Sāraṇīyadhamma.

In the phrases beginning with "akhaṇḍāni" (unbroken): for whoever a training rule (sikkhāpada) is broken at the beginning or at the end among the seven classes of offenses, that person's virtue is called "broken" (khaṇḍa), like a cloth torn at the edges. For whoever it is broken in the middle, it is called "perforated" (chidda), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. For whoever two or three rules are broken in succession, it is called "spotted" (sabala), like a cow with patches of a different color, such as black or red, appearing on its back or belly. For whoever they are broken here and there...
298:
The virtue of a monk whose virtue is broken here and there is called 'variegated' (kammāsa), like a cow marked with spots of a different color here and there. For one whose virtues are entirely unbroken, those virtues are called unbroken (akhaṇḍa), untorn (acchidda), unspotted (asabala), and unblemished (akammāsa). They are called 'free' (bhujissa) because they liberate one from the slavery of craving and make one a free person. They are called 'praised by the wise' (viññuppasattha) because they are praised by the Buddha and other wise people. They are called 'untouched' (aparāmaṭṭha) because they are not grasped by craving and views, and because no one can reproach them by saying, 'You have previously committed such and such an offense.' They are said to be 'conducive to concentration' (samādhisamvattanika) because they bring about either access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi).

'He dwells possessing common virtue' (sīlasāmaññagato viharati) means he dwells having virtue that has reached a state of equality with the monks dwelling in various regions. The virtue of noble disciples such as Stream-enterers is indeed identical to the virtue of other Stream-enterers living on the other side of the ocean or in the celestial realms. There is no difference in the virtue of the Path (magga-sīla). This was said with reference to that Path-virtue.

'This view' (yāyaṃ diṭṭhi) refers to Right View associated with the Path. 'Noble' (ariya) means faultless. 'It leads out' (niyyāti) means it is 'emancipatory' (niyyānika) because it leads out from the round of suffering. 'For one who acts accordingly' (takkara) means for one who practices in that way. 'For the destruction of suffering' (dukkhakkhayāya) means for the purpose of ending all suffering. 'Possessing common view' (diṭṭhisāmaññagato) means dwelling having reached a state of shared view. 'Foremost' (agga) means the chief. It is called 'comprehensive' (saṅgāhika) because it gathers all the rafters. It is called 'unifying' (saṅghāṭanika) because it makes a junction for all the rafters; it has the meaning of 'unifier' (saṅghāṭaniya). 'That which is the peak' (yadidaṃ kūṭaṃ) refers to that which is called the peak, known as the pinnacle of a gabled house (kūṭāgāra-kaṇṇikā). Palaces with five levels and so on stand only by being bound to the peak. If that peak falls, all parts of the building, starting from the clay, fall. Therefore, it was said so. 'Even so' (evameva kho) means just as the peak is the gathering point of a gabled house, so too, among these qualities of communal harmony (sāraṇīyadhamma), this Noble View should be understood as the foremost, the comprehensive, and the unifying.

In this context, 'And how, bhikkhus, is this view...' (kathañca bhikkhave yāyaṃ diṭṭhi) refers to the view of the Path of Stream-entry, which is said to be noble and emancipatory, leading one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering. The meaning is: 'In what way and for what reason does it lead out?' 'He is one with a possessed mind' (pariyuṭṭhitacitto va hoti) means that even by this much, he is indeed called one whose mind is possessed by defilements. This method applies everywhere. 'My mind is well-directed' (suppaṇihitaṃ me mānasaṃ) means 'My mind is well-established.' 'For the awakening to the truths' (saccānaṃ bodhāya) means for the purpose of awakening to the Four Noble Truths. In the terms such as 'noble' (ariya), that knowledge is called 'noble' because it belongs only to the Noble Ones and not to worldlings (puthujjana). It occurs only to those who possess the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma).
299:
Because that knowledge is specific to the Noble Ones and does not occur to other worldlings, it is called 'noble' (ariya). Because it occurs only to the Noble Ones who possess the supramundane Dhamma and not to other worldlings, it is called 'supramundane' (lokuttara). It means it is 'uncommon' (asādhāraṇa), not shared with worldlings due to their lack of it. This method should be understood in all sections (vāra).

'I gain internal tranquillity' (labhāmi paccattaṃ samathaṃ) means 'I obtain tranquillity in my own mental continuum.' The same method applies to 'extinguishment' (nibbuti). Here, 'tranquillity' (samatha) refers to one-pointedness (ekaggatā), and 'extinguishment' (nibbuti) refers to the subsiding of defilements.

'By such a view' (tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā) refers to the wisdom (view) of the Path of Stream-entry of such a nature. 'By nature' (dhammatāya) means by natural disposition. 'This is the nature' (dhammatā esā) means this is the natural way. 'The rehabilitation is known' (vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati) means the rising from an offense is evident either through a formal act of the Saṅgha or through confession (desanā). In fact, when a noble disciple commits an offense, among the heavy offenses (garuka-āpatti), he only commits those like the one concerning building a hut (kuṭikāra); and among light offenses (lahuka-āpatti), he only commits 'mindless' offenses (acittaka-āpatti) like those concerning sleeping in the same room (sahaseyya). Even in such cases, it happens without intention (asañcicca), not intentionally (no sañcicca). He does not conceal the offense he has committed. Therefore, He spoke the words beginning with 'Then, indeed, him quickly...' (atha kho naṃ khippameva).

'Young' (dahara) means youthful. 'Boy' (kumāra) means not old. 'Dull' (manda) means one who is foolish due to the immaturity of the eyes, ears, etc. 'Lying on the back' (uttānaseyyaka) means one who can only lie on the back because of being very young. It means he is unable to lie on the right or left side. 'Having stepped on a coal' (aṅgāraṃ akkāmitvā) means touching it with a hand or foot stretched out here or there. The hands of adults who touch it in this way do not burn quickly; indeed, some can even pick up a coal with their hand and walk a long distance while turning it over. However, the hands and feet of an infant are so tender that they burn just by touching, and he quickly pulls back while making a 'ciri' sound. Therefore, the infant is shown as an example here. An adult might endure it even while being burned, but this infant cannot endure it. For that reason too, only the infant is shown as an example.

'He confesses' (deseti) means if there is a person of similar status (sabhāga-puggala) to receive the confession, he does not endure it for a single day or night; even in the fourfold darkness of the night, he goes to the dwelling place of a fellow monk and confesses the offense.

'High and low' (uccāvacāni) means large and small. 'What should be done' (kiṃ karaṇီyāni) refers to duties to be performed after saying, 'What shall I do?' Among them, 'high duties' (ucca-kamma) refer to making and dyeing robes, whitewashing a stupa, and major tasks to be done at the Uposatha hall, stupa house, or Bodhi-tree house. 'Low duties' (avaca-kamma) refer to minor tasks such as washing feet or applying oil. Or else...
300:
At a stupa, work such as applying plaster is called noble work (*uccakamma*). At that same stupa, work such as boiling dye, carrying water, scrubbing with a scraper, and mixing resin is called lowly work (*avacakamma*). "*Ussukkaṃ āpanno hoti*" means reaching a state of diligence and performing necessary duties. "*Tibbapekkho hoti*" means having intense longing. "*Thambaṃ ca ālumpati*" means he eats by plucking grass repeatedly. "*Vacchakaṃ ca apacināti*" means he looks askance at the calf.

A cow with a young calf, having come together in the forest, does not go far, leaving the calf sleeping in one place; while grazing in the vicinity of the calf, she plucks grass, lifts her neck, and looks back specifically at the calf. In the same way, when a *Sotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) performs various duties, large or small, his mind is inclined towards those three trainings (*sikkhā*), and he performs them with unremitting fulfillment, strong desire, and intense longing.

In this regard, there is this story—it is said that while plastering work was being done at the Mahācetiya, a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) went up to the courtyard of the stupa holding a plaster bowl in one hand and a scraper in the other, intending to perform the plastering work. A monk who was fond of physical fitness went and stood near that elder. The elder, thinking, "The presence of another causes distraction (*papañca*)," moved from that place to another. That monk also went to that same place. The elder moved to another place again, and when the monk followed him to several places, the elder said, "Good man, the courtyard of the stupa is very vast; can you not find a place elsewhere?" Only then did the other monk depart.

"*Balatāya samannāgato*" means being endowed with strength. "*Aṭṭhiṃ katvā*" means making it beneficial (meaning, being one who has benefit). "*Manasikatvā*" means taking it to heart (performing attention). "*Sabbacetasā samannāharitvā*" means reflecting with the whole mind without even a slight distraction. "*Ohitasoto*" means lending an ear (attentive listening). Indeed, noble disciples are those who love hearing the Dhamma; they do not sit sleeping, talking with someone, or with distracted minds at the place of hearing the Dhamma. Instead, they listen until dawn without being satisfied, as if consuming the nectar of immortality (*amata*). Therefore, it was said thus.
301:
"*Dhammatā susamanniṭṭhā hoti*" means the nature of things is well-investigated. The term "*sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya*" is in the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*), meaning "by the knowledge that realizes the fruit of Stream-entry." "*Evaṃ sattaṅgasamannāgato*" means one who is endowed with these seven noble types of reviewing knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*). This which has been said is the consensus of the teachers. In truth, the supramundane path (*lokuttaramagga*) does not consist of many mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).

A *Vitaṇḍavādin* (sophist), however, says, "There is no path of a single mind-moment; according to the words 'one should develop thus for seven years,' path-development occurs for seven years." He says that although defilements are cut quickly, they are cut by seven knowledges. That *Vitaṇḍavādin* should be told, "Produce a Sutta passage." Then, certainly not seeing any other Sutta, he will produce and show only this Sutta: "This is his first knowledge attained... this is his seventh knowledge attained." Then he should be asked, "Is this Sutta of indirect meaning (*neyyattha*) or direct meaning (*nītattha*)?" Then he will say, "It is of direct meaning; the meaning is exactly as the Sutta stands."

He should then be asked, "What is the meaning in this passage: *dhammatā susamanniṭṭhā hoti sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya*?" He will certainly say, "It has the meaning of realizing the fruit of Stream-entry." Then he should be asked, "Does one endowed with the Path realize the Fruit, or one endowed with the Fruit?" Knowing this, he will say, "One endowed with the Fruit realizes it."

Then he should be told: "Monks, in this passage where it says a noble disciple endowed with seven factors is one endowed with the fruit of Stream-entry, would the noble disciple take only the fruit by jumping like a frog without developing the path? Do not say whatever you like just because you 'found' a Sutta. One who answers a question must live with a teacher, learn the Buddha's word, and understand the essence of the meaning before speaking." He should be made to understand: "These seven knowledges are only the reviewing knowledges of the noble disciple; the supramundane path does not consist of many mind-moments, it consists of only a single mind-moment." If he understands, let him understand. If he does not understand, he should be dismissed: "Go, enter the monastery early tomorrow and just drink your gruel." The remaining words are clear in all respects.

## The explanation of the Kosambiya Sutta
## in the Papañcasūdanī, the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, is finished.
302:
## 9. Commentary on the Brahmanimantanika Sutta

The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Brahmanimantanika Sutta. In this Brahmanimantanika Sutta, "pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ" refers to a base eternalist wrong view (sassata-micchādiṭṭhi). "Idaṃ niccaṃ" (this is permanent) means asserting that the Brahma realm, together with the physical bodies of the Brahmas residing there, is "permanent," even though it is actually impermanent. The terms beginning with "dhuva" are merely synonyms (vevacana) for that term "nicca." Among those three terms, "dhuvaṃ" means stable and firm; "sassataṃ" means existing at all times; "kevalaṃ" means whole and entire without decay; and "acavanadhammaṃ" means having the nature of not passing away. In the passages beginning with "idañhi na jāyati," it is said with reference to the fact that in this Brahma world, there is no one who is born, grows old, dies, passes away, or is reborn.

"Ito ca pana aññaṃ" (and other than this) means that Baka the Brahma had developed a powerful eternalist view that there is no other escape (nissaraṇa) superior to this Brahma realm, including its physical environment. Holding such a view, Baka the Brahma rejects all higher states, namely the three higher Jhana planes, the four Paths, the four Fruits, and Nibbāna. "Avijjāgato" means being possessed by ignorance, thus being devoid of knowledge and blinded. "Yatra nāma" refers to the one named Baka.

Monks, at that time, how did Māra the Evil One see the Blessed One? It is said that while sitting in his own abode, Māra would from time to time reflect on the Teacher, thinking, "Where is the recluse Gotama residing today, in which village or town?" At this time, while reflecting, he knew, "He is staying in the Subhaga Grove near the city of Ukkaṭṭhā." Looking to see where He was going, he saw Him proceeding to the Brahma world. He thought, "The recluse Gotama is going to the Brahma world. Before He can preach the Dhamma there and cause the assembly of Brahmas to transcend my domain, I will go and make Him weary of teaching the Dhamma." Thus, following closely in the Teacher's footsteps, he stood within the assembly of Brahmas with an invisible body. Knowing that "Baka the Brahma has been rebuked by the Teacher," Māra stood there as a support for Baka the Brahma. Therefore, it is said, "Atha kho, bhikkhave, māro pāpimā" (Then, monks, Māra the Evil One).

"Brahmapārisajjaṃ anvāvisitvā" means having possessed the body of one of the Brahmas in the retinue. He is not able, however, to possess the Great Brahmas or the Brahma Priests (Brahmapurohita). "Metamāsado" means "Do not rebuke this Brahma." "Abhibhū" (Overlord) refers to the chief who stands having conquered others. "Anabhibhūto" means one who cannot be conquered by others. "Aññadatthū" means...
303:
Aññadatthu is an indeclinable particle (nipāta) used in the sense of "certainly" or "surely." "Dasso" (All-seeing) indicates that he sees everything through the power of vision. "Vasavatti" (Wielder of Power) means he brings all beings under his control. "Issaro" (Lord) means he is the lord in the world of beings. "Kattā Nimmātā" (Maker and Creator) means he is the maker and creator of the world. It indicates that the earth, the Himālaya mountains, Mount Sineru, the universe (Cakkavāḷa), the great oceans, the moon, and the sun were created by this Brahma.

"Seṭṭho Sajitā" (Best and Appointer) means this Brahma is both the most excellent in the world of beings and the one who ordains. It shows him as the creator of beings, saying, "You be a Khattiya (noble), you be a Brāhmaṇa (priest), a Vessa (merchant), a Sudda (worker), a householder, or a renunciant; and even down to: you be a camel, you be an ox." "Vasī Pitā Bhūtabhavyānaṃ" means he is a master (vasī) due to his mastery over meditative attainments, and he is the father of beings who have been (bhūta) and those who are to be (bhavya). In that context, egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings are called "bhavya" while they are inside the eggshell or the womb. From the time they emerge outside, they are called "bhūta." Moisture-born (saṃsedaja) beings are called "bhavya" in their first thought-moment, and from the second thought-moment onwards, they are called "bhūta." Spontaneously born (opapātika) beings should be understood as "bhavya" in their first posture, and from the second posture onwards, they are called "bhūta." With the notion that all these beings are his children, it is said, "Father of those who have been and are to be."

"Paṭhavīgarahakā" (Revilers of earth) indicates that just as you now revile and loathe the earth as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," so too those others were revilers of the earth; it shows that you are not the only one. The same method applies to "revilers of water" (āpagarahakā) and so on. "Hīne kāye patiṭṭhitā" (Established in a low body) refers to those born in the four woeful states. "Paṭhavīpasaṃsakā" (Praisers of earth) means that unlike you who revile it, they were those who praised the earth and spoke in its favor, saying, "It is permanent, stable, eternal, inseparable, indestructible, and inexhaustible." "Paṭhavābhinandino" (Delighters in earth) means those who delight in the earth as "mine, I, or my self" through the power of craving and views. The same method applies to the remaining terms. "Paṇīte kāye patiṭṭhitā" (Established in a refined body) refers to those born in the Brahma world. "Taṃ tāhaṃ" means "For that reason, I [to] you." "Iṅgha" is an indeclinable particle in the sense of exhortation. "Upātivattittha" means "have transcended" or "passed." There is also a reading "upātivattito," but the meaning is the same. "Daṇḍena paṭippaṇāmeyya" means one would drive away by beating with a four-cubit-long club (muggara). "Narakapapāte" refers to a great abyss as deep as a hundred men's height. "Virādheyya" means one would be unable to grasp a place suitable for grasping with the hand or to stand on a place suitable for treading with the foot. In the Brahma's exhortation, "Monk, do you not see this assembly of Brahmas gathered here, shining, radiant, and brilliant?"...
304:
He shows the psychic power and majesty of the Brahmas who were standing there. Monks, Māra the Evil One approached me and led me to the Brahma assembly. "Bhikkhu, do you not see this Brahma assembly, resplendent and glowing with fame and glory? If you, too, do not transgress the word of the Great Brahma and do exactly as the Brahma tells you, you also will shine with fame and glory in this very way." Saying this, he led me and brought me near the Brahma assembly.

"Do not think so. Evil One, I know you: you are called 'Māra' because you cause the death of the multitude of beings, and you are called 'Pāpimā' (the Evil One) because you perform evil and base deeds that cause the loss of reputation for the multitude of beings," thus He said.

"Kasiṇaṃ āyuṃ" means the entire lifespan. "They are endowed with such great ascetic practice; but you were born only yesterday, and even now the smell of milk still wafts from your mouth—how could you know anything?" thus he speaks, harassing and oppressing. "Will cling to the earth" means overwhelming and swallowing the earth, grasping it through craving, conceit, and views. "Will be a companion who stays near me" means "You will be one who lives in my presence; when I go, you must follow; when I stand, you must stand nearby; when I sit, you must sit nearby; when I lie down, you must lie down nearby."

"Vatthusāyiko" means one who sleeps at my place. "One to be dealt with according to my desire, one to be cast out" means "You must be one who is treated according to my own pleasure as I wish; and after being cast out, you will be made lower than a jajjharikā bush, extremely stunted and small."

With these words, this Māra either entices the Blessed One or disparages Him. "Entices" means: "Bhikkhu, if you cling to the earth through craving and so on, you will be one who stays near me; when I go, you will go; when I stand, you will stand; when I sit, you will sit; when I lie down, you will lie down; I will set you above other people and make you an intimate confidant." This is how he entices. With the remaining words, he disparages. The intention here is: "If you cling to the earth, you will be one who sleeps at my place; you will have to wait for my going and so on before you can go, stand, sit, or lie down; you will have to keep guard for me at my place; and I will deal with you as I please."
305:
By casting him out and making him even more stunted than a jajjharikā bush—this is how he disparages. However, since this Brahma is rooted in conceit, only disparagement (apasādanā) is intended here. The same method applies to the elements such as water (āpo) and so on.

Furthermore, regarding "Brahma, I (know) you," the Blessed One now thought: "This Brahma is rooted in conceit and thinks 'I know'; intoxicated by his own fame, he does not see anything capable of even touching his body; it is proper to humble him a little," and so He began this discourse. In that text, "Gatiñca pajānāmi" means He knows the completion (the destination) of beings. "Jutiñca" means He knows the majesty. "Evaṃ mahesakkho" means one with such great fame and a great retinue.

"As far as the sun and moon revolve" means in whatever place the sun and moon wander. "The quarters shine resplendent" means they shine and glow in the directions, or the directions shine and glow because of them. "So far the thousandfold world" means a world of a thousand parts of that extent; this means a thousand world-systems (cakkavāḷa) together with this world-system. "There your power extends" means your authority prevails in this thousandfold world-system. "And you know the high and low" means you know the high and low, the inferior and superior beings within this thousandfold world-system. "And those with lust and those without" means not only knowing the high and low as "This one is prosperous, this one is an ordinary person," but also knowing people as "This one has lust, this one is free from lust." In "Itthaṃbhāvaññathābhāvaṃ," "itthaṃbhāva" refers to this world-system, and "aññathābhāva" refers to the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine world-systems. "The coming and going of beings" means you know the coming of beings by way of rebirth and their going by way of passing away within this thousandfold world-system. However, you have the perception "I am very great"; you are only a Sahassī Brahma (a Brahma of a thousand worlds). For others, the extent of Brahmas who rule over two thousand, three thousand, four thousand, five thousand, ten thousand, and a hundred thousand world-systems is immeasurable compared to you. Like one attempting to make a great canopy out of a worn-out cloth only four cubits long, you hold the perception "I am great"—thus He humbles him.

"Born here" means born here in the plane of the first jhāna. For that reason, you do not know that body (of a higher Brahma). To you...
306:
Even though I have reached the state of knowing, I am not equal to you. 'Abhiññāya' means having known. 'Kuto nīceyyaṃ' means 'How could there be a lower state for me than you?' (It is not possible).

It is said that this Brahma was one who arose in a lower realm (heṭṭhūpappattika). In the time before the Buddha's arising, he went forth as a hermit (isi), performed preliminary work for kasiṇa, and attained meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Having non-declining jhāna, when he passed away, he was reborn in the Vehapphala Brahma realm, a plane of the fourth jhāna, with a lifespan of five hundred aeons. After staying there for the full lifespan, desiring to be born in a lower realm, he developed the third jhāna and was reborn in the Subhakiṇha Brahma realm with a lifespan of sixty-four aeons. From there, developing the second jhāna, he was reborn in the Ābhassara realms with a lifespan of eight aeons. Then, developing the first jhāna, he was reborn in the first jhāna realm with a lifespan of one aeon. In the beginning, that Brahma knew his own past karma and the place of his rebirth, but as time passed, he forgot both and gave rise to the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). Therefore, the Blessed One said, "For that reason, you do not know that... how could you be lower?"

Then the Brahma thought, "The ascetic Gotama knows my lifespan, my place of rebirth, and my past karma. I shall ask him about my past karma." Thus, he asked the Teacher about his own past karma. The Teacher explained it.

In the past, this Brahma was born in a respectable family. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he thought, "I will make an end to birth, aging, sickness, and death," and having gone forth, he became a hermit. He attained meditative absorptions and, having gained the jhānas that serve as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), he built a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges and spent his time in the bliss of jhāna. At that time, merchants with five hundred carts were crossing a sandy desert. In the sandy desert, it is impossible to travel by day, so travel is done only at night. Then, the oxen yoked to the lead cart turned back and faced the direction from which they had come. The other carts turned back in the same way, and only when dawn broke did they realize they had turned back. That day was supposed to be the day they crossed the desert, but all their wood and water were exhausted. Therefore, thinking, "Now there is no life for us," they tied the oxen to the wheels, and the people went under the shade of the carts.
307:
They lay down. The ascetic also came out of his leaf-hut early and, sitting at the door of the hut, looking at the Ganges, saw a great torrent of water flowing like a rolling mass of jewels. Seeing it, he thought: 'Are there any beings in this world suffering from the lack of such sweet water?' As he was reflecting thus, he saw that caravan in the sandy desert and thought, 'Let these beings not perish. Let a great mass of water break off from this Ganges and go towards the caravan in the sandy desert.' He resolved this with the mind of direct knowledge (abhiññā). As soon as the thought arose, the water went there like water entering a canal. The people woke up at the sound of the water, and seeing the water, they were greatly delighted; they bathed, drank, and gave water to the oxen, and then reached their desired destination safely. The Teacher, wishing to show that past deed of Baka Brahma, spoke this verse:

'O Baka Brahma, you gave water to many people who were thirsty and oppressed by the heat. I, the Buddha, remember that old vow and virtuous conduct of yours, like one waking from sleep.'

At another time, the ascetic created a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges and lived depending on a forest village. At that time, robbers attacked that village, took away the valuable possessions, and led away the cows and the captives. The cows, the dogs, and the people all cried out loudly. The ascetic heard that sound and, reflecting 'What is this?', realized 'Danger has arisen for the people.' Thinking, 'Let these beings not perish while I am watching,' he entered the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, and upon emerging, he created with the mind of direct knowledge a fourfold army ready for battle in the path of the robbers. When the robbers saw it, thinking 'It is the King's army,' they abandoned their loot and fled. The ascetic resolved, 'Let whatever belongs to whom remain theirs,' and it happened exactly so. The multitude of people attained safety. The Teacher, wishing to show this also as his past deed, said:
308:
“You once released those people who were captured at the bank of the Ganges called Eṇīkūla and were being led away by robbers. I remember that ancient virtue and conduct of yours, like one waking from sleep.”

He spoke this verse. Here, “Eṇīkūlasmiṃ” means on the bank of the Ganges.

Furthermore, on another occasion, a clan living on the upper Ganges made a friendly alliance with a clan living on the lower Ganges. They lashed rafts together, loaded them with many kinds of food, perfumes, and flowers, and came down along the current of the Ganges. Those people, eating, dancing, and singing, were filled with great joy as if traveling in a celestial mansion. The Naga named Gaṅgeyyaka saw them and became angry, thinking, “These people do not even show me respect; now I will send them straight to the ocean.” He manifested a huge body, split the water in two, raised his hood, and stood making the sound “Sussū.” Seeing this, the people cried out in terror.

The ascetic sitting in his leaf-hut heard the sound and reflected, “These people were coming along singing, dancing, and full of joy, but now they are making a sound of fear; why is that?” He then saw the Naga King. Thinking, “Let these beings not perish while I am watching,” he attained the Jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), abandoned his own form, manifested himself in the form of a Garuḍa, and showed himself to the Naga King. The Naga King, terrified, withdrew his hood and dived into the water. The people reached safety. The Blessed One, wishing to show that past deed of Baka Brahmā, said:

“You forcibly released the boat seized in the current of the Ganges by the fierce Naga, along with the people. I remember that ancient virtue and conduct of yours, like one waking from sleep.”

He spoke this verse.

At another time, this Baka Brahmā went forth as an ascetic and became the ascetic named Kesava. At that time, our Bodhisatta was a youth named Kappa...
309:
...the youth named Kappa was the constant attendant and pupil of the ascetic Kesava. He was one who would ask his teacher what task he should perform, one who practiced what was pleasing, one endowed with wisdom, and one who acted for the teacher's benefit. The ascetic Kesava could not live without that youth and lived depending solely on him. The Blessed One, wishing to show that past deed of Baka Brahmā as well, spoke this verse:

“Kappa was your constant attendant; you considered him wise and virtuous. I remember that ancient virtue and conduct of yours, like one waking from sleep.”

In this way, the Blessed One revealed the deeds performed by the Brahmā in various past lives. While the Blessed One was speaking, the Brahmā reflected on them. Just as forms become clear when a thousand lamps are lit, all his past deeds became clear to that Brahmā. With a confident heart, he spoke this verse:

“O Venerable Gotama, you certainly know this life-span of mine; you know other things as well, for you are the Buddha. Because you know thus, this blazing majesty of yours stands illuminating the Brahma-world.”

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to reveal his peerless nature equal only to other Buddhas, said to that Brahmā, “Brahmā, I [know] the earth...” and so on. In that passage, “not experienced/reached by the nature of earth” means something that cannot be reached by the nature of earth. What is that? It is Nibbāna. Because Nibbāna has emerged from all conditioned things (saṅkhata), it is said to be unreached by the nature of earth. “Having known that Nibbāna with direct knowledge” means having known and realized that Nibbāna. “I do not take the earth” means I do not grasp the earth through the attachments of craving, views, and conceit (taṇhā, diṭṭhi, māna). The same method should be understood for water (āpo) and so on. The details should be understood according to the method already stated in the Mūlapariyāya Sutta.

“Friend, if you [say] ‘all’ by the nature of all [cannot be known]...” The Brahmā said this according to his own view, pointing to the word “Sabba” (All) and seeking fault in the word. Although the Blessed One spoke “Sabba” referring to Sakkāya (the five aggregates), the Brahmā referred to everything in its entirety. “You say ‘Sabba’; you say ‘not experienced by the nature of all.’ If it is not that all is unexperienced, then there is something experienced by him. Let not your [words] be merely empty...”
310:
“May your word not be empty, may it not be vain,” he said, attempting to refute the Teacher with a charge of falsehood. The Teacher, however, is a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand times superior in debate than this Brahma. Therefore, to crush the Brahma's argument, the Teacher brought forth the reason, saying, “I shall speak of the all, and I shall speak of what has not been experienced; listen to me,” and uttered the words beginning with “Viññāṇaṃ.”

In that text, “Viññāṇaṃ” refers to the Dhamma (Nibbāna) that should be specially known (through the knowledge of the Path, Fruition, and Reviewing). “Anidassanaṃ” is so called because it does not come into the range of eye-consciousness. By both these terms, Nibbāna itself is meant. “Anantaṃ” is so called because it is free from the ends of arising and falling away. This has also been said:
“Conditioned beings have an end; the unconditioned is infinite. Ends (arising and falling away) are seen in conditioned things; ends are made manifest in conditioned things.”

“Sabbatopabhaṃ” means fully endowed with radiance in every way. There is no Dhamma more radiant, more glowing, more pure, or more white than Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is “Sabbatopabha” because it exists prominently in every way and is not absent anywhere. It cannot be said of directions like the East, “Nibbāna does not exist in such a direction.” Or “pabha” is a name for a harbor; it is “Sabbatopabha” because it has a harbor for entry from all sides. Just as in the great ocean, wherever people wish to descend, that very place becomes a harbor and there is no place that is not a harbor; similarly, through whichever of the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) one wishes to enter Nibbāna, that very meditation subject is a harbor. There is no meditation subject that is not a harbor for Nibbāna. Thus it is said, “Sabbatopabhaṃ.”

“Taṃ pathaviyā pathavattena” means that Nibbāna is not reached (not experienced) through the nature of earth in earth, nor through the nature of water, etc., in the other elements like water. Thus, the Teacher established the argument that “Viññāṇa” (Nibbāna) is “anidassana, ananta, sabbatopabha, and ananubhūta” (not experienced) by way of the totality of all things belonging to the three planes of existence, which are the domain of those like you.

Then the Brahma, having had every view he clung to refuted by the Teacher and seeing nothing else to cling to, wished to play a trick and said, “Well then, friend, I will now disappear.” Here, “I will disappear” means “I will perform a miracle of invisibility.” “If you can” means “If you are able to disappear from me (then do so).”
311:
“Friend Gotama, disappear; perform a miracle,” (Baka Brahma said). (The Brahma thought,) “May I not be unable to disappear,” but he was utterly unable to disappear from me. What did that Brahma wish to do? He wished to go to his original rebirth-form. The original rebirth-form of Brahmas is subtle and does not appear in the range of others' vision; they remain only with a specially created body. The Teacher did not give that Brahma the opportunity to go to his original rebirth-form. Or, even without going to the original rebirth-form, he might wish to hide himself in whatever darkness to become invisible; the Teacher dispelled that darkness. Therefore, he was unable to disappear. Being unable, he hid in his celestial mansion, hid in a wish-fulfilling tree, and sat crouching. The host of Brahmas made fun of him, saying, “This Baka Brahma is hiding in his mansion, hiding in a wish-fulfilling tree, sitting crouching, yet he creates the impression, ‘O Brahma, you have disappeared!’” That Brahma, being mocked by the host of Brahmas, became crestfallen.

“Monks, when this was said, that Brahma said, ‘Well then, friend, I will now disappear in your presence,’ but seeing him unable to disappear, I said this; I spoke this verse,” (the Buddha said). Why did the Blessed One speak the verse? He spoke the verse while being invisible so that the host of Brahmas would not have the opportunity to say, “Is the recluse Gotama present in this place or not? How can we know?”

In that verse, “Bhavevāhaṃ bhayaṃ disvā” means: I have indeed seen danger in existence. “Bhavañca vibhavesinaṃ” means: Even while being one who seeks non-existence (Nibbāna) from this threefold existence such as the sense-sphere existence, I saw only existence again and again. “Bhavaṃ nābhivadiṃ” means: I did not welcome (delight in) any existence through the power of craving and views; the meaning is that I did not seek it. “Nandiñca na upādiyiṃ” means: I did not approach or cling to craving for existence. Thus, the Teacher taught the Dhamma, revealing the Four Noble Truths. At the end of the teaching, by leading them to the womb of insight (vipassanā) according to the sequence of the teaching, ten thousand Brahmas drank the ambrosia of the Path and Fruition.

“Acchariyabbhutacittajātā” means: They were filled with wonder, amazement, and joy. “Samūlaṃ bhavaṃ udabbahi” means: At the terrace of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), he uprooted existence along with its root for himself, and for many other devas and humans through various teachings; the meaning is that he extracted and destroyed it.
312:
Baka Brahma hid in his mansion, hid in a wishing tree, and sat crouching. "O Brahma, do you perceive that you have disappeared?" the Blessed One said mockingly. That Baka Brahma, being mocked by the assembly of Brahmas, became displeased. When this was said, "I, bhikkhus..." means that although Baka Brahma said, "O sir, I will now disappear from your sight," the Buddha, seeing that he could not disappear, spoke these words and recited this verse (gāthā). Why did the Blessed One recite the verse? It was so that the assembly of Brahmas would not have the opportunity to say, "Whether the recluse Gotama is here or not, how can we know?" Thus, while remaining invisible, he recited the verse.

In that verse, "Bhavevāhaṃ bhayaṃ disvā" means "I, the Buddha, having seen danger in existence (bhava)." "Bhavañca vibhavesinaṃ" means that while seeking Nibbāna, which is the cessation of existence, he saw only repeated existences in the threefold existence such as the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), and understood that nothing in that existence is to be grasped through craving or views. "Na abhinandiṃ" and so forth means he did not cling to or give rise to craving for existence. Showing these four aspects, the Blessed One taught. At the end of the teaching, he led ten thousand Brahmas to take up insight meditation (vipassanā) and let them drink the nectar of the paths and fruits (magga-phala), causing those Brahmas to experience unprecedented joy and delight. "Samūlaṃ vā udabbahaṃ" means that through various teachings given by himself at the Bodhi tree, he uprooted the existence of many other devas and humans along with the root of ignorance (avijjā).

At that time, the Evil Mara, overcome by anger, thought, "While I was wandering about, the recluse Gotama taught the Dhamma and released ten thousand Brahmas from my control." Overcome by anger, he possessed the body of one of the Brahmapārisajja Brahmas. To show this possession, the Buddha said, "Bhikkhus, at that time..." and so forth. In that Pali, "Sace tvaṃ evaṃ anubuddho" means "If you have thus personally realized the Four Noble Truths." "Mā sāvake upanesī" means "Do not lead lay disciples or ordained disciples to that Dhamma (to the penetrative realization)." "Hīne kāye patiṭṭhitā" refers to those established in the four woeful planes (apāya). "Paṇīte kāye patiṭṭhitā" refers to those established in the Brahma world.

To whom does this refer? It refers to the ascetics and wanderers who went forth outside the Dispensation. When a Buddha has not arisen, clansmen go forth as ascetics and, without consulting anyone, practice alone, attain meditative attainments (samāpatti), and are reborn in the Brahma world; it is with reference to them that this was said. "Anakkhātaṃ kusalañhi mārisa" means "O Gotama, not teaching others, not admonishing, not speaking the Dhamma is indeed good; such non-teaching is superior." "Mā paraṃ ovadāhi" means "Do not admonish others; do not wander sometimes to the human world, sometimes to the deva world, sometimes to the Brahma world, or sometimes to the Naga world; sitting in one place, spend your time with the bliss of jhāna, paths, and fruits."

"Anālapanatāya" means because of the state of not wishing to teach. "Brahmuno ca abhinimantanatāya" means because of Baka Brahma's invitation to the Brahma realm along with the realm itself, in the manner of "Sir, this Brahma realm is permanent," etc. Because of that invitation, this discourse (veyyākaraṇa) came to be known by the name, designation, and appellation "Brahmanimantanika Sutta." The remaining words are clear in meaning throughout the Pali.

## The Explanation of the Brahmanimantanika Sutta
## in the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikaya named Papañcasūdanī is finished.
## 10. The Explanation of the Māratajjanīya Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Māratajjanīya Sutta. In that sutta, "Koṭṭhamanupaviṭṭho" means having entered the belly, entered the intestines, and sat in the place of the rectum. "Garugaro viya" means like a very heavy and dull mass of stone.
313: "Māsācitaṃ manyeti" means like the belly of one who has eaten bean-rice, or like a bag filled with beans, or like wet beans. "Vihāraṃ pavisitvā" means if this heaviness was due to a digestive fault, he thought it unsuitable to walk in the open air, so he descended from the walkway, entered the leaf-hut, and sat on the prepared seat. "Paccattaṃ yoniso manasākāsī" means reflecting "What is this?", he attended to it in his mind using his own means. If the Elder Mahāmoggallāna had reflected on his own virtue (sīla) and thought, "Whether it be undigested food eaten yesterday, the day before, or the day before that, or any other incompatible fault, let it all be digested and let there be comfort," and had stroked his belly with his hand, the Evil Mara would have dissolved away. However, the Elder did not do that but attended to it wisely. "Mā tathāဂတံ ဝိဟေသေသီ" means just as harming children is harming the parents, harming the resident and attending pupils (saddhivihārika and antevāsika) is harming the teachers and preceptors, and harming the countryside is harming the king, so too, harming a disciple of the Blessed One is harming the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said, "Do not harass the Tathāgata." "Paccaggaḷe aṭṭhāsi" means he stood outside the door-leaf. The door-leaf is called "aggaḷa." It means he came out through the mouth, left the leaf-hut, and stood leaning against the door-leaf outside the hut. "Bhūtapubbāhaṃ pāpima" - why did he begin this teaching? It is said the Elder thought: "The scent of humans causes distress even to the sky-dwelling devas standing a hundred leagues away. For it is said: 'O Rājañña, the scent of humans distresses the devas for a hundred leagues.' But this Mara, though he is a city-dweller, pure, majestic, and a powerful king of devas, has entered my belly and sat inside the intestines in the place of the rectum; he must be extremely wicked. For one who can enter and sit in such a loathsome and repulsive place, what else will he not do? What else will he be ashamed of? If I say, 'You are my relative,' there is no one who would not become soft..."
314:
Thinking, "Now, having made him realize his lineage of relatives, I will release him by a gentle means," he began this teaching.

'You were then my nephew' means that at that time, you were related to me as a nephew. This statement is made by way of lineage. In the celestial realm, however, there is no such thing as the father's lineage or grandfather's lineage ruling as kings. One is reborn as a celestial king in the heaven through the power of merit, stays there for the duration of the lifespan, and then passes away. Another person, due to their own performed kamma, is reborn as the chief in that place. Thus, it should be understood that this Māra also passed away from that place at that time, performed merit again, and is now reborn in that position of authority.

'Vidhura' means one who is free from burdens, or one who is unique and unlike others. 'Appakasirena' means without suffering or hardship (easily). 'Pasupālakā' refers to those who tend goats and sheep. 'Pathāvino' refers to travelers on the road. 'Kāye upacinitvā' means having piled up and bound a pyre around the body. 'Aggim datvā pakkamiṃsu' means that, having estimated the size of the pyre to be sufficient for the body to be consumed, they set fire to it from the four directions and departed. Although the pyre blazed like a lamp flame, it was for the Elder as if he were sitting inside a water grotto. 'Cīvarāni papphoṭetvā' means that, having emerged from the meditative attainment, he shook out his robes while treading upon the smokeless embers that had the color of Butea flowers (kiṃsuka). There was not even a trace of heat in the Elder's body, and not even a single thread of his robes was burnt; this is the fruit of meditative attainment.

'Akkosatha' means "Revile him with the ten grounds for reviling." 'Paribhāsatha' means "Threaten him with words." 'Rosetha' means "Annoy or provoke him." 'Vihesetha' means "Cause him suffering." All these are synonyms for verbal assault. 'Yathā taṃ dūsī māro' means "Just like their Dūsī Māra." 'Labhetha otāraṃ' means "May they find an opportunity (an opening)," meaning may they find an object or cause for the arising of defilements. Regarding terms like 'muṇḍakā', although they could be called 'muṇḍa' because they are shaven-headed or 'samaṇa' because they are ascetics, these people used the derogatory forms 'muṇḍakā' (shavelings) and 'samaṇakā' (pseudo-ascetics) out of a desire to disparage them. 'Ibbhā' refers to wealthy householders. 'Kiṇhā' means those who are dark-skinned. In the phrase 'bandhupādāpaccā', 'Bandhu' refers to Brahmā. The Brahmins address that Brahmā as 'Grandfather' (Pitāmaha).
315:
'Pādāpaccā' means the offspring of the feet, meaning those born from the tops of the feet of Brahmā. Their belief is as follows: "Brahmins came from the mouth of Brahmā, Khattiyas from the chest, Vessas from the navel, Suddas from the knees, and Samaṇas from the tops of the feet." 'Jhāyinosmā jhāyinosmā' means "We are meditators, we are meditators." 'Madhurakajātā' refers to those who have become lazy. 'Jhāyanti' means thinking or brooding. Terms like 'pajjhāyanti' are expansions of the meaning through the power of prefixes (upasagga). 'Mūsikaṃ maggayamāno' refers to an owl that comes out of a tree hollow at night to find food and searches for a mouse on a tree branch. That bird remains motionless as if extremely peaceful, and when the opportunity arises, it quickly catches the mouse. 'Kotthu' is a jackal; it is also called 'soṇa'. 'Sandhisamalasaṅkaṭire' refers to the junctions of houses, sewage drains, and rubbish heaps. There, 'sandhi' is the gap or alley between houses. 'Samala' is the drain for discharging excrement. 'Saṅkaṭira' is the place where rubbish is discarded. 'Vahacchinno' refers to a donkey with a broken back that has come out of a difficult journey. 'Sandhisamalasaṅkaṭire' means in the house-junction, or in the sewage drain, or in the rubbish heap. That donkey also remains motionless as if bound, brooding and thinking.

'They go to hell' means—if Māra were to possess the bodies of people and act in this way, the unwholesome kamma would not belong to the people but only to Māra. However, without possessing their bodies, he merely displays inappropriate objects and unpleasant matters. Then, he creates and displays those monks as if they were fishermen overwhelming and catching fish, or catching fish with nets, or trapping birds with snares, or hunting in the forest with dogs, or sitting in a tavern holding women, or dancing, or singing, or as if inappropriate men were sitting or standing in the night-quarters or day-quarters of the bhikkhunīs. Although the people are in the forests, mountains, or monasteries, because they see those unpleasant sights, they return and say to others: "These monks perform deeds that are un-monk-like and inappropriate. How can one gain merit by giving to them? Do not give them anything at all." In this way, those people, by reviling virtuous monks in every place they see them, accumulate unwholesome kamma and become those who fill the lower realms and hell. Therefore, it is said, "They go to hell."
316:
"Anvaviṭṭhā" means being turned around (possessed). "Pharitvā viharimsu" means they did not merely dwell pervading. Rather, staying within the instruction of the Blessed One Kakusandha, they developed these four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), increased insight (vipassanā) based on meditative absorption (jhāna), and were established in the fruit of Arahantship.

"Āgatiṃ vā gatiṃ vā" refers to not knowing the place of coming by way of rebirth or the place of going by way of passing away. "Siyā cittassa aññathattaṃ" means there might be an alteration of the mind by way of joy (somanassa). "Saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti": here too, the meaning should be understood in the same way as before. For just as previously an object causing remorse was shown, so here an object causing faith (pasāda) is shown. It is said that at that time, Mara showed the monks to the people in their sight as if they were traveling in the sky, as if standing, as if sitting cross-legged, as if performing needlework in the sky, as if reciting texts, as if spreading robes in the sky to let the body take the heat, as if newly ordained monks were wandering through the sky, and as if young novices were standing in the sky picking flowers. Whether people went to the forest, the woods, or the monastery, they saw that practice of the monks and, upon returning, told others: "Among the monks, even the novices have such great psychic power and majesty; giving to these venerable ones is of great fruit; give to these venerable ones, show them respect." From then on, the people respected the Saṅgha of monks with the four requisites and, by performing much merit, became those who filled the path to heaven. Therefore, it is said, "They are reborn in the heavenly world."

"Come, monks, dwell contemplating the foulness (asubha) in the body." The Blessed One, wandering throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, went to the dwelling places of even just two or three monks and said: "Monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated with the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā), the mind shrinks, recoils, and turns away from the practice of sexual intercourse; it is not drawn to it; either equanimity or loathing is established. Monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated with the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūla-saññā), the mind shrinks from the craving for taste (rasa-taṇhā)..."
317:
...(the mind) shrinks, recoils, is not drawn to it; equanimity or loathing is established. "Monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated with the perception of non-delight in the whole world (sabbaloke anabhirati-saññā), the mind shrinks, recoils, and turns away from the diverse objects of the world; it is not drawn to it; either equanimity or loathing is established. Monks, for a monk who dwells frequently with a mind cultivated with the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā), the mind shrinks, recoils, and turns away from gain, honor, and fame; it is not drawn to it; either equanimity or loathing is established." (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Sattaka Nipāta). Having shown the benefits in this way—

"Come, monks, dwell contemplating foulness in the body, having the perception of repulsiveness in food, having the perception of non-delight in the whole world, and contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things (saṅkhāra)." He taught these four meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). Those monks also, while working on these four meditation subjects, increased insight, exhausted all taints (āsava), and were established in Arahantship. These four meditation subjects also calm the lineages of greed, hatred, and delusion, and they destroy greed, hatred, and delusion.

"Sakkharaṃ gahetvā" means taking a stone of a size that fits within the fist. This Mara, having failed to find an opportunity (to find fault) either by inciting brahmins and householders to abuse the monks or by causing gain and honor to arise for the Saṅgha of monks through the influence of brahmins and householders, now desired to make an effort with his own hand. He possessed the body of a certain boy and took such a stone. With reference to that, it is said, "Sakkharaṃ gahetvā."

"Sīsaṃ vo bhindi" means he split the head; the thick skin was cut and the flesh was split in two. However, the stone, without breaking the skull, hit the bone and fell back. "Nāgāpalokitaṃ apalokesi" means having heard the sound of the blow, he looked back like... (like a Great Elephant).
318:
When a great elephant (hātthināga) wishes to look in this or that direction, he does not turn his neck but turns with his whole body to look. In the same way, the Buddha turns with his whole body to look. Indeed, while the bones of ordinary people are situated touching end to end, and the bones of Paccekabuddhas are linked like the tips of elephant goads, it is not so for the Buddhas. The bones of the Buddhas are interconnected like the links of a chain. Therefore, when looking back, it is impossible for them to turn only the neck. Just as a great elephant turns with his whole body when wishing to look behind, so too must the Buddha turn. Thus, the Blessed One turned with his whole body like a golden statue turned by a machine and looked. Having looked and remained standing, he said, "This evil Dūsī Māra did not know his measure." The meaning of this is: this Dūsī Māra, in committing evil, did not know the limit and has acted beyond all measure.

"Simultaneous with the look" means at that very moment when the Blessed One Kakusandha looked. "Passed away from that place" means he passed away from that celestial realm and was reborn in the great hell (Mahāniraya). In truth, one who passes away does not pass away while remaining in just any place; therefore, he passed away after returning to the Vasavatti heaven. The phrase "simultaneous with the look" should be understood as merely indicating the time of his passing, and not that he passed away because the Blessed One looked at him. It should be understood that because he offended the noble Great Disciples (Mahāsāvakas), his life was cut off right there, like being struck by an axe.

"There are three names" means there are three designations. "Chaphassāyatanika" means being the cause of individual feelings in the six sense bases.

"Saṅkusamāhata" means being tormented by iron spikes. "Paccatta-vedaniya" means producing a feeling that is to be experienced by oneself alone. "Spike and spike would meet in the heart" means that the iron spikes would meet in the middle of the heart. It is said that those reborn in that hell have a body three gāvutas in height; the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna (as Dūsī Māra at that time) also had such a body. Then the hell-wardens, taking burning, blazing, and glowing iron spikes the size of palm-tree trunks, and turning them again and again, said, "This person planned and committed evil for this reason..."
319:
...pounding the middle of the heart as if pounding a cake in a mortar, fifty wardens go towards the feet and fifty wardens go towards the head, piercing him. Going in this way, they reach both ends in five hundred years, and returning again, they reach the middle of the heart in five hundred years. It was said with reference to that matter. "Vuṭṭhānimam" refers to the feeling of emergence from the result (vipāka-vuṭṭhāna-vedanā). It is said that this feeling is more painful than the suffering in the great hell. Just as the seven days of nursing (parihāra) are more painful than the seven days of drinking medicinal oil, so too, they say, the feeling of emergence from the result in the Ussada hell is more painful than the suffering of the great hell. "Seyyathāpi macchassa" (as of a fish) means that a human head is round; when one strikes it with an iron spike, the strike does not find a firm place and slips off. A fish's head, however, is long and broad, so the strike finds its place; it is easy to inflict torture without missing. Therefore, such a head [as a fish's] comes to be. 

"Vidhuraṃ sāvakamāsajja" means having offended the disciple named Vidhura. "Paccatta-vedanā" means producing individual feelings to be experienced by oneself. In this place, "Īdiso nirayo āsi" (such was the hell), the nature of hell should be explained by the Devadūta Sutta. "Kaṇha-dukkhaṃ nigacchasi" means, "O Dark Māra, you shall experience suffering." "Majjhe sarassa" (in the middle of the lake) means that in the middle of the great ocean, there are mansions (vimānas) arisen supported by the water that last for an aeon. Their color is like that of beryl (veḷuriya). Their flames shine like the crest of a fire burning in a reed-thicket on a mountain top. They are exceedingly radiant and endowed with splendor. In those mansions, nymphs of various colors, such as blue and so forth, dance. "Yo etamabhijānāti" means he who knows the story of this mansion. Thus, the meaning here should be understood through the Vimānavatthu and Petavatthu. The phrase "Pādanguṭṭhena kampayī" (shook it with his big toe) should be explained by the Pāsādakampana Sutta. "Yo vejayantaṃ pāsādaṃ" (who [shook] the Vejayanta palace) should be explained by the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhayavimutti Sutta. "Sakkaṃ so paripucchati" (he questioned Sakka) should also be explained by that same Sutta. "Sudhammāyābhito sabhaṃ" means near the Sudhamma hall. This Sudhamma hall is the one in the Brahma world, not the one in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. For there is no celestial realm without a Sudhamma hall. "Radiant in the Brahma world" means that in the Brahma world, together with great disciples such as Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākassapa, having entered the attainment of the fire element (tejo-dhātu)...
320:
I shall further elaborate on the radiance of the Blessed One while he was abiding in the attainment of the fire element (tejodhātu). On one occasion, the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of the assembly of Brahmas who were gathered in the Sudhammā hall in the Brahma realm and were thinking, "Is there indeed any recluse or brahmin of such great psychic power who is able to come here?", went to that Brahma realm. Sitting above the assembly of Brahmas, he entered the attainment of the fire element and willed for the arrival of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and others. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the others also went there, paid homage to the Blessed One, entered the attainment of the fire element, and sat in their respective directions; thus, the entire Brahma realm became filled with a single radiance. The Blessed One taught the Dhamma that explains the Four Noble Truths; at the conclusion of the teaching, many thousands of Brahmas were established in the paths and fruits. With reference to that establishment, these verses were spoken; this meaning should be understood through another Brahma Sutta.

'Vimokkhena aphassayi' means he touched (experienced) through the liberation of jhāna (jhānavimokkha). 'Vanaṃ' refers to the island of Jambudīpa. 'Pubbavidehānaṃ' refers to the island of the inhabitants of Pubbavideha. 'Ye ca bhūmisayā narā' refers to the inhabitants of Aparagoyāna and Uttarakuru. It means he touched all of them. This meaning should be understood through the taming of the Nāga king Nandopananda. That story has been elaborated in the Iddhikathā (Discussion on Psychic Powers) of the Visuddhimagga. 'Apuññaṃ pasavi' means he has acquired demerit. 'Āsaṃ mā akāsi bhikkhūsu' means "Do not entertain this desire, thinking 'I will harass the monks'." The remaining terms are clear in meaning in all places.

## The Explanation of the Māratajjanīya Sutta is finished.
## The Explanation of the Fifth Division (Vagga) is finished.
## The Commentary on the Mūlapaṇṇāsa is finished.
